title: One year later, regrading the 10 biggest deals from the 2025 NFL trade deadline
summary: From the Colts' disastrous gamble on Sauce Gardner to the Eagles' productive Jaelan Phillips rental, here is how last year's biggest deals have aged
full_text:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline has a tough act to follow. Last year saw 27 players traded in-season, which was the most in a single year in a quarter of a century. This is shaping up to be an active push to Nov. 10, but will it rival the mayhem of 2025? That remains to be determined. It is the quality of the transactions that matters more than the volume. Last year can be both a blueprint for how to pull off beneficial midseason moves and for what to avoid, because the high number of trades included multiple examples of both good deals and bad.
No deal withstood the test of time worse than the Sauce Gardner trade. It has since been panned as one of the most one-sided transactions in recent NFL history and should be a reminder that just because a player carries All-Pro bona fides, he might not be worth mortgaging the future to acquire.
The most beneficial trades are often the ones made on the margins, where teams secure mid- or late-round draft capital for players on expiring contracts. These tend to be mutually beneficial, as one team lands an instant-impact rental while the other secures future assets in exchange for someone who was destined to walk away for free. Last year's trade deadline featured a plethora of such deals.
After the 2025 deadline, we ranked every major trade . And now with the benefit of hindsight, let's re-grade the top 10.
The Gardner trade aged so poorly for Colts general manager Chris Ballard that it became a primary reason why the franchise fired him in the middle of the season. Nobody could have foreseen the stark regression the two-time All-Pro cornerback experienced upon his arrival in Indianapolis, but it is very real, and it looks awful in the context of what Ballard gave up to acquire him. Gardner has played the worst football of his career in his 17 games with the Colts, while the Jets constructed an exciting young offensive core with the assets they received in return -- plus they still have another first-round pick to add to it.
Since the Colts are trending downward this year and may emerge as sellers at the deadline as they barrel toward a potential rebuild, this is the exact situation in which they would prefer to own a 2027 first-rounder. Instead, with every loss they add to their tally, they watch the Jets lick their lips and prepare to cash in.
The Dallas defense is still a disaster, even with Williams offering solid run-stopping ability in the middle of the line. His six tackles for loss through the first six games of the year were the most by a Cowboys defensive tackle since 2013 and were tied for the most of any defensive tackle in the league this year. On an individual level, he is delivering what the Cowboys paid for when they parted with all those draft picks and signed him to a three-year, $105.9 million extension, even if it is short of the All-Pro caliber of production he logged at his peak in New York. The problem is that it has not translated to improvement on the defensive side of the ball at large.
On the Jets' side, they released Smith and have gotten practically nothing out of Ponds in the first five games of his career. He could still develop into a good cornerback, but he has only seen 59 snaps of action and allowed three catches and a touchdown on five targets in that small sample size. If he does not pan out, it will come down to the 2027 first-rounder to save this trade. That player needs to turn into a Pro Bowler to at least match what New York gave up in Williams.
The idea behind trading for Flacco was to keep the offense afloat last season until Joe Burrow returned from turf toe. It worked to an extent, as the veteran delivered a string of entertaining passing performances, including a 470-yard outburst and three consecutive games of at least 33 points. The defense was the real issue and the main reason Flacco went just 1-5 as the starter. At face value, the trade did not move the needle because of the poor record. But the offense was better with Flacco than Jake Browning , at least. Plus, the pick swap gave the Bengals another interesting young wide receiver.
Flacco was never going to be long for Cleveland as it churned through quarterbacks, so to package him in a trade swap that saw the Browns move up a round was a win for a non-contending team. A small win, but one nonetheless.
The Dugger deal was effectively a salary dump for the Patriots and one that benefited the Steelers immensely. The safety had fallen out of favor in New England to the point where the franchise bought out the remainder of a four-year extension they signed in 2024 in order to move him. It was an admission that the deal had failed and cost the Patriots $5.4 million in cash, plus roster bonuses.
Dugger was a winner from the trade because he reached unrestricted free agency two years early. The Steelers also came away on top because they got a productive version of Dugger for half a season at essentially no cost. He filled a hole in the lineup following DeShon Elliott's injury and delivered an impact with two interceptions (one of them a pick six), five passes defended, a sack, two tackles for loss and a safety. Not bad for a nine-game rental.
A third-rounder is a steep price to pay for eight games of Phillips, but when all is said and done, this trade should end up as a good one for the Eagles. Phillips was a pleasant addition to the defense, playing some of the best football of his career on a per-game basis to help Philadelphia secure a playoff spot. The Eagles elected not to re-sign him at the high price tag of four years and $120 million (which the Panthers awarded him in free agency), but they will not come away empty-handed, as his departure should net them a third-round compensatory pick in the 2027 draft. They will effectively get back what they put in.
Meanwhile, the Dolphins were unlikely to sign Phillips to an extension, too. They manifested a third-round pick instead of getting nothing in return for what would have been an exit in free agency. Everyone won here with the compensatory pick, essentially creating an invisible third piece in the trade.
Last year's Chargers offensive line was a MASH unit, and the 2026 group is only slightly healthier. Penning arrived midway through last season as an emergency fill-in and was called into action early this year, too, before he suffered a concussion of his own and landed on injured reserve on Oct. 10. That Los Angeles re-signed him at the end of his rookie contract salvaged some value from the trade, but this still is a bust of a former first-round pick whose main contribution is depth. His PFF pass-blocking grade in 2026 is the worst among all 74 qualified guards.
It was a shame that Penning did not catch on in New Orleans, considering the Saints used the No. 19 overall pick on him in 2022. At least he did not walk away for nothing.
Mike Macdonald said Monday that "early returns are positive" on Rashid Shaheed's knee after he suffered an injury in Sunday night's win over the Chiefs . His availability for the rest of the year would go a long way in cementing this trade as a fruitful one for the Seahawks, but regardless of his health, Seattle seems pleased with where it stands. Shaheed was never supposed to be more than a secondary receiving option behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba and, in fact, is more of a gadget offensive weapon and special teams threat than a downfield target. He returned two kickoffs for touchdowns last season, including one in the playoffs en route to a Super Bowl ring, and earned himself a three-year, $51 million extension at the end of his 12-game run in Seattle in 2025.
Shaheed was similarly a boom-or-bust asset in New Orleans and one who would have been phased out eventually had he re-signed as the Saints identified Chris Olave , Devaughn Vele and (once healthy) Jordyn Tyson as the future of their receiving corps. Turning his expiring contract into a pair of high-end Day 3 picks should be viewed as a success since the Saints are no worse off at…

title: Prisco's Week 8 NFL picks: Packers over Panthers, Lions hand Vikings their first loss
summary: Pete Prisco reveals all of his Week 8 picks, including the Bills to top the Ravens in a high-scoring game
full_text:
Going to the dogs last week turned out to be dog doodoo. I picked every dog against the spread last week and it looked good early, but then it collapsed late with five straight losses, including both prime-time games Sunday and Monday night.
I was 8-6 straight up last week and 6-7-1 against the spread. Hey, the spread record was an improvement, which tells you how bad I've been this season. My ATS record this year is 43-61-3, which is a long way from .500. My straight-up record is 62-44-1.
So this week, it's back to just picking the games. Forget all dogs. Trying to get to .500 makes me borrow a coaching cliché they all use.
One game at a time. One week at a time.
All lines via DraftKings ; All times ET
These two are both coming off losses. The Carolina loss featured the Bucs running over them for 258 rushing yards. It's been a problem all year. But the Packers don't run it very well, so something has to give. Carolina gave Jordan Love fits last year, but that will change here. Carolina gives up 27.7 points per game. Love lights them up and Josh Jacobs gets the run game going.
Pick: Packers 31, Panthers 24
Lamar Jackson could be back for the Ravens, but how much will his injured ankle impact his ability to move? The Bills are coming off a bye, so they will be rested. Baltimore's defense was bad in the loss to the Bengals last week, but Buffalo's defense has been awful. Look for a shootout here with Josh Allen getting the best of it.
The Titans are having major problems on offense, while the Bengals lit up the Ravens last week. Joe Burrow was special in the second half of that game and I think that will carry over here. Look for an offensive explosion from the Bengals as Burrow starts to get into the MVP talk.
Pick: Bengals 36, Titans 10
The Cowboys' offense came alive against the Eagles Monday night, especially on the ground, which isn't a good thing for an Arizona defense that is last in the league in scoring. The Dallas offense should roll and the Arizona offense won't be able to keep up. Dallas big — even on a short week.
Pick: Cowboys 37, Cardinals 21
The undefeated Vikings face a tough road game here against Detroit. The Lions offense against the Minnesota defense will be a treat to watch. Jared Goff is playing at a high level right now, but Minnesota's defense is the best in the league in terms of scoring. The Vikings offense is limited, but the Detroit defense has had major problems. But they were better last week, which I think carries over. Lions take it.
Pick: Lions 23, Vikings 13
Kirk Cousins stays in as the starter for the Raiders, but teams have blitzed him the past two weeks. That could be a problem here since the Jets are a top-10 team in blitz percentage. The Raiders have struggled to stop opposing offenses, giving up 28.1 points per game, so look for Geno Smith to have success. Jets win it.
This is a big game for the division lead in the AFC North. The Browns beat the Steelers earlier this year, but this will be a bigger challenge on the road. They are also playing consecutive road games, which will be a challenge. Look for Aaron Rodgers to play well as the Steelers take it.
Pick: Steelers 24, Browns 20
This is suddenly a big game in the NFC South with the Bucs upsetting Carolina last week and the Falcons upsetting the 49ers. The Tampa Bay running game has come alive, but Atlanta is stingy on the ground, giving up 3.8 per rush. That will mean this is a Baker Mayfield game. Tampa Bay gives up 3.5 per rush, which might make for tough going for Bijan Robinson. That's a problem for the Atlanta offense. Tampa Bay wins it.
The Colts are a mess; they are playing consecutive road games, and they haven't won at Jacksonville since 2014, when Andrew Luck was the quarterback. Oh, and they traded their best offensive lineman, Quentin Nelson. The Jaguars are coming off a bye, so they will be rested. This one will get ugly as the Jaguars bounce back from the loss to the Texans in London.
Pick: Jaguars 30, Colts 16
The battle of Los Angeles isn't quite the game many expected before the season. The Chargers, coming off a bye, haven't won yet and the Rams have been a disappointment. But the Rams won last week at Las Vegas to seemingly right things. They will win here, but the rested Chargers will keep it close.
Pick: Rams 23, Chargers 20
The Chiefs' offense was lifeless in Seattle on Sunday night and now faces a tough Denver defense. They have to find ways to get the running game going again with Kenneth Walker. Bo Nix showed some life last week in the victory over Arizona, but this Chiefs defense will be a challenge. Look for a low-scoring game won by Kansas City, with Walker getting going against Denver's defense, which gives up 4.6 yards per rush.
Pick: Chiefs 19, Broncos 14
The Dolphins won their first game last week and have been in a lot of their losses. But this New England team will be a challenge, even at home. The Patriots are coming off a bad road loss to the Bears, and they will be rested, having played on Thursday. The defense limits the Dolphins' offense, and Drake Maye will play well. New England wins it.
Pick: Pats 28, Dolphins 14
This might be an elimination game of sorts for these two. Both need a victory in the worst way — even in their horrible division. The Eagles are crippled by injuries, but Washington has plenty of their own. With the Eagles on a short week off a Monday night game and the Commanders off a bye, Washington will win it.
Pick: Commanders 28, Eagles 16
The Bears are riding high behind Caleb Williams and an improved defense. But this is a tough road trip against a Seattle team that showed what it can do on defense by shutting down the Chiefs Sunday night. Seattle also got the running game going. The Seattle defense will slow down the Chicago offense, and the Seahawks will win it.
Pick: Seahawks 24, Bears 17

title: Is it time to start the conversation about benching Cardinals QB Brissett?
summary: It appears that the 2026 version of the Arizona Cardinals is just the version of the team in 2025. Maybe the new boss is just like the old boss. At this rate, something needs to change. Yes, the Cardinals are 2-5-0. But 10 games remain. Is this team headed down the rabbit hole to another […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Jacoby Brissett #7 of the Arizona Cardinals reacts after his team was defeated by the Detroit Lions at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images It appears that the 2026 version of the Arizona Cardinals is just the version of the team in 2025. Maybe the new boss is just like the old boss. At this rate, something needs to change. Yes, the Cardinals are 2-5-0. But 10 games remain. Is this team headed down the rabbit hole to another double-digit-loss season? Or can they rebound? RELATED: WHEN SHOULD THE CARDINALS START THE CARSON BECK ERA? Arizona has a new offense, but geez, averaging 20.3 points a game is concerning. This side of the ball will drive up and down the field all game, then when they arrive in the Red Zone, the wheels come off, and the offense does not finish. Correct that statement: the offense rarely finishes. The offensive problems with this offense begin with one guy: QB Jacoby Brissett. It’s a sad, sad situation. His all-time starting record? 22-50-0. His starting record while with Arizona? 3-16-0. This new Mike LaFleur offense is ranked #19 overall in the league. They are #18 in total passing yards (1,607), #1 in attempts (283), #2 in completions (184), #13 in pass completion percentage (65.0%), #16 in touchdown passes (10), #23 in fewest interceptions thrown (6), #28 in passing plays of 20+ yards (13), dead last in passing plays of 40+ yards (0), and have given up the 16 th most sacks (15). Where are the explosive plays? Long plays just aren’t a thing with Arizona. They are the only club that hasn’t had a passing play go further than 40 yards, and look at the plays of 20-plus yardage. Just 13? In seven games? The Cardinals boast the league’s best tight end in Trey McBride, and have several dynamic pass catchers in Michael Wilson, Kendrick Bourne, and rookie Reggie Virgil. The offensive line is holding its own despite losing LT Paris Johnson and each week having to Band-Aid who is healthy and who is injured. In the past, Brissett was known for having huge games. He has 10 career 300-yard passing days and one in which he eclipsed 400 yards in the loss to the San Francisco 49ers last year in late November (452). But none of that is happening this year. In the Week 2 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, Brissett had a mere 95 passing yards. 166 in the loss to the New York Football Giants in Week 4. The issue is that Brissett is having to throw a lot in every contest. The average for a quarterback is 28 attempts. This year, Brissett has thrown 37, 28, 52, 35, 47, 35, and 48 attempts. What that means is that the Cardinals aren’t generating much of a running game, so their quarterback has to air it out for much of the contest. That is not sustainable. When the opposing defense realizes that Arizona can’t run, they stop looking for the run and blast off the snap every time, which gives them a distinct advantage. Should this offense sit Brissett? Statistically, his completion percentage is strong. He threw for 73.0% and 73.1% in two games, and in the 60s for four more. That is really a good sign. Any quarterback who can throw for a 65% completion ratio in any game has done his job. These are dream stats for any signalcaller. The main issue with Brissett at the helm is the offense’s inability to get into the end zone. The Cardinals can move the ball up and down the field for much of the game, but as soon as they cross the 20-yard line, it is like time stands still. Here's the story of the season so far: Arizona Cardinals are dead last in red zone efficiency (42.86%). Arizona Cardinals are dead last in points per game allowed (29.7). — Johnny Venerable (@JohnnyVenerable) October 26, 2026 Currently, Arizona is ranked dead last in Red Zone efficiency at 44%. Good teams, such as the San Francisco 49ers, come in at scoring a touchdown on 87% of their trips. Plainly put, the Niners finish drives, while the Cardinals spit and sputter and end up with three points instead of six. Which is gravy for Arizona kicker Chad Ryland. He is the king of having to come in and kick 23-yard field goals because the offense can’t find a way to get into the end zone. He is ranked #2 in field goal attempts, #3 in converted field goals, and he has converted on 89.5% of his attempts. To show how the offense relies on him to bail them out, he has converted 5 of 5 kicks in the 20–29-yard range, and 5 for 5 in the 30–39-yard range. It’s not like he is banging out a bunch of 50-to 60-yard kicks. Last weekend against the Denver Broncos, the Cardinals were 1-5 in Red Zone appearances. They got down to Denver’s 11, 7, and 23 without scoring a touchdown. Drives of 14 plays and 10 plays. While the Broncos were scoring six points a pop, Arizona was getting half that. The week before, in the 18-16 win over the Los Angeles Rams, Ryland did all the scoring. Brissett guided the offense on drives of 10 plays, 12, 15, and 14. The Cardinals were on the Rams’ 16, 12, 3, 19, 9, before Ryland kicked the 43-yard game-winner with no time remaining. Yet each drive ended up with yet another field goal. In the second quarter, Arizona had a first-and-goal at the eight, and after three plays had not punched it in. What about the 15-play drive that began at their own 25-yard line to start the third quarter, and the offense had a first-and-10 on the Rams’ 23 and could only get to the 19 before trotting out Ryland once again? Or the 14-play drive, as the period was about to expire, that volleyed over into Quarter 4 became a first-and-goal at LA’s eight. Four-yard run to the four-yard line, minus three-yard run, minus two-yard pass, field goal. Before this drive, the Cardinals were up 15-9. A touchdown here with just over nine minutes left in the game would have crippled the Rams. Two things about Brissett: He doesn’t have many picks (6), but he also doesn’t throw many touchdowns (10). Which makes absolutely no sense with having access to an exceptional pass-catching tight end like McBride. Raise your hand if this makes any sense. Here’s an idea: Sit Brissett for a few games. Insert backup Gardner Minshew and see what happens. What is the worst that can happen? The Cardinals will lose? They are doing that anyways. Maybe Minshew has a potion that will help this offense get into the end zone. Because the problem isn’t whether this offense can move the ball – it can. It’s getting into the end zone and collecting three points instead of six. By kicking field goals on the majority of drives, it keeps the other team in the ballgame. There is no extension of the lead – ever. Throw Minshew in there and let’s see if anything different pops out. Then, at some point down the schedule, put rookie Carson Beck in some games and see what Arizona has in him, because they will need to know before next April’s NFL Draft. Kick the tires on Beck and see what he can do in a live regular-season game against defensive starters. If Ryland ends up going to the Pro Bowl this year, the first person he should thank is Brissett. Maybe buy him a nice watch.

full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Falcons fans and fans across the country. It’s no surprise that the NFC South is up for grabs. Any division without a clear playoff team creates an opportunity for all four teams to compete. What can be viewed as a slight surprise is the Falcons being up there as the favorite to win the NFC South. After being largely projected to finish last, they have surpassed expectations so far, beating multiple playoff teams in 2025 and embarrassing their biggest rival in primetime. Kevin Stefanski has quickly instilled his philosophy to make the Falcons more efficient, cohesive, and disciplined. With Jeff Ulbrich’s excellent coaching, the team has a clear identity on both sides of the ball and is pushing toward the top of the NFC South. A win against Tampa Bay would give them an advantage over two divisional rivals. Given Carolina’s recent struggles and tough upcoming matchup, the Falcons could be in first place by the end of the weekend. A win would lead to plenty of discussion about their outlook. That raises the question of expectations going forward. Let us know your thoughts below. If the Falcons win this week, will they win the South? Are you confident in the Falcons? full_text: Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Michael Penix Jr. led the Falcons offense to a solid day on Sunday against the previously undefeated 49ers, completing 25 of 34 passes, a 73.5% completion rate, for 213 yards, three touchdowns, and no turnovers. His efforts did not go unnoticed, and Penix has been named the NFC Offensive Player of the Week for his performance. It’s Penix’s first time receiving the NFC Offensive Player of the Week Award. From the Falcons: … Penix is only the third quarterback in the league in the last 25 seasons to have at least three passing touchdowns with zero interceptions in a victory over a 6-0 or better team. Penix has completed at least 72% of his passes in Atlanta’s three wins this season. His 21 touchdown passes rank 10th in franchise history. Penix joins teammates Bijan Robinson (honored three times since 2025) and Kyle Pitts (Week 15, 2025), and former teammate Zane Gonzales (NFC Special Teams Player of the Week, Weeks 12 and 18, 2025), as NFC Players of the Week. Penix will speak to the media on Wednesday afternoon, and we will update this post once he comments on the honor. Congratulations to Penix on the well-deserved recognition, and here’s hoping we see that level of play for the rest of the season.

title: Week 7, 3 up and 3 down: Herculean efforts and efficient play led to a win
summary: The Atlanta Falcons fell behind early, but a sound game plan and sensational individual efforts helped them claw back and take this win from the San Francisco 49ers. Here’s the Week 7, 3 up and 3 down: 3 up Kendal Daniels After suffering a terrifying injury against the Bears, Daniels put that behind him and […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 25: Kendal Daniels #53 of the Atlanta Falcons reacts against the San Francisco 49ers following an NFL football game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons fell behind early, but a sound game plan and sensational individual efforts helped them claw back and take this win from the San Francisco 49ers . Here’s the Week 7, 3 up and 3 down: 3 up Kendal Daniels After suffering a terrifying injury against the Bears, Daniels put that behind him and had his coming-out party. In just his 7th start, the rookie linebacker wore the green dot and held down the fort while Divine Deablo nursed an arm injury. Daniels did more than survive; he thrived, accumulating a TFL and multiple turnovers. Daniels operated as the MIKE linebacker, and while he wasn’t perfect, his instincts made up for the small mistakes that popped up here and there. Those natural instincts and athletic ability made Jeff Ulbrich comfortable with the amount of work the rookie has been given, and you should feel the same. He’s raw, but he’s improving week to week, and he and Harold Perkins Jr. are competing for the title of biggest draft steal. Kendal Daniels' instincts pop on film. The LB has legit range and does a good job navigating through trash. Wore the green dot in just his 7th start. Falcons got a good one. pic.twitter.com/i9kEjKy3SI — Tre’Shon (@tre3shon) October 27, 2026 Jessie Bates III I really wanted to replace Bates on the list this week, but the safety made it impossible. He hauled what will likely be the most impressive interception of his career, a play that turned the tide when the Falcons desperately needed it. At the end, when it looked like the 49ers were driving for a touchdown, Bates called game with a lethal peanut punch. When wearing the red helmet, he’s the best safety in the history of the game. After a slow start that raised questions about his future in Atlanta, he now looks poised for an extension. Just another day at the office for Jessie Bates pic.twitter.com/QaJMHiXEjO — Tre’Shon (@tre3shon) October 27, 2026 Michael Penix Jr. We’ve seen Penix be efficient and manage the game when his running backs put up 200 yards, but we haven’t seen him lead the team that way without a run game. We can check that off the list. No, we did not see a high volume of deep shots, but that’s not what was needed to win. Raheem Morris took away the deep ball and dared his former quarterback to carve up his zone defense underneath, and that’s exactly what Penix did. We saw Penix work through his progressions and come off receivers who weren’t open, getting down to his 3rd, and at times 4th, option. It was great to see him celebrate National Tight Ends Day, and that’s an underrated storyline coming out of this game: eight different receivers caught a ball. 3 down Run Game The run game has been in a slow decline the last three weeks, and the unit had its worst performance in that span. Now, to be fair to the offensive line, the 49ers have stuffed everyone. They allow the fewest explosive runs in the league, and sold out to stop Bijan. Still, the Falcons have to get this operation back on track as they prepare to enter the second half of the schedule. They’ve started to implement more inside zone and duo concepts but have barely dipped their toes into power. We did see a few misdirection concepts, and that’s a great way to take advantage of run blitzes. Start mixing in more, and defenses will be forced to play more honestly. Jahan Dotson Dotson was the lowest-graded receiver in the game according to PFF . He wasn’t unplayable, but he is on a two-game skid now and needs to refocus. The drop was inexcusable. Dotson not only had the first down, but he also had room to gain those yards he claims to love . There have also been some noticeable effort issues, not anything egregious, but enough that they can’t be ignored. Dotson is still separating at a high level; he’s also great at drawing PIs, but it can be frustrating not getting many targets. He has to stay locked in so he’s ready when the ball comes his way. Xavier Watts This is a bit nitpicky, but Watts hasn’t really taken the year-2 leap we hoped for, and this felt like a good time to point it out. He was responsible for the 49ers longest pass play of the game and just hasn’t made the impact plays in coverage that he did as a rookie. With the secondary constantly shifting cast members, communication breakdowns are more likely, and that could be affecting the second-year safety. Watts has been fine, but we know he can be better, and hopefully he’s able to take that leap now that the secondary is starting to get healthy again. The Falcons are now sitting just below .500 at 3-4, and the NFC South is wide open. They have a chance to improve their title odds by burying the Buccaneers next week. Can they get it done?

title: Ravens film study: Cam Jurgens makes strong debut vs. Bengals
summary: The Ravens’ 35-13 loss to the Bengals left us with more questions than answers about the current state of the roster. After holding Cincinnati scoreless in the first half, Baltimore surrendered five second-half touchdowns, raising questions about the team’s consistency and effort. Despite the disappointing result, several players continued to play with a high motor […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - OCTOBER 25: Cam Jurgens #64 of the Baltimore Ravens snaps the ball during an NFL football game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Cincinnati Bengals at M&T Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Ben Hsu/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Ravens’ 35-13 loss to the Bengals left us with more questions than answers about the current state of the roster. After holding Cincinnati scoreless in the first half, Baltimore surrendered five second-half touchdowns, raising questions about the team’s consistency and effort. Despite the disappointing result, several players continued to play with a high motor throughout the game. Cam Jurgens provided much-needed stability along the interior offensive line in his first start as a Raven, Travis Jones reminded everyone of his ability to dominate in the trenches, and Ethan Burke stepped into an important role following Tavius Robinson’s season-ending injury. C Cam Jurgens 67 snaps | 26 run blocking | 41 pass blocking | 1 pressure allowed Jurgens made his first start for Baltimore since being acquired from Philadelphia on October 7th, providing some much-needed stability to an interior offensive line that has struggled throughout the season. One of the most noticeable aspects of his performance was his football IQ and awareness in pass protection. The center’s responsibilities extend well beyond snapping the football, as he is tasked with setting protections, identifying pressure and assisting neighboring offensive linemen. On multiple reps, Jurgens demonstrated his awareness against stunts and loops, absorbing contact and passing off defenders to prevent free rushers from reaching the quarterback. In one-on-one situations, he displayed a calm demeanor and a reliable anchor, allowing just one pressure across 41 pass-blocking snaps. Ravens C Cam Jurgens – 1 pressure allowed in 41 pass block snaps pic.twitter.com/GnaaSgPnLl — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) October 27, 2026 Jurgens also flashed his core strength and ability to operate in space. On one rep, he tossed a Bengals defender to the ground before releasing into space on a screen. In the run game, he consistently worked to establish favorable angles, flip his hips and seal rushing lanes for the ball carrier. Jurgens isn’t necessarily an overwhelming power blocker, but his ability to steal leverage, reach his landmarks and position his body between the defender and the ball carrier makes him an excellent fit for Baltimore’s rushing attack. His presence provides immediate stability to the offensive line while giving the Ravens a potential long-term answer at center for years to come. EDGE Ethan Burke 17 snaps | 11 run defense | 6 pass rush | 1 pressure | 2 stops Burke’s performance against Cincinnati may not jump off the stat sheet, but his contributions came in an important role for Baltimore’s defense. With Tavius Robinson suffering a season-ending pectoral injury, the Ravens needed another versatile edge defender capable of holding up against the run, and Burke demonstrated that he can fill that responsibility. His alignment versatility allows him to operate as a 7-technique outside the tight end or reduce inside into 5-technique and 4i alignments. On one rep, Burke aligned across from the tight end, established a firm point of attack, maintained vision into the backfield and disengaged to make a tackle for a minimal gain. On another, he absorbed contact from a tight end with momentum, worked off the block and made another stop near the line of scrimmage. Ravens UDFA Ethan Burke Welcome back Brent urban pic.twitter.com/Xzmc5DMEZ8 — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) October 27, 2026 As a pass rusher, Burke also demonstrated his motor and ability to generate pressure through pursuit. On one rep, Burrow escaped to his left, but Burke continued working toward the quarterback and nearly finished the play with a sack. Had he secured the tackle, Burke would have recorded three sacks over the last two weeks, highlighting his recent emergence as a contributor. While his pass-rush repertoire remains a work in progress, his ability to play multiple alignments, maintain gap integrity and pursue quarterbacks outside the pocket provides Baltimore with valuable defensive versatility. Burke’s role may not receive much attention, but his contributions against the run will be important as the Ravens navigate the remainder of the season without Robinson. DT Travis Jones 32 snaps | 11 run defense | 21 pass rush | 3 pressures | 2 stops Jones has had a relatively quiet start to the 2026 season after establishing himself as one of Baltimore’s most productive interior pass rushers last year. Part of that can be attributed to his responsibilities within Jesse Minter’s defensive front, where he has frequently been asked to two-gap and occupy blockers rather than attack upfield. Against Cincinnati, Jones finally had opportunities to play more aggressively, and his combination of play strength and explosiveness was on full display. On one rep, he deployed a hump move to drive the guard backward into Burrow’s lap, forcing the quarterback to escape the pocket. On another, Jones utilized an outside-arm swipe to clear the guard’s hands, create displacement and transition into power to generate pressure. His ability to combine technical hand usage with overwhelming strength makes him a difficult matchup for interior offensive linemen. Ravens DT Travis Jones – 3 pressures, 2 stops By far the best game from Travis this year, looks like he’s stronger than everyone out there. Deploying length, anchoring down vs the run and overpowering to collapse the pocket pic.twitter.com/MstDPvOAfT — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) October 26, 2026 Jones was equally impressive against the run, displaying the ability to both penetrate the backfield and control blockers at the point of attack. On one rep, he utilized a swipe move to defeat his blocker and penetrate into the backfield for a tackle for loss. On another, he stacked the center, maintained leverage and peeked into the backfield before disengaging to limit the runner to a minimal gain. Jones’ ability to collapse the interior of the pocket is particularly valuable for Baltimore’s edge rushers, as forcing quarterbacks to drift outside their protection creates additional opportunities for sacks. If Jones can consistently generate this level of interior disruption, it will have a significant impact on the effectiveness of the entire defensive front moving forward. How many games will the Ravens win in the regular season? | Baltimore Beatdown

title: Ravens’ reasons for concern and optimism
summary: The Jesse Minter era in Baltimore has hit its first major fork in the road. After giving up 35 unanswered points to the Bengals in the second-half of Sunday’s game, questions are starting to rain down on the Ravens. Unfortunately, Baltimore’s second-half meltdowns have now transcended multiple coaching staffs. Coming into Week 7, the team […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 25: Ja'marr Chase #1 of the Cincinnati Bengals catches a touchdown during the fourth quarter against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Todd Olszewski/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jesse Minter era in Baltimore has hit its first major fork in the road. After giving up 35 unanswered points to the Bengals in the second-half of Sunday’s game, questions are starting to rain down on the Ravens. Unfortunately, Baltimore’s second-half meltdowns have now transcended multiple coaching staffs. Coming into Week 7, the team had already blown double-digit leads to the Saints and Browns. However, Sunday’s collapse was on a completely different level. The Ravens didn’t just get beat in the second half; they were completely annihilated. Fans and media are predictably rushing to play the blame game and rebuild the roster, but it’s too early in the season to be calling for sweeping changes, especially after three straight games with a backup quarterback. A 1-2 record without Lamar Jackson is closer to an expected result than an outright disaster. It’s less that the Ravens lost those games and more how they fell apart when their best was needed. With a locker room, coaching staff, and front office searching for answers, let’s look at what aspects of the 2026 Ravens should be of concern, but more importantly, where there could be some light at the end of this currently dark tunnel. Reasons for Concern The blown leads are clearly a player-driven issue John Harbaugh’s firing in January led many to believe that the team’s history of collapsing late in games and blowing double-digit leads was over. Instead, the Giants have put forth several solid fourth quarters while Minter’s Ravens are still struggling down the stretch. Don’t get me wrong, it was time to move on from Harbaugh. If anything, this shows that there is clearly a systemic issue impacting the players in the second half. The moment any type of adversity hits, they collapse like a house of cards. When the Bengals scored coming out of halftime, fans all had the same feeling: it’s over. Based on the Ravens’ body language, they felt the same way. The game snowballed out of control from there. So what is the issue? It would be irrational to pin all of these collapses on one player. However, there are a few members of this defense who have been constants through different eras, like Marlon Humphrey, Kyle Hamilton, and Roquan Smith. This trio in particular is considered the leaders of the Baltimore defense, but only Hamilton truly rises to the title on the field. Humphrey and Smith have seen a gradual decline in performance over the years, and unfortunately, the Ravens are still paying them a lot of money. Aside from their play, Humphrey and Smith are supposed to be the veterans in the room who speak up, hold other players accountable, and rally the troops when adversity hits. However, this doesn’t seem to be the case. Humphrey is an extravagant off-the-field personality, which draws plenty of criticism. Smith was initially thought to be the next great linebacker and leader of the Ravens’ storied defense. Aside from his first two seasons in Baltimore, it hasn’t quite worked out that way. Both are still solid players, but not nearly as good as their price tags or reputations suggest. As Minter alluded to in his Monday press conference, he is looking for one of his players to step up, not just on the field, but on the sideline and in the locker room. Ray Lewis and Ed Reed aren’t walking through that door anytime soon. The Ravens need a powerful voice within their defense to rally the troops when adversity hits. I’m not even sure if the younger generation of players respond to that type of motivation. It’s possible that the players are being told to play loose and free in stressful moments. If so, they’re taking it too literally. This, in my opinion, is the root cause of these defensive collapses. Younger players rally around the vets. Lewis, Reed, and Terrell Suggs held those around them accountable, even the coaches. I’m not sure that personality exists in the Ravens locker room right now, and whether it be via trade or otherwise, someone needs to step up and re-establish the once-great Ravens defensive culture – if it even exists anymore. The performance on Sunday wasn’t merely a talent or play-calling deficiency – the players looked defeated, just like they did after the Texans, Chiefs, Bills, and Lions games last year. It’s a problem, and it needs to be corrected fast. Suspect roster construction Eric DeCosta is frequently thought of as one of the better general managers in football. The Ravens have been very good at drafting prospects, developing them into solid players, extending the best ones, and receiving compensatory picks when the rest eventually price themselves out of Baltimore. Most of the time, it works. However, the current state of the Ravens is defined by a glaring weakness in the trenches. Early in the Lamar Jackson era, DeCosta reallocated resources from the trenches and into the wide receiver and defensive back rooms. He still drafted a few good linemen like Tyler Linderbaum and Travis Jones, but in later rounds, there were a lot of whiffs. Before selecting Vega Ioane this year – who is looking like the Ravens’ next great guard – five of the previous seven first-round picks were spent on receivers and defensive backs. Obviously, Zay Flowers and Kyle Hamilton were hits, but returns on Rashod Bateman have been mixed at best and the jury is still out on Nate Wiggins and Malaki Starks. Overcorrections have been another issue. After multiple injuries at center, DeCosta had acquire for Cam Jurgens from the Eagles. He looked good in his Ravens debut, but the second-round price tag was steep. Similarly, the neglect of the edge rusher room forced DeCosta to first trade two first-round picks for Maxx Crosby and then give massive contract to Trey Hendrickson when Crosby’s knee scared Baltimore out of the deal. Hendrickson has been good despite his finger injury, but the moves reeked of overcorrecting to address a position that was not properly addressed in previous years. A number of DeCosta’s recent contracts have quickly looked like mistakes in hindsight. Mark Andrews looks like a shell of himself, and neither Jaylinn Hawkins nor John Simpson have lived up to expectations. This year, Andrews, Humphrey, and Smith currently comprise approximately 20% of the Ravens total salary cap. The Ravens are loyal to their players, perhaps to a fault. To compound the issue, they now are in a tight salary cap position that is preventing them from making any significant trade deadline moves. Any major trade would have to involve the other team eating a portion of the player’s salary – thereby raising the price of the deal – or the Ravens engaging in another round of cap gymnastics to either trade away one of their own or push more money into the future. The one saving hope is that these contracts are simply spillover from the Harbaugh era. The front office and coaching staff both collaborate on how the team should be built. If DeCosta can get a Jackson extension done and clear cap space by parting ways with underperforming veterans, Minter should be in position to build his vision of the Ravens. Reasons for Optimism There have been flashes of the Ravens’ full potential Let’s rewind to Week 2 of the 2022 season, in Mike Macdonald’s second game as the Ravens’ defensive coordinator. Similar to what we saw on Sunday, Baltimore surrendered 28 points in the fourth quarter to Miami, and blew a 21-point lead. This was not an anomaly in his tenure. Macdonald — the coach who, for better or worse, Minter will be compared to for the remainder of his time in Baltimore — also has a history of poor defensive performances early in the season, especially in the second half of games. In 2022, the Ravens were 23rd in defensive EPA/play in Weeks 1-9,…

title: Ravens survey and discussion: predicting Baltimore’s 2026 win total
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Ravens fans and fans across the country. The Baltimore Ravens entered the 2026 season with Super Bowl expectations and an 11.5-win over/under. But Jesse Minter is 4-3 through his first seven games and […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - OCTOBER 25: Head Coach Jesse Minter of the Baltimore Ravens looks on from the sidelines during the first quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at M&T Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Todd Olszewski/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Ravens fans and fans across the country. The Baltimore Ravens entered the 2026 season with Super Bowl expectations and an 11.5-win over/under. But Jesse Minter is 4-3 through his first seven games and sitting in last place in the AFC North with the NFL’s toughest schedule for the rest of the season. Can he bounce back and bring the Ravens to double-digit wins, or is Baltimore headed for another disappointing finish? Here are Beatdown’s thoughts: Nikhil Mehta I only see one clear win on the Ravens’ remaining schedule – Week 10 against the Chargers – and four more games in which I would favor Baltimore. That’s five at worst, nine as expected, and 10 or more at best if this team can stay healthy and field something resembling a second-half defense. But I have little reason to believe either of those things will happen, so I will land in the eight- to nine-win band. Frank Platko While the vibes around the Ravens are bleak right now, and for good reason, I still believe better days are on the horizon. That is, of course, assuming Lamar Jackson can return within the next couple of weeks without a dropoff in his performance. The Ravens have a tough schedule ahead but with Jackson under center, every game is winnable. I think the team can rally enough to roughly split the remainder of their divisional matchups, beat both NFC North teams (Panthers and Buccaneers), and earn at least one win against another non-divisional opponent (Bills, Jaguars, Texans, Chargers). Even if not exact, this ballpark projection would give the Ravens 10 total wins — meaning they’d have to go 6-4 the remainder of the season. Even amidst continuing injuries and inconsistencies in all three phases, this seems doable. 10-7 will most likely not be enough to win the division anymore but a wild-card playoff berth is still within striking distance. Stephen Bopst The Ravens, while in stress, aren’t nearly in as bad of a spot as they were at this time last year. Their record ultimately hinges on the health of Lamar Jackson, but that’s currently a big if. They should win 2/3 against the Browns and Steelers, that puts them at 6. From there, I expect them to win four out of the remaining seven against the Chargers, Bills, Bucs, Texans, Panthers, Bengals, and Jaguars. It they really want some breathing room, they’ll have to take one of these next two games against Jacksonville or Buffalo. If not, it could be tough to sneak into the playoffs and they’ll need a really hot finish. Regardless, I see this as a 10-7 team that should be in contention for a wildcard. Dustin Cox Even though it may feel like the Ravens’ season is imploding after consecutive divisional losses, this team can still make a run with a healthy Lamar Jackson. Any hopes of the top seed in the AFC are probably out the window at this point, and winning the division will be much harder now, but I still expect Baltimore to find their footing over the next month or so and become a dangerous team in the conference. I think 11-6 is a realistic record if Jackson can return this week and remain healthy for the remainder of the season. I expect them to split the next two games against the Bills and Jaguars while losing to the Steelers once and another loss coming to either the Texans or Bengals again. Just getting into the playoffs is all that matters at this point, and I think the Ravens still have the team and coaching staff to make some noise if they get there. Now, it’s your turn! title: Buffalo Bills trending up, trending down: The Ravens keep blowing leads, and the Bills need to be ready
summary: The Buffalo Bills continue their campaign, aiming for the AFC’s number one seed, this Sunday when they host the 4-3 Baltimore Ravens at the New Highmark Stadium. The Ravens have been road warriors this year (3-1 away from home) and should have their own franchise QB, Lamar Jackson, back for this game. A Bills victory […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills continue their campaign, aiming for the AFC’s number one seed, this Sunday when they host the 4-3 Baltimore Ravens at the New Highmark Stadium. The Ravens have been road warriors this year (3-1 away from home) and should have their own franchise QB, Lamar Jackson, back for this game. A Bills victory here might not put Baltimore away when thinking playoffs, but it certainly makes it tougher for them to still fight for the so precious number one seed. The Ravens have led by 10 or more points in all three of their losses, and the defense is the reason. ESPN’s Ben Solak, citing Next Gen Stats, found that Baltimore ranks 29th in completion percentage allowed (64.8%) and 26th in yards per attempt (7.8) when the likelihood of a pass is 75 percent or higher (reminds me of a certain defensive group…). The pass rush isn’t the problem. Baltimore pressures 42 percent of the time in those spots, above the league average. The problem is that 40 percent of those throws go to receivers with at least three yards of separation, the third-highest rate in the league. Joe Burrow posted a perfect passer rating in the second half against them on Sunday, in a 35-13 Bengals win. That is the defense the Bills (5-1) get after the bye, and it shapes this week’s list. Lamar Jackson is expected to play, with some uncertainty about how close to full strength he will be. Zay Flowers caught eight of 11 targets for 137 yards and a touchdown against Cincinnati, even with Tyler Huntley throwing to him. On the other side, we don’t have a Ja’Marr Chase to create all that separation, but having DJ Moore back would certainly help. With all of this in mind, here are my trending up and trending down Bills players who can be decisive in next Sunday’s matchup. HEROES Josh Allen, QB: The matchup is built for him Baltimore plays zone on 61 percent of obvious passing downs, and a zone defense that rushes well but doesn’t close on routes is the defense Allen punishes. He was efficient against the Raiders: 23-of-33 for 255 yards, two touchdowns, no interceptions, and he tied Jim Kelly’s franchise record for touchdown passes. Through six weeks, he leads the league in total dropback EPA at 58.6, per ESPN. Through five weeks, PFF had him first among quarterbacks in rate of positively graded plays (23.2%) and had him at a 90.8 grade in opponent territory, with ten red-zone touchdowns and no turnover-worthy plays. He is tied for the league lead with three fourth-quarter comebacks, per Pro Football Reference. Baltimore has blown three double-digit leads this season, and that is the kind of game he is best at finishing. We should see more of what we saw the last time those two teams met in Orchard Park, and Josh had to lead a comeback-from-behind victory. Christian Benford, CB: After Brock Bowers, Zay Flowers is the assignment Benford’s work on Brock Bowers deserves every bit of attention it got. Next Gen Stats counted 19 matchups against Bowers, 14 of them in man coverage, which was a career high against a tight end for Benford. Bowers was targeted five times with Benford on him, caught two for 23 yards, and had two pass breakups against him. Bowers’ two biggest catches, for 29 and 18 yards, came when someone else was covering him. CB played 64 of the defense’s 66 snaps. The Bills’ defense has allowed 15 touchdown passes, tied for the second-most in the league before Week 7. Jim Leonhard should have Benford traveling with Flowers on Sunday, and this matchup will be must-watch. HEAD-SCRATCHERS C.J. Gardner-Johnson, S: The experiment is not working He was ejected before halftime in Las Vegas for spitting at a Raiders player, after 28 snaps (42%). The league suspended him for a game, and that’s why he’ll miss the Ravens game. The Bills signed him as a one-year veteran to stabilize the back end and to give them “an edge” with his bold attitude. Instead, we’ve had missed tackles and an act that couldn’t be further away from how Buffalo Bills football is played and appreciated. It’s not just about his antics, though. His PFF grade last season was 51.6, 86th among 98 safeties, which is not far from where he is playing now. It seems he simply isn’t the starting safety he used to be. To be fair, there isn’t a big drop-off when Damar Hamlin plays in his place, and rookie Jalon Kilgore got 11 snaps against Las Vegas, with a third-down pass breakup and a touchdown allowed. He should be involved in the rotation going forward. Also, the safety spot is where I think a trade could change this defense the fastest. The deadline is November 10 at 4 p.m. ET, and Brandon Beane and Leonhard will decide whether the in-house options are enough. Terrel Bernard, LB: Sunday might be the final test of his role Bernard is the defense’s main communicator, and the defense has had communication problems. The coaches have already tested snaps without him, with Kaleb Elarms-Orr getting 22 snaps in Las Vegas, some of them next to Dorian Williams, while Bernard played 53 (80%). PFF graded him 53.9 overall (60th among 75 linebackers) and 44.8 in coverage (64th of 75), which should be his strength. His run defense has been ok (69.1, 28th of 75), but Henry will be a test. He ran 17 times for 45 yards against Cincinnati, averages 3.9 yards per carry, and has gone three games without a rushing touchdown, but with Lamar back, things normally get easier for him. Bernard has to start impacting games more often. He’s the captain, and it’s expected of him. He might be in danger of losing his job if not, after all, there are options — KEO has been getting opportunities, Shaq Thompson is on the practice squad, and a linebacker could be a deadline target too. HONORABLE MENTIONS Trending Up James Cook, RB : He ran for 95 yards and the go-ahead touchdown in Las Vegas. Baltimore’s pattern of losing leads in the second half, with their defense getting tired and allowing run games to succeed, means the Bills will probably have success insisting with the running game late in the game. Keon Coleman, WR : Without DJ Moore in Las Vegas, Coleman played 58 of 68 snaps and caught four passes for 59 yards and the touchdown that tied Kelly’s record. A defense with this much open-receiver trouble should give him room. Davison Igbinosun, CB : He played 42 snaps against the Raiders and allowed one catch on five targets, per PFF. Leonhard has said he has the majority of the snaps at the position, and with Flowers, Rashod Bateman, and Mark Andrews on the other side, he will be tested early. Trending Down Bradley Chubb, EDGE : He played 21 snaps against the Raiders and had one pressure on 11 pass rushes, while rookie T.J. Parker played 41 snaps and had two pressures on 29. Parker’s numbers aren’t dominant, but he has shown some potential. A rib injury opened the door, and if Chubb doesn’t raise his level, Parker’s share grows. The Bills got 12 pressures against Las Vegas and no sack of Cousins, and whether Jackson plays at full speed or Huntley starts again, they need more from the edge opposite Greg Rousseau. Maxwell Hairston, CB : He played 26 snaps (39%) in Las Vegas and has lost the starting spot to Igbinosun, while Tre’Davious White is back on the practice squad as a backup plan/warning. Hairston graded 40.0 overall this season (97th of 103 CBs), 36.4 in coverage (99th of 103 CBs), and 59.5 against the run (62nd of 103 CBs). Baltimore’s offense asks outside corners to tackle on screens and run plays, so his rotation snaps matter. FINAL THOUGHTS Baltimore’s defense is not a good one right now. It rushes the passer well enough, but it cannot cover, and it has been dreadful in second halves. That gives the Bills an edge on offense, but the defense still needs a fix. The safeties and the linebackers are the ones needing to step up the most, in my opinion. Two of the three starters are under scrutiny (Gardner-Johnson and Bernard), and the others aren’t exactly setting the world on fire either. I expect the Bills to target reinforcements at those…
author: Fernando Schmude

title: NFL trade deadline: Buffalo Bills trade candidate – Cam Bynum
summary: Let’s keep the safety carousel spinning for ideas for the Buffalo Bills ahead of this year’s NFL trade deadline. Taking center stage today is Colts safety Cam Bynum, a six-year steady veteran with over 5,000 career snaps on his NFL resume (counting playoffs) who resides on an Indianapolis team that appears to clearly be in […]
full_text: Let’s keep the safety carousel spinning for ideas for the Buffalo Bills ahead of this year’s NFL trade deadline. Taking center stage today is Colts safety Cam Bynum, a six-year steady veteran with over 5,000 career snaps on his NFL resume (counting playoffs) who resides on an Indianapolis team that appears to clearly be in fire-sale mode. This article is the seventh in the trade-candidate series I plan to sprinkle onto the site until the actual trade deadline until November 10, which is 13 days from now, and lands after Week 9. Past installments in this series: Derwin James , Brian Thomas Jr. Jessie Bates , Tariq Woolen , Amani Hooker , Antoine Winfield Jr. Age: 28 After a decorated career at cornerback for the University of California-Berkeley, Bynum was a fourth-round pick by the Vikings 2021. Minnesota’s coaching staff at the time immediately transitioned Bynum to safety, and he’s played that position ever since in the NFL. Bynum moved into a full-time role by his second season, when he played 100% — yes, 100% — of the Vikings regular-season defensive snaps. During that year, he racked up 81 tackles, defended six passes, and a pair on interceptions. In 2023, Bynum’s defensive snap percentage dipped to… 99.2%, and he was ubiquitous. That season, he made 137 tackles, knocked away nine passes, and snagged two more picks. The following season Bynum parlayed a three-pick, 96-tackle campaign into a four-year, $60 million deal that featured $26M guaranteed with the Colts. In 24 games in Indianapolis, Bynum has five picks and 10 pass breakups along with averaging 4.45 tackles per contest. 2026 snap splits Box: 24.8% Free safety: 60.6% Slot corner: 9.3% Wide corner: 4.4% *Bynum has played three snaps — of 430 total snaps — along the defensive line to date as well. Bynum has very much settled in as a true free safety. Despite aligning relatively far away from the football, he’s maintained high tackling numbers on a yearly basis. How he’d fit with Bills Given that the Bills might be in need of an every-down free safety — if we are to expect that C.J. Gardner-Johnson’s role will be diminished post-suspension — Bynum is the type of safety who’d fit exquisitely into the Bills defense. As a former cornerback, he boasts plus ball skills, and maybe most importantly given Gardner-Johnson’s struggles, Bynum is a spectacular tackler. His career missed tackle rate is 8.8% — anything below 10% is darn good for a defensive back. He’s been a staple of durability too. Bynum has three missed games in his NFL career to date, and they all came in his rookie season back in 2021. Financial obligation for Bills to trade for him 2026 salary: $10M If the Bills trade for Bynum after Week 9, they’d be on the hook for $5M in prorated 2026 base salary. He has roster bonuses that would add to $270k if he’s on the field for all nine regular-season contests in 2026. Over the next two seasons, Bynum’s base salaries are $13.4M and $14.4M but are not guaranteed. Re-doing Bynum’s deal if they traded for him would be most likely course of action for Buffalo, swapping large base salaries for future guaranteed money. Projected cost to acquire Using Syndicate32.com’s trade machine , and adding the “fire sale” stipulation to the assessment, the projected cost to trade for Bynm, is an early Round 3 pick in 2027. That feels about little high, especially considering the Colts are clearly looking to reset their roster. He’s a stable, high-volume safety but can be susceptible in coverage at times. Should the Bills trade for Cam Bynum? It feels like Bynum lands right in the sweet spot for what the Bills need and would be willing to spend draft-pick wise to acquire a defender at the deadline. He’s not a superstar by any stretch. Bynum would represent a respectable floor at free safety along with some semblance of upside. Overall, the Bills would know precisely what they’d be getting from him on a game-to-game basis, which is kinda-sorta the opposite of the Gardner-Johnson experience thus far. I don’t think I’d send a Round 3 pick for Bynum, though. If Indianapolis would be willing to part with him for one of Buffalo’s fourth-round selections, this is a trade I believe the Bills should very much consider.

title: Are Buffalo Bills fans’ expectations out of sync with 5-1 record?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bills fans and fans across the country. The bye week was fruitful for the Buffalo Bills. Losses by three key AFC foes in the New England Patriots, Baltimore Ravens, and Kansas City Chiefs […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NV - OCTOBER 18: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills warms up before kickoff against the Las Vegas Raiders during an NFL football game at Allegiant Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bills fans and fans across the country. The bye week was fruitful for the Buffalo Bills. Losses by three key AFC foes in the New England Patriots, Baltimore Ravens, and Kansas City Chiefs now set Buffalo up with a real opportunity to earn the one seed at season’s end. They just have to keep winning. The last time we saw the Bills in action, they pulled off a 33-30 road win over the Las Vegas Raiders. Saying “pulled off” against the .500 Raiders team may seem uncomfortable, but that’s what transpired in their 33-30 victory in Week 6. A game that many felt Buffalo should have had well in hand came down to the wire, thanks in part to a mostly ineffective defense that once again struggled to stop an opponent’s passing attack. It’s become a broken record, this continued discussion about what ails the Bills’ defense. In truth, it’s almost everything related to playing defense. Even the once-potent pass rush has cooled to a mild simmer more reminiscent of airport wings than your favorite Buffalo hang. Much of that is due to the way teams are playing the defense. Okay, yes, all is not doom and gloom for a 5-1 team that currently shares the lead in the AFC. It’s a long season and with that comes the potential for Buffalo’s defense to put it all together and make something big out of their first year under defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. Until and unless that happens, success is likely to hinge on the offense being able to score on nearly every drive. Take a step back for a minute though, and ask yourself if you thought the Bills would be 5-1 under rookie head coach Joe Brady? Maybe it’s an easy “yes” simply due to quarterback Josh Allen. Before deciding if that’s the case, consider the rash of injuries on offense, and some turnover-heavy performances. Then take a minute and reflect on the type of player Greg Rousseau has become, and what’s becoming true of defensive tackle Deone Walker. There are encouraging signs and plenty of tape to prove this team has enough to hang with the big boys. Remember, Josh Allen is one of the game’s most incredible players. So many fans believe that One Bills Drive should be doing more to pull off an impactful trade. Too much of that discourse fails to realize Buffalo’s current cap situations, which affords them around $4 million in available money. Even if they could finalize a trade for your favorite player, how are they fitting any impactful starter’s current salary on the books? With that said, how are you feeling about the team? After some time to think things over through the bye week, are you confident in the Bills currently under the direction of Joe Brady and president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane? title: Buffalo Bills trade deadline expectations should be dampened by salary cap space
summary: The Buffalo Bills don’t have very much salary cap space and don’t have very many good ways to create salary cap space right now, so you should probably reset your expectations for the NFL Trade Deadline on November 19th. There. Now that that is out of the way, we can get into the whys and […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills don’t have very much salary cap space and don’t have very many good ways to create salary cap space right now, so you should probably reset your expectations for the NFL Trade Deadline on November 19th. There. Now that that is out of the way, we can get into the whys and hows of it all, but I needed to form that base level of information before we moved on. How much salary cap space do the Bills have for trades? The Buffalo Bills are currently 27th in the NFL with just $4.5 million in cap space, per Spotrac. That isn’t very much for an addition for anyone with a base salary. Base salary is counted on this year’s cap and as such, the Bills would need to fit every dollar under the cap at the moment of the trade. How can the Bills create cap space for a trade deadline move? I see a few options for how the Bills can create what I will call “significant” cap space before the trade deadline. Of those few options, some are improbably and others are not what I would consider good options. Restructure Dion Dawkins’s contract Restructure Josh Palmer’s contract Trade Josh Palmer Outside of those moves, the Bills don’t have a lot of options with financial implications. Trading Max Hairston doesn’t clear up cap space as he’s on a minimum contract in terms of base salary. Restructuring Greg Rousseau gets you somewhere between $1 million and $2 million if you need it. Khalil Shakir restructuring would net maybe a million, as would Dalton Kincaid. I don’t want to restructure Dorian Williams if I don’t see future. I would save these for emergency injury replacements, if I had to. Nearly everyone else is playing for the veteran minimum right now. They’ve already pulled the rest of the levers. Let’s take a closer look at each potential option and why I don’t really like it. The Bills can restructure Dion Dawkins’s contract Taking the rest of Dion Dawkins’ available base salary and prorating it over five years, you can clear $10 to $11 million in cap space. It’s true and available. But then that is all added as dead cap in 2027 and beyond. His dead cap hit in 2027 would go from just under $14 million to close to $25 million. His cap hit on the roster is currently set to be $25 million. You’d get no cap relief from releasing Dawkins in 2027, so you’d be theoretically handcuffed to him. That also leaves you with four medium-to-big money contracts on the offensive line, allocating about 20% of your cap to four players there. If the Bills wanted to do this, they already would have as they have done multiple times in Dion’s career. I wrote about Dawkins more back in August after the O’Cyurs Torrence extension. The Bills can restructure Josh Palmer’s contract If the Bills restructured Palmer’s contract, they could push $5 million or so of cap space into the future. That would put his 2027 dead cap number at just under $10 million. This one makes more sense to me than Dion’s, if I am being honest. You save $600k in cap space and a bunch of money cutting Palmer in 2027 and it’s over and done. I don’t think anyone expects Palmer to make more than $8 million in compensation from Buffalo in 2027, so it’s a clean out. I don’t love having that much dead cap in 2026, but I think it works. The Bills can trade Josh Palmer This option seems to be gaining traction on social media, but I don’t see the upside for the other team. Buffalo could send Palmer and a fourth to another team for a sixth or something, but I doubt Beane wants to do that. Those type of salary dumps tend to happen in other sports, not football. You’d have to find a team that legitimately wants Palmer and his $6 million in base salary for the rest of this year. I don’t see that happening. Who are some budget-friendly players the Bills could trade for at the deadline? One notable player Bills fans have pointed to for a potential trade is Zack Baun, the Eagles linebacker. He only has a base salary of $1.345 million and the Bills would only pay 1/11th of that. It would be a steal for the Bills if the Eagles were willing. Philadelphia has their own problems making this move. They only have $9 million in cap space and Baun’s dead cap charge of $22 million would accelerate immediately. They would have to create a lot of space to make it work and it probably isn’t worth it. The Steelers’ Cole Holcomb could be an interesting add at linebacker instead. He is making league minimum base salary and buried on their depth chart with a lot of starting experience in the NFL. Not a great option, but someone to add to the mix. At safety, Budda Baker ($14 million), Jessie Bates ($13 million), and Derwin James ($11.5 million) are probably outside of the Bills’ salary cap range unless their existing teams eat base salary for more trade compensation. The Colts’ Camryn Bynum ($10 million) and Titans’ Amani Hooker ($8 million) make more sense as options. The list is pretty short. So align your expectations accordingly.
