title: Bills return from bye as Ravens collapse: Where do both teams stand in NFL power rankings?
summary: The Buffalo Bills didn’t play a single snap in Week 7, yet they emerged from their bye week sitting atop several NFL power rankings. Meanwhile, their next opponent, the Baltimore Ravens, is heading in the opposite direction. Apparently, the best way to move up in the NFL power rankings is to take the week off […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills didn’t play a single snap in Week 7, yet they emerged from their bye week sitting atop several NFL power rankings. Meanwhile, their next opponent, the Baltimore Ravens, is heading in the opposite direction. Apparently, the best way to move up in the NFL power rankings is to take the week off and let everyone else lose. At least, that strategy worked pretty well for the Buffalo Bills. While Buffalo enjoyed its Week 7 bye, two previously undefeated teams, the Kansas City Chiefs and San Francisco 49ers, suffered their first losses of the season. The result? The Bills climbed to No. 1 in several national power rankings without ever stepping onto the field. Buffalo enters Week 8 at 5-1, with its offense among the NFL’s best and a defense that continues to raise questions. Meanwhile, Sunday’s opponent, the Baltimore Ravens, has problems of its own. Baltimore enters the matchup at 4-3 after surrendering 35 unanswered second-half points in an embarrassing 35-13 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. So, are the Bills legitimate Super Bowl contenders, or simply the beneficiaries of everyone else’s struggles? And perhaps more importantly, are the Ravens still the dangerous AFC opponent we’ve grown accustomed to seeing? Let’s see what the national experts think. Buffalo Bills Week 8 Power Rankings The Bills are moving up across the board, with four of the eight outlets placing Buffalo at No. 1. Three placing the Bills at No. 2, and USA Today continuing the disrespect ranking them at No. 9. But the rankings come with a warning. The Bills’ offense has been outstanding, averaging 32.8 points per game while leading the league in yards per play, points per drive, and scoring drive percentage. Josh Allen and James Cook have provided one of the NFL’s most productive offensive combinations. Unfortunately, the defense hasn’t enjoyed the same success. The Athletic highlighted Buffalo’s struggles defending the pass, noting that the Bills rank among the league’s worst teams in expected points added per opponent dropback. Buffalo has surrendered more than 250 passing yards in five of its first six games. That’s not exactly the defensive résumé you’d expect from the NFL’s top-ranked team. The bye week gave defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard an opportunity to evaluate what hasn’t been working.Now comes the difficult part: fixing it. And with Lamar Jackson returning to Baltimore’s lineup, the timing couldn’t be more important. Baltimore Ravens: From AFC Contender to Question Mark? Remember when the Ravens were considered one of the AFC’s biggest threats? That feels like a long time ago. Baltimore entered the season with championship expectations, but consecutive losses have exposed problems that extend well beyond the absence of Lamar Jackson. The Ravens’ Week 7 loss to Cincinnati was particularly concerning. Baltimore carried a 13-0 lead into halftime before being completely dismantled over the final two quarters. The Bengals scored 35 unanswered points, and for the second consecutive game, the Ravens failed to score in the second half. And suddenly, a team that appeared capable of competing with anyone is struggling to finish games. The difference between Buffalo and Baltimore is striking. Buffalo’s average ranking is 2.38. Baltimore’s is 15.50. That’s a separation of over 13 positions between two teams that entered the season with significant expectations. The Ravens haven’t suddenly forgotten how to play football, but their inability to protect leads has become impossible to ignore.. The Lamar Jackson Factor: Can One Player Fix Baltimore? There’s no denying that Baltimore is a different football team with Lamar Jackson under center. Jackson has missed three consecutive games with a high ankle sprain, and the Ravens have gone 1-2 during his absence. His potential return against Buffalo would provide an immediate boost to Baltimore’s offense. But would it solve everything? Jackson wasn’t responsible for Baltimore surrendering 35 second-half points against Cincinnati. He wasn’t responsible for the defense’s inability to stop Joe Burrow and the Bengals. And he certainly can’t be expected to solve every problem on both sides of the football. The Ravens have now blown double-digit leads in all three of their losses this season. But let’s not be naive here. The Ravens’ No. 15 ranking reflects their recent struggles, but it doesn’t necessarily reflect the team Buffalo will face Sunday. A motivated Baltimore team with Lamar Jackson back under center is a completely different challenge. Bills vs. Ravens: Trending Up and Trending Down Buffalo Bills (5-1) TRENDING UP: Offensive dominance Buffalo’s offense continues to rank among the NFL’s best. Allen and Cook have provided the production needed to overcome defensive struggles, and the Bills enter Week 8 rested and sitting atop the national consensus rankings. TRENDING DOWN: Defensive consistency The Bills have allowed at least 30 points in four of their five victories. Jim Leonhard’s defense needs to show improvement, particularly against the pass, if Buffalo expects to remain among the league’s elite. Baltimore Ravens (4-3) TRENDING UP: Lamar Jackson’s return Getting Jackson back will immediately change the outlook for Baltimore’s offense. His ability to extend plays and create opportunities with his legs could present serious problems for Buffalo’s struggling defense. TRENDING DOWN: Second-half collapses The Ravens have failed to score after halftime in consecutive games. Their inability to maintain leads has become one of the team’s biggest weaknesses, and their defense has struggled to make adjustments when opponents gain momentum. Looking Ahead: Bills vs. Ravens Sunday’s matchup presents an interesting one. The Bills have one of the NFL’s most explosive offenses, but a defense that has struggled to consistently stop opponents. The Ravens have a potentially dangerous offense, depending on Jackson’s performance and health, but a defense that just surrendered 35 unanswered points. For Buffalo, the biggest question is whether the bye week allowed Joe Brady and Jim Leonhard to address the team’s weaknesses. For Baltimore, the question is whether Jackson’s return can provide enough of a spark to overcome the team’s growing list of problems. The Ravens may be ranked 15th, but nobody should mistake them for the NFL’s 15th-best team when Lamar Jackson is healthy and Buffalo might have climbed to No. 1 in most rankings without playing last week, but they are about to face their toughest opponent yet.. Now it’s time to prove the ranking belongs to them.
author: Sara Larson

title: Exploring Baltimore Ravens tendencies ahead of Week 8’s game against Buffalo Bills
summary: The Ravens are 4-3 entering Week 8’s game in the new Highmark Stadium against the Buffalo Bills after consecutive losses in the AFC North to the Browns and Bengals. Let’s dive into Baltimore’s tendencies before this clash of former MVPs on Sunday. Ravens offense First half vs. second half The Ravens own the league’s largest […]
full_text: The Ravens are 4-3 entering Week 8’s game in the new Highmark Stadium against the Buffalo Bills after consecutive losses in the AFC North to the Browns and Bengals. Let’s dive into Baltimore’s tendencies before this clash of former MVPs on Sunday. Ravens offense First half vs. second half The Ravens own the league’s largest disparity between first half and second half efficiency to date this season. In the first two quarters, Baltimore’s EPA per play on offense is third in the NFL (behind the 49ers and Bills). They’ve scored the most first-half points (118) and have the best point differential in the first half (+65), per Warren Sharp . In the second half, the script flips completely. Their EPA per play is 29th in football. They’ve scored the the second-fewest second-half points in the league and have the worst point differential after halftime at -70. this drop off is incredible and is why Declan Doyle needs to script plays for the second half imo and stop playing the scoreboard – it's killing Baltimore #30 in RB rushing EPA in the second half of games they cannot run the ball to hold onto leads to save their life https://t.co/fBUwFjE1uF pic.twitter.com/WToUnsnY8a — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) October 27, 2026 This is a trend to keep in mind, one that will be fascinating to monitor throughout this game. They’ve also struggled mightily on third downs inside their opponents’ 35 yard line to date despite massive success on third downs outside their opponents’ 35 yard line. Another TE-heavy offense Much like their last two contests against the Rams and Raiders, the Bills defense will see plenty of multi tight end looks against the Ravens in Week 8. (Clearly this has become a league-wide trend). Baltimore enters this contest seventh in 12 personnel usage, at 32%. The Ravens are also fifth in 13 personnel utilization at 14%. Mark Andrews remains the No. 1 tight end. Matthew Hibner and Durham Smythe have played 167 and 126 snaps respectively this season. Even Josh Cuevas as been on the field for 102 snaps. Lamar Jackson got out to incredible start before injury In the first four games of the season, the Ravens quarterback completed 70.8% of his passes at a sizable 10.1 yards-per-attempt clip, with six touchdowns and one interception, and he rushed 19 times for 144 yards with a score on the ground too. At the time, his 80.9% adjusted completion rate was the fifth-highest in the NFL among qualifiers. It appears Jackson will return this Sunday after missing the past three games, and we won’t know how close to 100% he is. However, the Bills should expect him to be fully operational when he’s on the field. And he was humming before the ankle injury. Ravens defense Baltimore lives in sub-packages Only the Browns (91.2%), and Seahawks (83.9%) have played a higher percentage of their defensive snaps in a sub-package than the Ravens (80.6%). And it’s sensible because beyond superstar Kyle Hamilton and former first-rounder Malaki Starks, the Ravens signed Jaylinn Hawkins in free agency. It’s mostly been Roquan Smith and Trenton Simpson, and the latter has really come on in his fourth season, at linebacker for the Ravens in the first half of the 2026 campaign. Trey Hendrickson’s unique production Hendrickson was the big-ticket item the Ravens signed this offseason, snagging him from the division-rival Bengals after the Maxx Crosby fiasco unfolded. He’s currently seventh in the NFL among qualifying edge rushers in pressure rate, at 16.9% (one spot below Greg Rousseau). Despite that, Hendrickson is 18th in pass-rush win rate %, which is the times at which charting suggests he “won” the rep, regardless of a pressure was ultimately registered on the play. The 31-year-old rusher still brings it around the corner, and mostly aligns on the right side of the Ravens front, so we’ll get plenty of Hendrickson vs. Dion Dawkins in this contest.

title: Bills vs. Ravens history: Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, and Derrick Henry
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Baltimore Ravens have a history that stretches back three decades, with plenty of memorable games along the way. From regular-season battles to playoff matchups with a trip to the AFC Championship on the line, these two teams have given fans plenty to talk about over the years.  But as the Bills […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills and Baltimore Ravens have a history that stretches back three decades, with plenty of memorable games along the way. From regular-season battles to playoff matchups with a trip to the AFC Championship on the line, these two teams have given fans plenty to talk about over the years. But as the Bills prepare to host the Ravens on Sunday, we’re taking a slightly different approach to this week’s Time Capsule. While there’s plenty of history between the two franchises, much of their recent history has been written by three players: Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, and Derrick Henry. Allen and Jackson have gone head-to-head since 2018, while Henry was giving Buffalo’s defense headaches long before he traded his Tennessee Titans uniform for Baltimore’s purple and black. So, rather than looking back at the teams as a whole, we’re going to revisit these matchups through the eyes — or arms and legs, as the case may be — of the players who’ve helped shape them. We’ll look at how Allen and the Bills’ offense has fared against Baltimore’s defense, what Jackson has done against Buffalo, and just how much damage Henry has caused over the years. _____________________________________________________________________________ Josh Allen & the Bills’ offense vs. Ravens’ defense Baltimore’s defense hasn’t always been kind to Josh Allen. Some of his toughest games have come against the Ravens, dating back to his rookie season. However, the Bills have also found ways to beat Baltimore even when the offense wasn’t putting up big numbers. Allen’s first taste of the Ravens’ defense came in the 2018 season opener when he replaced Nathan Peterman in a game Buffalo lost 47-3. Allen completed just six of 15 passes for 74 yards and he was sacked three times. Things weren’t much easier the following season when he made his first start against Baltimore. The Ravens sacked him six times, held him to 146 passing yards, and limited Buffalo to 17 points. The Bills finally got the better of Baltimore in the 2020 playoffs, winning 17-3, although the offense didn’t exactly light up the scoreboard. Allen threw for 206 yards and a touchdown, while Buffalo’s defense did much of the heavy lifting. Two years later, Allen helped the Bills climb out of a 20-3 hole in Baltimore. He threw for 213 yards and a touchdown, added 70 yards and another score on the ground, and Buffalo came away with a 23-20 win. It was the first time Allen had rushed for more than 25 yards against the Ravens, and his ability to make plays with his legs helped turn the game around. Baltimore got the upper hand during the 2024 regular season, holding Allen to 180 passing yards and no touchdowns in a 35-10 loss. But when the teams met again in the playoffs, Buffalo found a different way to win. Allen threw for just 127 yards, his lowest total in a start against Baltimore, but scored twice on the ground as the Bills won 27-25 to advance to the AFC Championship Game. Then came the 2025 season opener, and everything Buffalo had struggled to do against Baltimore’s defense seemed to change. Allen threw for 394 yards and two touchdowns, nearly doubling his previous high of 213 passing yards against the Ravens. He also added two rushing touchdowns, giving him four total scores in a game where Buffalo trailed by 15 points late in the fourth quarter. The Bills scored 16 unanswered points over the final four minutes to pull out a 41-40 win. Across seven meetings, including the playoffs, Allen has thrown for 1,340 yards, five touchdowns, and just one interception. He’s also rushed for 179 yards and five touchdowns, with four of those rushing scores coming in his last two appearances against Baltimore. For years, the Ravens managed to keep Allen from doing much damage through the air. His first six appearances against Baltimore produced just 946 passing yards combined, an average of fewer than 158 per game. Then he threw for 394 in one night. The numbers show how much this matchup has changed. Baltimore has made Allen work for just about everything over the years, but the Ravens have also learned that keeping him quiet early doesn’t necessarily mean he’ll stay that way. Josh Allen vs. Baltimore Ravens – Career (including playoffs) Season Result Pass Yds Pass TD INT Rush Yds Rush TD 2018 L 3-47 74 0 0 26 0 2019 L 17-24 146 1 0 9 0 2020 Playoffs W 17-3 206 1 0 3 0 2022 W 23-20 213 1 1 70 1 2024 L 10-35 180 0 0 21 0 2024 Playoffs W 27-25 127 0 0 20 2 2025 W 41-40 394 2 0 30 2 TOTAL 4-3 1340 5 1 179 5 _____________________________________________________________________________ Lamar Jackson vs. Bills’ defense While Baltimore’s defense has given Josh Allen plenty of headaches over the years, the Bills have returned the favor against Lamar Jackson. Buffalo has managed to keep Jackson’s passing numbers relatively low in most of their meetings, although stopping him from putting points on the board has been another story. Like Allen, Jackson got his first taste of this matchup as a rookie in 2018. He entered the Ravens’ 47-3 win in relief of Joe Flacco, throwing for just 24 yards. When he returned to Buffalo as Baltimore’s starter in 2019, he threw for only 145 yards but made the most of them, connecting on three touchdown passes in a 24-17 Ravens win. The Bills had considerably more success against Jackson when the teams met in the 2020 playoffs. Buffalo held him to 162 passing yards and no touchdowns, sacked him three times, and intercepted him once. That interception turned into one of the most memorable plays in Bills playoff history when nickel cornerback Taron Johnson returned it 101 yards for a touchdown. Jackson left the game with a concussion, and Buffalo went on to win 17-3. Two years later, the Bills again found ways to frustrate Jackson. He threw for 144 yards and a touchdown but was intercepted twice, including a fourth-quarter pick by safety Jordan Poyer in the end zone. Buffalo shut Baltimore out in the second half, erasing a 20-3 deficit to win 23-20. Jackson did manage 73 rushing yards, his highest total against the Bills to that point, but the turnovers proved costly. Baltimore turned things around in the 2024 regular season. Jackson completed 13 of 18 passes for 156 yards and two touchdowns, then added 54 rushing yards and another score in a 35-10 win. It was the first time he had scored three total touchdowns against Buffalo since 2019, and the Bills struggled to contain him after the Ravens had paired him with Derrick Henry. But the playoffs were a different story. When Jackson returned to Buffalo for the divisional round following the 2024 season, he put up his best passing numbers against the Bills to that point, throwing for 254 yards and two touchdowns. However, Buffalo forced him into two turnovers, including an interception by safety Taylor Rapp and a fumble recovered by edge rusher Von Miller. The Ravens lost another fumble later in the game, and the Bills held on for a 27-25 win. Jackson’s most recent appearance against Buffalo came in the 2025 season opener, and this time the Bills had little success slowing him down. He completed 14 of 19 passes for 209 yards and two touchdowns while adding 70 yards and another score on the ground. Jackson’s 144.4 passer rating was his highest against Buffalo, and Baltimore built a 15-point lead late in the fourth quarter. Of course, Bills fans know how that one ended. As we discussed above regarding Allen, Buffalo scored 16 unanswered points in the final four minutes to win 41-40, handing Jackson a loss despite one of his best-ever performances against the Bills. Across seven meetings, including the playoffs, Jackson has thrown for 1,094 yards, 10 touchdowns, and five interceptions. He’s been sacked 12 times, and Buffalo has held him below 165 passing yards in five of those seven games. The numbers tell an interesting story. title: Panthers vs Packers: Storylines to watch for Thursday Night football
summary: Hello CSR! Happy game week! I like many of you am reeling from a horrific showing by the Panthers against the Buccaneers on Sunday. BUT! None of that matters now, as we’re on to Green Bay and another prime time tilt for this Panthers squad. They sit at 3-3 and still very much control their […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - NOVEMBER 02: Carolina Panthers linebacker Trevin Wallace (32) hits Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) during a game between the Green Bay Packers and the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on November 2, 2025 in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Hello CSR! Happy game week! I like many of you am reeling from a horrific showing by the Panthers against the Buccaneers on Sunday. BUT! None of that matters now, as we’re on to Green Bay and another prime time tilt for this Panthers squad. They sit at 3-3 and still very much control their own destiny for the 2026 season, though the injury bug continues to haunt them. They’ll be missing several key pieces as they make the trip across the country for this game. Let’s dive right in. Defense: The stoppable force vs the movable object I don’t need to rehash it in too much detail, but the Panthers again found themselves getting run over on Sunday by the Buccaneers ground attack. What appeared to be an aberration of a week 1 destruction on the ground now could be closer to reality, as the Bucs also ran for 300 yards against an admittedly short handed defense. Luckily for the Panthers, they’ll be facing a Packers rushing attack that’s 32nd in every category but touchdowns per game in 2026 . Of course, the Packers were missing their start running back Josh Jacobs most of that span, and he’ll be back for his second game of the season this week. He wasn’t a very effective rusher last week as he shakes off the rust, but this is definitely a game where the Panthers rush defense can shake off a horrible loss and bounce back. They do have a bevy of weapons in the passing game, but making them one dimensional should help a bit. Offense: Get back on schedule The Panthers offense had an uncharacteristically chaotic game on Sunday, as they turned the ball over on two interceptions and a sack-fumble for a touchdown. Of course, the special teams didn’t help things either, but this was very much a game where the continuous pressure on Bryce Young finally had negative ripple effects for the offense. Bryce Young is having a good year, but when offensive linemen are getting beaten clean in key passing downs consistently, there’s only so much he can do. And that’s where I get to the theme of staying on schedule, and that’s going to start with Chuba Hubbard. Hubbard, to his credit, averaged 4.7 yards per carry on Sunday and caught 4 passes to keep the drives going. But, with the game script finding the Panthers quickly in the hole on the scoreboard, he only ran the ball 7 times. The Packers rush defense is basically in the middle statistically, while their passing defense is top 10 in yards per pass and yards per game. This is very much going to be a game where a balanced attack is going to matter. Bonus storyline: The special teams cannot be a problem again The Panthers biggest issues in some of their losses this year has been giving the ball away on routine punt and kick returns. They simply cannot do that against a Packers team that can easily score a play or two later through the air if the momentum shifts on a bad turnover like that. I know they’ve been cycling punt returners all season to try and right the ship, but this needs to be fixed now. I don’t care if the punt returner fair catches it every single time, the turnovers really have hurt this team when its trying to get cooking. And I would expect this Packers team to be looking for revenge after that ugly loss last season against the Panthers. What are you watching for in this game, Panthers fans?

title: Panthers vs Packers: Matchups to watch
summary: The Carolina Panthers are coming off one of their worst performances in recent memory, and that’s saying a lot for a team that has been rebuilding for the better part of the last decade. Carolina got embarrassed 43-13 at home against division rivals the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in a Baker Mayfield revenge game. It was […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 4: Will Lee III #24 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after defeating the Detroit Lions following an NFL football game on October 4, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers are coming off one of their worst performances in recent memory, and that’s saying a lot for a team that has been rebuilding for the better part of the last decade. Carolina got embarrassed 43-13 at home against division rivals the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in a Baker Mayfield revenge game. It was an awful outing that dropped the Panthers to 3-3 on the season and halted the team’s momentum-building two-game win streak. And now here come the 4-3 Green Bay Packers in a primetime Thursday Night Football showdown. The Packers had their own three-game winning streak snapped last week in a 20-17 defeat at the hands of the Detroit Lions on a last-second field goal. While there is still a lot of football to play this season, a win for the Panthers in this one to get to 4-3 would be a massive boost and cleanse the team’s collective palate of the bitter aftertaste lingering from the Tampa Bay debacle. Whether or not Dave Canales’s squad will come away with a much-needed victory will depend heavily on these four matchups: Carolina’s run defense vs Josh Jacobs The Packers come into this game as the least productive rushing team in the NFL. Green Bay averages just 59.9 rushing yards per game , which is last in the league by a country mile. The next worst rushing attack is the Las Vegas Raiders at 74.7 yards per outing, so on paper it looks like the Panthers should be able to bottle up the run. However (and you knew there was a “but” coming here), the Packers played their first six games without star running back Josh Jacobs due to suspension. Jacobs returned last week and had 11 carries for just 36 yards, but that could be viewed as a tune-up for Green Bay’s featured back. Jacobs, a three-time Pro Bowler, has averaged 74.0 rushing yards per game over his seven-year career, and the Panthers run defense will need to hold him well below that average to keep Green Bay’s offense one dimensional. The Panthers offensive line against the Packers defensive line According to the metrics, the Panthers offensive line is struggling this year. According to those same metrics, the Packers defensive line is struggling even more. ESPN produces a stat called “win rate” to measure how often offensive lines “win” in both run blocking and pass blocking. On the flip side, it also measures how often defenses “win” against both run and pass blocking. Coming into Thursday night the Panthers offensive line ranks 31st in run blocking and 25th in pass blocking. As subpar as those results may appear for the Panthers offensive line, they’re somewhat on par with Packers defense’s rankings of 28th in run stop win rate and 26th in pass blocking. Neither team has been particularly good across the line of scrimmage, so whoever wins in the trenches could go on to win this game. Jordan Love vs the Panthers banged-up secondary Packers quarterback Jordan Love is having perhaps his worst starting season in Green Bay. Now in his fourth year as a full-time starter, Love is mired in career lows in completion percentage (59.8%), passer rating (90.3), and quarterback rating (59.8). While he’s widely regarded as a good quarterback who can lead a good team to the postseason most years, Love has yet to be selected for a Pro Bowl. But Jordan Love is probably licking his chops looking at the Panthers cornerback room that’s being held together by band-aids and duct tape. The Panthers Week 1 starting duo of Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson is arguably the best cornerback duo in the league, when healthy. Both Horn and Jackson have been injured most of the season. In their absences, Carolina has been starting fourth-round rookie Will Lee and veteran Akayleb Evans. While this is Evans’s fifth year in the league, he had largely been relegated to special teams duty in the previous two seasons before being thrust into a starting role this year. While Jordan Love isn’t the second coming of Tom Brady, he’s a good quarterback who at times can be great. The Panthers are going to need their two fill-in corners to step up. Dr. Jekyll vs Mr. Hyde If you can figure out the 2026 Carolina Panthers, you are far wiser than I am. Dave Canales’s team definitely has a Doctor Jekyll and Mister Hyde vibe this year. Carolina’s defense can surrender 59 points in Week 1 against the Chicago Bears, then in Week 2 clamp down against the Atlanta Falcons and yield just three points. The Panthers can lose a headscratcher to the Cleveland Browns in Week 3, then pull off impressive back-to-back wins in the two following weeks against the Philadelphia Eagles and Detroit Lions. And just as soon as the Panthers look like they have things figured out and are ready to stake their claim as the best team in the NFC South, they can find themselves losing 33-6 at halftime at home against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers like they did last week. The 2026 Carolina Panthers suffer from multiple personalities. We’ll see if we get Dr. Jekyll or Mr. Hyde on Thursday night.

title: Chicago Bears NFL Trade Deadline Targets
summary: The rumor mill ahead of the November 10 trade deadline has been churning for weeks, and the Chicago Bears have been front and center for much of it. Yesterday, the Indianapolis Colts made the biggest trade splashes so far, sending guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: Jermaine Johnson II #11 of the Tennessee Titans rushes the passer during an NFL football game against the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The rumor mill ahead of the November 10 trade deadline has been churning for weeks, and the Chicago Bears have been front and center for much of it. Yesterday, the Indianapolis Colts made the biggest trade splashes so far, sending guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers, and reports were that the Bears checked on both players. While interest in Nelson was likely due diligence, their interest in Buckner was more serious because of their need on the defensive line. In ESPN’s latest trade deadline article from Jeremy Fowler (Insider) and Matt Bowen (Xs&Os), they speculate on several players who could be moved along with the best scheme fits. Here are who they see as logical for the Bears. No player has more buzz to the Bears than Khalil Mack, but the winless Los Angeles Chargers seem content to stand pat. Fowler writes, “Returning to the Bears is a natural fit for the equivalent of a quality Day 3 pick.” The Arizona Cardinals’ Josh Sweat (6’5″, 265) would give the Bears bookend Sweats up front. The 29-year-old had 12 sacks a season ago and 2 so far this season. The Bears have been rumored to be in on defensive end Jermaine Johnson II (6’5″, 254) before, and with the Tennessee Titans in rebuild mode, they may be willing to move the 27-year-old. The Titan who may make the most sense is cornerback Alontae Taylor, who has history with Chicago defensive coordinator Dennis Allen from their time in New Orleans. Taylor hasn’t fit in with the Tennessee defense and has been a healthy scratch the last two games. His contract would require some work to fit in, but “He plays a premium position, and he has the speed to cover receivers on the perimeter or play a disruptive role in the slot,” Bowen writes. The article also lists other corners and d-linemen potentially on the trade block, which could lead to a very active deadline. Looking around the league, several other teams could be sellers with defensive players the Bears could covet, including the Philadelphia Eagles, Washington Commanders, New Orleans Saints, Miami Dolphins, and New York Jets. The Jets have a former Bear Pro Bowler who has yet to play a snap on defense for them, and could be had for a late pick or a pick swap. Cornerback Nahshon Wright seemingly wants to return to Chicago (just look at his Twitter profile pic), and while he was boom-or-bust in coverage in 2025, he’d fill a need for a secondary that’s dealt with injuries all season. From ESPN’s Rich Cimini , who covers the Jets. Nahshon Wright tells ESPN that he’s “definitely frustrated” by having no role on defense. Asked if he has requested a trade, he said, “Not formally…(But) I’ve expressed my feelings (to the team) Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer believes the Bears are in the defensive tackle market, and he mentions Washington’s Daron Payne and Indianapolis’ Grover Stewart as possibilities. He also drops Mack’s name as a fit in Chicago. Bears head coach Ben Johnson was asked today how involved he is with general manager Ryan Poles and their trade talks as the deadline looms. “Well, yeah, there’s a lot going on,” Johnson said. “It’s certainly Ryan’s domain, and yet we have constant dialogue of what this team needs and where we can impact ourselves not just this year but, you know, years in the future as well. So he’s turning over every stone that he possibly can to improve this football team, just like he has ever since I’ve gotten in this building, and I feel really good about our process, and we’ll see what happens. Never know.” Do you expect any trade deadline additions?

title: Reviewing the Bears’ PFN grades from Week 7 vs. Patriots
summary: The Bears picked up a crucial victory over the Patriots on Thursday night, improving their record to 5-2 in the process. The rest of the football week can feel like it drags on after your team plays on a Thursday, but in the case of Chicago, there has still been plenty of buzz after defeating […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a touchdown against the New England Patriots during the third quarter of the game at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Bears picked up a crucial victory over the Patriots on Thursday night, improving their record to 5-2 in the process. The rest of the football week can feel like it drags on after your team plays on a Thursday, but in the case of Chicago, there has still been plenty of buzz after defeating the reigning AFC champions on primetime television. Each week, I’ll review how Chicago’s eligible performers graded by Pro Football Network’s Impact Scoring model. Now that the rest of the NFL has caught up, and the numbers have all been crunched, here’s how Week 7 looked. Offense Caleb Williams: 81.6 (8th of 26 QBs) D’Andre Swift: 75.5 (22nd of 42 RBs) Luther Burden III: 84.8 (5th of 54 WRs) Rome Odunze: 76.3 (20th of 54 WRs) Colston Loveland: 80.4 (3rd of 32 TEs) Cole Kmet: 75.5 (15th of 32 TEs) Theo Benedet: 76.1 (22nd of 52 OTs) Joe Thuney: 80.0 (7th of 44 OGs) Garrett Bradbury: 77.1 (17th of 51 Cs) Jonah Jackson: 74.0 (26th of 44 OGs) Darnell Wright: 83.2 (6th of 52 OTs) Among NFL starting quarterbacks in Week 7, Caleb Williams tied for second with 308 passing yards and ranked fifth with 0.40 EPA per dropback and seventh with +6.7 CPOE. His efficiency on Thursday was impressive, especially when targeting Luther Burden III. Burden’s 3.19 EPA per target led all wide receivers, and his perfect 100.0 efficiency grade also led the league. Along the offensive line, Darnell Wright was particularly elite, finishing third among offensive tackles with an 85.7 run-blocking grade and fourth with an 81.2 pass-blocking grade. Defense Daniel Hardy: 68.8 (30th of 88 EDGEs) Jamree Kromah: 64.0 (41st of 88 EDGEs) Austin Booker: 55.8 (70th of 88 EDGEs) Shemar Turner: 52.4 (81st of 88 EDGEs) Grady Jarrett: 72.0 (33rd of 91 DTs) Neville Gallimore: 58.2 (72nd of 91 DTs) Kentavius Street: 53.9 (94th of 95 DTs) D’Marco Jackson: 84.8 (12th of 75 LBs) Devin Bush: 66.6 (74th of 75 LBs) Malik Muhammad: 78.7 (25th of 89 CBs) Kyler Gordon: 75.7 (42nd of 89 CBs) Tyrique Stevenson: 73.0 (54th of 89 CBs) Jaylon Johnson: 70.7 (62nd of 89 CBs) Dillon Thieneman: 74.1 (48th of 78 SAFs) Cam Lewis: 63.5 (77th of 78 SAFs) As one could likely anticipate by Drake Maye’s stat line on Thursday, the Bears’ defense didn’t grade incredibly well in Week 7. D’Marco Jackson was the highest-grading defender of the bunch, having tallied six tackles and an interception and allowing a 52.8 passer rating when targeted in coverage. Malik Muhammad was the only other Bears starter who performed at an above-average starting level; both Tyrique Stevenson and Jaylon Johnson allowed passer ratings above 100.0 on Thursday, while Cam Lewis allowed a perfect 158.3 passer rating when targeted in coverage. Special teams (for the sickos) Cairo Santos: 77.4 (10th of 22 Ks) Tory Taylor: 78.6 (12th of 29 Ps) Even though he missed a field goal earlier in the game, Cairo Santos comes into the top ten after nailing a 58-yard field goal to give the Bears a two-score lead in the fourth quarter. On the punting end, Tory Taylor ranked eighth among 29 punters with a net punting average of 44.0 against the Patriots.

title: Bears vs Seahawks: Who can help limit Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba?
summary: The gauntlet of the Chicago Bears’ 2026 schedule rolls on, as they are facing a 2025 Super Bowl participant for the second week in a row, this time squaring off with the champs — the Seattle Seahawks. It’s no secret what the Seahawks win with — their defense is top five in almost any metric, […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 25: Jaxon Smith-Njigba #11 of the Seattle Seahawks scores a touchdown against Mansoor Delane #5 of the Kansas City Chiefs during the second quarter at Lumen Field on October 25, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The gauntlet of the Chicago Bears’ 2026 schedule rolls on, as they are facing a 2025 Super Bowl participant for the second week in a row, this time squaring off with the champs — the Seattle Seahawks. It’s no secret what the Seahawks win with — their defense is top five in almost any metric, with their total yards given up of 233 per game leading the NFL. The Bears will need to be methodical to score points on them. Meanwhile, their offense is far more pedestrian, sitting somewhere around league average in most categories like total scoring, total yards, passing yards, etc. But that doesn’t tell the full story of their offense. After losing a major contributor in Kenneth Walker to the Kansas City Chiefs, the Seahawks were staring down a talent drain on offense. Nobody told Jaxon Smith-Njigba. JSN, the shifty slot receiver for Seattle, is leading the league in reception yardage by more than 200 yards at 867 yards — with Ceedee Lamb in a distant 2nd with 651 yards. That gives JSN an incredible 124 yards per game, and a pace for over 2,100 yards on the season (a mark that has never been hit). To this point, the Bears’ defense has overperformed. But that’s not to say that they have been great — especially when it comes to shutting down a passing attack. Currently ranked at 18th in the league, the Bears average 226 yards passing against their defense per game. Even worse, their top corner coming into the season — Jaylon Johnson — looks like a shell of himself. Once known for locking up half the field, he’s now more likely to get beaten downfield while giving up chunk plays. So for this week, I am not expecting Johnson, Malik Muhammad, Tyrique Stevenson, or Kyler Gordon to lock up JSN. I think he will get his. I think the key to victory is to limit the damage. This brings me to Bears’ rookie Dillon Thieneman. Throughout his rookie campaign, Thieneman has been excellent, particularly in cleaning up plays on the back end. It’s felt like every game there are at least three occurrences where Dillon darts in for an open-field tackle to limit an 8-yard gain from turning into a house call. Dillon Thieneman with one of the CRAZIEST sequences of plays you’ll see from a rookie. Hawks down Saquon Barkley, stuffs Saquon at the GL, and then picks off Andy Dalton. The Bears found their FRANCHISE SAFETY in the 25th overall pick 😳🔥 pic.twitter.com/8CFR0CTyzP — Rookie Watch (@RookieWatxh) September 29, 2026 In the first 7 games, JSN has catches of 82, 45, 38, and 33 yards. A stat indicative of his explosive potential. His ability in the slot means that he will frequently be looking to take a crossing route for more than the initial depth of the catch. If the Bears are going to win on Monday, that is going to require Thieneman to support his CB room and limit these big gains.

title: Bears v. Patriots Upon Further Review – A Closer Look at the Referees
summary: Hello Chicago Bears fans! Thursday Night Football at Soldier Field and downtown Chicago was rockin’ and rollin’. Caleb Williams threw for 308 and two scores, D’Andre Swift found the end zone, and Cairo Santos hit a career-long 58-yarder to seal it. Chicago improved to 5-2. But about those yellow pieces of fabric? Let’s go to […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Cairo Santos #8 of the Chicago Bears reacts after missing a 53 yard field goal against the New England Patriots during the fourth quarter of the game at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello Chicago Bears fans! Thursday Night Football at Soldier Field and downtown Chicago was rockin’ and rollin’. Caleb Williams threw for 308 and two scores, D’Andre Swift found the end zone, and Cairo Santos hit a career-long 58-yarder to seal it. Chicago improved to 5-2. But about those yellow pieces of fabric? Let’s go to the tale-of-the-cloth. Official totals: Chicago 9–69, New England 10–71. The calls were fairly balanced on the surface. The tape told a bit of a different story. One illegal forward handoff, one declined OPI that should not have been thrown, one late roughing the passer that extended a scoring drive, and a late intentional offside that Vrabel admitted was coached. Upon Further Review — Grading System The series reviews every accepted flag and every meaningful no-call in a Chicago Bears game. Each play is graded against the rule, the tape, and the “clear and obvious” standard. The same scale is applied to both teams. The goal is a transparent differential, not a complaint. Correct — The flag matches the rule and the tape. Bright-line fouls (false start, delay, illegal formation, clear hold, late hit with force, etc.) are Correct. Judgment calls that a reasonable crew could make and that the available angles support are also Correct. Arguable — The contact or action is real, but reasonable observers can differ. Most holding, most illegal contact, most pass interference that is neither a clear push-off nor a clear non-call lives here. The flag is defensible; so is the non-call. Incorrect — The flag does not match the rule or the tape. Mutual contact with no restriction called OPI. A finished legal pancake called holding. A soft post-release shove called roughing the passer. A play still live (or not whistled dead) called unnecessary roughness. All-22 or clear broadcast angles reverse the call. Horrible — A bright-line miss that a crew should not make. The tape shows the opposite of the foul that was thrown, or shows a foul that was not thrown, with no reasonable ambiguity. Examples used in the series: a legal pancake finished and called holding; incidental or defender-initiated contact on a completed short conversion called OPI; a clear facemask or head/neck hit that is not flagged when the rule is written for it. The Four-Tier Scale Replay overturns are judged against the “clear and obvious” standard. If the call on the field was not clearly and obviously wrong, the reversal is Incorrect. Weight (1–4) Weight measures impact, not correctness. A Correct flag can be Weight 4; an Incorrect flag can be Weight 1. 1 — Housekeeping / pre-snap. False starts, delays, too many men, illegal formations that do not change field position or down-and-distance in a meaningful way. 2 — Drive disruption. Holds or contacts that wipe chunk plays, create third-and-long, or move the chains without scoring or red-zone leverage. 3 — Scoring or red-zone leverage. Automatic first downs that extend scoring drives, red-zone holds, personal fouls that set up points, or flags that turn a field goal into a touchdown opportunity (or the reverse). 4 — Wiped score, wiped turnover, or game-ending leverage. A takeaway erased, a touchdown erased, a flag that directly produces or prevents the final points in a one-score game. No-calls receive the same grades and weights. An unthrown flag that the tape supports is graded as if it had been thrown, then marked as a no-call. Compilation Every accepted flag and every graded no-call is listed by team. Counts are tallied: Correct / Arguable / Incorrect / Horrible for calls against the Bears and calls against the opponent. A combined crew grade is given. A differential is stated: which team received the better (or worse) treatment on the accepted flags, and which team benefited from the unthrown flags. The “Bears Tax” is noted when the pattern is repeated across games: holds or contacts that are flagged on Chicago are not flagged on the opponent in the same techniques and game states. First Quarter CHI 0, NE 0 Will Rouse (NE), offensive holding, 10 yards — 14:15. Opening drive. Wipes a completion. Correct. Wt 2. Marcus Williams (NE), encroachment, 5 yards — 7:00. On third down. Process. Correct. Wt 1. Darnell Wright (CHI), false start, 5 yards — 6:48. Offsetting the encroachment. Process. Correct. Wt 1. Santos from 43. 3–0. Swift from 4 after a 58-yard Burden catch. 10–0. Second Quarter CHI 10, NE 0 Chicago, defensive too many men, 6 yards — 13:42. Gives New England a first down. Process. Correct. Wt 2. Maye scores on a scramble after a successful challenge. 10–7. Chicago, illegal forward handoff (Caleb Williams to Joe Thuney), 5 yards — 7:49. 2nd-and-3 at the NE 8. Trick play. Williams fakes to Swift and hands the ball forward to the guard. Thuney gains a few yards. Flag. The rule is absolute: an interior lineman may only receive a handoff backward. Ben Johnson later said, “It’s got to be backward.” Williams said he didn’t know the rule. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 3. Sets up third-and-8. We will cover it in detail in the flag of the Game section. Rome Odunze (CHI), offensive pass interference, 10 yards (declined) — Next play. Incomplete in the end zone. Flag thrown, declined. Bears take the field goal. All-22 shows no restriction and mutual contact. The receiver is not the initiator of a push-off or grab that significantly hinders the defender. The flag does not meet the standard. Incorrect. Wt 2. 13–7. Rome Odunze commits OPI and can’t come down with the catch.. 2nd time this season he’s done this in the end zone https://t.co/eFDI0U9wth pic.twitter.com/YwsEQBrM5f — Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT (@jmthrivept) October 23, 2026 Charles Woods (NE), defensive holding, 5 yards — 2:58. Third down after the Maye interception in the end zone. Extends the drive. Correct. Wt 2. Zavion Thomas (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 2:43. Negates a Johnson gain. Arguable. Wt 2. Gabe Jacas (NE), roughing the passer, 15 yards — Same play. On a 22-yard Burden catch. Late hit after the release. Automatic first and yards. Correct. Wt 3. Takes Chicago to the NE 33 at the two-minute warning. Burden screen for the touchdown on third-and-17. 20–7. Stevenson 48-yard score as time expires. 20–14. Third Quarter CHI 20, NE 14 Graham Bradbury (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 11:55. Negates an Odunze catch. Arguable. Wt 2. Additional process flags on both sides pad the totals. Correct on the bright-line ones. Wt 1. Fourth Quarter Santos from 58 seals it. 30–24. Cory Durden (NE), offside / encroachment (intentional), 5 yards — Late, after the two-minute warning. Third-and-short. Vrabel confirmed postgame the coaches told Durden to jump to manage the clock and timeouts. Accepted. Correct under the rule (you cannot intentionally commit a foul to gain an advantage). Wt 2. Chicago still converted the field goal. Mike Vrabel shares that DT Cory Durden was instructed to go offside late in the game to save time. He also credits Cairo Santos for making the 58-yard field goal. pic.twitter.com/wdHDkRsG4Q — Mike Reiss (@MikeReiss) October 23, 2026 Calls against Chicago Play Grade Wt Wright false start Correct 1 Too many men Correct 2 Williams illegal forward handoff (Thuney) Correct 3 Odunze OPI (declined) Incorrect 2 Thomas holding Arguable 2 Bradbury holding Arguable 2 Other pre-snap / process Correct 1 9 accepted. 5 Correct, 3 Arguable, 1 Incorrect, 0 Horrible. The Thuney handoff is the cleanest Correct of the night. The Odunze flag is the Incorrect: All-22 shows mutual contact with no restriction. The rest of the Chicago ledger is mostly gray holds and process. Calls against New England Play Grade Wt Rouse holding Correct 2 Williams encroachment Correct 1 Muasau illegal…

title: Do the Chicago Bears have a good defense now?
summary: Okay, maybe “good” is too strong an adjective, but the Chicago Bears defense sure as heck isn’t the dumpster fire so many fans told me it’d be this season. I suppose the takeaway regression has hit in 2026, but it just hasn’t hit as hard as many predicted. They led the league in 2025 with […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: Austin Booker #94 and Dillon Thieneman #31 of the Chicago Bears sack Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots during the fourth quarter of the game at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Okay, maybe “good” is too strong an adjective, but the Chicago Bears defense sure as heck isn’t the dumpster fire so many fans told me it’d be this season. I suppose the takeaway regression has hit in 2026, but it just hasn’t hit as hard as many predicted. They led the league in 2025 with 33 (1.9 per game), and so far through 7 games, they are tied for 7th with 10 (1.4 per game). The Bears had 35 sacks as a team a season ago (2.1 per game), and this year they’re on a slightly better pace with 17 (2.7 per game). Top NFL defenses this season in causing "Havoc" which is the % of plays a defense gets a pressure, TFL, forced fumble, INT, or pass breakup pic.twitter.com/238tb5puHO — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) October 27, 2026 The Bears are allowing 20.4 points per game this year, down from 24.4 in 2025. The Bears are allowing a smidge fewer yards through the air this year (225.9) than in 2025 (227.2), but the rushing defense has taken a big turn in the last 7 games, allowing 87.6 yards per game down from 134.5 a season ago. However, they are allowing more yards per play in 2026 (6.3) compared to last year (6.0). Complementary football has helped the defense, as Chicago’s improved offense, which leads the league in time of possession (35:30), keeps opposing offenses on the sideline. But the defense still needs to get stops, and it leads the league in third-down conversions allowed at just 26.1% and ranks second in the league in opponent fourth-down conversion percentage (22.2%). NFL teams ranked by points allowed in the final 5 minutes of a game: pic.twitter.com/qMP6thQz3b — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 28, 2026 Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has done a good job scheming things up, but he’s also getting solid and surprising play from some of his players. Can the Bears keep it up on D? What would a defensive addition at the trade deadline do for their chances?

title: 3 keys to a Cincinnati Bengals victory vs. the Tennessee Titans
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals will be back at their home stadium for the first time since the Week 4 loss to Jacksonville. Somehow, the Bengals have only played two home games so far this entire season. They will be welcoming the 1-6 Tennessee Titans to Paycor Stadium. Now, let’s take a look at the Bengals’ biggest […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals will be back at their home stadium for the first time since the Week 4 loss to Jacksonville. Somehow, the Bengals have only played two home games so far this entire season. They will be welcoming the 1-6 Tennessee Titans to Paycor Stadium. Now, let’s take a look at the Bengals’ biggest keys to victory against a sneaky Titans squad. Don’t underestimate your opponent How many times over the years have we seen the Bengals lose a game that they had no business losing? We all remember the Mike White game against the Bengals during the 2021 season. Just last year we had another loss to the New York Jets that was absolutely brutal. Come to think of it, we should be thankful this game isn’t against the Jets this week. It is a similar feeling coming into the game, though. The Titans look overmatched on paper. They are 31st in passing yards per game offensively, while being 26th in rushing yards per game offensively. The Bengals defense, led by Dexter Lawrence, was lights out in the second half against Baltimore, after doing enough in the first half to at least keep the score within striking distance with the offense struggling. Meanwhile, the Bengals’ offense was able to put up 35 second-half points on the road against the Baltimore Ravens. Joe Burrow and the Bengals offense should be able to easily move the ball on Tennessee. However, this is the NFL. It is a week-to-week league. The Titans played the Browns close just last week, and probably should have been able to win that game after taking an early 14-0 lead. If you come out flat any given week, you can lose to anyone in this league. Contain Tony Pollard Tony Pollard had 129 rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns against Cleveland. He was the majority of the Tennessee offense during that game, adding another 26 yards receiving on three receptions. The Bengals have been inconsistent against the run this year. They were able to keep Derrick Henry in check last week. Henry averaged just 2.6 yards per carry against Cincinnati. If they can do something similar against Tony Pollard this week, they should be able to come out with the victory. Throw the ball from shotgun early I think the Bengals should just come out firing. When they basically dropped under-center for the majority of the second half against the Ravens, they looked like the offense we have grown accustomed to watching during the Joe Burrow era. I say keep that same attitude to start this one. You can always add in more under-center and run the ball more once you have built up a two-score lead. Be aggressive and don’t keep the Ferraris in the garage. Throw the ball to Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins so that those guys can do what they do. If we come out aggressive offensively and build a quick lead, I think you can roll this week. You never want to start off slow and allow a struggling team to gain confidence. If that happens, the Bengals could get upset at home against Tennessee. Once again, you just cannot take any opponent lightly in the NFL. We don’t want to be looking back at this game all season for one that we had no business losing, so come out firing from the jump. What’s your biggest key to getting this W?

title: Joe Burrow comments on Bengals trade deadline speculation
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are sitting at 4-2 to start the season after an electric win over the Baltimore Ravens this past weekend, 35-13. Despite the good start to the 2026 season, the Bengals still have plenty of needs to help solidify the roster before the trade deadline. The Bengals could still use another corner, safety, […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals are sitting at 4-2 to start the season after an electric win over the Baltimore Ravens this past weekend, 35-13. Despite the good start to the 2026 season, the Bengals still have plenty of needs to help solidify the roster before the trade deadline. The Bengals could still use another corner, safety, linebacker, running back, and now tight end with season-ending injuries to Erick All Jr. and Tanner Hudson. Fans have seen the Bengals in rumors for guys like Zach Baun and Johnathan Taylor, but there have been zero legitimate reports suggesting this will actually happen so far. Joe Burrow was asked about the trade deadline rumors during his weekly press conference with local media, and he shared his thoughts regarding them. “Number one, I feel really good about our team and the guys we have in there,” Burrow said. “Number two, I think every GM in football is probably exploring all options at this point, and very few ever end up materializing. But that’s something that I think all those guys think about critically, and whether it ends up happening or not, who knows. “But I feel really good about the team we have in there.” Burrow was then asked about the rarity of the Bengals front office making trades, and of course, Dexter Lawrence was brought up. “I don’t think there’s very often that a player like Dex becomes available. And then for one first-round pick in a high-need position for us…I think all those things together kind of created the perfect storm of a situation for us to involve ourselves. “And yeah, obviously it’s worked out great for us, and we couldn’t be happier with it,” Burrow stated. It will be fun to see what shakes out before the deadline, but it is clear the team is confident in the guys they have in the building right now.

title: 4 key matchups to watch in Bengals vs. Titans
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals improved to 4-2 on the season with a second-half surge against the Baltimore Ravens. The Tennessee Titans fell to 1-6 after a tough 27-24 loss to the Cleveland Browns. On paper, the Cincinnati Bengals should handily beat the Titans. Games are not played on paper, though, and just about any NFL team […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals improved to 4-2 on the season with a second-half surge against the Baltimore Ravens. The Tennessee Titans fell to 1-6 after a tough 27-24 loss to the Cleveland Browns. On paper, the Cincinnati Bengals should handily beat the Titans. Games are not played on paper, though, and just about any NFL team could have success vs. the Bengals if they play like they did in the first half of the Baltimore game. Now, let’s take a look at some of the key matchups this week. Jeffery Simmons vs. Dalton Risner and Ted Karras Jeffery Simmons is still one of the best pass-rushing defensive tackles in the NFL. He has 24 pressures and four sacks already this season for the Titans. Ted Karras and Simmons have some history, with Karras infamous for up yours Tennessee a few years back after getting into a scuffle with Simmons late in the game. Dalton Risner will see a lot of Simmons this week also. I thought Risner played his worst game of the season against Baltimore. It seems like his knee injury is still hampering his play on the field. A fully healthy Dalton Risner would have his hands full with Simmons, so we shall see if one that continues to play through injury can keep him from wrecking the game on the interior. Jermaine Johnson vs. Amarius Mims Jermaine Johnson was traded to the Titans from the New York Jets this offseason. He currently has 21 pressures and three sacks this season. He will be matched up against one of the best offensive tackles in the league, Amarius Mims, this week. Mims has allowed just four pressures the entire season. That is an absurd number through six games of the season in the NFL. While I don’t want to discredit Johnson here, I will just tell him good luck when matched up against Mims. Mims should be an All-Pro this season, and it is a shame that he doesn’t get more national recognition for his play this year. Amarius Mims vs. Miami Dolphins Mims has allowed 4 pressures according to PFF on 209 pass blocking snaps. The only players with less are Garrett Bolles with 3 pressures on 188 PBLK snaps, Jermaine Eluemenor with 3 pressures on 161 PBLK snaps, and Joe Alt with 3 pressures on just… pic.twitter.com/KeUtdiB0XB — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) October 13, 2026 Tony Pollard vs. Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter Tony Pollard had his best game of the season last week against Cleveland. Pollard rushed for 129 yards and three rushing touchdowns. He added 3 receptions for another 26 yards during the game. While Tennessee has struggled as a whole offensively, Pollard is one player that could give the Bengals’ defense some trouble this week. If they are going to contain Pollard, some of that responsibility will go to the second-year linebackers in Knight and Carter. Both guys have improved overall this season, but missed tackles can still be an issue at times. Carter has a 13.8% missed tackle rate on the season. Knight has a 10.7% missed tackle rate. If the linebackers can make plays that come their way without allowing big gains, the Bengals should have a chance to shut down the Titans offense. Austin Schlottmann vs. Dexter Lawrence Dexter Lawrence will see a ton of double teams, as he does on a weekly basis. One of the players who will be responsible for trying to contain him is center Austin Schlottmann. Schlottmann is 6’6” and 300 pounds. That frame alone suggests a player who is going to struggle with the power and leverage that Lawrence creates on the interior. Schlottmann has a 45.7 overall grade per PFF this season. He is 31 years old, and this will be the first season he is going to eclipse 400 snaps in a season. Dexter Lawrence, meanwhile, is arguably the most dominant defensive player in the league this year. He has 22 pressures with four sacks through just six games played this season. He is a force against the run, an elite pass rusher, moves better than guys that are 30-40 lighter than him, and commands so much attention that it frees up his teammates to make plays of their own. Dexter Lawrence could be in line for a massive game this week against Tennessee. At this point, we expect that from him every week. I will continue to say that Lawrence should get serious consideration for Defensive Player of the Year. He makes everyone around him better. A truly dominant player in the middle of the defense. Dexter Lawrence vs. Baltimore Ravens Lawrence should get serious consideration for the Defensive Player of the Year Award. He is that damn good. pic.twitter.com/MLKlPq8vH0 — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) October 26, 2026

title: Cleveland Browns news: A 51-point beatdown in Pittsburgh
summary: A 51-point beatdown in Pittsburgh The Cleveland Browns and Pittsburgh Steelers face off on Sunday in Pittsburgh. Some of the games have been competitive; many, especially since 1999, have not.  […]
full_text: (Photo by George Gojkovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images A 51-point beatdown in Pittsburgh The Cleveland Browns and Pittsburgh Steelers face off on Sunday in Pittsburgh. It will be the 148th meeting of what is the AFC’s most played rivalry, as the two teams have been playing each other since 1950. Some of the games have been competitive; many, especially since 1999, have not. But there is one game that stands out among the rest, and it took place in Pittsburgh on September 10, 1989. Cleveland was still a talented team, one that had made the playoffs the previous four seasons. But there were still some questions, as the game would be the debut of head coach Bud Carson, who took over after the departure of Marty Schottenheimer following a loss to the Houston Oilers the previous year in a Wild Card playoff game. The Steelers, on the other hand, had spent the decade grasping at the remnants of the 1970s after being displaced as the top dawg in the division by the Browns. OTD 1989 #Steelers #Browns Bud Carson makes his head coaching debut Clay Matthews TD David Grayson scores on a fumble recover and a pick 6 Manoa 2 TD’s 51-0 #DawgPound #PrimeTime pic.twitter.com/4tofda5kwd — Old Time Football 🏈 (@Ol_TimeFootball) September 10, 2026 Having broken the Three Rivers Jinx in 1986, and having won three consecutive games in Pittsburgh, there was a good feeling that the Browns would make it four in a row and open the season on a winning note. But no one could have predicted what took place that afternoon. Cleveland jumped out to a 17-0 lead at the end of the first quarter on the backs of defensive touchdowns from linebackers Clay Matthews and David Grayson. Having the Steelers down, the Browns stepped on the gas and the lead grew to 30-0 at halftime, 44-0 at the end of the third quarter, and 51-0 when the final whistle blew. The 51-point differential is still the fourth-biggest margin for a Week 1 game in NFL history. Thirty-seven years later, the result is as stunning as it was on the day it occurred. Sunday’s game carries extra importance as the Browns are looking for a season sweep of the Steelers while also maintaining their hold on first place in the AFC North Division. No one is expecting a repeat of the 1989 game, as a win by any margin at a stadium where the Browns have not tasted victory in the regular season since 2003 would do just fine. title: Browns HC remains singularly focused on the next game
summary: Being a fan of a sports team has always been different from being a player or head coach. Fans may live and die by the weekly results, but it isn’t their livelihood. Whereas the players and coaches know their continued employment relies on how they perform when it matters.  Fans are also invested more heavily […]
full_text: Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Being a fan of a sports team has always been different from being a player or head coach. Fans may live and die by the weekly results, but it isn’t their livelihood. Whereas the players and coaches know their continued employment relies on how they perform when it matters. Fans are also invested more heavily in the rivalries and the history of their favorite teams, as they have lived through it. While players and coaches may understand the importance of a game, such as a divisional game or a playoff game, it remains just the next game on the schedule. That does not mean they care less; of course, it is just that they are focused on one thing, while the fans are often focused on something else. Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken illustrated that during his media appearance on Wednesday. Monken and the Browns are preparing for Sunday’s game against the Pittsburgh Steelers, which has the added importance of the Browns having the opportunity to sweep the season series from the Steelers. There is also the not-so-small matter of the Browns not having won a regular-season game in Pittsburgh since 2003. But to Monken, and likely the players, the history takes a back seat to achieving the goal of simply winning another divisional game : “This year, whether it’s where we’re at record-wise, comparing the past or the history against the Steelers, it’s a divisional game. So, as I always say, what matters is what we do today, how we practice today, how we prepare today for any opponent. “It’s bigger because it’s obviously a divisional opponent. The fastest way to get in the playoffs is to win your division. That’s the fastest way to get in the playoffs. I mean, you’re guaranteed (a spot) in the tournament, and we’re a long way away from that. That’s not what I’m saying. That’s why the game is what it is, and rivalries are made up of good teams playing each other, and we’re fighting like hell to be a really good team.” Monken is also preaching to the players the importance of staying focused on the task in front of them, rather than the history between the two teams : “I know it’s a divisional game and I know it’s next, and they’re all important, and that’s why I try to not get too much into that, because it’s one of 17. It happens to be one-plus, because it’s a divisional game, but they’re all going to be important, right? The last one was critically important to get us to five. This one’s critically important to try and get us to six. And then you go from there. “But I try not to put too much emphasis on what-ifs, if this, if that, whether it’s win or lose. I don’t control that part of it. Me personally, what do I control? The messaging to the team, to our coaches, the game plan we put together, and getting our guys to have a practice today that’s worthy of the preparation we’re going to need to go play them Sunday.” It is an interesting way to approach each week, and probably a good one given that this team is mostly young and has not experienced much (if any) success at the NFL level. In the past we’ve seen Cleveland teams win a couple of games, start believing the headlines, and then fall flat. But if the Browns can win on Sunday, they will continue to change the narrative around the team, and exorcise one of the biggest demons haunting the franchise. And if that happens, despite Monken downplaying the history a bit, there is no doubt he will reference it in some way in the post-game press conference. And then turn his focus to the next critical game, in what could be turning into a special season in Cleveland. Bring the Dawg Pound with you on the SB Nation app! full_text: The more things change ( the Cleveland Browns winning five of their first seven games ), the more things stay the same ( quarterback stories drawing a ton of interest ). This week, as the Browns prepare to take on the Pittsburgh Steelers, QB Dillon Gabriel rejoined the 53-man roster, with the team reportedly planning to keep four quarterbacks , or at least prepared to, for the rest of the season. With the NFL trade deadline around the corner, GM Andrew Berry could take a number of routes with the team , including random quarterback-related trade suggestions , but few believe that Shedeur Sanders, Taylen Green , or Gabriel have a lot of value on the market. While most expected Sanders to remain in his backup role after Gabriel’s activation, Cleveland HC Todd Monken was noncommittal about what he would do behind starter Deshaun Watson : Monken asked how Dillon Gabriel's return to the active roster might affect Sunday's QB order / game day roster "I haven't gotten there yet." — Zac Jackson (@AkronJackson) October 28, 2026 It is very possible that Monken is just not concerned about the decision, wants to throw the Steelers off his plans, or just doesn’t care to explain his plans to the world. The Browns head coach is also aware enough of what his statements could elicit from fans and media. In the end, Monken and all of Cleveland’s fanbase just want wins, which Watson is currently helping with. The best-case scenario is that no one ever finds out who the backup quarterback is. That could only happen, however, if the Browns decide to keep three quarterbacks active on Sundays. For now, we wait to hear from Monken with the final decision between Sanders and Gabriel becoming official 90 minutes before Week 8’s kickoff, when the inactive reports come out. title: NFL trade deadline: How the Browns, GM Andrew Berry should proceed
summary: For the first time in a long time, the Cleveland Browns appear to be trending in the right direction. With the team sitting at 5-2, it is likely that the Browns will be buyers at the November 10th trade deadline instead of sellers. As the team prepares for their AFC North clash with the Pittsburgh […]
full_text: For the first time in a long time, the Cleveland Browns appear to be trending in the right direction . With the team sitting at 5-2, it is likely that the Browns will be buyers at the November 10th trade deadline instead of sellers. As the team prepares for their AFC North clash with the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 8, Cleveland has a rare opportunity in front of them. If the Browns were to win at Pittsburgh on Sunday, the possibility of making the playoffs would turn into a reality, considering how wide open the AFC is. GM Andrew Berry should be looking to improve their roster at the trade deadline without giving up major draft capital. Browns trade targets that don’t make sense Indianapolis Colts RB Jonathan Taylor Philadelphia Eagles RB Saquon Barkley Las Vegas Raiders EDGE Maxx Crosby Jacksonville Jaguars WR Brian Thomas Jr The Indianapolis Colts are having a fire sale. General manager Chris Ballard has already been fired and head coach Shane Steichen isn’t far behind. Jonathan Taylor doesn’t make much sense given the potential cost, and the Browns running game is starting to come together. The Philadelphia Eagles could be selling assets, but RB Saquon Barkley could be difficult to move because of his contract situation as well as age. It’s unlikely that the Raiders trade Maxx Crosby, but the Browns just traded away a superstar edge rusher in Myles Garrett and it wouldn’t make sense if they traded away Garrett just to trade for Crosby, who isn’t close to Garrett in terms of talent. Browns trade targets that fit for the right price Philadelphia Eagles OLB Nolan Smith Los Angeles Chargers EDGE Tuli Tuipulotu You’ll notice I’ve listed only two players here, but both are edge rushers. The Los Angeles Chargers are a disaster, and from what I was told, the team is looking to trade players to recoup draft assets. Chargers edge rusher Tuli Tuipulotu is playing on the last year of his contract and is slated to be a free agent this offseason. Acquiring Tuipulotu would boost the Browns’ edge rusher room but only for the right price. Cleveland doesn’t necessarily have to overpay to get him, but if they can, it has to be for the right price, maybe a combination of picks instead of one premium one. As for the Eagles, it’s an interesting case. The team is injured across the board, and if they choose to punt the season to regain assets, linebacker Nolan Smith could be dealt. Philadelphia picked up Smith’s 5th-year option, but it’s not likely that the Eagles will keep him long-term. It’s the NFL; you can’t keep everyone, and price tags fluctuate. Smith is more of a run stopper, but he’s shown signs of brilliance in his pass rushing. Browns trade targets that should be pursued ASAP Los Angeles Chargers EDGE Khalil Mack Arizona Cardinals EDGE Josh Sweat Washington Commanders CB Amik Robertson Los Angeles Chargers TE Charlie Kolar Houston Texans TE Cade Stover New Orleans Saints TE Noah Fant More names could’ve been included, but I chose to go with these specific ones. As mentioned earlier, the Chargers are selling assets and Khalil Mack is likely the first domino to fall. Despite his age, Mack is still playing at a high level. Mack is also playing on an expiring deal and general manager Andrew Berry has shown the ability to play players on expiring deals. As mentioned earlier, the edge room needs some more juice added to it, and Mack would help. The Browns tight end room is thin in terms of depth, and it also lacks an in-line tight end. Staying with the Chargers, tight end Charlie Kolar has familiarity with Todd Monken’s offense and would be a reliable TE2 for the Browns to utilize. The Washington Commanders cornerback room is already thin, but if the Browns can acquire cornerback Amik Robertson, it would benefit them. Robertson has been stout for the Commanders, he can play inside and outside, and the Browns slot corner has been a weakness for some time. Which of these Browns trade targets would you have the most interest in, assuming an appropriate trade price? Join the conversation! full_text: One of the major keys to the Cleveland Browns’ offensive success this season has been yards after catch. The Browns’ playmakers have really made the most of their targets and have been able to extend drives. It has really helped the offense push the ball down the field when other things aren’t working. KC Concepcion had one of the best games of his rookie year, and his ability to get yards after the catch was a massive part of that. On the opening drive for the offense, he was able to get a 23-yard gain from a short pass. This was an extremely valuable third-down play and it helped the offense to move the ball when the quarterback wasn’t pushing the ball down the field. Harold Fannin Jr. is another weapon that has been really successful in getting a significant amount of yards after the catch this season. He always fights through contact and gets those extra yards. He averages 6.2 yards after catch per reception thus far this season. This really helps the way that defenses have to approach the Browns since they have so many weapons. Let me know what you think in the comments – The Browns’ YAC: A Recipe for Offensive Success?

full_text: (Photo by George Gojkovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns head to Pittsburgh on Sunday looking to break a decades-long losing streak. The Browns have not won a regular-season game against the Steelers in Pittsburgh since 2003 – a span of 23 seasons! Sadly, this is not the first extensive losing streak for the Browns in the Steel City, as older fans will remember the infamous “Three Rivers Jinx.” Beginning with the opening of that concrete dump in 1970, the Browns made the annual trip 16 times, and 16 times they came home on the losing end. Sometimes it looked like the Browns would break the jinx as they suffered four-point losses in 1974 and 1977; three-point losses in 1979, 1980, and 1984; and a one-point loss in 1985. The franchise tried everything to change its luck, from taking a bus instead of flying and switching hotels, but nothing could break the jinx. Until the afternoon of October 5, 1986. The most memorable play of the day came when Gerald McNeil returned a kickoff 100 yards for a touchdown in the second quarter, Cleveland’s first touchdown return in 12 seasons. After the Steelers retook the lead in the third quarter, the Browns moved to within one point heading into the fourth quarter after a field goal from Matt Bahr. The deficit grew to four points after a Gary Anderson field goal, but Cleveland retook the least on Earnest Byner’s four-yard touchdown run. Pittsburgh had one final chance after Bahr’s second missed field goal of the day, but Cleveland’s defense held and the jinx was finally over. Cleveland’s next chance to break its latest streak comes this Sunday in a season that has been full of surprises.
