title: Detroit Lions tagged as ‘best fit’ for 4 trade deadline candidates
summary: The NFL trade deadline is just under two weeks away—Tuesday, November 10—and several trades have already been made. So ESPN insiders Jeremy Fowler and Matt Bowen put together a list of the top-25 candidates to get traded by the deadline. Interestingly, they also listed at least two teams that they view as the best team […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Riq Woolen #2 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on against the Carolina Panthers at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL trade deadline is just under two weeks away—Tuesday, November 10—and several trades have already been made. So ESPN insiders Jeremy Fowler and Matt Bowen put together a list of the top-25 candidates to get traded by the deadline . Interestingly, they also listed at least two teams that they view as the best team fits for a landing spot. In their list of 25 traded candidates, the Detroit Lions were listed as one of the best fits for four of those candidates. Let’s go through them one-by-one. Eagles CB Riq Woolen It’s not surprising the Lions are being paired with a cornerback, given their struggles at that position this year. Although it is interesting to see the Lions have some recent success at cornerback after utilizing some rotation with the players they have. The Eagles are 2-5 and will be without starting quarterback Jalen Hurts for the rest of the season. They definitely could be sellers at the trade deadline, and ESPN lists Woolen at a 35% likelihood of being traded. He’s on a very manageable contract, with the acquiring team only responsible for a prorated amount of his $6 million base salary. He would bring some height and length (6-foot-4) to the outside cornerback position, but his play hasn’t been as good as his best Seahawks days. This season alone, PFF credits him with 20 catches on 36 targets for 282 yards, 4 touchdowns—but he does have six passes defended and a forced fumble. Here’s what Matt Bowen had to say about his play this year: “Woolen has the length and long speed at 6-foot-4 to help a defense majoring in man coverage and two-deep zone. The tackling and eye discipline could improve, but Woolen is a disruptor on the perimeter.” Chargers CB Donte Jackson The Chargers are the only winless team remaining, and with the Rams, Ravens, Patriots, 49ers, Chiefs, and Broncos still on the schedule, their season is already toast. Jackson will be 31 next month, but he’s had an illustrious NFL career. Over nine years, he’s started 109 games, tallied 23 interceptions, and 68 passes defended. He was a captain for several years with the Panthers, so he’s high-character, as well. Financially, this is another easy one. It’s the same as Woolen: all the acquiring team would need is to fit a prorated amount of Jackson’s $6 million salary. Here’s Bowen’s analysis: “With his backfield vision and short-area closing speed, Jackson fits best as a zone corner. He’s a top-down defender with route awareness who can create on-the-ball production” Bengals EDGE Shemar Stewart While the Bengals are far from sellers at 4-2 on the season, they have been barely playing Stewart, who was the team’s 17th overall pick just last year. Stewart has played in just 17 snaps this season. Despite that, I think it’s unlikely Cincinnati moves on from Stewart this early in his career. He missed nearly all of training camp with a leg injury, and that was part of Zac Taylor’s explanation for having Stewart inactive this past week. “He’s doing all the right things. He’s getting better every week. (He missed) training camp for the most part. So, to get him back, I think he’s been doing a great job of practicing. We’re just in a really tough spot with our inactives right now. Sometimes we’re really healthy. Sometimes we’re beat up at a position where we need another guy up. So, unfortunately, we just had to pull from the d-line, and it’s a really deep d-line group, and it’s really difficult to choose who’s going to be inactive there.” But in the unlikely situation he’s on the block, he is a very good fit in Detroit. He’s long, strong, and extremely physical. Saints G Cesar Ruiz This is just a bizarre one. Ruiz could very well be on the block for a 2-5 Saints team, but it’s hard to imagine the Lions getting involved for a guard. Not only has Ruiz played right guard for almost his entire NFL career—where Lions’ second-year player Tate Ratledge is holding things down just fine—but the Lions have also been getting really solid play out of Christian Mahogany at left guard. And they have a good backup option in Juice Scruggs. Not sure what ESPN is thinking with this one. It ain’t happening.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: 5 Lions vs. Vikings thoughts after watching Minnesota’s win over Colts
summary: Like every week, I begin my preparation for the Detroit Lions’ upcoming game by watching their next opponent’s previous matchup. Here are five things I learned about the Minnesota Vikings after watching their 16-10 win over the Indianapolis Colts. Did Colts find a weakness in Vikings’ run defense? For the season, the Vikings’ run defense […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Dallas Turner #15 and Harrison Smith #22 of the Minnesota Vikings sack Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts in the second quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images Like every week, I begin my preparation for the Detroit Lions’ upcoming game by watching their next opponent’s previous matchup. Here are five things I learned about the Minnesota Vikings after watching their 16-10 win over the Indianapolis Colts. Did Colts find a weakness in Vikings’ run defense? For the season, the Vikings’ run defense has been almost as stellar as their outstanding pass defense. They’re only allowing a -0.212 rush EPA (second), they’re first in rush success rate allowed (31.2%), and ninth in run defense DVOA. But the Colts were able to run quite successfully against them last week. 33 carries, 154 yards (4.7 YPC), 1 TD -0.050 rush EPA (12th best of Week 7) 41.2% success rate (13th) The Colts’ running game kept them in decent downs and distances all game, which allowed them to convert on third downs 53% of the time against the Vikings—the highest percentage Minnesota has given up all year by far. For the season, the Vikings are allowing a third-down conversion rate of just 28.2% (third-best). If you get into a third-and-long, you can forget it. Minnesota has allowed just a 14.3% conversion rate on third-and-7+ (seven conversions out of 49 attempts, second-best). Now, it’s worth pointing out that the Colts have one of the best rushing attacks in football, and they still produced only an above-average day against the Vikings. Still, despite Detroit’s inconsistencies in the running game, it’s easy to imagine Detroit trying to attack on the ground to try and keep the Vikings’ aggressive pass defense at bay. Kyler Murray is struggling with accuracy Obviously, the Vikings’ offense has not yet found its footing with new quarterback Kyler Murray under center. They’re averaging just 20.8 points per game (23rd) despite constantly being given good field position (33.9-yard line average, third best), and they average just 4.7 yards per play (27th). But I was surprised to see how much of it appears to be Murray’s fault. He really struggled with accuracy against the Colts. Not only did he complete just 14-of-24 passes (58.3%), but his -12.2% completion percentage over expected (CPOE) was second-worst of the week—oddly only ahead of Patrick Mahomes. For the season, Murray is a more modest +0.7% CPOE (16th), but he’s near the bottom of the league in yards per pass attempt (6.5, 22nd) and EPA/dropback (-0.09, 23rd). And that’s despite rarely throwing the ball deep. His 7.0 average depth of target is just 7.0 yards (23rd out of 33). Run game is okay, but short-yardage is a problem The Vikings opened up the game against the Colts after a good kick return and found themselves in a third-and-1 in Colts territory. They squandered the opportunity with back-to-back Aaron Jones runs that went for a collective -1 yard. On their next drive, they managed to pick up a fourth-and-inches with a Murray sneak, but barely. It turns out their short-yardage running game has been a problem all year. They sport a power success rate (success on third- and fourth-and-short situations) of just 60% this year, which ranks 21st in the NFL. That is not a situation the Lions’ run defense has excelled at this year, allowing a success rate of 83%, tied for the highest in the NFL. So this is a weakness vs. weakness matchup. That said, their down-to-down rushing efficiency is at least okay. They rank 21st in yards per carry (4.0), but 27th in rush EPA and 27th in rushing success rate. With Aaron Jones’ health status unclear this week and Jordan Mason back in the lineup, it’s hard to know what to expect on the ground for Minnesota. They’re nasty on special teams It actually wasn’t their best game on special teams, with a 59-yard field goal blocked and a kick return of 43 yards allowed vs. the Colts. But the rest of their special teams units were great. Their punter, Brett Thorson, dropped both of his kicks inside the 20-yard line. Myles Price had a 46-yard kick return of his own. And Will Reichard has made every single kick this year outside of that one blocked. For the year, the Vikings rank first in punt return average (19.2), first in kick return average (30.7), eighth in punt coverage average (8.7), and 14th in kick coverage average (25.2). They’re first in special teams DVOA this year. But the Lions have been pretty dang good, too. They’re fifth in special teams DVOA, third in punt return average (14.4), 22nd in kick return average (25.0), fifth in punt coverage average (8.1), and fifth in kick coverage average (23.8)—and Jake Bates has yet to miss a kick. Fans of special teams units will have their Super Bowl on Sunday. Dear lord, their pass defense is scary The Vikings went viral this week for their outrageous 85.2 blitz rate against the Colts, the highest ever recorded in the NextGenStats era (back to 2016). That aggression led to four sacks, one interception, and at least three other passes that could’ve been picked off. The Colts managed just 108 passing yards (64 net), and a paltry 4.9 yards per attempt. They didn’t have a single passing play of over 13 yards. For the season, the Vikings aren’t just first in most categories; they’re first by a mile: 61.7 passer rating allowed (next best is 72.6) 10.6 sack percentage (next best is 9.4) 53.9 completion percentage allowed (next best 56.4) 68.4 blitz percentage (next best 42.3%) -0.30 EPA/pass allowed (next best -0.22) 35.5 dropback success rate allowed (next best 39.2%) The good news is that the Lions are one of the best teams against the blitz this year. When facing a blitz, the Lions rank: Eighth in lowest sack percentage (5.4%) Fifth in lowest pressure rate allowed (35.1%) Seventh in yards per attempt (7.2) First in EPA/pass (+0.25) But this is an entirely different beast in Minnesota, and we’ll see if Jared Goff, Drew Petzing, and the Lions offensive line have answers for Brian Flores.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Minnesota Vikings’ strengths, weaknesses
summary: From zero NFC North games to back-to-back divisional showdowns, the Detroit Lions are getting familiar with their biggest rivals. The Lions host the NFL’s lone undefeated team, the Minnesota Vikings, on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET at Ford Field for Week 8. Detroit is coming off a thrilling victory over the Green Bay Packers, their […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: T.J. Hockenson #87 of the Minnesota Vikings celebrates with Justin Jefferson #18 after scoring a touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts during the fourth quarter of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images From zero NFC North games to back-to-back divisional showdowns, the Detroit Lions are getting familiar with their biggest rivals. The Lions host the NFL’s lone undefeated team, the Minnesota Vikings, on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET at Ford Field for Week 8. Detroit is coming off a thrilling victory over the Green Bay Packers , their first divisional win of the season. Minnesota is off to a better start than anyone could’ve expected. When down 22-10 against the Packers in Week 1, the Vikings looked like many expected this year. Suddenly, the defense came roaring back, wreaking havoc and helping the offense rebound to win. Since then, that’s been the Vikings’ MO: rely on the defense to create enough problems so the offense doesn’t have to work as hard. Let’s take a deep look at the Vikings’ season so far as they head into Week 8. Minnesota Vikings 2026 season thus far (6-0) Week 1: Defeated Green Bay Packers, 39-22 Week 2: Defeated Chicago Bears, 9-3 Week 3: Defeated Tampa Bay Buccaneers, 23-16 Week 4: Defeated Miami Dolphins, 15-10 Week 5: Defeated New Orleans Saints, 23-13 Week 6: BYE Week 7: Defeated Indianapolis Colts, 16-10 Offensive stats: On offense, the Vikings try to take a balanced approach. Quarterback Kyler Murray hasn’t been as lights-out as people expected, averaging 162 passing yards per game with only three passing touchdowns. His legs have helped with 132 yards on 25 carries. That side of the offense has struggled most, as Minnesota hasn’t seemed to figure out how to coordinate its passing attack. The team has relied heavily on running back Aaron Jones, who leads the team with 105 carries for 436 yards and two touchdowns, averaging 4.2 yards per carry. Backup running back Jordan Mason missed four games with an injury, but he returned against the Colts and took some load off Jones, getting 15 carries for 59 yards and a touchdown. Minnesota is running the ball better than throwing it, averaging in the top half of the league in rushing yards per game. The usual suspects lead the receiving corps, with wide receiver Justin Jefferson catching 23 passes for a team-high 302 yards and three touchdowns. His partner in crime, Jordan Addison, has 13 catches for 183 yards and a touchdown, while tight end T.J. Hockenson leads the team with 27 catches for 237 yards and two touchdowns. Minnesota’s offensive line seems a bit better than last year, despite a worse PFF pass-blocking grade (69 in 2025, 68.8 in 2026), but the unit is ranked 10th, up from 14th. Only one injury is plaguing the line this time (guard Donovan Jackson) instead of multiple, so you can’t point the offense’s woes at them. This offense is struggling at the most important position (quarterback), and they don’t improve as the season goes on, it could be what keeps them out of the playoffs. Defensive stats: While the offense has been average, the defense is doing much of the heavy lifting. Edge defender Dallas Turner is in the midst of a breakout year and leads the team with 6.0 sacks. He’s followed by Blake Cashman (4.5) and Andrew Van Ginkel (4.0). According to PFF, the Vikings have the 12th-ranked pass rush (70.6 grade). Despite tying for the most sacks in the NFL, the Vikings have faced teams that could be inflating those numbers. In the secondary, cornerback Byron Murphy has started strong, leading the team with three interceptions and six pass deflections. Minnesota has seven interceptions, tying it for the fourth-most in the NFL. Like the defensive line’s pass rush, the pass defense’s success could be inflated by who they’re matched up against, as PFF ranks them 15th in coverage. Minnesota ranks top-10 in many other categories, but their secondary, despite the stats you’ll read below, could be their weak point on that side of the ball. The unit is good, but they haven’t played as complete a unit as the Lions so far. Green Bay has been the best offense they’ve seen yet, and without running back Josh Jacobs, they put up 22 points. They’ve faced the Chicago Bears (in a rainstorm) and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, both of which lost their quarterbacks in the fourth quarter. The already-poor offenses of the Miami Dolphins, New Orleans Saints, and Indianapolis Colts were missing either a starting running back or wide receiver when they faced Minnesota. Detroit is at full strength and will give this defense its toughest test all year. Injury notes Key players ruled out : S Jamal Adams (IR), G Donovan Jackson (IR), TE Josh Oliver (IR) Key players to monitor : RB Aaron Jones (knee) Unlike the Packers, the Vikings are coming in fairly healthy overall. Their biggest loss is starting guard Donovan Jackson, who is out for the season with a torn meniscus. Beyond that, injuries haven’t hit many star players. Safety Jamal Adams was placed on IR before the season started with a torn right quadriceps, hurting depth at safety and prompting Harrison Smith to return from retirement. Backup tight end Josh Oliver tore his biceps, and while he could return this season, he won’t play this week. Jones is the player to watch this week. He suffered a scary-looking knee injury against the Colts, but he is considered day-to-day, so his status for Sunday is unknown for now. If the Vikings don’t have Jones, expect Mason to lead the way. Biggest strength: Defense When people talk about the Vikings, they bring up their defense. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores is having his best year in Minnesota, and if he doesn’t land a head coaching job in 2027, the NFL is seriously wrong. Minnesota’s defense has been a problem all over, from the front seven to the back four; this unit is in pandemonium. On the pass defense, Minnesota has allowed the lowest completion percentage (53.9), the fewest passing yards (1,085), the fewest touchdowns (three), the lowest QB rating (61.7), and is tied for first in sacks (21). Their insane 68.4 blitz rate is over 25 percentage points higher than any other team. Vikings defense came to play 💪 INDvsMIN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/IiI1asgTY1 — NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026 It’s not just the pass defense causing problems; they are shutting down rushing attacks, too. They have allowed the third-fewest rushing yards in the NFL (587) and are tied for the fewest rushing touchdowns allowed (three). No matter what offenses try, this defense stops them. They’ve held five of their six opponents to under 17 points this season, so scoring is far from easy, no matter who they face. Biggest weakness: Offense While the defense is playing lights out, the offense still needs a lot of work. First, Murray has been playing fine at quarterback, but he’s not lighting up the stat sheet. The Vikings have the fourth-fewest passing yards on average, tied for fifth in fewest passing touchdowns (six), and have only one pass over 40 yards. The passing game just isn’t explosive enough right now, even with their new, shiny quarterback that people thought would help this offense score more points. Meanwhile, their former starting quarterback is lighting it up against one of the NFL’s best defenses . When you talk about the running game, there hasn’t been much there either. The Vikings average 4.0 yards per carry (t-22nd), have three total rushing touchdowns (tied for 31st), and only three runs over 20+, with the longest at 35. Again, this offense’s lack of explosive plays is being bailed out by its defense. Key matchup: Lions offense vs. Vikings defense The Lions offense is a tough machine to slow down, and last year the Vikings held Detroit to 24 and 10 points in the two games. Detroit’s offense should be a step up this year, with poor offensive line play and tight end…

title: Detroit Lions stock report: 19 risers, 9 fallers against the Packers
summary: The Detroit Lions will take the outcome, even if it wasn’t pretty. The team finally secured consecutive victories for the first time since the top half of last season, moving to 4-2 and 1-0 in the division after an unexpected slugfest. Much of the immediate aftermath surrounded outspoken criticism of the officiating and Dan Campbell’s […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-OCTOBER 25: Quarterback Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers gets sacked by defensive end Aidan Hutchinson #97 of the Detroit Lions during the first half of an NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, October 25, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Detroit Lions will take the outcome, even if it wasn’t pretty. The team finally secured consecutive victories for the first time since the top half of last season, moving to 4-2 and 1-0 in the division after an unexpected slugfest. Much of the immediate aftermath surrounded outspoken criticism of the officiating and Dan Campbell’s fourth-quarter decisions, but it was important for the Lions to win an ugly one, especially against a quality divisional opponent. They won despite the defense getting marched up and down the field on Green Bay’s first two drives before stiffening up in a big way, and despite an offense that wasn’t firing on all cylinders and missed opportunities throughout. They persevered and won a gritty one. They’re a better team for finding a way to win. Let’s get into the Week 7 stock report following Detroit’s first divisional victory of the season. Stock up: Brian Branch, S If you want to know what Detroit thinks of Brian Branch, just listen to Ford Field blow the roof off clear into Canada after his fourth-quarter interception. Branch really is a shapeshifter for the defense with what he’s able to do at the second and third levels, serving as a force multiplier for the other 10 players on the field. The Lions’ defense had by far its best, most complete four quarters of football with Branch back in black, and there was a comfortable, calming sense to his presence for the rest of the guys out there. Like Sam LaPorta, the other franchise pillar in a contract year who balled out against the Cardinals, Branch reminded everyone why he’s the defensive version of LaPorta: a versatile skeleton key who opens everything up for the unit. Branch finished with 45 of 67 defensive snaps (67%), ramping up his workload before being unleashed more consistently in the second half. He finished with four total tackles, three of them defensive stops, and one roaring, high-pointed, go-up-and-get-it interception. It was crucial for a team that had forced only two turnovers in its previous four games. With Branch back, and the lowly Vikings and Dolphins offenses next on the slate, the Lions’ defense could gain some traction and confidence before heading to Germany to face last year’s MVP runner-up, Drake Maye. Stock up: Amon-Ra St. Brown & Jameson Williams, WRs While Branch eased back into the swing of things in the first half, St. Brown and Williams collectively diced up the Packers on three first half drives that crossed into Green Bay territory, although those possessions resulted in only 10 points. In the first half, St. Brown recorded seven catches for 135 receiving yards, while Williams had three receptions for 51 yards and a touchdown. Both players made big plays to move the ball downfield and into the end zone on Detroit’s first scoring drive, helping the offense overcome its opening quarter slump. St. Brown then had a 40-yard catch-and-run to set up a field goal on their second drive . On the final drive of the half, which ended in a red-zone fumble, Williams and St. Brown helped get Detroit out from the shadow of its own end zone, control the clock, and move into scoring range. One of football’s best receiving duos combined for 14 receptions on 20 targets, 244 receiving yards, two touchdowns, and 12 first downs. In a huge divisional game against a legitimate Packers pass defense, with a running game that found some success but suffered enough negative plays to leave the offense behind the sticks, Detroit’s two playmakers at receiver rose to the occasion for Jared Goff and the team. Stock down: Christian Mahogany, Cade Mays, & Tate Ratledge, IOL In Cade Mays’ season debut, the interior offensive line took some lumps adjusting to its new partner in crime, with some rust to knock off. While the pocket was clean for Jared Goff for much of the afternoon, and Mays in his debut had some particularly stout pass-protection reps on play action to go along with Mahogany and Ratledge being rock-solid in pass pro this year, it was arguably the muddiest day of run blocking for the team this season. Jahmyr Gibbs was consistently contacted shortly after receiving the handoff, often behind the line of scrimmage. Some of those struggles could be attributed to predictable run designs, the Packers’ aggressive run blitzes and defensive slants, and a lack of play calls to counter that aggression. Still, there was entirely too much leakage in the run blocking, much of it coming through the A- and B-gaps. Mahogany and Ratledge are too boom-or-bust at times. The high-level plays are there, but their inconsistency also reveals fundamentals that still need correcting: losing early at the line of scrimmage, getting off balance and being unable to recover, lacking awareness to react to run-throughs, and too often failing to climb to the second level while working on double teams. Mays was also partially responsible for some of the blitz issues, where pre-snap adjustments could have helped, and was involved in one false start and, inadvertently, both fumbles. It’s a volatile interior trio with a high ceiling that will continue to develop throughout the season. The Lions can survive games like these when their elite skill players are able to be game-changers and lift up the team. Stock up: Aidan Hutchinson & Alim McNeill, DL The two other difference-makers on the Lions’ defense, aside from Jack Campbell, both had productive games up front to help hold the Packers’ offense to just 17 points and keep Jordan Love uncomfortable and on his toes, or on his heels with some of those back-foot fadeaway throws, for much of the day. Hutchinson had an underrated game but was seemingly everywhere, even lining up standing lurking over the guards. Not only did he have the lone Gumby-like sack, draw a holding penalty, and nearly pick off a screen pass in the red zone, but he also forced multiple incompletions, including blowing up a play-action rollout. He gave Anthony Belton and Jordan Morgan hell while also clobbering Josh Jacobs from the backside on one of the first runs of the game. Hutchinson also recorded an average time to pressure of 2.49 seconds, his fastest in a game so far this season. McNeill was similarly a problem, consistently generating pressure up the middle to crush the pocket and speed up Jordan Love into several inaccurate throws, while also registering a big-time run stuff on third-and-3 against Marshawn Lloyd. Both players could have used a little more pass-rush support from the rest of the defensive front. Quick Hits STOCK UP: Jared Goff, QB: Goff battled well, ripping play-action passes, intermediate throws, and a handful of money balls outside the hashes. Jahmyr Gibbs, RB: Gibbs was given minimal running room and was often under duress early in plays, finishing with -24 yards before contact while still mustering a rushing success rate above 48%. If the Lions had any other running back, they might not have won that game. Tyleik Williams, NT: Williams was fortunate enough to be matched up against backup center John Williams after both Sean Rhyan and Jacob Monk were injured early in the game. He took advantage, pushing him around and winning at the line of scrimmage for most of the afternoon. Derrick Moore, DE: Moore actually played quite a bit on early downs and appeared more forceful and stout in run defense from his two-point stance, shoving tight end Mark Redman into the hole on one goal-line run . He also whooped left guard Laken Tomlinson on an interior pass-rush rep, generating pressure on the incomplete deep ball to Golden where Khalil Dorsey wasn’t flagged. Perhaps the game is…

summary: The Green Bay Packers announced on Wednesday that the team has already ruled out three of their starters against the Carolina Panthers in Week 8: center Sean Rhyan, right guard Travis Glover and Mike linebacker Zaire Franklin. The Rhyan and Franklin rulings were expected coming into the week, but Glover being out for Thursday Night […]
full_text: (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers announced on Wednesday that the team has already ruled out three of their starters against the Carolina Panthers in Week 8: center Sean Rhyan, right guard Travis Glover and Mike linebacker Zaire Franklin. The Rhyan and Franklin rulings were expected coming into the week, but Glover being out for Thursday Night Football likely means that Kevin Zeitler will get the starting job in Glover’s place. According to head coach Matt LaFleur, the team wasn’t notified about Glover’s knee injury until Monday morning. Beyond the players ruled out, four players were listed as questionable: receiver Matthew Golden (shoulder/foot), defensive lineman Devonte Wyatt (ankle), defensive lineman Anthony Campbell (ankle) and edge defender Brenton Cox Jr. (quadricep). The expectation right now is that the Packers will scratch three offensive linemen (including both Rhyan and Glover), Franklin and running back Kaleb Johnson to get their 53-man active roster down to their 48-man game-day roster. With that being said, if Green Bay is down players at any other position (the players listed as questionable), they might need to call up bodies from the practice squad to backfill at those spots. On the Panthers’ side of the injury report, the team ruled out four players, including two starters in edge defender Jaelan Phillips and guard Damien Lewis. Carolina was already hurting on both lines of scrimmage, as their defense cannot stop the run, and the team already lost one starting offensive lineman — Taylor Moton — to the injured reserve. title: Devonte Wyatt, where art thou?
summary: After suffering a season-ending ankle injury last season, the future for former Green Bay Packers first-round pick Devonte Wyatt was in some doubt as he headed into his final year under contract. However, prior to training camp even opening this summer, the Packers and Wyatt agreed on a three-year $57M contract that would keep him […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 11: Devonte Wyatt #95 of the Green Bay Packers looks on during the game against the Chicago Bears at Lambeau Field on October 11, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Daniel Bartel/Getty Images) | Getty Images After suffering a season-ending ankle injury last season, the future for former Green Bay Packers first-round pick Devonte Wyatt was in some doubt as he headed into his final year under contract. However, prior to training camp even opening this summer, the Packers and Wyatt agreed on a three-year $57M contract that would keep him in Green Bay for the foreseeable future. The contract included a $20M signing bonus and $22M in true guarantees, but with the contract structure including a 2027 roster bonus, it functionally looks more like about $31M in functional guarantees before his contract is potentially on the chopping block after the 2027 season. At the time, the Wyatt contract was considered a pretty good deal. It came in materially lower in guarantees than John Franklin-Myers’ deal, despite Wyatt being less of a unique player. Rather than being the size of a classic 4-3 defensive end, Wyatt is built like a classic three-tech. While availability has been a rolling problem for Wyatt, when he’s been on the field, he was always disruptive, even if the actual sack production lagged the pressure numbers. His first three seasons saw pressure rates north of 9% in each of them, and last season, as his snap load increased prior to injury, still maintained a solid 20th ranking amongst defensive tackles in pressure rate, even as the rate itself fell to 7.7%. In 2026, the pressure rate decline has continued, with it now falling to a paltry 5.4%. The pressure rate decline is particularly problematic as Wyatt has never been a good run defender. Quantifying run defense is always difficult as even something like “stops” can be misleading since good run defense at defensive tackle is often about occupying the correct space within the overall context of the front and not letting holes open up. PFF grades continue to be less-and-less useful as the company has moved in a… different… direction, but his grades have been sub-standard in this department for years. His run defense grades, aside from his rookie season in more limited snaps, have been 52 or worse in each of the past four seasons. In 2026, he’s giving the Packers next-to-nothing. DT percentile grades in pass rush and run defense pic.twitter.com/lcUGCavzt8 — Jrfortgang (@throwthedamball) October 28, 2026 Also, goodness Chris McClellan… (I don’t think the graders ever know what they’re looking at with nose tackles, to be honest). One very nice surprise on this chart is Karl Brooks, who is having a career year despite playing more snaps than ever. While Wyatt is only playing just under half of the defensive snaps, Karl Brooks, in addition to being a special teams ironman, is playing over 60% of the defensive snaps. His pressure rate is solid, but his run stop rate is very high, rating as one of the best in football, despite him being a bit of an outlier in terms of the type of defensive tackle you would expect to pop in the run game. Brooks’ contract-year breakout has helped mask some of the shortcomings of Wyatt, but they became very glaring on Sunday when the Packers front was struggling mightily to create pressure as the Lions basically forced Lukas Van Ness out of the pass rush with their formation alignments. This left the Packers without their best pass rusher on most plays, and Wyatt’s disastrous 2026 continued as he didn’t register a single pressure, his second consecutive game doing so. With Javon Hargrave out for the year and likely a cut candidate this off-season, and Karl Brooks looking more-and-more likely to earn a good contract elsewhere this spring, the Packers desperately need a return of 2025 Devonte Wyatt sooner rather than later. If not for 2026, then at least for 2027 when perhaps maybe, just maybe, they won’t be decimated by apocalyptic injury luck for yet another year.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Micah Parsons looms
summary: It’s a bit later than I think we would have expected, but it looks like Micah Parsons’ return is drawing near. Head coach Matt LaFleur has indicated there’s a chance the Packers’ star edge rusher could start practicing next week, giving the Packers some hope that one of the league’s best players could finally be […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 18: Micah Parsons #1 of the Green Bay Packers looks on from the sidelines against the Dallas Cowboys during the fourth quarter at Lambeau Field on October 18, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s a bit later than I think we would have expected, but it looks like Micah Parsons’ return is drawing near. Head coach Matt LaFleur has indicated there’s a chance the Packers’ star edge rusher could start practicing next week, giving the Packers some hope that one of the league’s best players could finally be back in uniform. It seems to have been broadly understood that the Packers were going to be without Parsons for at least part of the season, and the goal for however long that portion turned out to be was to survive and position themselves to make some noise when Parsons came back. I think they’ve basically done that — to a point. Assuming Parsons is back next week, the Packers need to take care of business against the Panthers to give themselves a favorable outlook on the rest of the season once they’ve got their most critical defensive piece back. A win moves the Packers to 5-3, which isn’t great but it’s workable. They’d probably need to go 6-4 at least the rest of the way for a decent shot at the playoffs. But if they’d happen to lose, which we can’t rule out given how they’ve played to this point, their playoff odds drop to just 27% according to ESPN’s playoff scenario estimates. That makes Thursday’s game pretty close to a must win. And if they do win, who knows what happens next? The 2026 Packers are a mystery to themselves and others. They could be competitive in any game or lose to anyone. But getting Parsons back, even if he can’t fix their offensive line problems, would give them hope they haven’t had in a long time. Handle the Panthers first, and then see what happens. Matt LaFleur isn’t ruling out imminent practice return for Micah Parsons | ESPN What the Packers do this week will go a long way toward determining what kind of scenario Parsons will face when he returns. Packers CB Brandon Cisse not playing like a rookie | Packers.com There have been bumps in the road, but Cisse has been everything the Packers could have asked for. Packers rookie Brandon Cisse is turning heads with his rapid development | Packers News ($) Cisse spent a lot of time opposite Amon Ra St. Brown on Sunday and came out looking pretty good. title: Houston Texans NFL Power Rankings: Week 8
summary: So much for that win in London! Following Houston’s fantastic victory against the Jacksonville Jaguars one week ago to improve to 2-4, last Sunday’s game against the New York Giants was supposed to be another step back towards contention. Instead, both Houston’s offense and defense fell back on their old habits of poor blocking and […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 25: A Houston Texans reacts during the fourth quarter against the New York Giants at NRG Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images So much for that win in London! Following Houston’s fantastic victory against the Jacksonville Jaguars one week ago to improve to 2-4, last Sunday’s game against the New York Giants was supposed to be another step back towards contention. Instead, both Houston’s offense and defense fell back on their old habits of poor blocking and poor tackling, penalties galore, and the like as the Texans lost to the Giants 27-21 in overtime. This loss practically wiped out any hopes for a comeback season in Houston, giving the team a record of 2-5 and with some serious questions to answer during the bye week. One of the most stunning developments of this game was Giants QB J.J. McCarthy, who was starting his first game with New York after being traded by the Minnesota Vikings. He was such a colossal disappointment in Minnesota that head coach Kevin O’Connel went from drafting him tenth overall in 2024, to the birth of “nine” in 2025 after multiple grizzly performances, to demoting him to third-stringer in 2026 – behind QB Carson Wentz! Today marks a month since the Giants decided to deal a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Vikings for McCarthy, and they are looking like geniuses for that decision. In his first start since Minnesota’s 2025 regular season finale against the Green Bay Packers, McCarthy demolished what little reputation the Texans’ defense had left from last year, repeatedly targeting Giants star WR Malik Nabers and rookie Malachi Fields, who both combined for 11 receptions and 194 yards on just 14 targets. They practically embarassed the entire Texans’ secondary with those two receivers, which alone should give you idea on how far the Texans have fallen, especially without S Jalen Pitre on the field. pic.twitter.com/Xag0S46kaI — Performances (@NotPerformances) October 25, 2026 And once you get over the J.J. McCarthy angle of this loss, it only gets worse from there! Giants RBs Cam Skattebo and (former Texan) Devin Singletary gashed Houston’s defense over and over again, both finishing the game with a combined 165 rushing yards and two touchdowns on just 22 carries. Practically all of the Giants’ RBs were placed in the doghouse by head coach John Harbaugh last week as he aired his frustrations over their issues thus far, and the Texans defense became the catalyst to their “get right” game! Cam Skattebo and Devin Singletary – a RB that the Texans’ coaching staff and defense should know how to stop from his year here in 2023 – had their bounce back games against the Houston Texans! And RT Jermaine Eluemunor was gassed up in the Giants locker room postgame, too: "If you didn't hear [Will Anderson Jr.'s] name today, then I did a pretty good job. I'm not too shy about saying I'm the best right tackle in the NFL. People can go watch the tape and take from it what they will. I did my job today." – Jermaine Eluemunor pic.twitter.com/zrcT6uT8uU — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 26, 2026 Maybe it’s fitting the Texans lose like this a week before Halloween, because this might as well be a nightmare come to life! The shadow cast by Houston’s losing record grows ever longer as the days grow shorter, and the sense that time is running out climbs up their minds as a chill raises the hairs on their backs. At 2-5, Houston’s fight or flight response has been activated, but has the air of desperation come too late for these Texans? Well, let’s take a look at where everyone is ranking them following their 27-21 overtime loss to the New York Giants: NFL.COM : 18. Houston Texans (2-5) (Last Week: 22) Another tough loss has landed on the Texans’ ledger, reducing their room for error going forward. It’s fair to say this defense is no longer deserving of its respected reputation — especially when reflecting on how Devin Singletary ran right through the heart of the unit to a game-winning touchdown . I do believe C.J. Stroud will continue to keep Houston competitive. I’m keeping an eye on that connection with Marvin Harrison Jr. too; Stroud’s touchdown pass to his former Ohio State teammate on Sunday was exquisite. – Nick Shook ESPN: 21. Houston Texans (2-5) Week 7 result: Lost to the Giants 27-21 (OT) Week 7 ranking: 16 Best offseason addition: TE Foster Moreau The Texans didn’t have many big offseason acquisitions, but Moreau has provided help in the run game. And he has been a good red zone threat with three total touchdowns. Moreau has played 43% of the snaps, eating into the playing time of tight end Dalton Schultz , who is down from 70% in 2025 to 57% this season. Moreau helps Houston’s offense not be predictable when he’s in the game. Even though Houston has just two wins, its offense is averaging 24 points per game. And Moreau is a noteworthy part of the unit. – DJ Bien-Aime SPORTS ILLUSTRATED: 21. Houston Texans (2–5) Last week’s ranking: No. 14 Last week’s result: lost to Giants, 27–21 (OT) This week: idle I know great defenses are difficult to maintain from year to year, but the Texans’ fall from grace remains one of the most stunning moments in recent history. J.J. McCarthy would have been ripped to shreds by almost the exact same cast of characters a year ago (no offense). How do you not evolve over the course of an offseason? – Conor Orr BLEACHER REPORT: 22. Houston Texans (2-5) Last Week: 19 Week 7 Result: Lost vs. New York Giants 27-21 (OT) Back-to-back wins briefly revived Houston’s season. Sunday’s loss exposed how much work remains. There are a number of reasons why the Texans have struggled, but the most surprising has to be the team’s defensive collapse. Last year, Houston led the league in total defense and ranked first in the AFC in scoring defense. This season, Houston’s defense has been average—on a good day. The Texans allowed 420 yards of offense in Sunday’s overtime loss, including 188 yards and four scores on the ground. The offense isn’t without blame—taking on a Giants team short its best edge-rusher and green-dot linebacker, Houston had just 237 yards of offense and was 3-for-12 on third down. The Texans head into their bye week facing an unpleasant reality: There will be no return to the playoffs in 2026. – Gary Davenport CBS SPORTS 21. Texans (2-5) (Last Week: 15) Losing at home to the Giants just might be the death blow in their chances of winning the AFC South. The defense just isn’t good enough. – Pete Prisco USA TODAY: 24. Houston Texans (20): It may be a lost season in H-Town, but not if you’re Tank Dell. Welcome back, boss, and props. Tank Dell gets his first catch in 673 days for a 42-yard gain🥹 NYGvsHOU on FOX/FOX One Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/zwXKQWxxJs — NFL+ (@NFLPlus) October 25, 2026 – Nate Davis YAHOO! SPORTS: 21. Houston Texans (2-5, LW: 17) The Texans’ loss Sunday was one of the most damaging of the entire NFL season. They were double-digit favorites to beat the Giants, and a win over New York would have put Houston at 3-4, not far behind 4-2 Jacksonville with a head-to-head win over the Jaguars. And the Texans had a massive letdown in an overtime loss to the Giants. At 2-5, their margin of error is incredibly slim with 10 games to go. At this point it’s clear the Texans are nowhere near as good on defense as expected. They were 16th in defensive DVOA through Sunday’s games and 24th in EPA ( expected points added ) allowed. Needing a stop in overtime Sunday, Houston allowed runs of 42 and 30 yards on back-to-back plays that ended the game. “No magical elixir is going to drop out of the sky and … fix it,” Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans said according to AP. “We fix it by putting the work in and getting better at fundamentals of football and that’s where we’ve got to just own it. As coaches, as players, we’ve all got to own it and we’ve got to find a way to turn this thing around.” – Frank Schwab THE ATHLETIC:…

title: Playing the Texans Blame game
summary: As we sit here in the middle of the bye week it becomes apparent in these situations that someone is going to get blamed for why things are going the way they are going. The usual refrain is that you can’t fire the players. That’s actually a misnomer as players get fired all the time. […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 25: Head coach DeMeco Ryans of the Houston Texans looks on during the third quarter against the New York Giants at NRG Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images As we sit here in the middle of the bye week it becomes apparent in these situations that someone is going to get blamed for why things are going the way they are going. The usual refrain is that you can’t fire the players. That’s actually a misnomer as players get fired all the time. They are cut, waived, released, and demoted. Players see their roles increase and others see their roles decreased. However, talk radio and the sports debate shows don’t make their money talking about releasing or benching players. They make their money by talking about the guys wearing the polos and hoodies on the sideline. Sometimes, those discussions reach as high as the suits in the front office. Of course, I make no bones about the fact that this is one person’s opinion and I have never coached a down of football. I did play the game decades ago as a youngster and as the kids would say, that was a hot minute ago. However, the Indianapolis Colts have already fired Chris Ballard. The league usually turns over five or six head coaches a season and numerous assistants will get their walking papers. That will happen whether I bloviate or not. So, if we look at the Texans, here ia short list of who could be on the chopping block. Cole Popovich One hardly ever buys completely into stat services like PFF. However, at one point, Juice Scruggs was the highest rated center in the NFL. The fact is that he is the starting center for the Lions and they are generally thought to have one of the best lines in the NFL. Yet, he was deemed to be not good enough to stick around. One could hardly blame that evaluation based on his performance in Houston. So, either he suddenly got better or there is something going wrong in Houston. Every year we complain about the offensive line. Every year they change the guys up front. Every year we complain about the offensive line. It’s literally an O’Henry story ready to be written. Popovich was promoted from assistant to head offensive line coaches because of reasons. They didn’t even deem to interview anyone else. Somehow having the guy that was in the room when another coach failed seem like the right way to go. It still doesn’t make sense. Matt Burke This one hurts because I generally like Burke. However, you cannot go from one of the best defenses in football to one of the worst in one season without having some fallout. Goodness knows how much control he actually has over the situation. DeMeco Ryans is calling plays and two out of the three games looked exactly like the first four games did. Firing Burke feels like one of those “we gotta do something” moves that teams do when they feel that accountability is needed. Frank Bush The Texans routinely boasted one of the best special teams units in the league for the better part of a decade. They still have one of the best kickers in the business, but their punting game and coverage games have really fallen off this season. Everyone likes Bush, but in a season where things aren’t going well, fingers get pointed and we often look for areas where the team has seen a fall in production. I would put this one as one of the more unlikely results, but you never know what can happen if things get bad enough. Nick Caley Here is where things get interesting. When you look at the overall numbers, the Texans offense ranks in middle of the pack or better in most of the important offensive categories. They rank low in two important categories: running the ball and pre-snap penalties. Obviously, how you feel about Caley depends on your expectations and who gets to set them. It is clear that DeMeco Ryans wants a team that won’t turn the ball over and won’t have negative plays. Check and check. They are not the ball control team that Ryans wants. They will always be a square peg in a round hole as long as that is the expectation. So, how we feel about Caley depends on a lot of projection. There are times in the game when we collectively yell, “why in the hell are you running that play?” Usually it involves a slow developing running play that everyone in the stadium knows is coming. Yet, we have to ask ourselves if that is what he would do if he were completely left to his devices? It’s an important question because if you fire him thinking he’s the problem and have a head coach that demands ball control then you wind up right back in the same spot you were before. DeMeco Ryans I am one of those crazy people that thinks you don’t fire a coach after one bad season. That is of course unless you completely lose faith in that coach. If Ryans did a better job of coaching in games then it is possible this is a 3-4 or 4-3 football team right now. In that case we wouldn’t be having this conversation. Yet, he handled the Jacksonville game well and has shown that he can keep the team engaged after slow starts on multiple occasions. Of course, that begs the question of why we are always having slow starts. I see this as a Gary Kubiak circa 2010 situation. Kubiak engineered the best offense in the NFL according to some metrics, but they employed perhaps the worst defense in football. Ownership forced Wade Phillips on him and the rest is history. Hannah McNair (the real power behind the throne) might step up and force the issue on the offensive side of the ball. This is especially true if you pay your quarterback 60 million a year. He may get told he is changing styles and the offensive coordinator given more power. I really can’t see Ryans being shown the door because he is so popular and the first three years were so successful, but such a move would be putting him on notice. Nick Caserio Obviously, the person on top gets most the acclaim and most of the blame when things go wrong. The trade for Marvin Harrison Jr. might end up working out overall. If he is productive and raises the level of the passing attack then it will be a good trade in that vacuum. Of course, one will obviously point the opportunities that could have come with that draft capital. Could they have added a defensive player that would have impacted the level of the defense? Would another linebacker or safety benn more impactful? I suppose we will never know. Some of this is based on projection. We know he is responsible for much of the roster and the salary cap situation. Those situations seem fine. What we don’t know is how much control he has had over the assistant coaches. There seem to be a lot of buddy hires here and that could be an area where a Hannah McNair steps in and demands more control in that department. He also gets dinged for three consecutive years of offensive line shuffling that hasn’t worked. Is it the wrong players or the wrong coaches? Either way, like Ryans he might be relatively safe for now, but he will be put on notice.

The Colts conducted a walk-through today so therefore the injury report is only an estimation of a player’s participation if there was a practice. We conducted a walk-through on Wednesday. Wednesday's practice report is only an estimation of a player's participation if there was a practice. pic.twitter.com/KPXGomHyIA — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 28, 2026 Linebacker CJ Allen (ankle) was a full participant today. Allen was in line to start Sunday until he injured his ankle. Fellow rookie linebacker Bryce Boettcher (groin) missed practice today, he looks likely to miss another week with the groin injury. Whereas veteran linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (hand) was a full participant despite a hand injury. Cornerback Justin Walley (knee) missed practice today. Warren injured his groin at practice and has missed two games because of it. Right Guard Matt Goncalves (ankle) was limited at practice today. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, Indianapolis Colts starting slot wide receiver Josh Downs has requested a trade from the organization , after the team initiated a fire sale on Tuesday by trading two of its best players: DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson in order to jumpstart the now fully undergone rebuild. ‘ Per The Athletic’s James Boyd, Downs did little to dispel the notion that he requested a trade when asked on Wednesday during his post-team practice media availability: #Colts WR Josh Downs on trade rumors: “It is what it is. I’m where my feet are. …” pic.twitter.com/pgZnRw9GID — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) October 28, 2026 Originally a 2023 3rd round pick of the Colts, the 5,’9”, 171 pound wideout has transformed into one of the better natural young slot receivers in all of football—and also offers special teams value with his punt return ability. On the 2026 season, Downs has 26 receptions for 307 total receiving yards and 0 touchdown receptions during 7 games (5 starts). While he is still plenty young enough to be in the Colts’ long-term plans at 25-years-old, Downs also is currently a pending free agent at year-end, as a byproduct of being in the last year of his rookie contract. He probably see’s the writing on the wall as far as maximizing his production at wide receiver here, as Indianapolis could very well be looking at another new starting quarterback come 2027—for the 7th time in the last 8 years. It’s hard to build any consistent chemistry and rapport as a wide receiver with their quarterback position being a constant turnstile and in flux. Downs and his agent representation are presumably hoping that they can find an upgrade at starting quarterback over incumbent Daniel Jones in the interim before next year’s free agency, as playoff suitors such as the Kansas City Chiefs and Los Angeles Rams are among the teams that are expected to be interested in acquiring him. title: Colts’ Week 7 QB Analysis: What a Difference a Year Makes
summary: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. […]
full_text: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. Commentary will be brief but feel free to let me know in the comments that stats aren’t everything. (click charts for larger view) As of this week, out of 32 starting QBs, I have Daniel Jones ranked 30th for the season in efficiency. That’s quite a contrast to one year ago today, when I wrote this about him: “I think I could just copy and paste my comments from previous weeks, because Jones keeps delivering the same consistently strong performances. In Week 8, he was once again a top-10 QB in EPA efficiency and success rate, minimizing mistakes and mixing in high-impact plays to keep the NFL’s best offense rolling”. Let me just update that for the current year: I think I could just copy and paste my comments from previous weeks, because Jones keeps delivering the same consistently poor performances. In Week 7, he was once again a bottom-five QB in EPA efficiency, making mistakes and mixing in costly sacks to keep one of the NFL’s worst passing attacks sputtering. Here’s how the offense looked against the Vikings: After the first drive, there wasn’t a lot of movement down the field. The Colts could only manage a 31st place Drive Success Rate (65.2%) and that just isn’t going to cut it. The run game was capable and provided the only Colts’ touchdown of the day, but the passing was absolute garbage. Let me tell you that story in numbers. HOW WELL? mouseover definitions: arsr , edp , sg% , oz% , pr% , tip , ttt , adot , ay/c , yac , yacoe , yd/c , ac% , cpoe , aypa , drp , scr% , ta% , sck% , aa% , ny/d , ny/p , 1st% , td% , to% , qbsr , epa/p , adj/p The offense tried leaning on its run game on early downs and found moderate success. ( 15th ARSR; 26th EDP ) The Vikings have the #1 Pass Rush Win Rate in the league and it showed as Jones faced tremendous pressure from constant blitzing, causing him to rush his throws. ( 1st PR%; 19th TIP; 22nd TTT ) Jones was forced into short passes, and those completions produced very little yardage after the catch. The Colts finished at the bottom of the league in total yards per completion. ( 26th ADOT; 19th AY/C; 30th YAC; 31st YCOE; 32nd YD/C ) Jones struggled to complete passes, finishing well below expectations. Combined with the limited yardage on his completions, that left him dead last in yards per attempt. ( 27th AC%; 31st CPOE; 32nd AYPA ) Drops weren’t a factor, but sacks certainly were. Jones was sacked four times, while scrambling only once and throwing the ball away twice. His decision making in the face of pressure is poor ( 29th DRP; 13th SCR%; 7th TA%; 2nd SCK%; 2nd AA% ) Between the short passing game, poor completion rate and sacks, Jones finished dead last in the league in yardage efficiency, averaging just 2.6 yards per play. ( 32nd NY/D; 32nd NY/P ) With such poor passing, the offense struggled to generate first downs and Jones failed to produce a passing touchdown. ( 26th 1ST%; 30th TD% ) Jones’ interception was another damaging play in an already inefficient passing performance. ( 3rd TO% ) Ironically, Jones was reasonably consistent at producing positive plays, finishing near the middle of the league in success rate. The problem was that a lot of his positive plays were barely positive, while his negative plays were particularly costly, That is why his EPA efficiency was far, far worse than his success rate. ( 16th QBSR; 30th EPA/P ) mouseover definitions: ay< , dp% , ay/c , yac , yd/c , ac% , aypa , drp% , aypa , ta% , ypa , sck% , ny/a , scr% , ny/d , car% , ny/p , 1st% , any/p , td% , any/p , to% , any/p , epa/p , opd , adj/p Jones’ efficiency curve shows how his passing production fell apart. Although he generated decent air yardage on shorter completions, the absence of deep completions and very little production after the catch drove his average yardage near the bottom of the league. His inability to complete passes or make good decisions under pressure prevented him from improving on that. Jones had some productive plays scattered throughout the game, particularly in the first half, but they were repeatedly offset by costly negative plays. The biggest problems were four sacks, including two consecutive sacks early in the third quarter, and the fourth-quarter interception that removed any hope of a comeback. Jones actually produced positive EPA on half his quarterback plays (15 of 30), but the negative plays were considerably more damaging than the positive plays were valuable. He finished with just a 50.0% success rate and a god-awful -0.15 EPA per play. Jones’ recent struggles are becoming more apparent. His success rate has remained somewhat stable, hovering just below league average, but his EPA per play continues to fall, with five of his last seven games finishing in negative territory. Most concerning is the steady decline in net yards per QB play, which fell to the aforementioned 2.6 yards this week. HOW FAR? Jones never established much rhythm in the passing game, although he did put together a productive stretch of short completions during the second and third quarters. Nearly all his throws were short, with no attempts over 20 yards (1 incompletion of 20 yards). The interception was the dagger. After averaging 11.5 air yards per target in each of the previous two weeks, Jones returned to a much shorter passing game, with a 5.2 ADOT this week. His completions averaged 5.1 yards downfield, continuing a longer-term downward trend in the depth of his completed passes. Jones is averaging just 6.0 yards per attempt this season off of the 8th shortest passes. TO WHO? Keenan Allen led the Colts with 31 receiving yards on 3 targets. I guess Jones spread the ball around a lot, so that’s good… kind of. Tyler Warren has missed 2 weeks and he still leads the team in receptions. Not a lot of depth for anybody this week. Not a lot of value for anybody this season. HOW ACCURATE? Jones 59.1% completion rate was 11% lower than expected given the short throws he was making. That continues a season long decline in accuracy (CPOE). Looking at the season as a whole, Jones has been below league average at nearly every passing depth, with his biggest struggles coming on throws beyond 20 yards. HOW FAST? Jones averaged 2.57 seconds to throw this week, a significant drop from 2.93 seconds the previous week and somewhat quicker than league average. Unfortunately, a lot of that was hurried throws to avoid pressure. His season-long time to throw has been relatively normal for the depth of his targets, sitting close to the league trend line. TO WHERE? Jones had mixed results on shorter throws, finding considerable success on passes within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage, while struggling badly everywhere else. He didn’t attempt a single pass beyond 20 yards. Some of the worst deep throws in the league.

title: Stampede Blue Reacts Survey – Week 8
summary: The Indianapolis Colts’ disappointing season continued Sunday with a 16-10 loss to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings, dropping them to 2-5 and extending their losing streak to three games. While the defense delivered one of its better performances of the season, the offense struggled once again, with quarterback Daniel Jones completing just 13 of 22 passes […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 11: Anthony Richardson Sr. #5 of the Indianapolis Colts warms up prior to a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts’ disappointing season continued Sunday with a 16-10 loss to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings, dropping them to 2-5 and extending their losing streak to three games. While the defense delivered one of its better performances of the season, the offense struggled once again, with quarterback Daniel Jones completing just 13 of 22 passes for 108 yards and throwing a costly interception on the team’s final possession. Jones has now thrown just four touchdowns compared to seven interceptions through seven games, a significant departure from the quarterback who helped lead Indianapolis to an impressive start in 2025. With the Colts continuing to fall further out of the AFC playoff picture, questions are beginning to mount about whether Shane Steichen should consider making a change at quarterback. Anthony Richardson has yet to take a regular-season snap in 2026, but with the former fourth-overall pick approaching the end of his rookie contract, there is an argument for giving him another opportunity to prove himself. Richardson’s struggles with accuracy and decision-making have been well documented, although his athleticism and ability to create explosive plays could provide a different dimension to an offense that has become increasingly stagnant. Steichen, however, has maintained his confidence in Jones and has indicated that a quarterback change is not currently under consideration. Should Anthony Richardson start? Are you confident in the Colts? Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys: The uncertainty surrounding Indianapolis extends well beyond the quarterback position. Just over a week after firing general manager Chris Ballard, the Colts have now traded eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in exchange for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round selection. The decision to move one of the franchise’s most accomplished players suggests that Indianapolis is beginning to prioritize its long-term future, raising questions about whether other established veterans could be dealt ahead of the November 10 trade deadline. Last week’s Reacts survey showed that 47 percent of Colts fans remained confident in the direction of the franchise, potentially reflecting some renewed optimism following Ballard’s dismissal. However, another disappointing loss and the departure of Nelson could significantly change that sentiment. With the possibility of additional roster moves looming and the coaching staff facing mounting pressure to produce results, fans have plenty of reasons to question where this franchise is headed. Will the latest organizational changes restore some hope for the future, or will the Colts’ continued struggles push confidence even lower?

title: It may be hard to stomach but this is exactly what the Colts need to do
summary: Fires can be good, at least in the sense of forest fires. No one wants to see a fire raging out of control and wreaking havoc, but a fire, especially a controlled or non-life-threatening one, is essential. A fire removes dead debris and makes way for new life. It encourages diversity and the chance for […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: DeForest Buckner #99 of the Indianapolis Colts takes the field before the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fires can be good, at least in the sense of forest fires. No one wants to see a fire raging out of control and wreaking havoc, but a fire, especially a controlled or non-life-threatening one, is essential. A fire removes dead debris and makes way for new life. It encourages diversity and the chance for new opportunities for different species to thrive. The Indianapolis Colts are experiencing their own version of a controlled burn, and while it may be painful to witness, it is exactly what’s needed. Two pillars of the team are gone. Captains Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner have new teams. No, these men aren’t “dead debris” but they are older players with expiring deals. For this metaphor, we will consider them to be the underbrush that needs to be parted with to make room for new growth. They probably won’t be the last either as Grover Stewart, Jonathan Taylor, Josh Downs, and others are floating around the rumor mill as trade candidates. If all of those players leave, the Colts will resemble a burned-out forest, dead and a shell of its former self. That’s when the magic can happen, though. New players can rise to take their place. Those that might not have gotten much of a shot will get to demonstrate what they can do now that the path has been cleared. Through the restocking of draft picks, the new growth begins as well. Fresh faces and an infusion of young talent can start to take root and stand where the mighty pines once did. There is no guarantee that it all works out and the forest returns to its mighty glory. That could take several burns and restarts. What is guaranteed is that this current iteration of the Colts isn’t going anywhere. By trading the men they have, the Colts are accomplishing two things: they are providing cherished players an environment in which to thrive and are reaping draft capital to help restore what has been missing in this organization. The moves have been twofold so far and completely necessary. The top canopy of the forest is gone. When Chris Ballard was fired, it left the whole forest exposed. The Colts looked around and realized how desperately they needed a refresh. When the fire is calculated and controlled, it is most effective. Fans have to trust the Irsays to keep it that way, and if they do, this organization can reap the benefits. Watching long-time players leave is tough, but removing the old and restarting with new can bring a world of possibilities. The fire itself isn’t usually pleasant, but for the Colts, this one is essential to their future.

title: Chiefs News: Chris Jones is one of Chiefs’ pressing concerns
summary: Coming out of the Kansas City Chiefs’ 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, there was plenty to be concerned about with the Chiefs. The receivers, the offensive tackles, the pass rush — all of it is under a critical eye heading into the remainder of the schedule. When thinking about the Chiefs’ lack of sacks, […]
full_text: (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Coming out of the Kansas City Chiefs ’ 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks , there was plenty to be concerned about with the Chiefs. The receivers, the offensive tackles, the pass rush — all of it is under a critical eye heading into the remainder of the schedule. When thinking about the Chiefs’ lack of sacks, one player comes to mind: defensive tackle Chris Jones, who has half a sack this year, three quarterback hits and just one tackle for loss through six games. Which can be fixed? | The Athletic “Room for progression, I think, so far,” Jones said. “It’s about getting better every game. Haven’t reached my sack number. I think I’ve got point-five of a sack right now. It’s all good. It’s not how you start. It’s how you finish.” The good news for Jones is he still has time to rewrite this season’s narrative if he produces his typical splash plays. So far, though, there hasn’t been much on-field evidence that better days are coming. There’s no backup plan for when the league’s top-paid defensive tackle isn’t producing like himself. The Chiefs have no choice but to keep Jones in his current role, while hoping he can recapture some of his previous magic. ‘We’ve had the right conversations’: Mahomes discusses report Chiefs kicked Simmons from meeting | KCTV5 “Stuff like that doesn’t really bother me,” Mahomes said of the report, “because I’m so in the moment and in the team. When you’re in this building, you don’t even really hear stuff like that unless (Chiefs Vice President of Football Communications Brad Gee) tells you that stuff.” Simmons, who has dealt with a back injury since the middle of August, was placed on injured reserve a day after the alleged incident, which Mahomes did not deny. “We’ve had the right conversations now. We’re moving in the right direction,” said Mahomes, who in his 10th season with the Chiefs is also a team captain. “You have to have hard conversations at some point and I think we’ve had those. We’ve had great conversations after, and we’re moving in the right direction and that’ll be great for the team.” Kansas City Chiefs just gained a bit of an advantage against the Denver Broncos in the worst way for Week 8 | A to Z Sports The Broncos do not throw the ball well downfield. They don’t do that well with Waddle. Add in that Waddle may be out, and this could be huge for the Chiefs. Next Gen Stats show that quarterback Bo Nix was highly effective on short passes, connecting on 11 of 13 attempts under 10 air yards for 114 yards and a touchdown. However, he completed only four of 12 deeper throws for 108 yards. Notably, 66.2% of Nix’s passing yards came after the catch, bringing his season total to 64.4%, the second-highest mark in the league behind Jalon Daniels of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Chiefs’ Travis Kelce, Patrick Mahomes had harsh words for Justin Tucker in 2024 | The Kansas City Star “But me and Pat, we’ve been having the same mentality for this game all week long. And it was you’ve got to go in there and have the right mindset and we just weren’t in a joking mood. We were ready to get after it and So Justin, sorry if we took it to a level that you didn’t think it’d get to. If you’re gonna be a (jerk), I promise you I can one-up you every time.” Mahomes said at the time that he wasn’t surprised Tucker pulled the stunt. “I’ve had like seven years of kind of doing that same warmup routine, and there’s only been, I think, like three occasions where there’s been a kicker that … wasn’t necessarily moving out of the way or kind of sharing the field in the right way,” Mahomes said at the time on 96.5 The Fan. “And it was in Baltimore all three times, so he does little stuff I think to try to get under our skin.” ‘The Chiefs don’t scare me’: Packers star does not hold back on Patrick Mahomes and Co. | Yahoo! Sports “The Chiefs don’t—they don’t scare me. Like, watching that game, I’m not—I was not scared,” Parsons declared on The Edge. He then revealed that his lack of fear is because he doesn’t feel Mahomes has a weapon on offense that can take the top off of a defense vertically and went on to call out Chiefs wide receiver Xavier Worthy personally. “They need someone to be able to take the top off… We have to stop this madness. Just cuz you buy Tyreek Hill speed don’t mean you buying Tyreek,” Parsons said of Worthy. Your speed could be efficient, but people forget Tyreek’s strong. And it’s not even just his speed. Reek was stopping on the dime.” Around the NF L Winless Chargers sticking with Mike McDaniel as offensive playcaller | ESPN “We’re very confident in Mike and his talent, his work ethic and his ability,” Harbaugh told reporters, according to The Athletic. “We continue to be.” Harbaugh made the decision after the organization’s self-scouting over their bye week. “I feel like every stone, any part that we could look to better, that’s the way we responded,” Harbaugh said. New study estimates 75 percent of former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 had CTE | Pro Football Talk A new study from JAMA Network Open by researchers at Boston University, Mass General Brigham, and the Concussion & CTE Foundation has found that an estimated 75 percent of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE. “Many cases may have been early stage at the time of death and possibly symptom free,” the paper said, via Shwetha Surendran of ESPN. That observation speaks to one of the basic realities of CTE. It’s unknown how many people have it. And it’s no surprise that the vast majority of former NFL players who die with CTE symptoms are later determined to have had CTE. Josh Downs landing spots after Colts WR reportedly asks out, Indy continues fire sale | CBS Sports Wide receiver Josh Downs has requested a trade, per ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler. Downs is in the final year of his rookie deal and has reportedly fetched interest from multiple teams. With the Colts rebuilding, he seems to want out now. “It is what it is,” Downs told reporters in the Colts locker room on Wednesday, per The Athletic. “I’m here today, but whatever comes my way comes my way.” Downs has caught 26 passes for a team-high 307 yards and zero touchdowns in seven games this season. He and Keenan Allen, along with tight end Tyler Warren, have been shouldering the load in the passing game with Alec Pierce sidelined by an ankle injury. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Third-down failures doomed the Chiefs’ offense in Seattle No phase of the offense was good, but the Chiefs’ inability to sustain drives and convert on third downs doomed them. The Chiefs converted just three of 11 third downs, which helped them muster only a field goal in a game where each team had just eight total offensive drives. With so few possessions, every third down carried extra weight, and while the Chiefs converted two fourth downs, third-down issues stalled drives and kept them from even coming close to the end zone.
