title: Miami Dolphins: Malik Willis problem solved, well, at least for one week
summary: I slightly altered the lyrics to “Friday, I’m in love” by The Cure! Verse 1 I don’t care if Monday’s blueTuesday’s grey and Wednesday tooThursday I don’t care about youIt’s Sunday Malik, I’m in love Verse 2 Monday you can fall apartTuesday, Wednesday break my heartThursday doesn’t even startIt’s Sunday Malik, I’m in love From […]
full_text: I slightly altered the lyrics to “Friday, I’m in love” by The Cure! Verse 1 I don’t care if Monday’s blue Tuesday’s grey and Wednesday too Thursday I don’t care about you It’s Sunday Malik, I’m in love Verse 2 Monday you can fall apart Tuesday, Wednesday break my heart Thursday doesn’t even start It’s Sunday Malik, I’m in love From the 1992 album “Wish” I hope someone else hasn’t said this and I will profusely apologize to those who have but I am digging the home uniforms on the road! I have avoided walking underneath ladders and spilling salt. I am now compelled to beg you all to watch the old comedy ”Used Cars” starring Kurt Russell where another main character is majorly superstitious. Pure genius! Without further ado….. My thoughts on Malik’s performance against the NY Jets. To quote Christopher Walken playing the Continental “Wowwie wow wow! This calls for the……wait for it….Champaign!” ok, the photo isn’t from the Continental but I love Walken, so there. This is the good Malik, the one us Phins’ fans have been waiting for. I will humbly refer you all to my last column “How to solve a problem like Malik?” Now since I know that Jeff Hafley and Malik Willis read my column (ha) because Malik took SOME of my advice to heart and to mind. DIGRESSION BEFORE PROCESSION Before my hero worship of Malik’s techniques (rhymes!) commences, I must note: that late hit on Malik was such a cowardly hit, but had that been Tua on the receiving end, he would have died. Malik might secretly be Luke Cage(look it up – one of my favorite Marvel characters). That hit barely fazed him. What a badass kung fu master! I was in shock on how stout he is and how he just brushed that dirty hit off. It was like a 5-year-old child hitting him. Very zen!!! That “shock absorption” was worth millions to this organization and for that alone Sullivan gets major kudos. That said, since I love Malik, I need him to survive and thrive. Malik, make you the one and only Malik! Don’t take the big hits that other mobile QBs took e.g. Francis Jean Tarkenton, Randall Cunningham, Lamar Jackson, Archie Manning, Michael Vick. All those dudes took big hits to their upper body and lower body. I see scrambling QBs as analogous to riding motorcycles on the city streets. Sooner or later if you scramble too much, you’re gonna take a big hit involving strong kinetic energy from yourself AND the person that hits you (meaning double the kinetic energy), meaning it is gonna hurt with significant potential for short term and long-term damage. Never forget the hits are CUMULATIVE. that said, Malik blowing up Minkah at the pylon WAS LEGENDARY! OBSESSION WITH PROCESSION Somethings we know that happen with the earth that we can measure but cannot control: The earth orbits the Sun The earth spins on its axis giving us day and night. As the earth spins, it also wobbles slightly every 23,000 years or so. That is called Procession. Some things we know that happen with Malik that we can measure AND that he can control He has elite NFL throwing strength He has elite NFL speed. He made those pocket “take-offs” look easy. Not easy. He can vary his delivery using change of speeds and arm angles. He has the build of a NFL linebacker. To the game! There were throws on the first drive and others against the Jets where Malik threw it perfectly. PERFECTLY! His weight was forward and the football went where it was aimed. Just like I said on my previous column. In football, your feet are as equally important as your hands. Ask any offensive tackle. The whole “west coast” offense is based on the QB’s feet position. The QB reads “deep, then intermediate, then short (check down)” with his feet rotating and dictating where he’s throwing the ball. If his feet are at 45 degrees, he’s generally throwing to the TE or WR but on possession routes. I watched Joey Harrington (remember him?) give a great demo on the West Coast offense back in the day. Back to the good Malik, he was making the QUICK throws on that first drive. It was very similar (like I mentioned in my last column) to the preseason game where Malik matriculated us down the field. Just a thing of beauty! Where I got nervous, is on that first drive, when Malik held it for an extra beat and hit Dulcich for the big seam completion. But I am sure you noticed, that he was in rhythm. One, two, three—throw!!!! All the simple but proven techniques work. I cannot also go any further without talking about the o-line and TE work. They made things happen but more importantly, they fit in the rhythm of the offense. Destroying defense lines in the mode of the 1970s Dolphins is glorious, but that isn’t necessary if things are in rhythm. And the whole offense was “on-time and on-target.” Dang near impossible to stop. This is a pattern that I like seeing. This is something to build upon. We may have won ourselves away from Jeremiah Smith but we now know Malik CAN do it. Let’s some positive karma his way!
author: Paulie Dorsal

title: One win does not a season make, but it sure does keep it from being a waste
summary: The Miami Dolphins won their first game of the 2026 NFL season this past weekend, beating the New York Jets in Week 7. The 28-25 victory improved Miami to 1-5 for the year. One win through seven weeks is not something about which fans should be bragging – but at least the Dolphins are not […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 25: Ollie Gordon II #0 of the Miami Dolphins reacts after winning the game against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on October 25, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins won their first game of the 2026 NFL season this past weekend, beating the New York Jets in Week 7. The 28-25 victory improved Miami to 1-5 for the year. One win through seven weeks is not something about which fans should be bragging – but at least the Dolphins are not the Los Angeles Chargers. There was talk throughout the summer and into this season – even up until the end of the Jets game – that the Dolphins might be the first team to go 0-17 for a season. There were analysts who could not see a way for Miami to win a game this year, and they had practically written off the Dolphins. “Obviously, you could feel the energy and the excitement,” head coach Jeff Hafley said on Monday. “It’s what I thought, there’s a lot of young guys, a lot of this team has never won an NFL game. So a lot of it today, it’s their first Monday. I mean, I didn’t even have to give a victory Monday, because most of the players on our team don’t even know what a victory Monday is. They’re too young. But you could see the energy and the excitement and the confidence.” One win does not a season make, but it sure does feel good. And it makes sure this season is not a waste. Miami has the youngest roster in the NFL. They are a team that stripped the franchise to the bare bones: roster, coaching staff, front office, everything. This is a complete reset for the Dolphins, and one that was needed. Miami had spent years building a team based on speed, pre-snap motion, and creating mismatches. They added high-priced veterans to both the offense and defense in an effort to win now. But the wins did not come. Miami has not won a playoff game since 2000. Think about it like this. The Jets have the longest playoff appearance drought in the major North American leagues, the NFL, Major League Baseball, National Hockey League, and National Basketball Association. The Jets have not seen the postseason since the 2010 season, giving them 15 straight years without making it to the playoffs. The Dolphins’ playoff winless streak is 10 years longer than that. Miami has made cameo appearances in the playoffs, but their last win came under head coach Dave Wannstedt. Nick Sabin, Cam Cameron, Tony Sparano, Joe Philbin, Adam Gase, Brian Flores, and Mike McDaniel could not get the Dolphins a single postseason victory. Not a Super Bowl run, not an AFC Championship Game appearance. Just a win. One single Wild Card round victory – shut out. It appears, with this rebuild, owner Stephen Ross decided to no longer put a bandaid on his team and hope it stopped the hemorrhaging. The Dolphins have completely reset the team and now, it is as matter of execution. And execute the team did in Week 7. For one game in a season that will be filled with growing pains, the Dolphins looked like a mature team. They put a complete performance together, they withstood a lull in the middle of the game, and they made the plays that mattered when they mattered most. The offense put points on the board, bent but did not break on defense, and they make special teams showed up. One win does not a season make, but one win can keep the season from being a waste. The Dolphins are a team that is learning. They are adjusting to the speed of the league. They are working on their communication. They are adjusting to new roles, new assignments, and new responsibilities. They are experiencing the complex looks, schemes, and systems teams in the NFL routinely use every snap. They Dolphins are becoming a better team through their struggles. “When I watch the tape with them, it’s win or lose, we got to be real with each other and turn on the tape,” Hafley said. “And when you watch the tape, it’s always nice to put the result aside, win or lose, and just focus on what we did well, what we need to do better, and move on…The guys were happy last night and there’s good energy in the building, but I think though it’s a young group, it’s a mature group and they understand that after they leave the building today it’s over and we have a really good team coming into play us at home. So we’ve got work to do and we got to get back to it.” And now, they are learning how to win. It was one game. It was against the Jets, who cannot seem to win an AFC East rivalry game. But, in the NFL, winning is hard. And the Dolphins won. That means something. Wide receiver Malik Washington explained, “I think for us it’s somewhat of a confidence boost; I think we’re going to operate business as usual, whether we won or lost. We’re going to come in, we’re going to work, we’re going to see what details we need to clean up. But this is somewhat of a confidence boost to know like, hey, we can do this and we can keep pushing forward. So I’m excited to see us do it again this Sunday.” Rookie safety Michael Taaffe added, “I think the win was awesome. I think it was really cool for us. So fun to see all of our hard work come to fruition. But I gotta credit our coaching staff and the leaders on the team because today it felt like every other Monday. We’re not going to change, we’re not going to be somebody different. We’re going to look at how we need to improve and we’re going to say good job about the plays that we did well on. And so I thought that was really cool because I’ve been on other teams that aren’t like that. Sometimes the problems are masked by the result. And so they did a really good job today of not masking the problems just because we got a win and showing, hey, we need to get better. And in order to win against New England next week, we got to do things to correct. And so I think they did a really good job with that.” This team is learning. They are growing. They are correcting their mistakes. And, for at least one weekend, they are winning. This team is getting better, they are figuring it out, and they are setting themselves up for a better future. One game. It is not going to suddenly change the direction of the season. But, it was the first taste of victory for these players and this team. This is not a 0-17 team. This is a team that, for all their struggles and a steep learning curve, will remember this feeling, they will remember what it was like to win, and they will want it even more. One win does not a season make, but for this team it sure makes sure the season was not a waste.

title: Understanding Brian Flores’ Blitz-Heavy Scheme
summary: The Minnesota Vikings under defensive coordinator Brian Flores run a unique scheme that has become a hot topic around the league after dominating every opponent en route to a 6-0 start for the Vikings. It is a blitz-heavy scheme but it’s not about simply dialing up pressure and hoping not to get burned. It’s Not […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Eric Wilson #55 of the Minnesota Vikings celebrates with Blake Cashman #51 against the Indianapolis Colts during the first quarter of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings under defensive coordinator Brian Flores run a unique scheme that has become a hot topic around the league after dominating every opponent en route to a 6-0 start for the Vikings. It is a blitz-heavy scheme but it’s not about simply dialing up pressure and hoping not to get burned. It’s Not Just About Rushing the Passer The first thing to know about Flores’ blitz-heavy scheme is it’s not just about rushing the passer, it’s a total defensive philosophy designed to stop the run and pass, dictate the terms of engagement, and make execution for the offense more difficult- forcing mistakes. There are several intertwined elements to what is really a unique scheme in the NFL at the moment, which is rare. Foundational Elements and Principles The foundation of Brian Flores’ scheme is a five (or more) man front paired with a secondary playing zone coverage. That is what you are likely to see on around 80% of the Vikings’ defensive plays. A 5+ Man Attacking Front The defensive front operates an attacking, aggressive style, with defensive linemen penetrating gaps and linebackers blitzing and twisting. This contrasts with other schemes where defensive linemen are tasked with defending a gap-and-a-half or two gaps by catching blocks or taking on double-teams to keep linebackers clean. Edge rushers are tasked with setting edges, rushing the passer, or dropping into coverage. Beyond that, Flores will often place or walk-up other defenders to the line of scrimmage, either bringing or simulating additional pressure. The key in all of this is to pressure the quarterback and offense both physically and mentally- and not just occasionally but every down. Zone Coverage On the back end, the Vikings play a variety of zone coverages, frequently disguised pre-snap, and also man coverage on rare occasions. This contrasts with the man coverage that has typically accompanied blitzing fronts in the past. One key here is that the zone shell coverage is better able to prevent or limit the explosive plays that can result when a blitz doesn’t get home in time. The other key is that the coverages vary and can be difficult (or impossible) for a quarterback to differentiate pre-snap and often early post-snap as well. Numbers, Angles, Matchups- and Chaos The object of every football play or scheme is to create advantages in numbers (players), angles, and/or matchups. Brian Flores’ scheme is no different in that regard. But the high blitz rate on every down and the variability of blitz packages and coverages adds a degree or two of difficulty for opposing quarterbacks and offenses to deal with that can wear them down mentally as well as physically over the course of a game. Flores’ pressure packages are designed to either create a free (unblocked) rusher by bring more numbers in a given space than the offense has blockers; and/or by creating angles that give defenders an advantage over their blockers; and/or by creating matchup advantages by forcing typically weaker blockers such as tight ends or running backs to block the Vikings’ edge rushers or blitzing linebackers. Flores also uses numbers, such as 8-man fronts, to confuse offensive protection plans. Flores may end up actually rushing anywhere from three to eight men in such fronts, but which are coming and which are dropping is a constant struggle for offenses to identify. And even post-snap which players rush and which drop can be dictated by the blocking scheme employed. Deception and trickery are part of Flores’ scheme in this regard, as defenders may rush two steps to see if they are blocked or not and those that draw a lineman may then drop into coverage- leaving the lineman blocking nobody- while the ones that don’t draw a blocker continue their rush. Add to that twists and games by the linebackers and defensive linemen and it becomes even more difficult to defend. No one runs double-mug alignments more than the Vikings. Most teams use these presentations on 3rd Downs, but Minnesota will use theirs on any down. When Brian Flores wants to use a double-mug on a passing down, he typically tries to isolate the RB with a Center or Guard… pic.twitter.com/pVgqc2A4zb — Cody Alexander (@The_Coach_A) October 13, 2026 On the backend, the Vikings play a variety of zone coverages that are designed to both takeaway deep passes while also making underneath passing more difficult. The typical offensive counter to a blitz is to employ a ‘hot’ route, or a receiver running a quick route such as a slant or out or a screen that gives the quarterback a preplanned option in the event of a blitz. Or sometimes against man coverage the quarterback may throw a deep route hoping his guy comes down with it- particularly if there is a mismatch in his favor. Using a zone coverage shell makes that a guessing game as a quarterback is unlikely to know if his receiver is or will be open by the time the pressure arrives. Zone coverage also differs from man coverage in that defenders have eyes on the quarterback while man coverage defenders are focused on the receiver. That can make hitting hot routes more difficult as defenders clue in on the target by watching the quarterback. Defenders also know based on the blitz call and offensive formation where the hot route is likely to be – and can look to shut that option down. And the variety of zone coverages- along with presnap disguises- forces a quarterback to try to read the coverage post-snap as the pressure in coming- which can lead to mistakes or holding the ball too long. Brian Flores's defense in Minnesota has become synonymous with all-up alignments and max pressure. But there is nuance to how he attacks protections; he doesn't treat every situation like a nail to hammer. Against the Colts, he shows this with a boundary overload that gets… pic.twitter.com/soAVmcmDe7 — Cody Alexander (@The_Coach_A) October 28, 2026 On running plays, stacking the line of scrimmage can also complicate run blocking assignments, overload blockers, clog rushing lanes, and either bring down the ball carrier or contain him in a small space until more defenders arrive to make the tackle. Fitting the run is the cultural backbone of any defense. It is non-negotiable. Everyone has to show up in the fit. Minnesota is currently 9th in Run DVOA with the #1 EPA/Run (-.230). Only Jacksonville has a lower YPC than the Vikings' 3.5 (FTN). The clip is a great… pic.twitter.com/LXYewiJZdM — Cody Alexander (@The_Coach_A) October 28, 2026 A lot of attention on Flores and blitz scheme/rate – especially after a historic outing vs DJ17… but watch some of this gorgeous run defense from Vikings yesterday Levi Drake Rodriguez #50 & Van Ginkel #43 – edges being set and LDR squeezing the play from backside. Gorgeous.. pic.twitter.com/GtVos5dHj6 — Ben Fennell (@BenFennell_NFL) October 26, 2026 Below is an excellent video outlining some of the main concepts Brian Flores employs as part of his scheme. Setting the Terms of Engagement Brian Flores’ uniquely aggressive blitz-heavy scheme allows him to set the terms of engagement, creating a playbook advantage as well. Opposing offenses are forced to react to what Flores and the Vikings defense is doing, rather than dictating the terms of engagement themselves. The constant threat of pressure on every down through various blitz packages can limit opposing offense’s gameplan and playbook. Some plays and concepts simply won’t work very well against Flores’ scheme. Equally, Flores’ pressure packages can limit protection plans and route combinations. By forcing opposing offenses to adapt to Flores’ unusual scheme or pay the price, it adds a degree of difficulty not normally encountered on…

full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions plays against the Green Bay Packers at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings and Detroit Lions released their first injury reports in advance of their Sunday afternoon matchup at Ford Field. Here they are. Minnesota Vikings Player Name Position Injury Wednesday Thursday Friday Injury Designation Donovan Jackson* LG Knee DNP DNP DNP IR-OUT Joe Huber* LG Knee DNP Aaron Jones* RB Knee DNP Brian O’Neill* RT Knee LP Detroit Lions Player Name Position Injury Wednesday Thursday Friday Injury Designation Kerby Joseph* S Knee LP Ennis Rakestraw Jr.* CB Ankle LP Jacob Saylors RB Neck LP Jahmyr Gibbs* RB Shoulder DNP Aiden Hutchinson* DE NIR-Rest DNP Alim McNeil* DT NIR-Rest DNP Penei Sewell* LT NIR-Rest DNP Amon-Ra St. Brown* WR Ankle DNP Tyleik Williams* DT Illness DNP D.J. Wonnum* DE NIR-Rest DNP Injury Report Terms and Glossary FP = Full participant in practice. LP = Limited participant in practice. DNP = Did not participate in practice. NIR = Not injury related. PUP = Physically unable to participate list. IR = Injured reserve. Note: only starters on IR are listed. Player Name* = Starter. Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day. Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. Notes on Injured Players For the Lions, Kerby Joseph had his 3-week window to return from the PUP list opened this week, but he is unlikely to play on Sunday. Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown did not practice Wednesday with shoulder and ankle injuries, respectively, which is something to keep an eye on the rest of the week. For the Vikings, Kevin O’Connell didn’t seem overly concerned about either Aaron Jones or Joe Huber. Jones is considered day-to-day while Huber sitting out practice on Wednesday was more precautionary than a sign he won’t play on Sunday. Brian O’Neill continues to play through a minor knee injury. Bottom line, I wouldn’t be surprised if the Vikings don’t have any injury designations on Friday. We’ll see how it plays out with injury updates tomorrow and Friday. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

title: Blake Cashman Named NFC Defensive Player of the Week
summary: The Minnesota Vikings played a football game this past Sunday. And, because it’s now Wednesday, that means it’s time for one of their players to be recognized with a weekly award from the National Football League. The league has just announced that Vikings’ linebacker Blake Cashman has been named the NFC’s Defensive Player of the […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Blake Cashman #51 of the Minnesota Vikings celebrates after a play during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings played a football game this past Sunday. And, because it’s now Wednesday, that means it’s time for one of their players to be recognized with a weekly award from the National Football League. CASH!!! 💵💵 @blockayyy has been named NFC Defensive Player of the Week. 📰: https://t.co/BSAR8c1Kns pic.twitter.com/YJd6iksx37 — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) October 28, 2026 The league has just announced that Vikings’ linebacker Blake Cashman has been named the NFC’s Defensive Player of the Week for Week 7 of the 2026 NFL season. If it seemed like Cashman was all over the place in the Vikings’ 16-10 victory over the Indianapolis Colts this past Sunday, that’s only because. . .well, he was. Cashman recorded 12 tackles on the afternoon, including eight solo tackles and two tackles for loss. He also had two quarterback sacks (a career high), three quarterback hits, and four passes defended. It was the twentieth game of his NFL career with at least ten tackles, and his sixteenth since joining the Vikings. Sunday’s game was also the seventeenth straight game where Cashman recorded at least seven tackles, which is the longest current streak in the NFL and the longest streak for a Viking dating back to at least 1987. He’s the first player to have two sacks and four passes defended in a game since Alex Brown of the Chicago Bears did so in 2005, and the first player since at least 1982 (when the NFL first started recording sacks) to have at least twelve tackles, two sacks, and four passes defended in a game. Seems like a pretty solid outing, all things considered. We’re now seven weeks into the season, and this is the fifth week where a member of the Vikings has been recognized with a weekly award. The only weeks where a Viking was not recognized were Week 1 when they defeated the Packers and Week 6 when they were on their bye week. Cornerback Isaiah Rodgers, return specialist Myles Price, and kicker Will Reichard were named NFC Special Teams Players of the Week in Weeks 2, 3, and 4, respectively (with Price being named the NFC’s Special Teams Player of the Month for September for good measure), with cornerback Byron Murphy being recognized as the NFC’s Defensive Player of the Week in Week 5. Congratulations to Blake Cashman for being named the NFC’s Defensive Player of the Week for Week 7 of the 2026 NFL season!

title: Week 7 Observations: Unconvincingly Undefeated
summary: “A win is a win.” “You are what your record says you are.” As I took my dog for the traditional postgame walk on Sunday, those two statements served as a mental shield against a bombardment of negative thoughts about the Minnesota Vikings’ 6-0 start. This is the fourth time the Vikings have started 6-0 […]
full_text: “A win is a win.” “You are what your record says you are.” As I took my dog for the traditional postgame walk on Sunday, those two statements served as a mental shield against a bombardment of negative thoughts about the Minnesota Vikings’ 6-0 start. This is the fourth time the Vikings have started 6-0 since 2000, and this is the most worried I’ve been about any of them. In 2000, it didn’t seem out of sorts at all, despite rookie Daunte Culpepper leading the offense, given the successes of 1998 and 1999. In hindsight, I should have been more concerned about 2003, but a more experienced Culpepper and prime Randy Moss justified optimism. 2009 was exactly what it was supposed to be, and only bad luck kept us from a Super Bowl appearance. We did thoroughly outplay the eventual champion New Orleans Saints, after all. The usual group of national talking heads who give the Vikings the Rodney Dangerfield treatment whenever the team is putting together a strong season are up to their typical antics. The consensus view: “Elite defense. Offense can’t be trusted. The moment it needs to shoulder the burden and win a game, it’ll fall apart. The whole thing is built on sand. The Vikings will be the Vikings.” What’s unusual is how I reacted. In the past, I rolled my eyes and dismissed it all—just their biases running wild. Haters gonna hate. I convinced myself that whatever concerns were raised were, at best, exaggerated and, at worst, pure fantasy. This time it’s different. While I’m not going anywhere near booking a seat on their stupid “fraud train,” I’m not opposed to giving them a fair hearing, even if it goes against my wishes. They may have a valid point. It sucks, but it has to be done. I’ll get the good news out of the way before it gets depressing. ANOTHER DEFENSIVE GEM If you’re looking for another extensive write-up that heaps praise on Brian Flores and the defense, this isn’t it. Sure, Blake Cashman and Dallas Turner solidified their First-Team All-Pro resumes. And that doesn’t even touch on the terrific seasons guys like Jalen Redmond, LDR, and our entire cornerback room are having. Sure, first-ballot Hall of Famer Harrison Smith reached the magical 40 INTs/20 Sacks mark in his career. Sure, they held another team to 10 points and just over 200 yards. Sure, the unit is continuing at its historic pace. While “officially” allowing only 12.3 points per game, it’s actually 11.3 if you remove the Saints’ defensive touchdown. Oh, and that includes 3 points in the 4th quarter… all season . That’s utterly ridiculous in the modern NFL era. It’s not supposed to happen, yet here we are. ESPN’s Bill Barnwell also wrote a good article about it. Now that I’ve gotten that out of the way… DON’T TRUST THE PROCESS Anyone who’s read my work since I started the gig here as a Daily Norseman contributor knows I admire Kevin O’Connell. I believed he was the one to end our perpetual suffering and deliver a Super Bowl championship. I still believe so. But… that doesn’t mean changes aren’t needed. KOC isn’t going to give up play-calling duties. I don’t believe that’s realistic, especially given what happened with the Denver Broncos this season. Sean Payton gave them to offensive coordinator Davis Webb. It didn’t work, and Payton took them back. It’s a mess. KOC is from the Kyle Shanahan/Sean McVay School. It ain’t happening. But that doesn’t mean the day-to-day game planning, strategic responsibilities, and processes can’t be altered. Move people around. Bring fresh insights from different situations. Bring in an outside voice. Drill down on predictability in the scheme and situational play-calling. Mix things up. What’s the worst that could happen? We land in a situation where our kicker has scored more than the rest of the offense? Wait a minute… We only know what we know. Right now, we know the 2026 Vikings offense is worse than the 2025 version in nearly every major statistical category through six games. If I had told you that before Week 1, would anyone believe we’d be sitting at 6-0? And I know I’m sick of these headlines: Kevin O'Connell: We're confident we're not far off offensively. https://t.co/aJUYHPHuih — ProFootballTalk (@ProFootballTalk) October 26, 2026 I’ve collected the excuses, and I’m all stocked up. The atrocious first series, when the Vikings ruined another great Myles Price return, foreshadowed another rough day for the offense against another statistically porous defense. And before I hear it in the comments: Yes, Sunday’s game would have looked different if Jauan Jennings had made that difficult catch and scored, and if the questionable (and unnecessary) holding call hadn’t negated the big Jordan Addison play late in the game. Like against the Saints, we just need to hold onto the ball. But there comes a time when it has to happen. It’s Week 7. The final game in October is over. Every team deals with injuries. You don’t sign a proven veteran quarterback in March and tell the press: “You know, we hope to be able to score multiple touchdowns in a game consistently by November. That’s the goal.” You’d be rightly laughed out of the building. I’m pretty sure OTAs/minicamps and the preseason are there to make sure you hit the ground running in Week 1. And I want to be clear: this is not just about Kyler Murray. Not even close. Yes, he isn’t getting the ball downfield and appears to have missed a few big-play opportunities. That’s more evidence the issues run far deeper. Since Week 17 of the 2024 season, the Vikings’ passing offense has ranked among the least efficient and productive. In those 25 games, the team has averaged about 188 passing yards per game, well below the NFL average. I don’t care if your quarterback is Uncle Rico; that’s inexcusable given the offensive weapons this team has. This makes me want to puke: the Minnesota Vikings are only undefeated team left on early downs this season, their offense: #32 with 29% success rate #32 with 18% of plays gain a 1st down #32 with 24.0% of plays gain 7+ yards 62% of its series reach 3rd down #1 most in the NFL — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) October 27, 2026 Kwesi Adofo-Mensah took the blame for the J.J. McCarthy/Sam Darnold catastrophe. Now Nolan Teasley has shipped McCarthy out for a couple of AMC Theatre movie vouchers. Let’s hope Groundhog Day isn’t playing. Darnold won the Super Bowl last season. After stopping in for a cup of coffee and a few quick pleasantries, McCarthy just beat the Houston Texans on the road and has two straight games with 240+ passing yards (in just five quarters). It’s been over a year since the Vikings managed that over eight full quarters. This is my favorite (and by “favorite,” I mean the equivalent of pulling my nails out with pliers): Malik Nabers and J.J. McCarthy already have a better connection than Justin Jefferson and J.J. McCarthy 😳 pic.twitter.com/fJz57q083w — Underdog (@Underdog) October 25, 2026 I’d absolutely love to hear someone try to explain that one away. “IF” HAS OFFICIALLY ENTERED THE CHAT For the past few weeks, I’ve framed the issues on offense as not a matter of “if” things will turn around, but “when.” Now? Far too close to neck-and-neck for my liking. It was only a matter of time, I told myself. I mean, look at the defenses we’re playing. They’re bad! Here comes the 45-point onslaught! Nope. Then last week. Everyone healthy. We’re at home. Murray ascending. Momentum building. The Colts just lost to the winless Tennessee Titans. Morale in the toilet. Practically their entire secondary was banged up. It’s go time! Nope. Can it still happen? Sure. This team has too much offensive talent. But unlike my view a month ago, it’s no longer inevitable. This could be who we are. If so, you can kiss any Super Bowl dreams goodbye. Watching the Seattle Seahawks’ defense annihilate the Chiefs on Sunday night made me genuinely wonder whether we could reach 9 points and 150 total yards of offense with how we’re playing. Then again, I could also see our defense hold…

title: Patriots have plenty of familiarity with Dolphins’ new quarterback
summary: Despite being in his fifth year in the NFL, Malik Willis has not yet faced off against the New England Patriots in his career. That will change on Sunday, when his Miami Dolphins will host their division rivals at Hard Rock Stadium. Given their apparent lack of history with one another, one could assume the […]
full_text: Despite being in his fifth year in the NFL, Malik Willis has not yet faced off against the New England Patriots in his career. That will change on Sunday, when his Miami Dolphins will host their division rivals at Hard Rock Stadium. Given their apparent lack of history with one another, one could assume the Patriots are unfamiliar with Willis. That is not the case. Back in 2022, he entered the league under none other than current New England head coach Mike Vrabel. The Titans, who were coached by Vrabel at that time, selected Willis in the third round of the draft out of Liberty. And while he never developed into a viable starting option in his two years in Tennessee, his former coach has kept a close eye on him and his career ever since. “Malik’s continued to develop, and that’s the thing that I’m proud of him for,” Vrabel said earlier this week. “I know that he should be proud of himself to continue to battle and go to Green Bay. I try to stay in communication with him, tell him congrats and that I’m happy for him, and then he gets a deal in Miami.” Willis was the third QB off the board in the 2022 draft, and regarded as a possible successor to Titans starter Ryan Tannehill. He did end up starting three games during his rookie season, but his performance were not up to the standard of a team hoping to make the playoffs; he ended up ceding the No. 2 position to future Patriot Joshua Dobbs down the stretch. When the Titans drafted Will Levis in the second round the following year, his fate was essentially sealed. He ended up playing just 22 snaps his sophomore season, and was traded to Green Bay in August 2023. Once out of Tennessee, his career started trending up again. He was still no full-time starter but did look promising whenever asked to step in for Jordan Love — so much so that Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley took him to Miami with him when he was named Dolphins head coach earlier this year. Since signing a three-year, $67.5 million contract in March, Willis has not necessarily set the league ablaze. He has gone 87-of-151 for 1,057 yards with four touchdowns and four interceptions, plus three rushing touchdowns, while the Dolphins lost five of six games and are ranked toward the bottom of the league in several metrics. And yet, Mike Vrabel sees him making strides and starting to play to his natural abilities. “He’s very talented,” he said. “He’s got a strong arm, can throw at different platforms. He’s a strong runner. I think he’s starting to see things a little quicker, a little clearer, just as he’s developed in the NFL.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: A.J. Brown not making excuses as he works back from injury
summary: The production has not been there for A.J. Brown since returning to the field from a high ankle sprain. Through two games, Brown has hauled in just six of 16 targets for 75 yards. That included him dropping multiple passes in his first game back against the Jets. “I’m trying to put my best foot […]
full_text: The production has not been there for A.J. Brown since returning to the field from a high ankle sprain. Through two games, Brown has hauled in just six of 16 targets for 75 yards . That included him dropping multiple passes in his first game back against the Jets. “I’m trying to put my best foot forward. I know obviously I’m working through something, but it’s no excuses. I made none in the first week I was out there,” Brown said. “The things I can control, I try to control. That’s the only thing. I don’t look at anything as positive or negative, if that’s what you’re looking for. It’s information.” After playing two games in five days, Brown said he was feeling “OK” physically. The 29-year-old expectedly appeared to be working his way back to full explosiveness Thursday night. “Yeah, sometimes. Sometimes I see it, and sometimes I’m pushing through,” Brown said. “None of that stuff even matters. I’m out here, so I’m going.” While Brown did not have any drops in Chicago, the receiver missed several blocks in the run game. That included failing to sustain a downfield block on a cornerback, a missed opportunity that could have helped Rhamondre Stevenson find the end zone. Brown acknowledged those mistakes Wednesday. “I won’t make any excuses. I missed a couple blocks,” he said. “I’m going to leave it at that.” The Patriots will have an opportunity to get Brown going this weekend in Miami against a Dolphins defense that has struggled against the pass. Miami’s young secondary has been part of the league’s worst pass defense this season, giving Brown and the New England offense a chance to build some momentum. Brown knows they’re close to getting there. “There’s still room for improvement. We’ve done some good things. We just got to take it to another level. All 11 guys doing the same thing at the same time to help the offense stay on the field to complete the drive,” Brown said. “We are close.” For Drake Maye, the quarterback is excited to watch Brown get going. “He’s just getting things going,” Maye said. “I think he’s a had a tough road battling IR and coming back to try and find a flow. We had a Thursday night game where’s there’s not a full week of practice. We really had our third or fourth practice out there [Wednesday] with him running and getting in the groove of the game plan. “We got to keep that big picture in mind. We got full trust in him and he’s gonna make plays. It’ll be fun to watch him when he does.”

title: Carlton Davis injury: Patriots CB ready to make return vs. Dolphins
summary: New England Patriots cornerback Carlton Davis III is ready to make his return to the field this Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. Davis initially injured his neck in the season opener against Seattle and missed the Week 2 contest against the Steelers. He came back for the following two weeks before missing the Patriots’ last […]
full_text: New England Patriots cornerback Carlton Davis III is ready to make his return to the field this Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. Davis initially injured his neck in the season opener against Seattle and missed the Week 2 contest against the Steelers. He came back for the following two weeks before missing the Patriots’ last three games. The cornerback feels his initial return was too soon, but he is now ready to go. “Just day in, day out, trying to look for ways to get better,” Davis said. “Not trying to rush the process, but really trying to be efficient, recovering, and getting back out there, being a guy that my team can depend on. “I think the worst is just sitting on the sideline, watching plays being made or being a bystander. Last year, I played in every game. This year I was looking to do the same, and it’s a bit disappointing to not be able to do that. But I’m back here and ready to go.” The Patriots secondary has not been at full force since Week 1 in Seattle. In addition to Davis, New England has played without safety Craig Woodson for one game and cornerback Christian Gonzalez for two. Now healthy, the group is excited to be back on the field together. “It’s going to be great having all the guys back, being at full power and being able to go out there and feed off each other and make plays together,” Davis said. Gonzalez, who battled an illness last week, shared he was feeling better on Wednesday. He was excited as well to get his fellow cornerback back. “It’s everything. CD is a great vet, somebody that I lean on a lot, able to talk to, pick his mind about certain things,” Gonzalez said. “He’s seen a lot of ball, so just having him back out there is amazing. So, excited to get all of us back. I think this is the first game since the first week it’s going to be all of us out there. So excited for that to get back on the field with all that.”

full_text: Even though they have already matched their total losses from last year, the New England Patriots once again look like a legitimate contender for a playoff spot in the AFC. However, in order to get there, they will have to find a way to overcome the injuries that have ravaged their roster over the first two months of the regular season. While the expectation is that they will get several players back from injured reserve at some point, they also could go for a more radical approach in hopes of improving their team and gearing up for a stretch run in 2026. title: Patriots announce date, time for Rob Gronkowski Hall of Fame induction
summary: One of the best players in NFL history will take his rightful spot in the New England Patriots’ Hall of Fame next month. Rob Gronkowski, the most productive tight end to ever wear the franchise’s uniform, will be inducted in a public ceremony on November 7. As was announced by the team on Wednesday, the […]
full_text: One of the best players in NFL history will take his rightful spot in the New England Patriots’ Hall of Fame next month. Rob Gronkowski, the most productive tight end to ever wear the franchise’s uniform, will be inducted in a public ceremony on November 7. As was announced by the team on Wednesday, the event will kick off at 1 p.m. ET and take place at the Patriot Place Plaza. The Gronk returns ‼️ Join us on 11/7 at 1:00 PM for @RobGronkowski 's HOF induction ceremony. pic.twitter.com/PSSNymQKU5 — New England Patriots (@Patriots) October 28, 2026 Gronkowski will receive the famous red jacket in his first year of eligibility, after he beat guard Logan Mankins and kicker Adam Vinatieri in a fan vote in April . The 37-year-old will become the 38th inductee since The Hall was established in 1991, and the second tight end after Ben Coates in 2008 to receive the honor. A second-round draft pick by the Patriots in 2010, Gronkowski spent the first nine seasons of his career with the organization. The Arizona product saw action in 115 regular season games and recorded 521 receptions for 7,861 yards and 79 touchdowns. He added 81 catches for 1,163 yards and 12 scores in 16 playoff contests. One of the most productive and decorated players in franchise history, Gronkowski won three of his four total Super Bowls during his time in New England — he later won another ring as a Buccaneer in 2020 — and was voted to five Pro Bowls and named All-Pro on four occasions. He also is a member of the Patriots’ All-Dynasty Team and 2010s All-Decade Team, and the NFL’s 100th Anniversary Team. “It’s just such a prestigious honor to be inducted into the Patriots Hall of Fame, especially as a first ballot,” Gronkowski said in a media call back in April. “And to do it after so many others have led the way — Tom two years ago, Julian last year, you got the Tedy Bruschis the Willie McGinests — just so many guys that are just so great. And to be in the same category as them, it is just an absolute honor. There’s no doubt about that.” The Patriots will host the Green Bay Packers at Gillette Stadium on the weekend of Gronkowski’s induction. Kickoff for the game is scheduled for 4:25 p.m. ET on Nov. 8.

title: Patriots vs. Dolphins preview: Players to watch, stats, more for Week 8
summary: Coming off their mini-bye, the New England Patriots return to their division. On Sunday, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will visit the Dolphins in Miami. The Dolphins are in the middle of a rebuild. They brought in Jeff Hafley and Malik Willis as the head coach-quarterback combo this offseason to replace the departed […]
full_text: Coming off their mini-bye, the New England Patriots return to their division. On Sunday, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will visit the Dolphins in Miami. The Dolphins are in the middle of a rebuild. They brought in Jeff Hafley and Malik Willis as the head coach-quarterback combo this offseason to replace the departed Mike McDaniel and Tua Tagovailoa, and have invested heavily in rookie talent: no team made more picks in this year’s draft than Miami’s 13. The organization is building for the future, even though there are some current growing pains. At 1-5 and ranked 30th in scoring differential thus far, the Dolphins have been one of the worst teams in the NFL this season up to that point. That said, they might be trending up. Let’s meet them. Dolphins key stats The Dolphins’ problems are reflected by their statistics. They are ranked near the bottom of the league in most major categories on both offense and defense. Dolphins Patriots Record 1-5 (4th AFCE) 4-3 (2nd AFCE) Scoring diff. -59 (30th) +17 (10th) Points /game 16.3 (30th) 22.9 (19th) Points allowed/game 26.2 (25th) 20.4 (9th) Off. yards/game 293.5 (27th) 375.0 (7th) Off. EPA/play -0.122 (29th) 0.052 (10th) Off. EPA/dropback -0.116 (28th) 0.215 (5th) Off. EPA/run -0.130 (20th) -0.200 (26th) Def. yards/game 337.7 (16th) 315.7 (10th) Def. EPA/play 0.106 (29th) 0.017 (20th) Def. EPA/dropback 0.284 (31st) 0.077 (18th) Def. EPA/run -0.115 (13th) -0.081 (22nd) Turnover diff. -3 (t-21st) -7 (31st) Giveaways 8 (t-15th) 14 (31st) Takeaways 5 (29th) 7 (20th) Offensively, the Dolphins have struggled moving the ball both through the air and on the ground. There have been flashes, but the consistency is lacking even though the team has been able to keep turnovers in a comparatively reasonable range (especially when looking to New England’s much more talented offense). On defense, a lack of takeaway has plagued the unit, as has an uneven pass rush and an inability to get off the field on third down (52.1%; 31st). The run defense has been a relative bright spot, but considering that opponents are throwing all over the Dolphins — fourth-most attempts (175), highest net yards per attempt (7.5), highest scoring percentage (49.1%) — there simply is no need to run into a veteran D-line on a regular basis. Dolphins 2026 season The Dolphins started their season with five straight losses, including the first three by multiple scores. Since then, however, they have shown some improvement. Their scoring margin of -7 over the last three games is a distinct improvement, as is being able to finally earn a victory last Sunday against the lackluster Jets. Week 1: 27-13 loss at Las Vegas Raiders (0-1) Week 2: 35-13 loss at San Francisco 49ers (0-2) Week 3: 24-10 loss vs. Kansas City Chiefs (0-3) Week 4: 15-10 loss at Minnesota Vikings (0-4) Week 5: 31-24 loss vs. Cincinnati Bengals (0-5) Week 6: Bye Week 7: 28-25 win at New York Jets (1-5) What stands out about Miami’s schedule is that it featured the last three unbeaten teams in the league — the 49ers, Chiefs and Vikings — and the toughest strength of schedule among all 32 teams (.667). Granted, the Dolphins being fairly bad played into that, but they have played, and lost to, some very good teams and beaten the worst one they have faced so far. Dolphins active roster Roster up-to-date as of Oct. 28, 5 a.m. ET | *denotes nominal starter Quarterback (2): Malik Willis* (2), Kyle McCord (14) Running back (3): Ollie Gordon II* (0), Jaylen Wright (5 | KR), Kaytron Allen (30) Fullback (1): D.J. Herman (34) Wide receiver (6): Malik Washington* (6 | PR), Chris Bell* (18), Caleb Douglas* (7), Kevin Coleman Jr. (21), Jared Wayne (86), Jalen Tolbert (1) Tight end (4): Greg Dulcich* (85), Will Kacmarek (89), Seydou Traore (83), Justin Joly (80) Offensive tackle (4): Patrick Paul* (52 | LT), Austin Jackson* (73 | RT), Caedan Wallace (77), Chukwuebuka Godrick (79) Interior offensive line (6): Kadyn Proctor* (74 | LG), Aaron Brewer* (55 | C), Jonah Savaiinaea* (71 | RG), Jarrett Kingston (62), Andrew Meyer (60), D.J. Campbell (63) Interior defensive line (4): Zach Sieler* (92), Jordan Phillips* (94), Kenneth Grant (78), Zeek Biggers (93) Defensive edge (5): Joshua Uche* (9), Chop Robinson* (44), Malik Herring (90), Rob Beal Jr. (51), Rodney McGraw (59) Linebacker (5): Jacob Rodriguez* (10), Jordyn Brooks* (20), Willie Gay Jr. (40), Jackson Woodard (42), Shaka Heyward (45) Cornerback (6): Chris Johnson* (3), Jason Marshall Jr.* (4), JuJu Brents* (8), Jaylin Simpson (32), Reese Taylor (35), Marcellas Dial Jr. (24) Safety (5): Michael Taaffe* (16), Dante Trader Jr.* (11), Zayne Anderson (23), Julius Wood (25), Kyle Louis (19) Specialists (2): Bradley Pinion (48 | P/H), LS Tucker Addington (46 | LS) The first thing that stands out about the Dolphins is their commitment to rebuilding from the ground up. As part of that process, they have six rookie starters in their lineup: wide receivers Chris Bell and Caleb Douglas and left guard Kadyn Proctor on offense, plus linebacker Jacob Rodriguez, cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe on defense. Furthermore, several of their key reserves are first-year players as well, including fullback D.J. Herman, WR4 Kevin Coleman Jr, and their entire three-man backup tight end group. How soon the Dolphins will add a quarterback to the mix will be seen. For now, however, they are riding with free agency signing Malik Willis. Willis has started all six of the team’s games since signing a three-year, $67.5 million contract to move from Green Bay to Miami alongside his head coach. In those games, he has completed 87 o f 151 pass attempts (57.6%) for 1,057 yards with four touchdowns and interceptions each. He also has been sacked 16 times and scored three rushing touchdowns. Willis is a hit-or-miss thrower with big-play potential, but overall has been uneven as evidenced by his 31st ranking among quarterbacks in EPA per play (-0.115). Part of the reason might be his supporting cast, which is missing its best player — running back De’Von Achane — and relying on a whole lot of young talent. That said, Willis’ top two receivers this year are both veterans: wide receiver Malik Washington (26/289/0) and tight end Greg Dulcich (18/213/0). At running back, meanwhile, Ollie Gordon has stepped up since Achane’s season-ending knee injury. He has carried the. ball 72 times for 339 yards and a 4.7-yard average per carry; Gordon also has scored a team-leading four times. Miami’s offensive line, meanwhile, is a collection of highly-drafted players. The only non-first- or second-round pick is center Aaron Brewer, a former undrafted free agent who started his career with Mike Vrabel’s Titans in 2020. On the other side of the ball, Miami is led by a veteran defensive line. The top players among the group are Zach Sieler and Chop Robinson, who are tied for the team lead with two sacks each. Robinson, meanwhile, has posted a team-high 20 quarterback pressures. Also high on both lists is ex-Patriot and started edge Joshua Uche, who has one quarterback takedown among his 13 pressures. The second level of the defense is led by the aforementioned Jacob Rodriguez, who has impressed since arriving in the second round of this year’s draft. His running mate off the ball is first-team All-Pro Jordyn Brooks, who signed a three-year, $48.1 million extension through 2029 this offseason. The Dolphins are banking on Rodriguez and Brooks leading their defense for years to come, and for good reason: both are very good players. The secondary doesn’t have the same consistent talent, even though it has received some solid contributions from its youngsters and veterans alike. Safety Michael Taaffe, for example, is leading the team with two interceptions and tied for the team lead with a forced fumble. Overall, however, as illustrated by the EPA per dropback ranking, the Dolphins’ pass defense has some ground to make up — and an inconsistent secondary is a big reason for that.…

title: Examining the roster ties between Patriots, Dolphins ahead of Week 8
summary: There’s a Rolodex to flip through before head coach Mike Vrabel’s New England Patriots visit head coach Jeff Hafley’s Miami Dolphins. Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, 11 players in the fold for Sunday’s AFC East matchup have been members of both locker rooms during their NFL journeys. Here’s the list of […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Uche #9 of the Miami Dolphins gets set during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s a Rolodex to flip through before head coach Mike Vrabel’s New England Patriots visit head coach Jeff Hafley’s Miami Dolphins. Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, 11 players in the fold for Sunday’s AFC East matchup have been members of both locker rooms during their NFL journeys. Here’s the list of former Patriots and former Dolphins ahead of the 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff at Hard Rock Stadium. MIAMI Jalen Reagor, wide receiver — Reagor joined the Dolphins in June and was retained on the practice squad at its formation after being released in August. The 27-year-old wide receiver spent the previous two campaigns with the Los Angeles Chargers. Before then, he appeared in 11 games for Bill Belichick’s former club in 2023 and outlasted the initial 53-man roster deadline in 2024 only to be released, signed to the practice squad and then released from the practice squad. Entering the NFL with the Philadelphia Eagles in the first round of the 2020 draft at No. 21 overall, the TCU product had been traded to the Minnesota Vikings before finding his way to Gillette Stadium. Reagor now stands 64 games and 27 starts into his career. He has caught 86 passes for 1,037 yards and four touchdowns. An additional two visits to the end zone have arrived as a kickoff and punt returner. Caedan Wallace, guard — During training camp in August, the Patriots traded Wallace to the Dolphins in a pick swap involving a 2028 sixth-rounder and a 2029 seventh-rounder. The 26-year-old Penn State product had arrived in Foxborough in the third round of the 2024 draft class at No. 68 overall. He appeared in 10 games during his previous AFC East stop, starting a pair while going between offensive tackle, guard and jumbo tight end. Wallace has since checked into six games during his time in Miami Gardens, reporting as eligible for 14 offensive snaps while also working in protection on field goals and extra points. Joshua Uche, linebacker — Selected in the second round of the 2020 NFL draft at No. 60 overall, Uche’s Patriots tenure spanned 76 tackles and 20.5 sacks. A season featuring 11.5 sacks arrived along the way for an outside linebacker who once lined up across from the red-sleeved Matthew Judon. After 58 games off the edges, the stay reached its end ahead of the trade deadline in 2024. Uche headed to the Kansas City Chiefs as a sixth-rounder in the 2026 class headed back. The 28-year-old Michigan alum moved on to the NFC East on a one-year deal last campaign before returning to the AFC East on a one-year deal in March. He has made five starts this fall and stands 82 games, 134 tackles, 22.5 sacks, three forced fumbles and two recoveries into his career. Amari Gainer, linebacker — Gainer signed to the Dolphins’ initial practice squad after being waived by the Patriots at the 53-man roster deadline. The 26-year-old outside linebacker landed on New England’s practice squad last winter and was retained on a futures contract following Super Bowl LX. Originally entering the NFL with the Las Vegas Raiders as an undrafted free agent in 2024, the former transfer from Florida State to North Carolina appeared in all 17 games during his rookie year in the AFC West and was credited with five tackles through 328 snaps on special teams and 12 snaps on defense. Marcellas Dial Jr., cornerback — Dial was claimed off waivers by Miami after being let go by New England leading up to August’s cutdown deadline. The 25-year-old cornerback by way of Georgia Military and South Carolina had been chosen by the Patriots in the sixth round of the 2024 NFL draft at No. 180 overall. He was the last selection left from that class beyond All-Pro quarterback Drake Maye. Dial would make 17 appearances and one start as a rookie while seeing 60 snaps on defense and 378 snaps on special teams. A dozen tackles and a forced fumble were registered along the way. But a torn ACL saw Dial’s 2025 season end on injured reserve in training camp. He has since appeared in two games on the other side of the division. Tucker Addington, long snapper — Between summers, falls and winters, Addington had three separate stints with the Patriots from 2022 through 2024 as longtime long snapper Joe Cardona dealt with injuries. The 29-year-old specialist’s last came as a standard elevation from the practice squad before reverting and being released. Undrafted out of Sam Houston State, Addington has also been a member of the Houston Gamblers, Dallas Cowboys, Jacksonville Jaguars, Houston Texans and Washington Commanders. He has also been in Miami Gardens on more than one occasion, too. Addington’s NFL journey includes 16 games and a trio of tackles. NEW ENGLAND Ryan Miller, wide receiver — The Patriots signed Miller to the practice squad midway through October after placing wide receiver Romeo Doubs on injured reserve with a shoulder injury. The 26-year-old went undrafted out of Furman in 2023 and spent three seasons between the 53-man roster and practice squad of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers before being claimed off waivers by the New York Giants. Miller then became a waiver claim at Hard Rock Stadium amid training camp. He has played in 30 NFL games, including six starts, while totaling 17 receptions for 254 yards and four touchdowns. His most recent TD took place in a Dolphins uniform from 77 yards out in September. Mack Hollins, wide receiver — Placed on injured reserve due to a calf injury in October, Hollins has caught 61 passes for 759 yards and two touchdowns through 19 games and 16 starts with the Patriots. The 2017 fourth-round pick out North Carolina earned a Super Bowl LII ring as a member of the Philadelphia Eagles and was later claimed off waivers by ex-Miami head coach Brian Flores & Co. A Dolphin from 2019 through 2021, Hollins served as a special teams captain before making stops with an additional three teams. The 33-year-old’s NFL career has featured 228 receptions for 2,828 yards and 17 visits to the end zone across 131 appearances. Julian Hill, tight end — The Patriots lost Hill to season-ending injured reserve in June. The 26-year-old inline tight end had agreed to terms on a three-year pact in March after not being tendered by the Dolphins as a restricted free agent. Hill spent the past three campaigns there while appearing in 45 games, including 26 starts, on the way to reeling in 33 receptions for 288 yards. The 2023 undrafted addition out of Campbell recorded 1,298 snaps on offense and 496 snaps on special teams. Tanner Conner, tight end — Conner had been among a group of tight ends in Foxborough for workouts before signing to the practice squad in September. The 28-year-old Idaho State alum entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2022. He made the Miami Dolphins’ initial 53-man roster as rookie and went on to appear in 33 games during his first AFC East stop. Finishing 2025 on the practice squad of the New York Giants before being released in August, Conner’s career includes 12 catches for 107 yards across 251 snaps on offense and 413 snaps on special teams. K.J. Britt, linebacker — The Patriots reached a one-year deal with Britt in March and the veteran linebacker agreed to remain on the practice squad after initially outlasting the 53-man roster deadline. One standard elevation has followed thus far, spanning 14 snaps in the kicking game and a tackle on a kickoff return. Selected in the fifth round of the 2021 NFL draft at No. 176 overall, Britt stands 77 games and 16 starts into a run hat began with Tampa Bay. The 27-year-old Auburn product spent last year with the Miami Dolphins and finished atop the team with 76.9 percent of the workload on special teams. His career stretches 162 tackles, half a sack, four…

title: Gayle Benson Shares Letter of Gratitude Following Saints’ Game in Paris
summary: While the New Orleans Saints did not come away with a win in Paris, the game was a tremendous success in other areas, marking a historic milestone for the franchise and the NFL’s continued efforts to expand its international presence. The event provided a unique opportunity to showcase the Saints organization, strengthen connections with international […]
full_text: PARIS, FRANCE - OCTOBER 25: A general view during the National Anthem prior to the game between the New Orleans Saints and the Pittsburgh Steelers at Stade de France on October 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images While the New Orleans Saints did not come away with a win in Paris, the game was a tremendous success in other areas, marking a historic milestone for the franchise and the NFL’s continued efforts to expand its international presence. The event provided a unique opportunity to showcase the Saints organization, strengthen connections with international fans and celebrate the rich cultural ties between New Orleans and France. Beyond the final score, the experience helped introduce the excitement and traditions of Saints football to a broader audience while further establishing the team’s presence on the global stage. Saints’ owner Gayle Benson released a letter today expressing her sincere appreciation and gratitude to everyone who played a role in bringing the league’s first game to France, recognizing the collaborative efforts that extended well beyond the football field. Dear Friends, What an extraordinary and memorable week in Paris! As we return home, I want to express my heartfelt appreciation to each of you who traveled to France to be part of this historic Saints game. Your presence made the occasion even more meaningful to me and our entire organization. I know this journey required an enormous amount of time, planning and commitment. Whether you joined us as a devoted fan, corporate partner, business leader, community advocate, or elected official, I am deeply grateful that you chose to share this special experience with us. While the outcome on the field was not what we had hoped for, we have much to be proud of from our time together. We represented the New Orleans Saints, our beloved city and the entire state of Louisiana with class and pride on an international stage. Everywhere we went, you shared the warmth, hospitality and passion that make our community so special. The week also offered valuable opportunities to strengthen the ties between Louisiana and France. Conversations among government officials, business leaders and cultural organizations opened many doors for business development, investment, tourism and cultural exchange. I look forward to seeing these relationships grow and bring lasting benefits to both our city and state. Above all, I will treasure the people: familiar faces so far from home, new friendships, thoughtful conversations and the joy of sharing this historic occasion. Your enthusiasm was a wonderful reminder that wherever the Saints play, the Who Dat nation is there with us. I also want to extend my sincere gratitude to Commissioner Roger Goodell and the National Football League for their leadership in bringing this historic game to Paris, to our gracious French hosts for their hospitality, and to everyone who worked so hard to welcome and care for those who made the trip. Football brought us together in Paris, but the memories, friendships and partnerships we built will endure well beyond the game. Thank you for cheering us on and bringing a piece of home to Paris. Your friendship, loyalty and continued belief in the New Orleans Saints and the future of our great city and state mean so much to me. It was a privilege to share this remarkable experience with you, and I will always be grateful that you were part of it. With heartfelt appreciation and warmest regards, Gayle Benson New Orleans Saints Owner & CEO

full_text: PARIS, FRANCE - OCTOBER 25: Alvin Kamara of the New Orleans Saints looks dejected after the NFL game between Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints at Stade de France on October 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Photo by Franco Arland/Getty Images) | Getty Images With a return to losing, the New Orleans Saints’ power rankings in the NFL could take a hit. NFL.com – 23 (-3) “The Saints have become a team that gives its best effort but just doesn’t seem to have enough collectively to beat most opponents. Sunday’s Paris game was certainly winnable, but when operating with a smaller margin for error, the small misses — a Daniel Carlson field goal attempt that missed wide right , a four -and-out on their final possession in a one-score game — become magnified. A complete lack of a running game (18 net yards vs. Pittsburgh) doesn’t help, either.“ Fox Sports – 25 (-1) “For a second-year coach, Kellen Moore sure feels like he’s barely clinging to his job as his team tumbles into its bye week after losing to the Steelers in Paris. The Saints have just been such a disappointment, especially offensively, which was supposed to be Moore’s specialty. And injuries (to RB Travis Etienne and rookie WR Jordyn Tyson ) are only a part of it. The Saints have now lost four of five, and their lone win was a hold-on-for-dear-life nailbiter against the Giants. And when they come out of the bye week, there are no breaks in the schedule until nearly Christmas. Things could get ugly, fast. “ Bleacher Report – 25 (-1) “Heading into 2026, the New Orleans Saints felt like a team that was poised to make a big jump. After seven weeks, it’s clear that New Orleans is still at least a year away from being a legitimate contender. Tyler Shough showed franchise-quarterback potential late in his rookie campaign, and he’s largely built on last year’s success this season. However, he hasn’t been perfect enough to consistently carry an offense that has struggled to move the ball on the ground. On Sunday, he made a couple of big red-zone mistakes that cost the Saints in a very tight contest. Defensively, New Orleans has been a total disappointment. The Saints entered Week 7 ranked 29th in yards allowed and 31st in points allowed. While they did hold the Pittsburgh Steelers to 16 points, they coughed up 343 total yards and allowed Pittsburgh to convert 10 of 16 third-down attempts. Franchise owner Gayle Benson told reporters earlier in the season that the Saints “must do better.” If things don’t start to change on the field before the end of the season, changes to the front office could come after it. — Knox ” CBS Sports – 27 (-1) “Their lack of a running game is killing this team. They are way too one-dimensional to consistently win games.” Sports Illustrated – 28 (-3) “Jordyn Tyson is still not in a place where we’re talking seriously about him being a part of the game plan. With a handful of immediate impact players having been taken immediately after Tyson, and the Saints in freefall, a broader look at the Saints’ draft strategy may soon be in order.

title: State of the NFC South: Week 7
summary: Two massive wins in the NFC South, including one of the most unlikely blowouts in a while. Here is how each team did in Week 7 Tampa Bay Buccaneers: Against all odds, the Buccaneers beat the Panthers 43-13 in Charlotte. Not sure anyone expected this result, but it is the NFC South, so maybe that’s […]
full_text: PARIS, FRANCE - OCTOBER 25: Aaron Rodgers of the Pittsburgh Steelers runs with the ball during the NFL game between Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints at Stade de France on October 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Photo by Franco Arland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Two massive wins in the NFC South, including one of the most unlikely blowouts in a while. Here is how each team did in Week 7 Tampa Bay Buccaneers : Against all odds, the Buccaneers beat the Panthers 43-13 in Charlotte. Not sure anyone expected this result, but it is the NFC South, so maybe that’s on me. This game marked the return of Baker Mayfield to the lineup, but hilariously, he only threw 11 times, completing 7 passes for 64 yards and a touchdown. And yes, he did play most of the game. Bucky Irving was the star for the Buccaneers offense, getting over 100 yards rushing and two touchdowns. I’ll talk a bit more about the Buccaneers defense in the next section. Carolina Panthers : And then we have the Panthers. This was Carolina’s worst game this season, and with the defense struggling, the offensive issues only made it worse. Bryce Young was sacked 5 times, threw two interceptions, the run game was horrible, and the Panthers fumbled once. This was one of those games Carolina should put behind them, but their first-place lead just got much smaller. Atlanta Falcons : With the upset of the week, the Falcons somehow beat the undefeated San Francisco 49ers. What made this win even more impressive for the Falcons was that they didn’t need to rely on Bijan Robinson’s rushing ability to win, which has been their recipe for success. Michael Penix had a strong game, controlling the offense and avoiding turnovers, while the defense forced turnovers that made the difference. New Orleans Saints : Due to the Buccaneers’ win, the Saints are now last in the division after their loss to the Steelers. This wasn’t as embarrassing as some of their previous losses, but it made clear once again that the season’s issues persist. What made it worse was that the Saints’ massive red-zone improvement regressed. Heading into the bye, the team must make changes across the roster, and although Kellen Moore may be safe, one more loss could end his time in New Orleans.
