title: Perfect Seahawks extend perfect season with perfect shellacking of imperfect Chiefs
summary: The Seattle Seahawks defense quieted the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday Night Football to improve to 7-0 on the not-so-young-anymore season. It was an exceptionally gratifying victory, considering — — oh, the whole team? They’re 4-3. Just the Seattle defense is undefeated. “The Dark Side” may have their moments when they look and act mortal, […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks defense quieted the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday Night Football to improve to 7-0 on the not-so-young-anymore season. It was an exceptionally gratifying victory, considering — — oh, the whole team? They’re 4-3. Just the Seattle defense is undefeated. “The Dark Side” may have their moments when they look and act mortal, but they cannot be beaten unless the call comes from the inside of the house. Specifically, in the form of three silly turnovers per game, or an unlikely fumble in their own end zone that could’ve been prevented by running straight ahead, or some equally inexcusable meltdown like tossing two picks after the two-minute warning. All those self-destructive scenarios unfolded, and they all led directly to three roundabout losses. The ’Hawks D has dropped exactly zero games all calendar year, extraordinary really, with November looming around the bend. I want to dive in today, forty percent through the season and three days after their latest preposterous triumph — not allowing an Andy Reid-Patrick Mahomes team to enter the red zone — to the statistical thoroughness that defines their dominance. There should also be time to gently touch on a potential Achilles heel. Which might be fake. It would be weblog malpractice, however, to shame the offense any further without conducting our weekly worship of the solar system’s best wide receiver. Jaxon Smith-MegatroNjigba has ascended into the national consciousness, somehow strengthened his case for repeating (!) as Offensive Player of the Year, and… there’s really nothing defenses can do about it? Double him? Okay, they’re already doing that. Triple-team him? That’s how you run out of players. For the second time in two seasons, JSN is on pace to surpass Calvin Johnson’s all-time yards receiving record. All he’s managing so far is to lead the league in yards (843), first downs (43), touchdowns (8), and yards per touch (14.7). Put another way, if the stat contains the word “downs,” “touch” or “yards,” chances are Smith-Njigba is at the top, looking down on his subjects from the type of throne no Seahawk has occupied since 2005 Shaun Alexander. With that out of the way, it’s time to shower the defense with superlatives, rinsing and repeating along the way. The Seahawks rank first or second in the following (deep breath, fill both lungs): Defensive DVOA Yards per play, 4.0 Passing yards/game, 144 Net yards/attempt, 4.4 Passing first downs/game, 7.7 Average depth of target, 6.3 yards QB knockdown percentage, 16.9 Punts per play, .10 Yards per carry, 3.5 (JAX 3.2) Pressure rate, 30.9 (MIN 35.7) Total first downs/game, 14.8 (MIN 13.2) Turnovers forced, 12 (GB 13) EPA/play, -0.17 (MIN -0.21) Third down conversion percentage, 28.0 (CHI 26.1) ANY/A, 3.5 (MIN 3.4) The list goes on, but especially after watching them against the Chiefs, you get the picture tailored swiftly. It’s a complete defense, we knew they were trouble when they walked in, with nothing but champagne problems (I’m done now, it’s safe to read again). If there’s a component important to winning defensive football, the Seahawks are at the top. They can’t be attacked through the air or the ground, they kill you on third down, and they’re coached by the best mind in the game. They’re 18 men deep. We know this because both starting safeties missed time, they rotate seven men across the d-line and their third inside linebacker is blossoming in relief of another starter. One of my favorite toy stats in the list is punts per play. The .10 mark means opponents spend ten percent of their time punting. If they run 60 plays that’s six punts. Not exactly a recipe for points. In fact, only one other team this decade (the ‘23 Browns) has posted a mark as high. Add in interceptions and fumbles, which the Seahawks cause on exactly five percent of plays, and you’re watching foes give them the ball right back fifteen percent of the time, or one out of every seven snaps. On average, the poor offense opposite Seattle runs six plays for a handful yards then doesn’t get to move the ball anymore, because they’re relieved of that duty. However. All season long there’s been a breaking point for the law firm of Witherspoon, Jones, and Williams (feat. jr. partner Nick E.). And that’s on possessions past the tenth drive. I have a pretty chart. Team Drives 1-10 Plays/drive After drive 10 Plays/drive Drives 1-10 Points/drive After drive 10 Points/drive Patriots 7.6 1.1 Cardinals 4.7 0.7 Commanders 4.2 8.3 2.3 1 Chargers 4.4 9 1.3 3.3 49ers 3.6 10 1.4 5 Broncos 5.2 2.8 1.4 3 Chiefs 6.6 0.4 TOTAL 5.1 8.4 1.3 2.9 Note: the Patriots, Cardinals and Chiefs did not have an eleventh drive. Kneeldowns are omitted. Four out of five times, past the tenth possession, Seattle’s defensive drive stats suffered substantially. The plays per drive doubled or more; the points per drive followed accordingly. In weeks 3-5, the difference was most acute. Hell, if the Seahawks never allowed an opponent to begin an eleventh drive, they might well still be authentically undefeated. It kinda sucks, but that can be laid at the feet of the offense once again. Sam Darnold & Co. dominated time of possession by 13 and 12 minutes against the Cards and Chiefs and won handily; they split it against the Commanders and Chargers, two of the NFL’s weakest teams, and barely escaped with a 1-1 record. Longer possessions for Seattle means fewer drives for everyone, which means fewer times for the opposing coordinators to scheme solutions. My working theory is not that the defense gets tired; they keep producing three-and-outs. Instead, it’s that all 32 coaching staffs employ capable men who are getting paid good money to win the chess match throughout the game. Usually from the Kyle Shanahan or Sean McVay tree. (We will never be free from them.) Thus the best place for the Seahawks offense to start and help their defensive teammates is with ball security, bringing us full circle to the inescapable topic or turnovers. Maybe it really is all about the ball. That being said, should we be worried about stale defensive game plans? Not necessarily, according to friend of the site cmikespinmove: Mike Macdonald appears to be quite aware of the value of self-scouting and breaking tendencies. You don’t get to be a defensive genius without having some off-speed pitches. McVay and Shanahan have had to tweak their offenses to stay ahead of the defense; for example, McVay ran 11 personnel 95 percent of the time in 2018 when the rest of the league was at 60 percent. He then utilized 13 personnel (three TE) a full 30 percent of the time last season, more than twice as often as the next-highest coach. Macdonald won’t go stale or run out of ideas and tactics. Finally, before we laud some predators, it should — and will be — noted that the Seahawks have already played: DVOA-leading San Francisco Mahomes’ previously undefeated Chiefs Both AFC title game participants from last season The schedule has been treacherous, and still Seattle’s three losses have famously come by a total of eight points. A pick six sank them in Washington, Darnold set himself on fire late in Denver, and a no-call-personal-foul-JSN-drop parlay prevented them from forcing overtime against the Niners. Granted, those are things that cost you games for a reason, they’re egregious errors, but they’re also not representative of the team’s overall quality. Everyone else has said this in some form or another, but dang, if you just turn it over one less time in each of those three losses and play regular sloppy instead of ultra sloppy, you’ve swept your way to 7-0 for reals and everyone is talking about how you haven’t even his your stride yet on offense. Since this is a lookback on the first 40 percent of the season, a few predators have emerged as leaders, besides JSN, Destroyer of Worlds and Wrecker of Wills. Ernest Jones and Nick Emmanwori The best thing I can say about Jones? You feel like there must be two of him on the field because…

title: How Quenton Nelson can transform the Seahawks offensive line
summary: John Schneider has never been particularly hesitant to pursue veteran help when he believes a roster is close to contending. The Seattle Seahawks’ acquisition of Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts is the latest example, and it addresses one of the team’s most pressing needs without costing a first- or second-round draft pick. Seattle sent […]
full_text: John Schneider has never been particularly hesitant to pursue veteran help when he believes a roster is close to contending. The Seattle Seahawks’ acquisition of Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts is the latest example, and it addresses one of the team’s most pressing needs without costing a first- or second-round draft pick. Seattle sent Indianapolis a third-round selection in 2027 and a fifth-rounder in 2028, while taking on approximately $9.777 million in prorated salary for the remainder of Nelson’s 2026 contract. For a team sitting at 4-3 and hoping to make a serious postseason run, the move is a clear attempt to improve an offense that hasn’t consistently delivered. The rationale is straightforward. Seattle needs to give Sam Darnold a cleaner pocket and create more room for its running backs. Nelson has spent much of his career doing both at an exceptionally high level. The question isn’t whether his résumé justifies the move; it’s whether his current form can help Seattle overcome the problems that have held the offense back this season. At 30, Nelson already has six All-Pro selections and eight consecutive Pro Bowl appearances to begin his career. According to the Elias Sports Bureau, since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970, only four offensive players have made the Pro Bowl in each of their first eight seasons: Nelson, Hall of Fame running backs Franco Harris and Barry Sanders, and offensive tackle Joe Thomas. That is an extraordinary group to join. Seattle isn’t acquiring a developmental prospect or trying to rehabilitate a player who has fallen out of favor. It is bringing in a veteran whose track record suggests he can still be a difference-maker at one of the most physically demanding positions on the field. A 2018 Draft Connection Comes Full Circle Nelson’s arrival also creates an unexpected connection with Seattle’s quarterback. In the 2018 NFL Draft, the New York Jets moved from No. 6 to No. 3 overall to select USC quarterback Sam Darnold. The Colts remained at No. 6 and selected Nelson. The price for New York was substantial: the sixth overall pick, two second-round selections in 2018 and another second-rounder in 2019. The Jets used the third pick on Darnold, while Indianapolis landed the offensive lineman who would become one of the defining players of his position. Eight years later, those two careers intersect again in Seattle. The Seahawks are hoping Nelson can help create the conditions for Darnold to operate more effectively, particularly by limiting interior pressure and giving the running game a more reliable foundation. Why the Seahawks needed help inside The Seahawks’ offensive struggles have been reflected in several underlying metrics, and the run game has been especially concerning. Seattle ranked last in the NFL in yards before contact on runs designed through the B gaps, averaging just 0.3 yards per attempt, 0.5 yards less than 31st. The broader picture is equally troubling. Seattle ranked 26th in offensive EPA per play, 31st in EPA per designed run and 27th in run-block win rate. Its running backs averaged 3.6 yards per designed run, good for 28th in the league, while the team also ranked 28th in yards before contact on designed runs. Pass-block win rate placed the Seahawks 21st. No single statistic explains every problem, but together they point toward an offensive line that hasn’t consistently won its assignments. When the interior fails to establish leverage or create movement, running backs are forced to make decisions before reaching the line of scrimmage. In pass protection, losses up front allow defenders to collapse the pocket and shorten Darnold’s decision-making window. Nelson’s skill set directly addresses those concerns. His combination of power, hand placement and leverage has made him a particularly effective interior blocker, capable of creating movement at the point of attack while maintaining control of his assignment. There is evidence that his pass protection can still be a strength. Through Week 7, Nelson had logged 275 pass-blocking snaps without allowing a sack, with a reported pressure rate allowed of 2.2% in one statistical breakdown. His overall numbers, however, deserve closer attention. ESPN’s win-rate data placed Nelson in the 66th percentile in pass protection and the 37th percentile in run blocking in 2026. Those figures are below his marks in the previous two seasons, particularly as a run blocker. That doesn’t necessarily mean his best football is behind him. Nelson experienced a dip in 2022 and 2023 before returning to an elite level in 2024 and delivering another strong season in 2025. Seattle will be betting that the player who reestablished himself among the league’s best can bring that level of performance to a line that badly needs it. Joe Thuney offers a useful point of comparison. The Chiefs signed Thuney in 2021, when he was around the age Nelson is now. After arriving in Kansas City, Thuney earned three consecutive first-team All-Pro selections. Nelson could provide a similar boost, particularly if Seattle can work out an extension and keep him in the lineup beyond this season. The trade cost is manageable. The next contract…. The draft compensation is relatively modest for a player with Nelson’s credentials. Seattle gave up a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, then assumed approximately $9.777 million of his remaining 2026 salary obligation. The larger financial decision may come after the season. Nelson is approaching the end of his current contract, and acquiring him could be only the first step if Seattle wants to keep him in the lineup long term. The guard market offers a useful reference point. Peter Skoronski’s deal averages $25 million per year, followed by Trey Smith at $23.5 million and Chris Lindstrom at $21.8 million. At center, Tyler Linderbaum’s reported annual value is $27 million, while Creed Humphrey’s is $18 million. Given Nelson’s résumé, an extension approaching +$25 million annually would not be surprising. Schneider has made several notable in-season acquisitions over the years, including LT Duane Brown in 2017, S Quandre Diggs in 2019, EDGE Carlos Dunlap in 2020, DL Leonard Williams in 2023, LB Ernest Jones IV in 2024 and WR/KR Rashid Shaheed in 2025. Those trades haven’t always come with an immediate contract extension. Seattle can take a similar approach with Nelson, using the remainder of 2026 to evaluate his performance before deciding how much to invest in his future. The new deals for Ernest Jones IV and Leonard Williams turned out to be strong values, while the price Seattle paid to retain Rashid Shaheed felt like an overpay. Nelson presents another test of Schneider’s ability to balance immediate impact with long-term value. Whether the Seahawks can keep him beyond this season—and at what price—will be just as important as what he delivers on the field. How Quenton Nelson fits into Seattle’s starting line The most straightforward lineup adjustment would be to put Nelson at his established position of left guard and move Grey Zabel to right guard. That would allow Nelson to operate on the side where he has built his reputation while giving Seattle a chance to improve the interior without completely rebuilding the offensive line. Anthony Bradford, who recently returned from injured reserve, would be the most likely candidate to lose his starting spot under that arrangement. Zabel’s versatility makes the switch possible, but his experience on the right side should not be overstated. He played just three games on RG during his time at North Dakota State. His work at multiple positions during Senior Bowl practices demonstrated an ability to learn different assignments, although practice experience is not the same as an established track record in a particular role. Moving Zabel to center appears less likely. The position requires more than the ability to block one-on-one: the center must deliver the snap consistently and help…

title: Seahawks swap practice squad tight ends, sign Ben Sims
summary: The tight end room has seen a swap to begin Week 8. A week after the Seattle Seahawks signed veteran tight end Josiah Deguara to their practice squad, in the wake of Elijah Arroyo’s season-ending shoulder injury, they released the seven-year pro to make room for fellow tight end Ben Sims. full_text: The tight end room has seen a swap to begin Week 8. A week after the Seattle Seahawks signed veteran tight end Josiah Deguara to their practice squad, in the wake of Elijah Arroyo’s season-ending shoulder injury , they released the seven-year pro to make room for fellow tight end Ben Sims. Sims, in his fourth season, spent training camp and preseason with the Miami Dolphins before he was placed on injured reserve and ultimately waived with an injury designation early in September. The former Baylor Bear went undrafted in the 2023 NFL Draft, signing with the Minnesota Vikings as a UDFA. Sims was released by the Vikings ahead of his rookie campaign and signed with the Green Bay Packers, where he spent his first two seasons, playing in all 34 games, before he was released early last season. He finished the season back with the Vikings, suiting up in eight games. Across 45 career games, Sims has caught 11 passes for 93 yards and one touchdown. With Arroyo on injured reserve, Seattle has AJ Barner, Eric Saubert, and Nick Kallerup to call from at tight end on the 53-man roster, while Sims now rounds out the group on the practice squad.

title: Seahawks All-22 review: The good and bad from a big Seahawks win over the Chiefs
summary: The Seattle Seahawks 20–3 win over the Kansas City Chiefs was fantastic. As I pointed out in the preview, a loss could have put the Seahawks in a difficult position, while a win would restore some confidence and put Seattle back in the mix. Winning the division is still a long way off, but this […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks 20–3 win over the Kansas City Chiefs was fantastic. As I pointed out in the preview, a loss could have put the Seahawks in a difficult position, while a win would restore some confidence and put Seattle back in the mix. Winning the division is still a long way off, but this result shows that there is enough talent on the field and on the coaching staff to make the necessary adjustments. After losses to the Washington Commanders and Denver Broncos, beating a quality opponent was essential. You can’t just rack up wins against weaker teams and then struggle when the level of competition goes up. Of course, we have to account for the Chiefs’ injuries, especially along the offensive line. Seattle had its own injury issues, though, and that shouldn’t take away from a defense that held Patrick Mahomes and company to just three points. The offense still showed some glaring issues, but there were also signs of improvement. The offensive line played a more solid game, the rushing attack grew as the game went on, and the defense showed it can compete against elite opponents. This win doesn’t solve every problem, but it gives the Seahawks something they desperately needed: confidence and an opportunity to build some momentum. The Good 1. The Seahawks defense was dominant It’s hard to imagine a much better defensive performance than this one. The Seahawks held the Chiefs to just 3 points, 213 total yards, and 11 first downs, without allowing a single trip into the red zone. The three points tied the lowest total in any game started by Patrick Mahomes, while the 213 yards, 11 first downs, and zero red-zone trips were all new lows for the quarterback across his 153 career starts. Seattle also outgained Kansas City by 197 yards. Across Mahomes’ 153 starts, only one game had featured a larger yardage differential against his team: the AFC Championship Game against the Patriots during the 2018 season. That puts Seattle’s dominance into perspective. And this wasn’t simply a bad night for Kansas City; it was a normal night for the Seahawks defense. According to ESPN Research, Seattle became the first team since the 1984 Cleveland Browns to hold each of its first seven opponents of the season under 180 passing yards. The defense was also allowing just 3.99 yards per play, the lowest mark in the league and the fewest by any team through seven games since the 2019 New England Patriots. The Seahawks’ performance against explosive plays reinforces that impression. They had allowed just 26 explosive plays through their first seven games — defined as runs of at least 12 yards or passes of at least 16 yards. According to TruMedia, that’s tied with the 2007 Indianapolis Colts for the fewest explosive plays allowed by any team through its first seven games since 2000. All of this becomes even more impressive when you consider the opponent. Mahomes is one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL, Andy Reid remains one of the league’s top offensive minds, and Kenneth Walker III is capable of turning an ordinary play into a big gain. Seattle still contained the ground game and suffocated the opposing offense. Walker finished with just 36 rushing yards on 14 carries. Kenneth Walker III entered the matchup averaging 133 rushing yards per game, leading the NFL in rushing production. Against his former team, however, he was held to just 36 yards on 14 carries, averaging 2.6 yards per attempt. The Seahawks consistently set the edge and played sound team defense against the run. There were a few missed angles, but because the defense rallied to the ball as a unit, it was still able to make the play. On the rep above, Leonard Williams forces the running back inside, and Tyrice Knight makes the tackle for loss. The defensive tackle is the one who creates the play. Another game in which Byron Murphy was unstoppable as a stand-up pass rusher. Great angle and plenty of explosiveness off the snap. 2. Nick Emmanwori showed his potential Nick Emmanwori deserves a section of his own. Despite entering the game questionable, he played 100% of the defensive snaps and has shown unusual versatility for such a young player. He has played at least 50 snaps in each of the last four games. His usage helps explain the potential Seattle has in this player. This season, Emmanwori has lined up approximately 36% of the time in the slot, 34% as a linebacker, and 27% near the line of scrimmage as an EDGE. His ability to play so many different roles allows the defense to change its looks without necessarily substituting personnel. It took me a while to realize that Nick Emmanwori was the one making the tackle. He’s lined up on the opposite end of the line, and he isn’t just acting as a backside defender. He explodes off the snap and tracks down the ball carrier on the other side of the formation. Here, he’s playing as an EDGE. Even though Travis Kelce, who isn’t exactly an elite blocker, has him engaged, Nick sheds the block after initially biting on Walker’s inside cut and still makes the tackle. Now he’s impacting the game from the slot, covering a receiver downfield. When he’s asked to defend a vertical route without a double move or a change of direction, he can win the rep as if he were prime Richard Sherman. Here, he shows outstanding instincts. He’s responsible for a zone with a tight end in his area, but he recognizes that the play is developing toward another receiver. He tries to help by closing the space and ends up getting a hand on the pass. Incredible. It’s just as impactful as that sensational pass breakup against the Texans last year. This is pure athleticism. He reads the flow of the play, realizes Mahomes still has the ball, and takes off after the quarterback. No. 15 tries to work his magic, but under pressure, he ends up throwing an interception. Nick deserves a share of the credit for that turnover. 3. Jaxon Smith-Njigba continues to be the engine of the offense Jaxon Smith-Njigba is putting together an extraordinary season and once again proved that he’s the engine of the Seahawks’ offense. Against Kansas City, he finished with 9 receptions for 150 yards and a touchdown. His impact was especially impressive in the first half, when he recorded six catches for 129 yards and a touchdown. According to ESPN Research, those 129 receiving yards were the most JSN has recorded in any half of his NFL career. It was also the most receiving yards in a first half by a Seahawks player since Tyler Lockett recorded 133 yards on the road against the Arizona Cardinals in 2020. His performance is part of a historic start to the season. JSN became the sixth player in NFL history to record at least 100 receiving yards in six of his team’s first seven games. He also became the fourth player in NFL history to reach at least 55 receptions and 800 receiving yards through his team’s first seven games. He also passed Darrell Jackson to reach 28 receiving touchdowns in his first four seasons, the fifth-most in franchise history over that span. I’ve seen people saying the Chiefs shouldn’t have put a rookie in Mansoor Delane on JSN. He played tight coverage against JSN on several occasions, including on the touchdown. Here, though, JSN absolutely burns the defensive back. The rookie tries to challenge him in press coverage, which isn’t a great idea against JSN. The safety providing over-the-top help takes a terrible angle, and JSN makes Kansas City pay with yards after the catch. 4. Signs of life from the offensive line and rushing attack Emanuel Wilson finished the game with 24 carries for 100 yards and a touchdown, averaging 4.2 yards per attempt. What’s most interesting is how his production was distributed. He had just 22 rushing yards in the first half but finished with 78 in the second. Over Seattle’s final three offensive drives, Wilson recorded 54 rushing yards, including the 21-yard touchdown run. Wilson isn’t an explosive running back, and his limitations in burst and big-play ability remain…
author: Alexandre Castro

title: Seahawks Week 8 national power rankings: Seattle slightly rises after dominant win
summary: Entering Week 7, the Seattle Seahawks continued their downslide in the national power rankings after dropping their second game in a row to the Denver Broncos. Now, after an impressive, dominant victory over the Kansas City Chiefs, how much will the Seahawks bounce back in power rankings? Let’s take a look at five national media […]
full_text: Entering Week 7, the Seattle Seahawks continued their downslide in the national power rankings after dropping their second game in a row to the Denver Broncos. Now, after an impressive, dominant victory over the Kansas City Chiefs, how much will the Seahawks bounce back in power rankings? Let’s take a look at five national media sites ( NFL.com , CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (B/R), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle. Let’s start with the lowest rankings. Despite the dominant victory, PFT still kept the Seahawks ranked number 7. PFT did not provide much reasoning, although they did ask whether Seattle’s defense can repeat their same performance last week against Caleb Williams next week. B/R also ranked the Seahawks as 7th best , however this was two spots up from last week. B/R brought light to the dominant defensive performance by Seattle, however they also noted the flaws they have on offense – particularly the interception woes by Sam Darnold along with the struggling running game. It would be interesting how B/R’s ranking and analysis would have changed had they known about the recent trade acquisition of offensive guard Quenton Nelson . CBS sports moved the Seahawks up one spot, from 7 to 6 . Contrary to B/R, CBS Sports was positive about the running game, noting that the “running game came alive [and] that’s a must for this team’s offense to succeed.” ESPN also moved Seattle up one spot, from 6 to 5 . In their rankings this week, ESPN talked about each team’s biggest offseason addition. This is awfully ironic considering Quenton Nelson being acquired just a few hours later. Nonetheless, for Seattle, ESPN mentioned running back Emanuel Wilson as the team’s best offseason addition. In their reasoning, ESPN notes that Wilson has helped keep the struggling run game afloat. The highest ranking the Seahawks earned this week was from NFL.com who moved Seattle up two spots from 6 to 4 . In their ranking, NFL.com explains that the team was able to put together the “blueprint the 12s know and love”, one consisting of a strong run game, Jaxon Smith-Njigba terrorizing the other team, and a defense that completely shuts down the opposing team’s offense. Overall the national landscape seems to be cautiously optimistic about the team. The remaining doubts are all around the offense. It would be interesting to see how much any of these opinions would change with the recent trade for Quenton Nelson. Entering Week 7, the average power rankings between the five polled sites was 7.8. Entering Week 8, that average has risen to 5.8. Next week the Seahawks face the 5-2 Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football. Time will tell whether Seattle will be able to continue their positive momentum.

title: 49ers release struggling cornerback
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have released cornerback Jack Jones to make room for DeForest Buckner. It was a relatively easy decision after Jones had a rough outing against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 7. That wasn’t the only time Jones struggled this season. In Week 3, Jones gave up 53 yards in coverage on five […]
full_text: (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have released cornerback Jack Jones to make room for DeForest Buckner. It was a relatively easy decision after Jones had a rough outing against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 7. That wasn’t the only time Jones struggled this season. In Week 3, Jones gave up 53 yards in coverage on five targets. Atlanta picked on Jones in coverage. He allowed four of his five targets to be completed for 49 yards, allowing a passer rating of 107.5. In five games this season, Jones was targeted over 30% of the time when he was on the field. Teams were not scared of him. Against Atlanta, Jones allowed 5.8 yards of separation on five targets. Add in the penalties, and he became unplayable, since the run defense and tackling were a struggle. With Upton Stout out, Deommodore Lenoir moved to nickel, and Jones played Lenoir’s boundary role in obvious passing situations. Once Jones was benched, the Niners turned to rookie Ephesians Prysock. The 49ers will actually save money by releasing Jones, according to Over the Cap. He signed a one-year deal, and the contract has no guaranteed money beyond what appears to be a $140,000 signing bonus. Cornerback Nate Hobbs remains on the injured reserve. That’s a potential veteran replacement in the second half if the 49ers don’t address cornerback ahead of the trade deadline.

title: Explosive play rates: A tale of two sides for the 49ers
summary: As the San Francisco 49ers enjoy their bye week and evaluate their season through seven weeks, the front office has been busy making calls around the NFL. DeForest Buckner is back, and an educated guess would be that the organization isn’t done making moves. With a 6-1 record, even after a frustrating loss to Atlanta, […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the San Francisco 49ers enjoy their bye week and evaluate their season through seven weeks, the front office has been busy making calls around the NFL. DeForest Buckner is back, and an educated guess would be that the organization isn’t done making moves. With a 6-1 record, even after a frustrating loss to Atlanta, the 49ers couldn’t ask for a better start, especially with wins over tough defenses like Denver and Seattle. How have the 49ers done it? Explosive play rates on both sides of the ball. In this case, an explosive play is a run over ten-plus yards and a pass over 20-plus yards. The 49ers offense is top five in explosive play rate at 9.5%. The top four offenses in explosive play rates are Buffalo, Miami (what the hell?), Kansas City, and Baltimore. A closer look shows the 49ers’ rushing attack at number four with 14.1% and a passing attack at 5.6%, which is good for 11th in the league. With Mike Evans returning and others, that number should be trending upwards. What about defensively? The 49ers defense is first in explosive play rate allowed at 3.2%. With the best rushing defense number of 2.9% and the fifth-best passing defense at 3.5%, the 49ers defense will see a decrease in those numbers with Buckner and Nick Bosa playing next week and for the rest of the season, hopefully. Last week, the 49ers defense struggled to generate pass rush, but they weren’t hit over the top against Atlanta. Unfortunately, the deep Cover 3 zones run by Raheem Morris, paired with the struggling pass rush, allowed Michael Penix and the Falcons offense to convert underneath methodically. The 49ers’ run defense did a great job bottling up one of the most explosive backs in the NFL, Bijan Robinson. The NFL as a whole has converted to a two-man safety shell look, which is designed to limit explosive plays and keep everything in front of second- and third-level defenders. If the 49ers continue at this pace, they will be just fine. However, it is fair to expect an increase in explosives on offense and a decrease on defense. That is how the 49ers have a 6-1 record.

title: Brock Purdy’s slump: Why the 49ers QB has struggled since Week 5, and what fixes it
summary: As the 49ers took the field last Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, they had exactly four eligible wide receivers for the game — Brandin Cooks, Jacob Cowing, Christian Kirk, and Jordan Watkins. Yes, they had George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey (albeit a Christian McCaffrey who missed most of the first half with […]
full_text: Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images | Getty Images As the 49ers took the field last Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, they had exactly four eligible wide receivers for the game — Brandin Cooks, Jacob Cowing, Christian Kirk, and Jordan Watkins. Yes, they had George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey (albeit a Christian McCaffrey who missed most of the first half with a quadriceps injury), but the absences of Mike Evans (Achilles tendon), Deebo Samuel (hamstring), and Demarcus Robinson (ankle) were going to limit Brock Purdy’s options, and it doesn’t take a football expert to figure that out. In the 49ers’ first loss of the season — a frustrating 29-20 result after the 49ers had a 14-3 second-quarter lead — Purdy completed 27 of 40 passes for 288 yards, one touchdown, two interceptions, an EPA per pass of -0.06, and a passer rating of 75.8. Not what you want from a guy who was a legit NFL Most Valuable Player candidate in the first four weeks of the season , and this is not a throwaway one-week negative blip. The splits between Purdy’s first four games, and the last three, are pretty glaring. Per SumerSports : Split ATT COMP COMP% YARDS YPA TD INT RATING EPA/DROPBACK Weeks 1-4 113 79 69.9% 1,007 8.91 11 1 126.2 +0.505 Weeks 5-7 98 67 68.4% 741 7.56 4 3 91.4 -0.087 What’s the problem? Purdy’s performance against the Seattle Seahawks in the 49ers’ 32-29 Week 5 win was its own animal — the Seahawks have the NFL’s best defense by DVOA for the second straight season , and Purdy has struggled more against this defense than any other . Purdy was good enough against the Washington Commanders’ 23rd-ranked defense in Week 6, but what happened against the Falcons’ 11tth-ranked defense raised some eyebrows. Primary among the negative plays were Purdy’s two interceptions. Purdy has thrown two or more picks in a game just 11 times in his career, so that’s not something you expect, especially after the hot start. The first interception came with 5:41 left in the third quarter, and featured an amazing sideline toe-tap catch by Falcons safety Jessie Bates III. The 49ers were in 11 personnel with Cooks, Cowing, and Kirk on the field, and the Falcons responded with Cover-1 — man coverage across with a single-high safety. Purdy didn’t like what he saw, and then, it got weird. The Falcons flipped their box and deep safeties after the snap, and while Purdy is usually great against coverage disguises , the disguise won this time. Brock Purdy wanted to throw this ball away. Jessie Bates III said TOE DRAG SWAG instead. pic.twitter.com/5gYYWgapay — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 28, 2026 “I thought maybe Christian Kirk on the scramble was going to be there,” Purdy said postgame of Kirk’s out-and-up route. “But then, towards the end of the throw, as I was going to throw, I was like, ’No, it’s not.‘ I went to just throw it away by the sideline and then Bates, all of a sudden, came across and made a play. I was like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me.’ In that moment, I’ve got to completely throw the ball away if I’m not going to make an attempt to a receiver. I’ve got to learn from that in a tough way.” The second interception, which came with 2:42 left in the game with the 49ers down 26-20, was the killer. Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich called a double-mug look in Cover-3 (zone with a single deep safety), with linebackers Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. clogging up the middle of the offensive line. At the snap, both linebackers dropped into coverage — Perkins to hook/curl over the middle, and Daniels to the left flat. Purdy tried to get the ball to Watkins on a 15-yard in-cut, but Daniels both deflected and intercepted the pass. in which the falcons fool brock purdy on a frosty mug look pic.twitter.com/ptixqO1yxO — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 28, 2026 “The linebacker was mugged up on the line of scrimmage and then thought we had an alley outside to, I think, it was Jordan Watkins,” Purdy said. “I was going to throw. It was there, and I thought it was going to be a drive-by kind of play. All of a sudden, I threw the ball and he came from the backside, tipped it up to himself; I didn’t see him or anything. So credit to him. He made a good play. “In that moment, I’d like to say, ‘Yeah, I need to see [Daniels].’ But at the same time, it’s pretty tough to drop back and see a backer mugged up on the line, dropping from the opposite side and stuff. It was a good play calling [by] them and good execution by the linebacker.” Normally, Purdy is as good as it gets when it comes to seeing the field, understanding what’s in front of him, and making the right throw at the right time with the proper anticipation. Physical and mental mistakes (failing to throw the ball all the way out of bounds, and missing a dropping linebacker) happen to every quarterback. This is not a five-alarm fire. But it is disconcerting to see two such plays in one half from any quarterback who generally knows better. Communication breakdown? So, how much of this is on Purdy, and how much is on the receivers with whom Purdy doesn’t have the necessary connection yet? Kyle Shanahan’s passing game is all about timing, rhythm, and anticipation, and it’s why Purdy is his ideal quarterback. But if Purdy’s targets aren’t on the same page, that’s obviously a problem. McCaffrey and George Kittle did their level best to mitigate the damage with a total of 14 catches on 17 targets for 149 yards, and Kyle Juszczyk caught Purdy’s lone touchdown pass… but the receivers managed seven catches on 14 targets for 107 yards. That was Cooks, Cowing, and Watson; Kirk didn’t have an official target. “I mean, yeah, they’re new guys and stuff, so you’ve got to learn how they run routes and how they play for sure,” Purdy concluded when asked about the depleted receiver corps. “That’s a real thing. But I think just with our preparation and how Kyle goes about the week with getting us ready as an offense, I think it’s pretty… not easy, but he makes it pretty smooth for these guys to come in and learn what they need to do and be on time and all that kind of thing. I thought they did a great job today for what was handed to us. We need to limit the turnovers, yes, and we sort of shot ourselves in the foot with that. But we were out there [with] those new guys out there running routes for us and creating separation and making plays. “I thought I saw a lot of really cool things from Jordan Watkins [and] Jacob Cowing. Obviously, I’m trying to get the rock to Brandin Cooks and Christian Kirk, too, and see what they can do. You know, that will all come. But I thought they did a good job. It’s our first game all together as a unit with the receivers that we had. We’ve just got to keep working and stuff. But I thought it was a positive performance on their end. We’ve just got to keep chipping away.” Let’s get healthy! It will help that after the 49ers’ Week 8 bye, there’s a very good chance that they’ll have a lot of reinforcements back from the injury pool — and not just at receiver. “Yeah, I think all those guys from, you’ve got [DL] Nick [Bosa], [WR] Mike [Evans], [LB Luke] Gifford, Deebo, [S Marques] Sigle, [LB Garret] Wallow, D-Rob, [DL] C.J. West, all those guys have a chance after the bye week, but none are guaranteed,” Shanahan said on Monday. “So, big week of rehab for all of them, and we’ll see where they’re at next week.” With Evans and Deebo back in particular, that Shanahan passing game should be back on track. And there’s the eventual return of rookie De’Zhaun Stribling — possibly in December. Very good news for the team. Because we may have seen the line of demarcation from which not even Brock Purdy can escape.
author: Doug Farrar

title: Can past midseason trades for the 49ers signal potential future trades?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are on bye week, but trade rumors and speculation are swirling around the team. The Seattle Seahawks traded for All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson, and the Niners countered by sending a fourth-round pick for our old friend DeForest Buckner. Based on rumors and reports, it doesn’t seem like the team is done […]
full_text: (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are on bye week, but trade rumors and speculation are swirling around the team. The Seattle Seahawks traded for All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson, and the Niners countered by sending a fourth-round pick for our old friend DeForest Buckner. Based on rumors and reports, it doesn’t seem like the team is done adding to the roster. The choices are more defensive line help (yes, please), a wide receiver to improve depth or a true difference-maker, and possibly cornerback depth. Truthfully, the 49ers shouldn’t be done trading. The team has a golden opportunity in front of them to play for the title on Valentine’s Day. Could past midseason trades give fans an idea of what to expect in the coming days and weeks before the trade deadline? In 2019, the 49ers traded for veteran receiver Emmanuel Sanders to solidify a young receiver room with Deebo Samuel and Kendrick Bourne. The team came within minutes of a Super Bowl win. Sanders wasn’t the flashiest name, but the move was exactly what the team needed, as he brought leadership and stability to the receiver room. 2020 saw the 49ers trade for Jordan Willis, who would later etch his name in 49ers postseason lore with his massive blocked punt against the Packers. In 2021, Charles Omenihu was a find as the defensive lineman revitalized his career with the 49ers, and the team played in the NFC Championship Game. Christian McCaffrey’s trade was the biggest splash for the 49ers in 2022. The team fell short in the NFC Championship Game against Philadelphia as the 49ers ran out of quarterbacks, but that deal proved the team wasn’t afraid of a big splash, and who can argue with his production in San Francisco? During the magical 2023 season, the 49ers gambled on Chase Young and added veteran EDGE Randy Gregory. Young was impressive in the Super Bowl, but ultimately moved on to New Orleans, where he has transformed into the pass rusher Washington envisioned when they drafted him. 2024 was a small trade for Khalil Davis, and last year the 49ers made one of the more savvy, underrated moves by trading for DE Keion White. White’s play has warranted a valid discussion about a potential extension with the team. So, what does the past tell us about a potential trade for the 49ers in 2026? It’s completely feasible to see the 49ers take a big swing (Garrett Wilson? Nico Collins?), but for the most part, the team adds high-floor players to improve depth. Now, the past is an indicator of the future, but I’d argue this season has different circumstances than past seasons. 2023 was a loaded team, and Young was a sprinkle on top of that, but not a big swing. That was a low-risk, high-reward move. Also, in past seasons, the options for a big splash weren’t as plentiful. This season is completely different. The team should have the urgency to get a high-end EDGE option and a big-time wide receiver. Opportunities like this don’t present themselves often. Nothing is promised next season. Fans are tired of hearing, “This team will be back” next season. I don’t blame them. Go for the Lombardi now and worry about the rest next season. Plugging up roster holes and doing salary cap gymnastics is far easier with the sixth Super Bowl trophy in the case. Keep going, John Lynch and Kyle Shanahan. Go get the ring and kill the “can’t get it done” narrative.
author: Jason Aponte

title: 49ers listed as a best fit for 4 potential trade candidates
summary: The San Francisco 49ers upgraded at defensive tackle on Tuesday by adding DeForest Buckner. But are they done? Should they be? Adding an edge rusher and a wide receiver remain popular topics that we’ve discussed. If the 49ers didn’t face the Raiders coming out of the bye, Maxx Crosby might already be a Niner — […]
full_text: Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers upgraded at defensive tackle on Tuesday by adding DeForest Buckner . But are they done? Should they be? Adding an edge rusher and a wide receiver remain popular topics that we’ve discussed . If the 49ers didn’t face the Raiders coming out of the bye, Maxx Crosby might already be a Niner — but it’d also require the Raiders to be willing to do business with San Francisco. Khalil Mack for a fifth-rounder feels a notch below Buckner on the inevitability trade chart. Will McDonald is in the final year of his rookie contract with the Jets, although I’d argue that’d be redundant with Romello Height on the roster. If the Cardinals are open to it, Josh Sweat is an option, though he hasn’t been as impactful as he was in years past. Sources: Colts WR Josh Downs is requesting a trade from Indianapolis. pic.twitter.com/rwGaVGMTFf — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) October 28, 2026 If you’re going to get a wide receiver, to me it makes sense to go get a “guy.” I’m not sure Josh Downs falls under that category. The 49ers also have enough small-ish wideouts on the roster. You get the allure with Brian Thomas. If you’re going to swing, Garrett Wilson seems awfully unhappy in the Big Apple. Russell Wilson, who apparently is the voice of reason for the 49ers this season, said on NFL on CBS , “The 49ers have a chance, and if I’m Garrett Wilson, I’m checking out the 49ers. Kyle Shanahan should make the call. Mike Evans can make plays down in the red zone, but to find a player who can run every route for you, that’s Garrett Wilson.” Why are we ignoring cornerback after everything we’ve seen this season? If the Colts are having a fire sale, they have this player, Charvarius Ward, who has allowed a 39.1% completion rate and given up zero touchdowns this season. If you’re getting the band back together, get Mooney. ESPN ranked the top-25 trade candidates. The Niners were linked to a few, including No. 2 2. Brian Thomas Jr., WR, Jacksonville Jaguars What Fowler is hearing: League execs are sensing the end for BTJ in Jacksonville, as his targets and playing time have dipped. How Jacksonville has struggled to make this relationship work is still a mystery. Thomas is an elite mover with size who draws coverage deep, setting the stage for teammates Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers to eat underneath. But that plan for Thomas hasn’t materialized this season. And teams are circling with interest. Kansas City and Pittsburgh are among those exploring receiver help. Predicted chance of getting traded: 45% What Bowen sees on tape: Thomas’ numbers have declined over the past two seasons, but he has the traits to still draw interest. At 6-foot-3 and 209 pounds, Thomas has the profile of an X receiver who can separate at multiple levels of the field. I see legit straight-line speed and ball-tracking ability. He had 87 receptions and 10 touchdowns as a rookie in 2024, but he has been limited to a 9-105-1 line so far this season. Team fits: Chiefs, Steelers, 49ers We’re two years removed from Thomas Jr. having nearly 1,300 yards as a rookie. You get him this year and next year. Maybe he just needs to be on a team with Mac Jones to be successful again? At 6’3, 209 pounds, you’d think the Niners could find a place for him. If the player is a clear upgrade from Demarcus Robinson or Jordan Watkins, the answer should be easy. But if they are a run-of-the-mill type who would blend in with the other role players, then there should be pushback. 3. Josh Sweat, EDGE, Arizona Cardinals What Fowler is hearing: Rival teams could see him getting moved. “Sweat to Dallas makes a lot of sense to me,” an NFC exec said. “That’s a profile fit.” Rumblings persist that Sweat would want a new contract — he’s in the second year of a four-year, $76 million deal — and that could complicate things. But many teams are looking for an edge rusher. Predicted chance of getting traded: 40% What Bowen sees on tape: A long, angular mover who can win with speed-to-power, Sweat had 12 sacks and 37 pressures in Arizona last season. But his numbers haven’t been as solid in 2026, with two sacks and 10 pressures. Still, Sweat’s ability to threaten the edges of offensive tackles with his quickness off the ball fits pass-rush fronts across the league. Team fits: Cowboys, Bears, 49ers The contract and the division all but take the Niners out of the running for Sweat, who, again, has been underwhelming this season. It might be a motivational thing, but he has fewer tackles for loss, impact plays, sacks, pressures, and a pass-rush win rate 5% worse than Keion White. The 49ers were not listed as a fit for Khalil Mack, who ESPN ranked No. 7 and gave a 35% chance of being traded. The new team would inherit Mack’s $8 million salary, which is the prorated version of his deal. Another player who is on the list but not listed as a fit is Eagles left guard Landon Dickerson. Philly could be another team selling off parts in what appears to be a lost season. This is the final year of guaranteed salary in Dickerson’s deal, who is 28. ESPN lists him with a 25% chance of getting traded. Dickerson just played his first game since Week 1 on Monday night. It’s unclear what any compensation involving him would look like. 16. Jauan Jennings, Wide receiver, Vikings What Fowler is hearing: The Vikings’ free agent addition is not a focal point of the offense and is considered a trade candidate leaguewide. But he did catch two passes for 34 yards Sunday against the Colts for a Minnesota passing game that’s not exactly thriving right now. Jennings, who’s on a one-year deal, could prove a low-cost option for teams looking to add to their receiver room. The 49ers are an obvious fit. Predicted chance of getting traded: 50% What Bowen sees on tape: Jennings has seen very limited opportunities in Minnesota this season, catching just four of eight targets. However, he has proved to be a reliable target in previous seasons. He’s a consistent route runner who plays through contact and makes himself available to the quarterback on in-breaking targets. Team fits: Rams, Falcons, 49ers Let’s put it like this: If Jennings went to the Rams, would that strike fear in Raheem Morris? Probably not. It’s one thing to bring back proven commodities with All-Pro history like Buckner and Mooney. Jennings is a different discussion. 20. Quentin Johnston, Wide receiver, Chargers What Fowler is hearing: Teams have considered Johnston a trade candidate dating back to March. The Chargers shut that down at the time and even exercised his fifth-year option. But the Chargers’ 0-6 plight is resurfacing his name in league circles. Predicted chance of getting traded: 25% What Bowen sees on tape: With his physical tools at 6-3 and 208 pounds, plus the straight-line speed to create explosives, Johnston can help a team as a No. 3 receiver. The drops have been an issue in his four-year career (11 total), and he has been limited to only eight receptions this season. However, Johnston has 18 career touchdowns, and he produced 700 or more receiving yards in both 2024 and 2025. Team fits: 49ers, Raiders, Steelers It hasn’t clicked for Johnston in four years. He has three drops compared to eight receptions this year. He could potentially be a big-play asset in the 49ers offense, but trust could be a bigger issue if he’s inconsistent.

title: Making the case for and against the 49ers to go all in
summary: At 7-1, the San Francisco 49ers are the favorites to win the Super Bowl this season, even after their first loss of the year, as they enter a needed bye week to get healthy. Coming out of that bye week, though, and looking towards the second half of the season, their team could look different. […]
full_text: (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) At 7-1, the San Francisco 49ers are the favorites to win the Super Bowl this season, even after their first loss of the year, as they enter a needed bye week to get healthy. Coming out of that bye week, though, and looking towards the second half of the season, their team could look different. The 49ers already traded for defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, sending a fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts for the 32-year-old on an expiring contract. And more could be coming, with the 49ers still having a few gaps to fill on their roster. Following the 7-1 start, many have looked for San Francisco to push all the chips in for a Super Bowl this season, which would involve sending serious capital for stars. The 49ers are no stranger to trade deadline moves, although some, most notably the Christian McCaffrey trade, have had more magnitude than others. Over the years, we’ve seen teams go all in and hurt themselves for the future, while others have taken the pieces they’ve acquired with them on a Super Bowl run. Does it make sense for San Francisco to go all in here? Let’s make the case for both sides. Why they should As I mentioned at the top, the 49ers are the clear favorites to win the Super Bowl currently, followed by the Buffalo Bills, Kansas City Chiefs, Seattle Seahawks, and Los Angeles Rams. We know the 49ers flaws, with injuries easily being the main issue. But when you look at the NFL, it’s easy to poke holes in nearly every contender. Buffalo’s defense has been a major question mark. Kansas City still doesn’t have those top-tier receiving threats, and their defense lost some key talent over the offseason. Seattle has struggled without Klint Kubiak at times offensively, and Sam Darnold has been erratic. And the Rams have just outright struggled on both sides of the ball at times. The field is quite wide open right now. And after all the failures and miscues with reaching and winning a Super Bowl in the last few years, this could be San Francisco’s shot to do it all. If they do win the trophy, there’s no worrying talk about going all in at all. San Francisco also has very few holes on its roster. Realistically, they could just push all their chips in on an edge rusher and call it a day. They could also go for rotational pieces that can be more complementary to their depth. The 49ers core is getting older. This team is as well-coached as any in the country. It feels like this is the widest-open race San Francisco has been in in some time, hence the idea of going all in. Additionally, the teams underneath them will very likely make trades as well. They’ll need to respond. Why they shouldn’t We’ve seen teams make Hail Mary moves that have seriously backfired on them, and the 49ers could be in danger of doing the same. The 49ers would have to part with legitimate draft capital to go all in, and that could seriously hamper them in future years. We saw the major trade back in 2021 ahead of the draft and the ramifications it had on the 49ers over the next few years with the draft. In today’s NFL, you need young, cost-controlled talent on your roster to win a Super Bowl, and the 49ers have been doing a good job acquiring that over the last two years to put together a roster that can compete for a championship. Their formula is working. Going all in could also hamper development, as an edge rusher takes away reps from Keion White and Mykel Williams, among others. The 49ers have some solid 2027 draft capital with one pick in every round, although they lost a fourth in the DeForest Buckner trade. With as old a roster as they have, and as well as they’ve drafted recently, is it worth it to splurge and lose the capital? Final Thoughts I haven’t been a full proponent of going “all in” in years past, but this year’s case feels different for the 49ers. It truly feels like it could be their last shot at such an open title race. Contracts are only going to get more expensive, and the team’s stars are going to continue to age. There are also inherent flaws in nearly every team around them, and the biggest competition right now comes in the AFC in terms of title odds. An edge rusher feels like a must. Perhaps that’s all they need to do, but the 49ers have a true chance here to really separate themselves on paper, and it doesn’t have to be an expensive deadline either. We’ve seen the 49ers draft well and construct rosters as good as any other team in the NFL. They should be able to sustain success even if they lose another draft pick or two, but it would be tough knowing they lost out on a chance for the Super Bowl in a few months because a different contender made the trade they needed to.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: Where else could the 49ers add after trading for DeForest Buckner?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers made an early splash this season, trading for and reuniting with Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner a few weeks ahead of the trade deadline. Buckner, 32, had accumulated 31 tackles, four sacks, and three pass breakups for the lowly Colts this season, and was entering the final year of his […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers made an early splash this season, trading for and reuniting with Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner a few weeks ahead of the trade deadline. Buckner, 32, had accumulated 31 tackles, four sacks, and three pass breakups for the lowly Colts this season, and was entering the final year of his contract. In return, the 49ers sent just a fourth-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. Heading into the deadline, the 49ers are considered a clear buyer and could end up being one of the more active teams in the NFL. They addressed one area on Tuesday with the addition of a defensive tackle, giving them another reliable option next to Osa Odighizuwa and some much-needed depth. Where else could the 49ers add ahead of the deadline after trading for Buckner? Defensive end The obvious choice is in the same position group, but on the edge rather than up the middle. The 49ers had perhaps an even bigger need at edge, given the standout play from rookie Gracen Halton to open the year. Without Nick Bosa, the 49ers have found a way to manage, thanks to the creativity of Raheem Morris and his scheme. But as San Francisco continues to face playoff-caliber teams, they should add another pass rusher on the edge, even with Bosa in the mix. And this market should have a ton of them open, with names mentioned including Maxx Crosby, Khalil Mack, and others. Now, San Francisco does have a lot of young talent, with Halton, Romello Height, Keion White, Mykel Williams, and others on the defensive line. But a trade for a proven edge rusher will add more depth, keep bodies fresh, and provide the 49ers with a strong tandem once Nick Bosa is healthy. Cornerback The secondary has certainly been a strength for the 49ers this season, and Raheem Morris’s background as a defensive back seems to be playing into it. The cornerbacks are playing more confidently, which has resulted in more plays made, while the safety room led by Malik Mustapha has done its job and more. However, the 49ers could use one extra depth piece here, as top reserve Jack Jones has continued to struggle when thrust into action over the past few weeks. The 49ers have responded by trying out a variety of different lineups, but getting some corner depth to replace Jones could be a different priority. Wide Receiver Now, I don’t think the 49ers will look only short-term at wide receiver, with Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, Christian Kirk, De’Zhaun Stribling, and Demarcus Robinson all expected to play in the coming weeks. But there are avenues the 49ers can still improve their receiver room with a minor trade. First off, that group still has injury concerns, which could haunt San Francisco closer to playoff time. Adding a younger receiver that fits well in the room (perhaps Josh Downs?) could be what the 49ers need as that final depth piece. Still, with so many new faces in the receiver room, San Francisco could benefit from adding a younger, controllable option who can contribute now while remaining part of the team’s long-term plans. Other moves Many clamored for the 49ers to get into the Quenton Nelson sweepstakes, but even at a very reasonable price, I don’t see the Niners trading for an offensive lineman with the way their unit is currently playing. Everywhere else, they’re pretty set depth-wise. They’ve got pieces at quarterback, running back, and tight end, while linebacker is one of the more loaded groups as a whole on the roster. That allows the 49ers to shoot high for their targets at the positions listed above, and they could part ways with some serious draft capital to do so. The 49ers probably don’t make moves at all three positions on top of the Buckner move. But reports suggest they’ll be aggressive heading into the deadline, and these are the few spots where they can really improve.

title: 49ers News: Welcome back, DeForest Buckner!
summary: This moves me. I especially like the mentorship angle about this move. There’s a lot of young defensive linemen on this team that could really benefit from elite peer wisdom.  Kawakami: Adding DeForest Buckner might be just the start of the 49ers’ trade action (paywall)“They’re almost certainly checking in on the Raiders’ Maxx Crosby and […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JANUARY 19: DeForest Buckner #99 of the San Francisco 49ers heads to the sideline after recovering a fumble during the game against the Green Bay Packers at Levi's Stadium on January 19, 2020 in Santa Clara, California. The 49ers defeated the Packers 37-20. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images This moves me. I especially like the mentorship angle about this move. There’s a lot of young defensive linemen on this team that could really benefit from elite peer wisdom. Kawakami: Adding DeForest Buckner might be just the start of the 49ers’ trade action (paywall) “They’re almost certainly checking in on the Raiders’ Maxx Crosby and the Chargers’ Khalil Mack, among others; and hey, if you’ve got a good edge rusher you might let go for a third-round pick, give Lynch a call. He’ll pick up the phone. I guarantee it. If he hasn’t already dialed you up 10 or 20 times. Sitting at 6-1 and in great playoff position heading into the bye, in the 10th year of the Shanahan/Lynch reign, the 49ers are moving all-in. You could feel the momentum for this gaining inside team HQ for weeks, and now it’s here.” The 49ers have traded for DeForest Buckner “The move for Buckner allows players like Valdez and Odighizuwa to become role players. It takes some off Gracen Halton’s plate. The pecking order and domino effect should make everybody better. Plus, the Buckner is used to playing against double teams. In the first month of the season, Buckner was double-teamed on 36.4% of his pass rushes. That’s a number that’s actually down from 49.5%. That’s because Buckner has aligned at 5-technique or wider on 13.3% of his snaps, the highest rate since he entered the league. Through the first four weeks of the season, Buckner recorded three sacks, which was tied for the second-most among interior defensive linemen. What sets Buckner apart is his ability to turn pressures into sacks. Per Next Gen Stats, Buckner was converting 30% of his pressures into sacks, which was the highest rate of any season for a defensive lineman since 2018. Theoretically, Buckner should see an increase in production with the number of times the 49ers use a 5-down front, not to mention having Nick Bosa on the field.” Colts trade DT DeForest Buckner to 49ers in another major move “Buckner, 32, is entering the final year of his deal with the Colts and is slated to become an unrestricted free agent after the season. Had Buckner signed this offseason with another team, the highest compensatory draft pick the Colts could have received was a 2028 fifth-round selection since he is an 11-year NFL veteran. With the trade, the Colts netted a 2027 fourth-round pick instead.” 49ers game review: Dre Greenlaw’s yelling points to screaming need for cornerback depth (paywall) “ Before the snap, Greenlaw was animatedly clapping his hands, telling Jones, who was playing left outside cornerback, to protect the left flat. Instead, Jones covered wide receiver Zachariah Branch, who ran a go route. The result: QB Michael Penix flipped a 19-yard completion to the all-alone Robinson. After Greenlaw tackled Robinson on the right sideline, he got up in balled-fist fury and began barking at Jones.” 49ers minutia minute: Brock Purdy didn’t complete a pass to a WR until the third quarter (paywall) “The 49ers had only seven missed tackles, though two of them were by Brown. He leads the team with seven missed tackles, one more than Warner and Greenlaw.” 49ers overreactions: Would trading for star left guard be most helpful? “The defensive line also is an area where the 49ers could look to add. The 49ers deploy a nine-man rotation along the D-line, so they never can have too many good players to cycle through during the course of a game.”

full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 4: Antoine Winfield Jr. #31 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers returns a turnover against the Green Bay Packers during the game at Raymond James Stadium on October 4, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tampa Bay Buccaneers released their initial injury report Wednesday ahead of their Week 8 matchup against the Atlanta Falcons, with three players sitting out practice and two others participating on a limited basis. Running back Kenny Gainwell (hip), offensive tackle Luke Goedeke (calf) and linebacker Josiah Trotter (illness) were all listed as non-participants to begin the week. There was some encouraging news for Tampa Bay, however. Quarterback Baker Mayfield (right thumb) and safety Antoine Winfield Jr. (rib) were both full participants Wednesday. Mayfield returned to action in last week’s 43-13 victory over the Carolina Panthers, while Winfield’s participation is another positive development for the Buccaneers’ defense. Atlanta also opened the week with several players sidelined. Defensive back Billy Bowman Jr. (hamstring), linebacker Divine Deablo (forearm) and running back Brian Robinson (hamstring) did not participate in practice. Defensive end Za’Darius Smith was also held out for rest. The Falcons had six players listed as limited participants, including defensive end Samson Ebukam (hamstring), defensive linemen LaCale London (chest) and Charles Snowden (back), offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor (hamstring), cornerback Avieon Terrell (illness) and wide receiver Olamide Zaccheaus (shoulder). Wide receiver Beaux Collins (hip) and offensive tackle Cameron Williams (ankle) were full participants. Both teams will continue monitoring their injured players throughout the week, with Thursday’s practice providing another indication of their progress before Friday’s final injury designations. The Buccaneers (2-5) host the Falcons (3-4) on Sunday, November 1, at Raymond James Stadium. Kickoff is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET.

title: Can Todd Bowles save his job?
summary: With where the Buccaneers are and are going, many people (which may be an understatement) think, expect, and want to see Todd Bowles sent packing after or even during the season. Tampa Bay is 2-5, an unfortunate start to what was hoped to be a promising season. The Buccaneers have not been good this year, […]
full_text: First-year Buccaneers head coach Todd Bowles is entering his second stint as an NFL head coach. Syndication The Tennessean | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co With where the Buccaneers are and are going, many people (which may be an understatement) think, expect, and want to see Todd Bowles sent packing after or even during the season. Tampa Bay is 2-5, an unfortunate start to what was hoped to be a promising season. The Buccaneers have not been good this year, but at the same time it’s been a weird season. Tampa has played both good and bad teams and has been in almost exclusively close games. The Bucs actually have a positive point differential on the season (+11)— The positivity of that differential is largely in part due to last Sunday’s blowout win versus the Carolina Panthers, however, even without last week’s outing they would still only be at a -19. Not only has Tampa has been in every game they’ve played, but Todd Bowles’ side of the ball has probably been the team’s strongest unit. Bowles’ defense has some statistics you might believe if you haven’t been paying attention. The unit is ranked third in the NFL in yards allowed— They hold teams under 300 yards per game (294.7). The yards teams do come by against the Bucs are not on the ground. The Buccaneers’ rush defense is also top-5 in the league, only 77.3 yards per game allowed— Good for second best league wide. An easy argument against those defensive statistics might be that yards don’t win or lose games, points on the scoreboard determine the outcome of games— True, but the Buccaneers are actually first in that category. No team allows fewer points per game than the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, captained by Todd Bowles . At just 138 points surrendered on the season, the Bucs’ defense has let up under 20 points per game on average (19.8). The defense has had its highs and lows this season. For every instance like last Sunday’s dominance, there’s a fourth quarter meltdown like the Pittsburgh Steelers game two weeks back. Still, the Buccaneers’ defense has been good, arguably great, in 2026. “Todd Bowles is the head coach, so he’s the coach of the whole team and not just the coach of the defense.” How is the rest of the team doing? The Buccaneers’ special teams unit has been substantially improved this season. Todd Bowles spent a large portion of his offseason rearranging his coaching staff and one of his largest additions to the coaching staff was special teams coach Danny Smith. Smith’s taken the group to a new level and Bowles deserves credit for the hire, another check for the retainment of coach Bowles. Todd Bowles also brought in a new coach for the offensive side of the ball— Zac Robinson. This hire has not been as bountiful in its results. Robinson has been severely disliked by fans since his arrival in Tampa and hasn’t had many games this year where he looked the part. Aside from the last week, Tampa’s offense has had a difficult time functioning. The offense’s performance against Carolina, while one for the books speaks less to gameplanning, elite scheming or coaching, and more to circumstances (Carolina committing four turnovers) combined with psychical domination by the players on the field. Robinson has the Bucs’ offense ranked in the back half of the league. If that level of output should continue, than Robinson will unequivocally be a bad hire, but the story of the season isn’t completely written yet. The Bucs’ offense is coming off of their best game of the season and both of Tampa’s wins have come inside of the last three weeks of football. Each win featured a strong run game and improved play in the trenches, potential signs of growth from the group. If enough season remains for Zac Robinson to save face can the same be said for Todd Bowles? Many fans minds were made up on Todd Bowles before this season ever began, before the 2025 season, in all likelihood from the moment he got the job in 2022 there was a heavy contingent of fans that were not in favor of him as their team’s head man. Bowles’ record in four and a half seasons as Tampa Bay’s leader is 39-43— His claim to fame? Three NFC South crowns. Last season, was his first year missing the postseason and Tampa did so in dramatic team-wide collapsing fashion. This year, seems somehow worse. So what does a job-saving season look like for Todd Bowles at this point? First and foremost, without any dispute, the Buccaneers would need to make the playoffs. Anything short of a hellacious run to end the season and sneak into the playoffs as the kings of the South should lead to an immediate departure a head coaching search in January. A return to the postseason following last year’s leave should not be considered enough— If for no other reason than anyone who would’ve been asked six months ago what a successful season for the 2026 Tampa Bay Buccaneers would be wouldn’t have checked the box for seven or eight wins followed by a first round playoff exit. If Todd Bowles is able to rally his team and make run to the postseason with a season that will likely have more losses than wins the performance in the playoffs must play a factor. In the scenario that Tampa is the NFC South’s representative in this year’s postseason, Bowles’ Bucs would be matched up against a superior team. They would be an underdog at home in January. For Bowles to have a chance of survival, that first home playoff game would need to be a win. Game two of the playoff run would be a road playoff game, again as an underdog— Likely a very heavy underdog. A win in round one followed by a competitive loss in that round two game— That was the 2023 Tampa Bay Buccaneers. A playoff win and a close loss in round two is not a step forward, it’s a step backwards, back to where this team was three years ago. If Todd Bowles is able to take this team on the road and secure a second playoff victory that would mean the Buccaneers would have advanced to the NFC Championship Game— One game from Super Bowl. This becomes the point in time where Bowles has a chance. If Tampa Bay trecks their way through the rest of the regular season, winning enough games to burst into the playoffs, pulls out multiple playoff wins against quality contenders, and finds themselves 60 minutes from a Super Bowl appearance, Bowles has a chance. The narrative for the season would no longer be the doom and gloom Buccaneers. It would be that the team added a lot of new coaches with new pieces and simply needed to work out the kinks, that they just needed to get Baker Mayfield back healthy and that they were hamstrung by an undrafted rookie free agent quarterback earlier in the year, that Bowles has developed guys like Zyon McCollum and Jacob Parrish, and how his defense is playing at the highest level it has played at in years. A competitive showing in an NFC Championship Game setting is in all likelihood enough for Todd Bowles to retain his position as head coach of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers moving into 2027. It may be beyond unlikely and it may scare some fans to think about, but Todd Bowles can still save his job.

summary: We’re approximately two weeks away from the NFL trade deadline (Nov. 10). The 1-6 Tennessee Titans could be sellers. ESPN’s Matt Bowen and Jeremy Fowler recently published an article listing 25 players around the NFL as candidates to be […]
full_text: Tennessee Titans cornerback Alontae Taylor (24) talks with the media after the joint practice with the Seattle Seahawks at Vanderbilt Health Football Center Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co We’re approximately two weeks away from the NFL trade deadline (Nov. 10). The 1-6 Tennessee Titans could be sellers. GM Mike Borgonzi could certainly use additional draft capital as he continues rebuilding a young roster. ESPN’s Matt Bowen and Jeremy Fowler recently published an article listing 25 players around the NFL as candidates to be traded. The following three Titans made the list. We’ve paired our reactive analysis to each player with snippets of ESPN’s thoughts. DE Jermaine Johnson II Trading Jermaine Johnson II would make sense. The veteran pass rusher is on an expiring contract and would probably be useful to a playoff contender. The Titans acquired Johnson via trade in the offseason in exchange for T’Vondre Sweat. That makes the optics of trading him less than ideal, but rebuilding teams should always be interested in getting draft picks for veterans on expiring deals. “ Teams in the market for an edge rusher believe Johnson could be available at the right price ,” Fowler wrote . RB Tony Pollard Running back Tony Pollard also fits the criteria of being a useful veteran on an expiring contract. Earlier this season, Borgonzi apparently declined interest in trading Pollard. We’re not entirely sure we’re buying that. What does complicate the situation is how much more difficult his departure would make it to evaluate Cam Ward and the offense. “ Several teams could use a running back, and Pollard is an attractive fallback plan if the Colts stand pat on [Jonathan] Taylor ,” Fowler noted . CB Alontae Taylor Alontae Taylor makes an appearance after the Titans benched him in consecutive weeks. The optics here are brutal, with Taylor, a Tennessee native, having signed a three-year, $58 million contract in free agency this past offseason. His bloated contract probably makes it extremely difficult for Borgonzi to trade him. The Titans need to focus their energy on getting him to play better in this scheme. “ Taylor is not an easy player to trade because of his contract, which guarantees his entire 2027 salary of $20.5 million ,” Fowler wrote .
