full_text: Date/Time: Sunday, November 1, 2026 | 8:20 p.m. ET Location: Northwest Stadium (Landover, MD) The Washington Commanders come off their bye week with a 1-4-1 record and serious questions surrounding both the fate of their season and the future of head coach Dan Quinn. Terry McLaurin was lost for the year in their Week 6 matchup, while running back Bill Croskey-Merritt remains on the injured reserve list. In McLaurin’s absence, Dan Quinn expects Antonio Williams’ snaps to increase , with Chig Okonkwo’s role as a receiving threat expected to grow as well. Washington will look to use a committee approach in the backfield with Rachaad White, Austin Ekeler and Jeremy McNichols. Fortunately for Dan Quinn and the Washington Commanders, they face a 2-5 Eagles team that has lost five straight games, their longest winless streak since 2016. Paired with the season-ending loss of Jalen Hurts due to blood clots, the Eagles could be in tank mode as they head to Northwest Stadium in Week 8. Backup quarterback Tanner McKee has struggled behind an offensive line that has been reshuffled multiple times following the trade of Pro Bowl center Cam Jurgens and retirement of long-time right tackle Lane Johnson. Left tackle Jordan Mailata is the only player to play 100% of the team’s offensive snaps this year, while veteran Tyler Steen currently mans the right guard slot. Left guard Landon Dickerson and center/guard Drew Kendall both returned from injuries Monday night, while third-round rookie tackle Markel Bell made his first career start in Week 4. In two starts , McKee has thrown for 426 passing yards, 2 TDS, and 1 INT with a QBR of 35.4 this season. Saquon Barkley has been hampered by injuries over the past few weeks, and his status for Sunday night’s game is still uncertain. The Eagles placed backup Dameon Pierce on injured reserve Wednesday and signed practice squad running back Jaydon Blue to the active roster. Blue would be in line for more opportunities if Barkley misses any work Sunday night. Wide receivers Devonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks still lead the team in receiving, but first-round selection Makai Lemon had the best game of his rookie season on Monday night as McKee managed three solid quarters of play against a beleaguered Dallas defense. Makai Lemon had his best game as a pro, setting career highs in catches and yards while scoring his first NFL touchdown. 7 REC, 67 REC YDS, 1 TD vs Cowboys pic.twitter.com/jS220ShZmu — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) October 27, 2026 It was the defense that surprisingly failed the Eagles as Vic Fangio’s squad came apart on Monday night at Lincoln Financial Field. Missing only two starters, the Eagles defense was gashed for over 200 yards on the ground by a Dallas rushing attack that ranked 30th in the league coming into the game while giving up over 400 yards of total offense. Eagles' Defense All22 Thread vs. Cowboys. Buckle up. 1) The Cowboys absolutely destroyed the Eagles with Jumbo (6 OL) personnel. The Eagles had no answers all night. Some of the gaps were as big as you will ever see at this level. No single player or reason made it so bad. But… pic.twitter.com/ulxLxZueEn — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 27, 2026 It is possible that the defense finally broke under the weight of an offense that has struggled all season. As noted by Bleeding Green Nation , through their first seven games, the Eagles’ defense has been on the field for 67.3 plays per game, 4th-most in the NFL. This is due to Philadelphia’s offense leading the league in three-and-outs. Fangio’s defense has been on the field an average time of possession of 32:19, which is the second most in the league. No matter the reasons, the Eagles have struggled on both sides of the ball this season. The Eagles offense in 2026: – 29th in EPA/play – 30th in success rate – 26th in dropback EPA – 31st in dropback success rate The Eagles defense in 2026: – 27th in EPA/play – 25th in success rate – 29th in rush defense success rate – 31st in rush defense EPA Bad team. — Jake Rabadi (@JakeRabadi) October 27, 2026 Unfortunately for Quinn and the Commanders, the Eagles’ weaknesses mirror their own. While Philadelphia’s defense ranks 31st with a 28.7% pressure rate, the Commanders’ offensive line is allowing pressure 39.9% of the time. Similarly, while the Eagles offensive line is allowing pressure with a 41.7% rate , Washington’s defense ranks 17th in pressures with a 34.4% pressure rate and each defense has been extremely poor at generating quick pressures . Both teams have been bad in the trenches, but something will have to give on Sunday night. Coming off the bye, it will be interesting to see how the addition of Steve Wilks impacts Washington’s defensive game plan. full_text: Commanders head coach Dan Quinn announced that receiver Stefon Diggs would be held out of Wednesday’s practice, leading up to Sunday night’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles. He quickly followed that up with the fact that he’ll be a full go on Thursday. This isn’t related to the shot Diggs took to his hand during a Week 6 loss to San Francisco . While he didn’t say so expressly, this seems like veteran workload management. Diggs was formally listed with hand and hamstring issues, but was also designated as being given veteran rest. The Commanders have done things like this in the past, to help veterans be fresh and at their best on game day. That’s the most important thing for a player like Diggs, who will be instrumental with Terry McLaurin out for the season with a torn patellar tendon. Defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw was also held out of practice, and Quinn made it seem like a longshot that he’ll play against the Eagles. He was formally listed with a knee injury. Tight end John Bates didn’t practice with a shoulder injury. Those are injuries to monitor, considering the important roles they play. Receiver Treylon Burks (foot) and defensive lineman Charles Omenihu (groin/ankle) were limited. Quarterback Marcus Mariota (knee) was a full participant. Defensive lineman Johnny Newton’s 21-day practice window was opened on Wednesday, following his formal designation to return off injured reserve. title: Commanders Film Session: Antonio Williams is ready for more
summary: The season-ending loss of Terry McLaurin leaves a massive void in the Washington Commanders’ receiving room. Regardless of where you believe McLaurin ranks among the NFL’s best receivers, he has been the heartbeat of the Washington Commanders since entering the league. His ability to win contested catches, stretch defenses, and create explosive plays after the […]
full_text: The season-ending loss of Terry McLaurin leaves a massive void in the Washington Commanders’ receiving room. Regardless of where you believe McLaurin ranks among the NFL’s best receivers, he has been the heartbeat of the Washington Commanders since entering the league. His ability to win contested catches, stretch defenses, and create explosive plays after the catch made him an invaluable weapon. Furthermore, his overall intensity is what made him a spark plug for the team and the fan base. Replacing that production will require a collective effort from Washington’s receiver room, but rookie Antonio Williams should immediately become a priority in the offense. Through the first six games of his rookie season, Williams has demonstrated that he is far more polished than his experience suggests. While he lacks elite speed and overwhelming physicality , his understanding of coverage, defensive leverage, and route manipulation makes him a difficult matchup for opposing defenders. What stands out most is how consistently Williams attacks his routes with a plan. His versatility creates unpredictability for defenders, as he combines quickness and acceleration off the line of scrimmage with suddenness, sharp changes of direction, and underrated play strength at the top of his routes. More importantly, he understands how to use those traits to create separation rather than relying solely on athleticism. Williams has already shown flashes of his potential when given opportunities. Against the San Francisco 49ers, in Terry’s absence, he caught all three of his targets in the second half, finishing with 50 receiving yards. Through six games, Williams has totaled 18 receptions for 205 yards and, according to SumerSports, ranks 44th in the NFL in EPA per target among receivers who have run at least 50 routes. His production, combined with the technical skillset displayed on film, makes a compelling case that he is ready for a significantly larger workload. The question isn’t whether Williams can replace McLaurin’s production single-handedly. It’s whether Washington has a young receiver capable of taking on greater responsibility and consistently winning his individual matchups. Based on the film, Williams has earned that opportunity. In this Trap or Dive film session, I break down his first six games, highlighting the route-running intelligence, technical discipline, and versatility that make him an intriguing weapon in Washington’s offense moving forward. full_text: Johnny Newton suffered a torn pectoral muscle in the first Commanders preseason game. That’s normally a season-ender. It’s not the case this time. The second-year defensive lineman had his 21-day practice window opened on Wednesday, formally designating him to return off injured reserve. By rule , Newton must be activated within that window or he’ll be held on season-ending injured reserve. “He has worked his ass off,” head coach Dan Quinn said . Getting Newton back would be important for the team, considering his talents as an interior pass rusher. That wasn’t the only roster move Washington made on Wednesday afternoon. The Commanders formally placed receiver Terry McLaurin on injured reserve. He suffered a season-ending torn patellar tendon during a Week 6 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. Van Jefferson was promoted off the practice squad in a corresponding move. Jefferson was chosen over Jaden Bradley, and provides a more veteran presence in terms of depth. title: How Commanders LB Sonny Styles removed all doubt with stellar start
summary: The Commanders used a top 10 NFL draft pick on a non-premium position. Selections that high are normally reserved for a handful of spots, valued above all others, including quarterback, edge rusher, cornerback, offensive tackle and, at times, receiver.   An off-the-ball linebacker isn’t in that mix. Yet the Commanders confidently and without hesitation took Ohio […]
full_text: The Commanders used a top 10 NFL draft pick on a non-premium position. Selections that high are normally reserved for a handful of spots, valued above all others, including quarterback, edge rusher, cornerback, offensive tackle and, at times, receiver. An off-the-ball linebacker isn’t in that mix. Yet the Commanders confidently and without hesitation took Ohio State linebacker Sonny Styles at No. 7 overall . There are exceptions to every rule. Styles was one. The athletic freak with an off-the-charts RAS was confidently taken, as a defensive anchor point for years to come. Styles has played just six games to this point, but the evaluation’s pretty clear. This dude is legit. We officially learned that in Week 3, when he covered Seattle running back Jadarian Price like a blanket on a deep pass, which he expertly knocked away with an outstretched arm. Price runs like a gazelle. Styles is 6-foot-5 and 245 pounds. Guys that big shouldn’t run like that. The play we recall here wasn’t the biggest stat. We’re talking about a pass defensed on a day where he had five tackles, a forced fumble and an interception . Sonny Styles with the PBU 🔥 @SEAvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/F6KiZsymMY — NFL (@NFL) September 27, 2026 He was named NFC defensive player of the week after that showing. Yet, somehow, the man has done better. He had 13 tackles against the Giants. And 13 more against the 49ers heading into last week’s bye. It’s even more than the stats. It’s instinctual plays like this: Sonny Styles is improving every week. This coverage play is one that very few other LBs can make. The range to cover the ground, the awareness to know where the danger is, the length to get his hand in to the catch point and knock the ball out. Incredible play pic.twitter.com/ffktJPalPW — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) October 21, 2026 Or when he introduced himself to the NFL by obliterating Saquon Barkley in Week 1. What a PLAY by the rook, Sonny Styles 💪 WASvsPHI on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/KjyjZPPBcZ — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 The bye provides us a time to check in on Washington’s first-round pick, who sure seems like a foundational player already. title: REVISITED: One thought on 27 Commanders 2026 free agents
summary: NOTE: THIS IS A REVISIT OF AN ARTICLE THAT I ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED ON MAY 7th OF THIS YEAR. I HOPE YOU ENJOY MY CURRENT RUMINATIONS ON MY PRESEASON THOUGHTS ABOUT 27 FREE AGENTS. full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Chig Okonkwo #85 of the Washington Commanders runs with the ball after making a catch against the San Francisco 49ers during the second quarter of the game at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images NOTE: THIS IS A REVISIT OF AN ARTICLE THAT I ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED ON MAY 7th OF THIS YEAR. I HOPE YOU ENJOY MY CURRENT RUMINATIONS ON MY PRESEASON THOUGHTS ABOUT 27 FREE AGENTS. The 5 o’clock club is published from time to time during the season, and aims to provide a forum for reader-driven discussion at a time of day when there isn’t much NFL news being published. Feel free to introduce topics that interest you in the comments below. CLICK HERE to see the full 5 o’clock club archive A note from Bill: As always, it’s worth noting that I am no more qualified than any other NFL fan to assess players. My role as a writer on Hogs Haven is based primarily on having sufficient time and motivation to post articles daily combined with the ability to spell most of the words correctly. What follows is a repeat of an exercise I did last year — basically just a long comment that I am throwing out for your consideration on this fine May morning, now that the roster is nearly complete. Today seems like a good time to go on record with my thoughts about the men who comprise Washington’s 2026 veteran free agent signings & re-signings. No. 1 QB Marcus Mariota (re-signed, 1 year) In 2024, I was deeply disappointed when I learned that the Commanders had signed Mariota to a $6m one-year deal. Well, MM made me a believer with everything he did that season. Last year, I was thrilled to have him back at $8m. This year, I might’ve been ready to move on to a younger, cheaper backup if there hadn’t been so much turmoil; with the change at OC, QB coach and OL coach, continuity with Mariota feels like it’s worth the $7.3m cap hit that OTC reports for the position. Hopefully, next season, the backup will be Athan Kaliakmanis, or someone similar. UPDATE : It feels as if the Week 3 win over the Seahawks has already justified the investment in Mariota. I hope he’ll spend the rest of the season on the bench. Bonus thought: I thought the Week 4 glimpse of rookie Athan Kaliakmanis was promising. No. 2 P Tress Way (re-signed, 1 year) Normally, I’d be saying that a 36-yr-old punter being paid over $3m per year should be replaced by a younger, cheaper option, but Tress, our longest-tenured player, is a good punter, great holder, locker room leader, and active in the community. As long as he keeps doing all those things well for a cap hit of around $1.5m on a 4-year qualifying contract, I’m happy to see him coming back for another year. Here’s hoping he’s on the sidelines for the opening game at the new stadium in 2030! UPDATE : Tress has now said that 2026 is probably his final season, and that’s okay. He has also said he wants to take his family back to Oklahoma, which is a shame for the fans because I always envisioned him retiring in the DC area and becoming a fixture in local NFL media. He’s had to do far too much work in the early part of the season; let’s hope he spends much more time on the sidelines in the final 11 regular season games of his fine career. No. 3 OL Trent Scott (re-signed, 1 year) Washington is Trent Scott’s 4th team, and in every year of his 8-year career, he has started at least one game (and has 27 total starts in his career, including 3 last season) although he saw the field for just 82 snaps in 2025. In 2024, he seemed to surprise everyone when he stepped in at RG and played pretty well when Sam Cosmi was lost to an ACL tear. A year ago, it felt inevitable that he would make the 53-man roster. This year, I think he may be on the roster bubble behind Tunsil, Conerly, Coleman, and Wylie. I could see him ending up on the practice squad or signing with another team. UPDATE : It seems like I got the temperature read just about right on this one; Trent Scott did, indeed, end up on Washington’s practice squad. It almost makes me wonder if he should get a shot at playing on the left side of the line. Nos. 4 – 6 WRs Dyami Brown, Treylon Burks & Van Jefferson (all 1 year) Each of these guys got a contract worth between $1.26m and $1.99m in 2026. I think Van Jefferson ends up being the odd man out, with Burks & Brown both getting regular snaps, but with neither likely to have more than 30 or so catches or more than 300 or so yards ; however, if one catches fire, the other will probably be relegated to the end of the bench. Any of these guys could get displaced by a great training camp & preseason by a player like Ja’Corey Brooks or Jacoby Jones. UPDATE : If you read the sentence that I bolded, it seems to have played out pretty much exactly as expected though Burks & Brown are slightly ahead of my projection. Jefferson is on the practice squad (and he could possibly see some regular season playing time if injury continues to cut into the current WR room). Brown is on track for 266 yards in 17 games while Burks in tracking for 430 yards. Dyami has contributed as a special teams returner; Treylon has not. No. 7 RB Jeremy McNichols I like McNichols, but the Commanders RB room is competitive enough that there may not be room for him to make the 53-man roster for the 3rd year in a row. I think that Bill Croskey-Merritt, Fatman Allen and Rachaad White are roster locks. For McNichols to make the 53-man roster, I think the team will need to keep 4 backs, and I have him ahead of Jerome Ford if they do. Despite an unimpressive career stat sheet, McNichols could end up on another NFL roster if the Commanders don’t have him on the Week 1 roster. Hopefully, he would land on the Washington practice squad instead. He’s a valuable back who has had 2 solid seasons in a Commanders uniform. UPDATE : While injury has limited McNichols’ 2026 availability, the rest has played out pretty much as projected, with the team opening the season with Bill, Kaytron & Rachaad on the 53-man roster. Of course, Kaytron got nicked off of the waiver wire, which made McNichols more valuable when he was healthy enough to play. In his sole appearance this season, he ran for 13 yards on 5 carries. No. 8 CB Amik Robertson (signed, 2 years) I just haven’t been able to work up any enthusiasm for Robertson. His contract indicates that the Commanders aren’t fully sold on him either, as it is basically a 1-year, $7.5m deal with a team option for a second year at about the same price. Undersized and his best season now 3 years past, this feels like a roster band aid that isn’t completely adequate and not sticky enough for long-term duty. UPDATE : Bill-in-Bangkok swings…and MISSES THE BALL ENTIRELY!! I couldn’t have been much more wrong about Robertson, who may be the Commanders player who is performing closest to a Pro Bowl season through 6 weeks. He has been, at times, the only player in the defensive secondary who looked fully competent for an entire game. If things continue on the current path (including coaching staff), then Robertson will certainly be back in ‘27 vying for a starting position for the 2nd year in a row. He has been the most pleasant of surprises to me, though apparently, his play was not a surprise to the front office or coaching staff. I’m thrilled to have been wrong here. No. 9 OL Andrew Wylie (re-signed, 2 years) When he was the starting right tackle, I felt the team could do better. As a back up guard/tackle earning $3.75m per year, I’m fine with Wylie. It feels like the right role and pay for the 8-year veteran. UPDATE : Yep. We know who Wylie is and isn’t at this point. No. 10 EDGE Charles Omenihu (signed, 1 year) At 6’6”, 275 pounds, Omenihu offers the versatility to line up anywhere from 3-tech to 9-tech and play effectively. At $4m for one season, the price is right. He should provide a lot of what Daronte Jones will be looking for in 2026. If he provides it, he can be…

title: NFL trade deadline grades: DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson dealt by Colts, more
summary: Does Buckner make the 49ers Super Bowl hopefuls? Will Quenton Nelson upgrade the Seahawks' O-line? We're grading NFL trades ahead of November's deadline.
full_text:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline , which is Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET.

 When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

 Here are our evaluations for the first deals of trading season, including the Colts sending guard Quenton Nelson to Seattle and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to San Francisco. Check back through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

 

 
 Jump to a trade: 
 Buckner |  Nelson | Harrison   
 Jurgens  |  Porter | McCarthy 

 
 

 

 Colts trade DT Buckner to 49ers 

 49ers get: DT DeForest Buckner 
 Colts get: 2027 fourth-round pick

 49ers grade: A- 
 Colts grade: B-

 As soon as the Colts emerged as a team that might engage in a trade-deadline teardown, it wasn't hard to see the dots connecting Buckner back to the 49ers. That became a reality Tuesday.

 Though his numbers have dipped, Buckner, 32, can still help the 49ers get after the quarterback. He has four sacks this season, but his pass rush win rate ranked in the 45th percentile among defensive tackles, alongside a 69th percentile pressure rate. That is a drop from last season, when he was in the 90th and 88th percentile in those metrics, respectively. However, that 2025 performance is a positive sign for what he could bring to the 49ers the rest of this season.

 Extra pass-rushing help will be welcome in San Francisco, which ranks 19th in pass rush win rate. The 49ers have been without Nick Bosa , who has been out because of  a calf injury since Week 3 but is expected to return soon. Their pass defense is the only one of their major units (run and pass on offense and defense) that ranks outside the top seven in EPA per play (13th).

 

 I'll admit I'm a little surprised the 49ers made this move considering they already have Osa Odighizuwa as a pass-rush-first defensive tackle. But he can play next to Buckner -- especially on passing downs. Also, San Francisco's rash of defensive line injuries makes any help welcome.

 This type of roster-bolstering move makes sense for San Francisco. The 49ers are the Super Bowl favorites, according to ESPN's Football Power Index . In fact, they are the favorites by a lot , with the FPI giving them a 23% chance to win the Super Bowl (every other team is below 11%). Adding Buckner to reinforce those chances is worthwhile.

 The cost was also quite reasonable. The 49ers are surrendering a fourth-round pick and taking over the prorated remainder of Buckner's $13 million salary, assuming his contract is untouched. While compensatory picks are never a guarantee, there's a decent chance that San Francisco might recoup most of that draft capital back via a comp pick if Buckner signs elsewhere in free agency next offseason, especially given that San Francisco is low on 2027 cap space.

 That also is why I'm a little critical of the Colts' move here. Don't get me wrong, it absolutely makes sense for Indianapolis to trade him. The Colts are rebuilding, and Buckner is a 32-year-old in the final year of his contract -- of course they should have dealt him before the deadline.

 

 Perhaps this was the best offer Indianapolis received for Buckner today , but they also didn't have to trade Buckner right now. There are two weeks left until the Nov. 10 trade deadline. I would have thought they could have at least squeezed another Day 3 pick in addition to the fourth-rounder. -- Walder 

 
 

 Colts trade G Nelson to Seahawks 
 Seahawks get: G Quenton Nelson 
 Colts get: 2027 third-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

 Seahawks grade: A- 
 Colts grade: B+

 The reimagination of the Colts is officially underway, with longtime Indianapolis stalwart Nelson heading to the defending Super Bowl champions to bolster the interior of their offensive line.

 Nelson, 30, started his career with three consecutive first-team All-Pro selections. His level of play dropped in 2022 and 2023, but the 2018 first-round pick battled back to elite form in 2024, when he posted pass block and run block win rates that were each in the 90th percentile, along with earning second-team All-Pro honors. He earned a second-team All-Pro spot last season, too, along with a 91st percentile and 74th percentile pass block and run block win rates, respectively.

 His win rates haven't been quite as strong this season (66th and 37th percentile, respectively), but Nelson's reputation is still superb, and having such consistent results the previous two years suggests he probably remains one of the best guards in the league if we're projecting the rest of the season.

 

 The Seahawks presumably will keep Nelson at left guard and move Grey Zabel to right guard. That will push Anthony Bradford , who recently returned from injured reserve and has played two games this season, to the bench. Bradford recorded 30th and 33rd percentile pass block and run block win rates last season, respectively, so Nelson is a substantial upgrade.

 The Seahawks have Super Bowl aspirations but must get better play out of an offense that ranks 26th in EPA per play and 31st in EPA per designed rush. They rank 27th in run block win rate, 28th in yards per designed running back carry (3.6) and 28th in yards before contact on designed run plays. They also rank 21st in pass block win rate. So the team needed some offensive line help and upgrading their right guard or center made sense.

 Nelson is on an expiring contract, so unless his deal was altered, the Seahawks will take on the prorated remainder of his $16 million in salary for this season, which is a bargain for the quality of play he brings. The Seahawks could sign Nelson to an extension or a new deal after the season, but they could also let him walk in free agency and possibly collect a compensatory pick to mitigate the draft capital lost in this trade.

 It makes a lot of sense for the Seahawks to push their chips in on their current team. History tells us how hard it is to sustain elite defensive success, so the Seahawks need to take advantage while they have it.

 This was also an easily logical move for the Colts. The 2026 season is lost, and Nelson is a pending free agent. Whatever value he would bring to the team in the second half of the season pales in comparison to what he brings to the Seahawks, and the draft capital return is more than they would get in compensatory picks (which are never a guarantee, anyway) had Nelson left in free agency. Plus, they save money on the remainder of his 2026 salary.

 

 Ultimately, this is a win-win trade. Considering Seattle's contention window, positional (and overall offensive) need, the draft capital required and Nelson's contract, this is a sound move. -- Walder 

 

 

 Cardinals trade WR Harrison Jr. to Texans 
 Texans get: WR  Marvin Harrison Jr ., 2027 seventh-round pick 
 Cardinals get: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pick

 Texans grade: C+ 
 Cardinals: A-

 Minutes after the Texans completed their 26-3 blowout win over the Titans, news broke that the rumored trade of Harrison, who was inactive Sunday because of the expected move, would be completed. The Cardinals sent him to Houston for a second-rounder and a sixth-rounder in 2027.

 Similar to a lot of trades for young players, there are two simple questions: How much of our opinion of Harrison should be shaped by the league's predraft opinion of him and how much should be based on what we've seen from him in the NFL so far?

title: 2026 NFL trade deadline: Ranking the top 25 candidates to move, plus team fits
summary: Could the Colts listen on Jonathan Taylor? Would Josh Sweat help a contender's defense? We stacked the top players who might move before the Nov. 10 deadline.
full_text:
We're less than two weeks away from the 2026 NFL trade deadline  (Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 4 p.m. ET). Which players could potentially be available? And which trade candidates could make the biggest impact with new teams if they do get moved?

 NFL analyst Matt Bowen and national NFL reporter Jeremy Fowler worked together to build a comprehensive list of the top 25 possible trade candidates. To be clear: Players are ranked here by the potential value they'd provide a new team if traded -- not their likelihood of actually being dealt.

 That said, we did include our estimated percentage chances for each player to move, weaving in what we're hearing. Jeremy shared the latest buzz on each player, while Matt broke down what he sees on the tape. We even included some interesting team fits for each candidate. Some players have better odds of changing cities than others on the list, but all 25 are at the very least being discussed in trade conversations. Let's dive in.

 

 
 Jump to the top-ranked: 
 QB | RB | WR | TE | OL 
 Edge | DT | LB | CB | S 

 
 

 

 1. Jonathan Taylor , RB, Indianapolis Colts 
 What Fowler is hearing: Teams I've talked to aren't totally sold that Indianapolis will trade Taylor despite heavy interest  -- at least not yet. He is signed long term and would be a boon for next year's coaching staff, whether it's the current group or entirely new. But what Kenneth Walker III has done for Kansas City shows how a premier running back can put on new jersey colors and immediately reimagine a team's season. And the tenor of Indy's season is getting ugly, which affects all key players and could spark even more movement.

 Predicted chance of getting traded: 30%

 What Bowen sees on tape: Taylor is averaging 109.3 total yards per game this season, and he's tied for first in rushing TDs with eight. He's a volume runner with home run speed and pass-catching ability on screens and swings. His 17 rushes for 10 or more yards are tied for the fourth most in the league. Taylor would be an immediate upgrade for a team in need of a lead back who is decisive with the ball.

 

 Team fits: Seahawks, Commanders, Saints, Broncos, Vikings

 
 

 2. Brian Thomas Jr ., WR, Jacksonville Jaguars 
 What Fowler is hearing: League execs are sensing the end for BTJ in Jacksonville, as his targets and playing time have dipped. How Jacksonville has struggled to make this relationship work is still a mystery. Thomas is an elite mover with size who draws coverage deep, setting the stage for teammates Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers to eat underneath. But that plan for Thomas hasn't materialized this season. And teams are circling with interest. Kansas City and Pittsburgh are among those exploring receiver help.

 Predicted chance of getting traded: 45%

 What Bowen sees on tape: Thomas' numbers have declined over the past two seasons, but he has the traits to still draw interest. At 6-foot-3 and 209 pounds, Thomas has the profile of an X receiver who can separate at multiple levels of the field. I see legit straight-line speed and ball-tracking ability. He had 87 receptions and 10 touchdowns as a rookie in 2024, but he has been limited to a 9-105-1 line so far this season.

 

 Team fits: Chiefs, Steelers, 49ers

 
 

 3. Josh Sweat , Edge, Arizona Cardinals 
 What Fowler is hearing: Rival teams could see him getting moved. "Sweat to Dallas makes a lot of sense to me," an NFC exec said. "That's a profile fit." Rumblings persist that Sweat would want a new contract -- he's in the second year of a four-year, $76 million deal -- and that could complicate things. But many teams are looking for an edge rusher.

 Predicted chance of getting traded: 40%

 What Bowen sees on tape: A long, angular mover who can win with speed-to-power, Sweat had 12 sacks and 37 pressures in Arizona last season. But his numbers haven't been as solid in 2026, with two sacks and 10 pressures. Still, Sweat's ability to threaten the edges of offensive tackles with his quickness off the ball fits pass-rush fronts across the league.

 Team fits: Cowboys, Bears, 49ers

 

 
 

 4. Yaya Diaby , Edge, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 What Fowler is hearing: Tampa Bay beat Carolina handedly in Week 7 , with Diaby exploding for three sacks. A loss would have put the Bucs at 1-6 and closer to dealing mode. Diaby, 27, is still on the radar, though, because Tampa is not poised to pay the 2027 free agent, and the emergence of second-year rusher David Walker (four sacks) gives the Bucs a natural replacement. Diaby needs a new contract, but an acquiring team could get a compensatory pick for him if he signs a substantial deal with another team in free agency.

 Predicted chance of getting traded: 35%

 What Bowen sees on tape:  Diaby is a powerful and physical edge rusher with the temperament to set the edge against the run. He has three sacks and six tackles for loss in 2026, and he had 40 or more pressures in each of his past two seasons (with 11.5 total sacks over that time). He should be viewed as a quality starter.

 Team fits: Browns, Seahawks, Cowboys

 
 

 5. Jerry Jeudy , WR, Cleveland Browns 
 What Fowler is hearing: The Browns are not actively sending out feelers on Jeudy, but they would at least consider a substantial offer. Key word here is "substantial," though. I'm not sure, say, a fourth-round pick would move anyone in Cleveland, for example. Jeudy is part of the Browns' three-receiver sets and the veteran in that room for a good team in the playoff hunt. That dynamic diminishes his chances of being dealt. But as always, teams are looking for receiver help.

 Predicted chance of getting traded: 20%

 What Bowen sees on tape: Jeudy has the route traits and stop-start speed to separate as a multilevel route runner. He's sudden at the break point. However, the inconsistent hands have been an issue as a pro (33 career drops), and Jeudy lacks the frame and physicality to win on 50-50 throws. Jeudy had a career-best 1,229 receiving yards in 2024, yet he has just 16 receptions this season.

 

 Team fits: Chiefs, Raiders, Commanders

 
 

 6. Daron Payne , DT, Washington Commanders 
 What Fowler is hearing: Washington dealt key defensive pieces at the deadline three years ago and could be faced with a similar predicament this time with Payne, who's 29 and still has value. Payne is a 2027 free agent with a $16.4 million base this year. But the NFC East is also winnable, despite Washington's 1-4-1 record, so that could be a point in favor of the Commanders keeping him. Jacksonville is a potential fit, with some in the league noting the Jaguars could use a versatile interior player with pass-rush ability and have looked for that since the offseason.

 Predicted chance of getting traded: 25%

 What Bowen sees on tape:  Payne can still provide an interior presence due to his foot quickness and strength in one-on-one matchups, plus he will impact the run game from multiple alignments. He had a career-best 11.5 sacks in 2022, but he has totaled only 12 over his past four seasons.

 Team fits: Jaguars, Giants, Buccaneers

 
 

 

 7. Khalil Mack , Edge, Los Angeles Chargers 
 What Fowler is hearing:  Mack is productive and affordable. The Chargers gave him a $10 million signing bonus in March, so a new team would inherit the prorated version of his $8 million salary to close out his one-year deal. Returning to the Bears is a natural fit for the equivalent of a quality Day 3 pick. The Chargers have held off trading pieces such as Mack up to this point, though.

 Predicted chance of getting traded: 35%

 What Bowen sees on tape: Mack doesn't display the same level of explosive speed on tape, but he can still disrupt the pocket due to his play strength and advanced counter moves. Mack has 14.5 sacks and 83 pressures over his past three seasons, and he can play as both a pass-rushing linebacker or defensive end with third-down upside.

 

 Team fits: Bears, Browns, Bills, Cowboys

title: How the Falcons' two biggest stars bond off the field
summary: Bijan Robinson and Drake London are like brothers off the field, and on it, they're among the NFL's best.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- The first time Bijan Robinson  communicated with Drake London , it was about a number.

 The Atlanta Falcons drafted Robinson with the eighth overall pick in 2023. At Texas, Robinson wore No. 5, which was in use by London, who was selected by the Falcons with the exact same pick a year earlier.

 Robinson got London's cell phone number from then-head coach Arthur Smith and shot the wide receiver a text. He wasn't sure exactly how it would go. Robinson didn't know London and some players can be attached to their numbers. So, Robinson, as is his way, asked in the most polite way possible.

 London, to Robinson's relief, was amenable to giving up No. 5. London had worn No. 15 at Southern California. But when London found out that No. 15 wasn't available -- wide receiver Van Jefferson was going to wear it -- he told Robinson he was going to stay with No. 5. Robinson ended up choosing No. 7.

 "It all worked out," Robinson said.

 

 Robinson and London are now close friends and make up the offensive foundation for the Falcons -- and will for the foreseeable future. Both signed long-term contract extensions in the offseason, which will ostensibly keep them in Atlanta together through the 2030 season.

 The Falcons (3-4) have had uneven results so far this season, as well as in the three previous years Robinson and London have been together. The team has failed to make the playoffs or have a winning season, but it is through no fault of its star duo.

 Robinson has emerged as arguably the best running back in the NFL, leading the league in rushing this season (704 yards) and in scrimmage yards (2,298) last season. London has cemented himself as an elite wideout and is fourth in the NFL with 616 receiving yards. His touchdown Sunday helped the Falcons upset the San Francisco 49ers .

 Individual accomplishments aside, Robinson and London share a collective goal: getting the Falcons back to the promised land. Atlanta has not made the playoffs since 2017, the second-longest drought in the NFL. (The Jets haven't reached the postseason in 15 seasons.) And the Falcons have never won a Super Bowl. Robinson and London want to be part of the core that changes that.

 "[Bijan and I] talk about that before every season," London said. "This is the one where we got to do it. We're still striving for that and not even just together, but for this team, for this city, for the fans.

 "I always say that, and that's exactly why I wanted to stay here. You'll be the first to ever do it. I don't care where you're at [on] the totem pole of this team, you're going to be the first to ever do it. And that means something. I know this city will go up if we do that."

 Why the Robinson-London duo is among the NFL's best 
 Robinson and London sat shoulder to shoulder on the Falcons' bench. It was late in a 34-3 loss to the Carolina Panthers at home in Week 2. Robinson and London could both be seen talking to one another and shaking their heads, almost trying to figure out how the game had come to that.

 "We were just talking about how to fix that situation, that game," Robinson said. "What can we do better? How can we be better? And that was the key to that conversation, man. Just how can we help improve this offense? How can we help improve this team to the best of our ability? And that's really what it was about right there."

 There were some extenuating circumstances. The Falcons were playing third-string quarterback Cooper Rush with both Michael Penix Jr . (ACL) and Tua Tagovailoa (oblique) injured. Rush was dealing with back spasms himself, but played through them.

 

 The following week, with Penix back, Robinson and London both went off. Robinson had 194 yards on the ground and London, fittingly, had the exact same total receiving in a 35-14 win over the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field.

 It was the third time Robinson and London each went over 150 yards in the same game, an NFL record for a running back-wide receiver duo.

 "I mean, that's cool and all, but sometimes I'll be talking to my friends back home, and I'll be tripping out that Bijan [texts] me and stuff like that," London said after the game. "You know what I'm saying? He's going to be a [gold] jacket wearer. ... So it's really, really cool and just blessed to be a part of something like that."

 Robinson refers to London as his "real-life brother." The pair have been through two coaching changes in Atlanta, from Smith to Raheem Morris to Kevin Stefanski. The front office execs who drafted them are mostly gone. They have had a different starting quarterback to begin the season all four years they have been together.

 "I call him my blood brother because we really are," Robinson said. "We do everything together. We work hard together, we train together, do things off the field.

 "We talk about everything, and just seeing some of the adversity that we got to face throughout our career together and for these kinds of moments to happen is pretty special and I know he's enjoying it. I'm enjoying it, too."

 The stars' families have grown close, too. Robinson's grandparents often meet up with London's parents the night before games and go to dinner together. It is a strong bond.

 "They ended up clicking, and just every now and then we'll go out and eat and share a few words and stuff like that," London said. "My parents really do look up to them just as great people because of the age difference and stuff like that."

 

 The two complement each other on the field, as well. London is one of the best blocking wide receivers in the league. Falcons offensive coordinator Tommy Rees has lauded London for how unselfish he is despite being the team's star wideout.

 "When your best player, best receiver is selfless and willing to do those things and actually enjoys doing those things, I think it creates buy-in across the board," Rees said.

 Without London's blocking, Robinson might not be able to break those long runs like that 55-yard scamper he had against the Packers. And without Robinson's ability, London said, he wouldn't have as much room on the outside because teams are forced to stack the box to contain the threat of the ground game.

 "We got to lean on each other to make this train go," London said.

 Both are great players, but London is the fiery one 
 Robinson said he believes he and London are very similar. They're both homebodies and somewhat introverted off the field. You won't find either of them partaking in Atlanta's nightlife.

 On the field, though, teammates say they are very different. Both are extremely competitive, it just comes out in separate ways.

 In that lopsided loss to the Panthers, London fired back verbally to a fan who was lobbing insults at him. London so badly wants to win that if things don't go that way he can lose his cool at times. Robinson always remains even-keeled, regardless of game results.

 

 "On the field, Drake is more loud, screaming, but Bijan, he's always calm and not really saying [much]," Penix said. "But in the locker room, they're both the same. They talk, they're quiet, humble, humble guys. Just on the field, Drake shows it, expresses it more than Bijan does verbally."

 Has Robinson ever gotten angry and acted out?

 "I've never seen him get upset," Penix said.

 Tight end  Kyle Pitts Sr ., who got to Atlanta the year before London, echoed the sentiment.

 "Definitely game day, Drake's probably the more fiery one," Pitts said. "Bijan's definitely not fiery. He's very competitive, but fiery, I don't know. He's not a super yeller, but he'll show leadership when he needs to for sure."

 Robinson said London's intensity is one of the things he likes about his teammate and friend. It's one of the things, Robinson said, that gives the team the juice that can help it get over the hump, which both he and London are desperate to do.

 

 "He's passionate, man," Robinson said. "And I try not to get in the way of that because that's what builds…

title: Ranking the best 2026 NFL rookies: Arvell Reese, Denzel Boston, others in top 10
summary: Who are the NFL's most impressive rookies through Week 7? Who is overperforming or underperforming? We stacked the top 10 -- and have a tie at No. 1.
full_text:
The 2026 rookie class has had a unique start to  the NFL season , specifically at quarterback. According to ESPN Research, the 308 snaps by rookie QBs through Week 7 are the fewest since 2007. Tampa Bay's Jalon Daniels is the only rookie QB who has started so far, and his three starts are also the fewest at this point in the season since 2007.

 Because of this, zero quarterbacks made our debut top-10 rookie rankings -- sorry to Daniels, who just  handed the Bucs' starting gig back to Baker Mayfield . But there are plenty of intriguing players from six other positions who made our top 10.

 We polled five NFL analysts and reporters -- Matt Bowen, Kalyn Kahler, Jeff Legwold, Jordan Reid and Ben Solak -- to form a consensus ranking through Week 7. Our experts also predicted when quarterback Fernando Mendoza will start for the Raiders, picked out the most impressive position group, named one underperforming first-rounder and selected one overperforming late-rounder.

 

 Jump to a section:  
 Top 10 | Just missed 
 Big questions 

 

 

 T-1. Arvell Reese , Edge/LB, New York Giants 
 Stats: 56 tackles, 1.5 sacks, 1 INT 
 Drafted: No. 5

 Just as we saw during his final season at Ohio State, Reese's physicality and speed have shown up right away at the NFL level. He is comfortable attacking downhill as a run defender, and his consistency in coverage has been excellent. His four pass breakups are tied for the second most among all linebackers in 2026.

 Reese is the ultimate playmaker who can not only be used on the second level but is also equally as effective as a blitzer. He has 10 pass-rush wins and two pass breakups on 93 blitz attempts this season. Reese is a key building block for the Giants' defense alongside 2025 first-round pick  Abdul Carter .  -- Reid 

 
 

 

 T-1. Sonny Styles , LB, Washington Commanders 
 Stats: 46 tackles, 1 sack, 1 INT, 1 FF 
 Drafted: No. 7

 Styles' speed is what made him a top-10 pick, and he has put it on full display this season. In Washington's only win , he went stride for stride with Seattle running back Jadarian Price to break up a deep pass. Later in the third quarter, he caught up with tight end Eric Saubert  and stripped the ball at the goal line -- though Saubert recovered it for a touchdown. (He also had his only interception in that game.)

 Styles even made a strong debut, trucking Eagles running back  Saquon Barkley on his way to sacking quarterback Jalen Hurts . Styles has 13 tackles in Washington's past two games, which suggests he's only improving as his rookie year continues. -- Kahler 

 
 

 3. Denzel Boston , WR, Cleveland Browns 
 Stats: 20 receptions, 372 yards, 3 TDs 
 Drafted: No. 39

 The physical 6-foot-4 receiver is second in air yards per target (16.1), a full yard ahead of Detroit's Jameson Williams . Boston has become the Browns' dangerous deep threat, and though he has had a quiet couple of weeks, he is also second in yards per reception (18.6).

 Cleveland's offense features multiple playmakers equally. Boston sees 20% of the Browns' total targets, but fellow rookie KC Concepcion sees 21.8% and tight end Harold Fannin Jr . is just behind at 18.9%. It will be interesting to monitor whether that distribution shifts throughout the rest of the season.  -- Kahler 

 
 

 4. Josiah Trotter , LB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 Stats: 62 tackles, 1 sack, 1 INT 
 Drafted: No. 46

 Trotter's play recognition stands out on the tape. He is quick to diagnose against the run, getting eyes on formation keys and pulling guards to make tackles. His 43% run stop win rate ranks 10th among all linebackers, and he has the physical play style to drop the hammer on contact.

 Plus, Trotter has created some on-the-ball production in coverage, which includes a pick-six on quarterback  Joe Burrow and the Bengals. He's an ascending player who can also be schemed as blitzer in Todd Bowles' defense. -- Bowen 

 
 

 

 5. Olaivavega Ioane , G, Baltimore Ravens 
 Stats: 7 starts, 89.2% PBWR, 69% RBWR 
 Drafted: No. 14

 Ioane has already shown some versatility with 196 snaps at center and 182 at right guard. The Ravens have been forced to throw him into the deep end because of injuries, including three centers being put on IR.

 The injury bug caught up with Ioane himself, as he sprained an MCL  at right guard in a Week 7 loss to the Bengals . It's considered a short-term injury, but so far Ioane has played with physicality, and his pass block win rate at center (94.5%) is third best in the league. Ravens coach Jesse Minter has already said he believes Ioane deserves Offensive Rookie of the Year consideration. -- Legwold 

 
 

 6. Jacob Rodriguez , LB, Miami Dolphins 
 Stats: 61 tackles, 1 INT 
 Drafted: No. 43

 At the center of Miami's rebuild, Rodriguez has been among the most impressive rookies regardless of position. After ranking 27th in the FBS with 8.6 tackles per game last season at Texas Tech, he is third in the NFL through seven weeks (10.2).

 Rodriguez is a quick-footed linebacker who's consistently able to diagnose and attack downhill on run plays. He has also shown the ability to close throwing windows and make plays in the passing game. -- Reid 

 
 

 7. Mansoor Delane , CB, Kansas City Chiefs 
 Stats: 27 tackles, 1 INT, 5 PD 
 Drafted: No. 6

 It's almost impossible to excel as a rookie corner in the NFL. Just ask Delane, who had perfect positioning and an elite strike on Seattle's  Jaxon Smith-Njigba  but still got beat for a touchdown in Week 7 . Regardless, Delane has consistently been in the hip pocket of top NFL receivers; he has the physicality and ball skills necessary to develop into a premiere ball hawk.

 With a 20% pass breakup and interception rate (league average for corners is 15.3%) and a tight window forced on 32% of his targets (league average is 25.3%), Delane is answering the call as a top-10 draft pick. -- Solak 

 

 
 

 8. David Bailey , Edge, New York Jets 
 Stats: 35 tackles, 5.5 sacks, 3 FF 
 Drafted: No. 2

 Bailey leads all rookies in sack totals, and his 24 pressures rank sixth in the league. He entered the draft as the most pro-ready pass rusher after four collegiate seasons, and that is evident on the tape.

 Bailey combines his quickness and lower-body agility with a refined set of counter moves to work the edges of offensive tackles. Plus, he can create production late in the down by tracking the quarterback outside of the pocket. His 23.8% pass rush win rate ranks third highest among qualified rookies.  -- Bowen 

 
 

 T-9. Blake Miller , OT, Detroit Lions 
 Stats: 5 starts, 91% PBWR, 65.7% RBWR 
 Drafted: No. 17

 After Miller made 54 consecutive starts to close out his career at Clemson, there were some NFL evaluators who believed he was one of the safest picks in April. He looks every bit the long-term solution at right tackle for the Lions, who moved All-Pro  Penei Sewell to left tackle over the offseason.

 Miller's current pass block win rate ranks 10th in the league and tops among all rookies. He has surrendered one sack and been clean with his handwork -- no penalties for holding, illegal use of hands or hands to the face. -- Legwold 

 
 

 T-9. KC Concepcion , WR, Cleveland Browns 
 Stats: 30 receptions, 315 yards, 0 TDs 
 Drafted: No. 24

 Concepcion's career-best game against the Titans in Week 7 -- eight catches, 129 yards and a touchdown with 23 rushing yards to boot -- was strong enough to catapult him into our top 10. If he had more stable quarterback play, he would be an easy leader among rookie receivers in receiving yardage and receptions.

 Concepcion is lightning quick and able to make tough catches away from his frame. He looks like a three-down receiver; his designed touch and field-stretching ability is in the mold of Baltimore's  Zay Flowers or New Orleans'  Chris Olave . -- Solak

title: NFL Week 8 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips: What we're hearing
summary: Are changes coming for the Jets? Could the Chiefs add at the trade deadline? Will the Colts keep unloading? And what's going on in the AFC North standings?
full_text:
It's Week 8 of the  2026 NFL season , and we're under two weeks away from the trade deadline. Insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been calling sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 Which teams are most likely to bring in help before the Nov. 10 deadline? Which players are likeliest to end up in a new city? And will the Colts continue dealing players? Jeremy and Dan have updates on the trade market. Plus, we look into what's happening with the struggling Jets and what's going on in the chaotic AFC North, where the Browns are in first and the Ravens are in last.

 It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 8.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Aggressive teams at the deadline 
 Players likely to move  | Colts dealing 
 Jets changes  | AFC North chaos 
 Fantasy advice  | More intel 

 
 

 Which team is most likely to be aggressive in acquiring help at the deadline? 
 Fowler: The Chiefs appear poised to do something at wide receiver. Injuries to Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton have created holes in the passing game that running back Kenneth Walker III can't mask alone. The Chiefs have managed to win games despite those injuries, but Sunday night in Seattle was a reminder of how ugly things can look without adequate downfield playmakers.

 Enough receivers will be available in the coming weeks, so the Chiefs can get good value trading for the high-impact players or lower-cost options. The Colts' Josh Downs would be a fit for the Chiefs. The Browns' Jerry Jeudy  would also fit, though Cleveland is not inclined to deal him now barring a significant offer.

 Graziano: The Chiefs always seem to do something at wide receiver at the deadline. Usually it's a smaller move such as  Kadarius Toney or late-career DeAndre Hopkins , but the team has a history of targeted trade-deadline additions at the position. I expect Kansas City to be active in trying to add a player or two to boost the offense, be that another pass catcher, an offensive lineman or both.

 The teams that are most interesting to me are the surprises. Would the first-place Giants believe they're in position to trade a draft pick or two for a win-now player? Would the AFC North-leading Browns feel compelled to reward their current roster for its surprising first-half success by adding a player who can help take them to the next level? We saw the Colts do this last year with the big swing for Sauce Gardner .

 

 Of course, last year's Colts are proof that this approach doesn't always work , but what do you think? Would the Browns veer from their long-term building plans to try to make a 2026 run with Deshaun Watson at QB?

 Fowler: Cleveland is a low-key team to watch at the deadline. The Browns are 5-2 and like to make deals. Defensive line help will be available if they tap into it. And adding a versatile blocker, either at tight end or H-back, would be timely, perhaps providing a player similar to what Todd Monken had in Baltimore with Patrick Ricard .

 Seattle has already made a move with the deal for Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson . Edge rusher and running back are positions Seahawks GM John Schneider could monitor, as well.

 Graziano: Yeah, Tuesday was a big day in the NFC West arms race. It makes me wonder what the Rams are thinking. They obviously made their big moves in the offseason, but things haven't worked, and everyone's favorite superteam has fallen behind the 49ers and Seahawks in the division. I wonder whether there's another move for the Rams to make -- they could use a speedy wide receiver if one is available -- and whether they still have the draft picks and/or desire to add more to a roster that was already supposed to be loaded.

 I'm also very curious to see what the Jaguars do. They see themselves as a top AFC contender. I agree with them, but they could use one more piece up front on defense. Remember, the Jags were kind of a surprise at last year's deadline with  their move for Jakobi Meyers , who helped fuel their second-half run.

 

 
 Which player are you most confident will get traded somewhere before the deadline? 
 Fowler: Let's go with Jaguars receiver Brian Thomas Jr . Several execs I've spoken to believe Thomas' days in Jacksonville are numbered due to his diminished role in Year 3. He has trade value, and the Jaguars would be smart to explore that option. One potential deterrent: Jacksonville is in a winning window and needs all hands on deck for the stretch run. Thomas, at worst, still commands defensive coverage, but he hasn't caught a pass in the past two games and was essentially benched in London in Week 6 .

 None of the top trade options around the league is a slam dunk to happen, but place Thomas in the Marvin Harrison Jr . category of a receiver badly needing a fresh start . The safer bet might end up being Vikings wide receiver Jauan Jennings , who isn't a primary option in that offense and is also a trade candidate.

 Graziano: Thomas is my answer, too. He clearly hasn't been a big part of Jacksonville's offense since coach Liam Coen arrived last season. Thomas would surely prefer to either be a bigger part of the Jaguars' offense or go to a team where he can have a sizable role. And there are plenty of teams around the league that still view him as a high-end talent at a premium position and would give up something of value to get him.

 

 Like you said, this closely mirrors the Harrison situation. Thomas is two months younger than Harrison, was also drafted in the first round in 2024 and showed enough promise as a rookie that there's reason to believe a change of scenery could bring out the best in him. Thomas hasn't made any public noise about wanting out, but neither did Harrison. Still, Harrison and his agents were able to work with the Cardinals behind the scenes to find a solution that made everyone happy. I expect the same thing to happen for Thomas.

 Going back to your Jennings mention, I agree that the most likely guys to be traded are the slightly lower-profile names if simply because they won't cost as much to add. But I also imagine Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat will be of interest to teams needing defensive help over the next couple of weeks.

 Fowler: Yeah, Dan, Sweat certainly fits the profile of a prime trade candidate, and some around the league have linked the Cowboys to his services.

 

 
 What about the Colts? Are more moves coming after they dealt Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner ? 
 Graziano: With the Colts tearing things down, veteran wideouts such as Keenan Allen and Laquon Treadwell might have appeal as depth players on contenders that need help at receiver. Defensive tackle Grover Stewart and wide receiver Josh Downs are also on expiring contracts and didn't get extensions this offseason.

 The guy who did get an extension , running back  Jonathan Taylor , might be the most interesting of the bunch. Even after his recent extension, Taylor has a tradeable contract. The Colts would have to absorb $10 million in dead money next year, and the acquiring team would have to take on whatever prorated portion of Taylor's $8 million salary plus bonus compensation is left for this season. He's scheduled to make $16.02 million next year, and right now that's not guaranteed, though it converts to a full guarantee five days after the Super Bowl.

 So technically, you could acquire Taylor without any commitment beyond this season, but you'd also retain the ability to keep him past 2026 if you are comfortable with that price. I believe Tennessee's Tony Pollard is the more likely running back to be dealt, ahead of Taylor or Saquon Barkley , but if the Colts are in full rebuilding mode, you can't rule anything out.

title: Panthers' consistency starts in the trenches, rests with DC Ejiro Evero
summary: From offensive line woes to a troubled run defense, Carolina (3-3) faces its problems entering Thursday night's game at Green Bay.
full_text:
The Jekyll-and-Hyde-ish nature of the Carolina Panthers' start to the 2026 NFL season has led to more questions than answers through six games. Everyone loves a Slinky until it becomes the best way to describe their team's up-and-down season.

 Entering Week 8's "Thursday Night Football" matchup against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field ( 8:15 ET, Prime Video ), the Panthers are a team of extremes. This is a squad that gave the Atlanta Falcons a 34-3 shellacking on the road in Week 2 and overcame the Detroit Lions' No. 2-ranked offense at home in a Week 4 win . They're also the group that gave up 552 net yards and eight total touchdowns to the Chicago Bears in Week 1 and got run over by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Bank of America Stadium to the tune of 258 rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns in a 30-point blowout loss on Sunday.

 

 While it would be easy to pile on Carolina's inconsistent defense, the offense -- which ranks fifth in the league entering Week 8 -- is not without its own lumps. There are concerns to be had around the roster, and while the Panthers (3-3) sit at the top of the NFC South, their hold on the division will only loosen if they continue to yo-yo their way through the campaign.

 The Packers, who have a top-five passing offense and a top-10 passing defense, will presumably test the Panthers differently than the Buccaneers did last week. And with such a fast turnaround between a home letdown and a primetime battle on the road, Carolina will need to regroup quickly, even if Green Bay's league-worst rushing attack won't present the same challenges as Tampa Bay.

 Here are the biggest concerns -- and a reason for optimism! -- for the Panthers entering the midway stretch of their season:

 

 Panthers' run defense under coordinator Ejiro Evero has been troubled for years 
 Carolina's run defense was trending in the right direction heading into Sunday's nightmare afternoon against Tampa Bay. After giving up a franchise-record 59 points, along with 291 rushing yards and six rushing touchdowns, to the Bears, Carolina saw its rushing yard allowance continually tick downward over the following four weeks. The defense held top-tier running backs Bijan Robinson of the Falcons and Jahmyr Gibbs of the Lions to 72 and 46 rushing yards, respectively, in impressive wins.

 But against the Buccaneers, who had an injured Baker Mayfield -- wearing a uniquely designed glove for his dislocated thumb -- lining up under center, the Panthers allowed the rushing lane floodgates to open. Named defensive coordinator in Carolina in 2023, Evero oversaw a league-leading 12th occurrence (and third against the Buccaneers) of an opposing offense rushing for 200 yards or more against his unit since his hiring. The Panthers have allowed an opponent to rush for 200 or more yards six more times than any other defense in the league since the start of the coach Dave Canales era in 2024.

 

 "That's what we're working on right now -- I don't really want to get into the specifics of it," Canales said Monday after facing questions about the team's recent history of poor run defense. "I feel like there's the adjustments and the things that we need to do. I don't want to really air that out, but just understanding that we got to do it. We got to execute it well."

 The Panthers, because of their awful run outings against Chicago and Tampa Bay, are the worst-ranked run defense in the NFL through seven weeks (153.2 rushing yards allowed per game, which is 7.5 yards more than No. 31 Dallas Cowboys at 145.7).

 But it's also worth noting that the woes against the run aren't new to the system or the scheme. In 2024, Evero's unit allowed a league-worst 3,057 total rushing yards (179.8 per game) while becoming the first defense since 1980 -- and the first with an expanded 17-game schedule -- to give up 3,000 or more rushing yards in a season.

 While Evero's defense has its strengths, most notably in coverage, it's fair to wonder if (or when) the stark (and recurring) letdowns of the run game will eventually sour his standing in Carolina. Evero signed a contract extension in 2025 with the pact running through the 2027 season, a league source with knowledge of the deal confirmed to ESPN this week.

 The defensive coordinator, who is well-regarded in league circles, has been a routine head coaching candidate over the past five years. But his time with the Panthers might eventually reach an impasse, as the team has invested a lot of draft capital and cash in upgrading the defense over the past two offseasons and the results haven't been particularly illuminating.

 Though, notably, top free-agent outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips (hamstring) and the team's top two cornerbacks, Jaycee Horn (calf) and Mike Jackson (groin) -- both on injured reserve -- didn't play against the Bucs, and the Panthers, in general, have been dealing with a litany of notable injuries -- outside linebacker Nic Scourton , a 2025 second-round pick, included -- this season. Phillips and fill-in starting CB  Akayleb Evans  (knee/triceps) were both ruled out for Thursday's game.

 "Together, we've got to coach it better, collectively," Canales said. "We've got to have that plan, so that when it becomes the same type of concepts, that our players feel prepared, they feel ready to attack whatever it is."

 

 Carolina's makeshift offensive line is showing cracks in pass protection 
 Longtime right tackle Taylor Moton's return from offseason blood clot treatment was short-lived. It lasted just seven quarters. He suffered a fractured fibula in the third quarter of the loss to the Buccaneers, and will undergo season-ending ankle surgery, according to Canales.

 

 The Panthers are left with few options on the starting offensive line. This year's first-round pick Monroe Freeling , who was selected as a long-term developmental left tackle, will (again) be thrust into fill-in duty at right tackle with Moton sidelined. Freeling allowed three pressures in 22 pass sets against Tampa Bay, according to NFL Next Gen Stats, while Moton gave up none in his 16 pass snaps before injury. The rookie, in five games, has surrendered 18 total pressures (including four sacks), according to Next Gen's tracking data.

 Left tackle Rasheed Walker , who was signed to fill in for longtime starter Ikem Ekwonu (patellar tendon), was overmatched throughout the loss to the Bucs. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Walker allowed three sacks and seven total pressures in Week 7. He has given up a team-leading 34 pressures on the season.

 The interior line hasn't fared much better. Center Luke Fortner and left guard Damien Lewis  (who has been ruled out heading into Week 8 with a knee injury) have each been credited with four sacks allowed, while former Pro Bowl right guard Robert Hunt was beat cleanly on Sunday for what would become a strip-sack touchdown for Tampa Bay.

 With Moton out, the Panthers need to lean on Walker and Freeling until Ekwonu is ready to return, and even then, the 2022 first-round pick might not be able to play up to his standard after knee surgery and a long stint on the physically unable to perform list. At center, the Panthers drafted Sam Hecht in the fifth round to be a potential long-term starter, but he was a healthy scratch on Sunday in favor of waiver-wire pickup Corey Bullock and  Torricelli Simpkins III , who was promoted from the practice squad earlier this season. Simpkins, though, was listed as out for the matchup against the Packers with a left ankle injury.

 
 

 Yes! There is reason for optimism entering Thursday night's game 
 Against Tampa Bay, quarterback Bryce Young had unquestionably his worst game of the season, giving up three turnovers (sack-fumble for a score and two interceptions). But entering that matchup, Young was on fire, setting the franchise record for passing touchdowns (11) through the first five games of the season.

title: Bowen: Four players (and a defense) that have changed my mind
summary: Matt Bowen discusses a few disappointments, a couple of surprises and what to expect going forward.
full_text:
We're almost at the midpoint of the NFL season, and the fantasy football trade deadline is a little more than a month away. With that in mind, we have seen enough football to highlight some realizations that differ from early-season opinions and expectations.

 Yes, there is still a lot of football to be played here, and players can make a quick turnaround if they see a jump in usage or take advantage of a positive matchup. I get that.

 But after seven weeks, we can identify the players (and one defensive unit) who have been better or worse than anticipated, and what you can expect going forward.

 
 

 Justin Jefferson is no longer a clear WR1 
 I've often called coach Kevin O'Connell 's offense one of the more "QB friendly" systems in the league. It's the play design and the defined throws. Scheme guys open. Isolate players in positive matchups. Take shots off play-action. There should be a feeling of tempo and rhythm.

 

 But after watching the Vikings this season -- with Kyler Murray under center -- there is still a genuine lack of identity in the pass game. And we are seeing it even more with Jefferson's declining production.

 Jefferson opened the season in Week 1 by dropping 31.2 points on the  Green Bay Packers , in a game where Murray left early due to a concussion. Carson Wentz stepped in and Jefferson went on to catch two touchdowns.

 But in the three full games Jefferson has played with Murray, he's scoring 10.8 fantasy PPG. Plus, he's averaged 5.3 targets, with only two in the red zone during this three-game stretch. In fact, Jefferson has yet to post a game this season with double-digit targets, and he now plays in a low-volume throwing offense, as the Vikings have attempted only 164 passes this season (second fewest in the league).

 Now, I don't expect fantasy managers to give up on Jefferson. There's too much talent and upside despite the recent usage. Plus, Jefferson has some prime matchups over the next two weeks against Detroit and Buffalo, two defenses ranking in the bottom five versus wide receivers. But unless we see a big jump from Murray and the Minnesota pass game, it's fair to question if Jefferson can finish as a top-15 wide receiver by season's end.

 

 

 Blake Corum is more than just a bye-week fill-in 
 I said the following early in the season on Corum: "Bench stash. Insurance play behind starter Kyren Williams . A running back with some value in deeper formats." 

 But that's changed given Corum's recent usage and production in the Rams backfield.

 Corum, who saw a team-high 17 carries in the Week 7 win over the  Las Vegas Raiders , is scoring 15.8 fantasy PPG over his last three, with double-digit touches and at least one touchdown in each game. Corum has also caught six of seven targets during this stretch, while averaging 77.7 scrimmage yards per game.

 With the expectation that Williams remains the No. 1 in L.A., Corum's ceiling is somewhat capped. However, he is getting enough work to be played as a flex in 10- and 12-team leagues, with RB2 value in deeper formats. Plus, the upcoming schedule (LAC, @WSH, @ARI) creates more opportunities for Corum to produce weekly value ahead of the Rams' bye in Week 11.

 
 

 The Cincinnati Bengals are a solid starting D/ST 
 If you were to ask me about the Cincy defense in previous seasons, I would 100% disagree with this take. You couldn't put the Bengals in the lineup with any confidence outside of an extremely friendly matchup (and even then, only in deeper leagues).

 But this year's defense? The team made some really strong offseason additions to this unit, one that is now scoring 8.0 fantasy PPG (fifth most in the league). The Bengals are also allowing 20.3 PPG this season (eighth fewest), with multiple sacks in every game played and at least one turnover forced in four of them.

 The trade for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II gave the Bengals an anchor. He's a game changer. Plus, the team added veterans Jonathan Allen and Boye Mafe to build the front, with a secondary featuring coverage corners Dax Hill and DJ Turner II . There's talent here in defensive coordinator Al Golden's system. And with a positive upcoming schedule (TEN, @ATL, PIT, @WSH, NO, @CLE), the time is now to add a Bengals defense currently available in more than 55% of ESPN leagues.

 
 

 Garrett Wilson is a WR2 at best 
 Wilson had the look of a clear-cut WR1 back in September, as he scored 19.1 fantasy PPG from Weeks 1-3, seeing nine targets per game with two touchdown grabs.

 

 Since then, Wilson has scored fewer than 10 points in three of the past four games, and his Week 5 game versus the Browns (23.4 fantasy points) is the only outlier. And the volume is rapidly declining here, too, as Wilson has six or fewer targets in three of the four games.

 The emergence of rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr . factors in here. Cooper, who missed time due to ankle injury, has scored at least 22 fantasy points in back-to-back games, with at least five targets and a touchdown in each. He's a powerful and explosive mover, and it's pretty clear the Jets are scheming for Cooper in the game plan.

 Wilson is still a highly talented receiver, one capable of breakout weeks. But given Cooper's quickly expanding role and an upcoming schedule featuring some tougher matchups (LV, @KC, BUF, @LAC, MIA), Wilson has dropped down in my ranks as a mid-to-lower-tier WR2.

 
 

 Chase Brown is no longer a lineup lock 
 Heading into Week 8, Brown is scoring 12.5 fantasy PPG, but he's posted fewer than 10 points in three of his past four, and he hasn't found the end zone since Week 1. His single-game high this season -- 19.1 in Week 4 versus Jacksonville -- was boosted by 11 receptions on a day where he rushed for 10 yards on nine carries.

 Looking deeper at the tape and the numbers here, Brown's lack of rushing efficiency and explosive-play ability are major concerns. Brown is averaging only 3.4 YPC (33rd in the league), while his 7.3% explosive run rate is tied for 59th ... with Alvin Kamara . Not great. And Brown isn't breaking tackles at a high rate, averaging just 1.63 YPC after first contact (34th).

 Plus, the Bengals' No. 2, Samaje Perine , led the team in carries in Week 5 versus Miami (before the bye), and he was given an opportunity on the goal line last Sunday in the win over the Ravens, cashing in on a 1-yard score.

 With the lack of capable running backs, you can't really sit Brown in deeper formats. I get that. And the upcoming schedule should work in a Brown's favor based on the matchups (TEN, @ATL, PIT, @WSH). But at this point, you can't call Brown a must-start if you have other options to drop in the RB2 spot.
