title: NFL survivor power rankings: Why this is the week to use Bengals, Patriots
summary: ESPN NFL survivor pool strategy, predictions and ranking the top six options for Week 8.
full_text:
This season continues to have no mercy for Survivor players. Another 41% of the remaining entries were chopped off last week, leaving just 2.3% of the initial entries remaining after Week 7.

 At least one favorite of at least seven points has lost in each of the first seven weeks, the first time that has happened since 1972. In each of the past two weeks, the only double-digit favorite on the board lost outright. Two weeks ago, the Los Angeles Rams fell to the Arizona Cardinals . Last week, it was the Houston Texans losing in overtime against the New York Giants .

 Over 39% of the remaining entries have been eliminated in every week except Week 4. Last week, the New York Jets also made a significant dent in the pool, as users who adhered to the fade-Miami strategy were burned.

 This week, the biggest favorite on the board is the Cincinnati Bengals , and they will likely be the most popular pick despite only being 51% available. The Bengals have the easiest schedule remaining in the NFL according to ESPN Analytics, but they will have no better spot than this week, so the chalk is justified.

 

 After that, there are several other strong options. The Jacksonville Jaguars are nearly as big of favorites as the Bengals at a lower selection. The Rams,  New England Patriots and Dallas Cowboys  are all favored by about a touchdown, and all three have less future value than the Bengals or Jaguars.

 There are even more viable options down the board. The Washington Commanders are off a bye hosting the Philadelphia Eagles . The Pittsburgh Steelers face a Cleveland Browns team they have beaten 22 straight times at home in the regular season. Even the Buffalo Bills could be a good pick against the Baltimore Ravens if Lamar Jackson is ruled out.

 With so many players eliminated, it has never been more important to plan your route and know your competition. Check what teams your competitors still have available. If there are only a few people left, look at their tendencies in past weeks. Start to map out your picks for the remaining 12 weeks.

 My top pick will vary from contest to contest. For single-pick contests like on ESPN, I like eating the chalk with the Bengals, or perhaps pivoting to the New England Patriots or Dallas Cowboys . If my group has double-pick weeks coming up, I prefer to save the Bengals and opt for the Patriots, Rams or Cowboys.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet .  

 1. Cincinnati Bengals (vs. Tennessee Titans ) 
 

 The Bengals are the simplest choice if you're just looking to pick the biggest favorite and move on. While they have plenty of future value, as they should be favored in every remaining game, this is clearly their best spot as of now. In contests like Splash, that would be enough for me to pivot off of them and save them for a double-pick week down the road at low ownership. But on ESPN, it is hard not to take the win equity now. Just make sure to look at your group's availability, because their ownership could vary widely based on pick availability.

 
 Chance to win: 87% (ESPN Analytics), 94% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Bengals -10 (-500 moneyline) 
 Future value: Ninth 
 Availability: 51% 
 ESPN Selection: 25% 
 

 2. New England Patriots (at Miami Dolphins ) 
 

 The Patriots are a perfect 13-0 outright as a favorite of at least three points under Mike Vrabel, so they have been trustworthy as big favorites. He is also 5-0 after a loss, while the Dolphins could be in a flat spot coming off their first win of the season against the Jets. Though Miami has historically been a house of horrors for the Patriots, this seems like a great spot for the Patriots on extra rest against a team that still grades out as the worst in the NFL. The Patriots still have games left against the Los Angeles Chargers , Jets and Dolphins after this week, but the home Dolphins game doesn't come until Week 18 while the other two games are both on the road.

 
 Chance to win: 80% (ESPN Analytics), 78% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Patriots -7 (-340 moneyline) 
 Future value: 15th 
 Availability: 50% 
 ESPN Selection: 16% 
 

 3. Dallas Cowboys (vs. Arizona Cardinals ) 
 

 The Cowboys will be a strong pick in three of the next five weeks, including this one. In Week 11, they host the Tennessee Titans, though there will likely be other strong, widely available picks in that week like the Bills and Chicago Bears . But Week 12 is the one to watch. Obviously things can change, but as of now, you want to be able to have either the Bengals, Cowboys or Jaguars available for that week. If you can cover Week 12 without Dallas, then the Cowboys are a much better pick this week. If not, there are enough good options this week where I would save them.

 
 Chance to win: 78% (ESPN Analytics), 86% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Cowboys -6.5 (-310 moneyline) 
 Future value: Fifth 
 Availability: 87% 
 ESPN Selection: 16% 
 

 4. Los Angeles Rams (vs. Los Angeles Chargers ) 
 

 The Rams have the toughest remaining schedule in the NFL according to ESPN Analytics, so a "home" game against the winless Chargers is hard to pass up. Still, this spot looks similar to the Dolphins last week -- coming off a bye, looking for their first win against a rival -- and the Chargers don't have to get on a plane. I would be more likely to use them on Splash than on ESPN or Circa, given their lack of future value for Splash and multiple prime-time games for Circa.

 
 Chance to win: 74% (ESPN Analytics), 91% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Rams -6.5 (-290 moneyline) 
 Future value: 11th 
 Availability: 86% 
 ESPN Selection: 17% 
 

 5. Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. Indianapolis Colts ) 
 

 The Jaguars are one of the highest-value teams in Survivor. They still have two games against the Titans, a home Commanders game, and road games against the Colts and Giants. They will likely be the biggest favorites on the board in Weeks 10 and 12, which will likely be the two toughest weeks in November. That makes me lean towards wanting to save them, especially with their ESPN selection likely to increase throughout the week. They are just 68% available on ESPN, and even lower on other sites, so if you can get through this week, there will be other strong spots to use Jacksonville.

 
 Chance to win: 73% (ESPN Analytics), 83% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Jaguars -9.5 (-425 moneyline) 
 Future value: Third 
 Availability: 68% 
 ESPN Selection: 14% 
 

 6. Washington Commanders (vs. Philadelphia Eagles ) 

 The Commanders are seemingly in the dream spot this week, as home favorites coming off a bye with their opponent coming off Monday Night Football. However, since 2000, those teams are just 4-7 outright and 1-9-1 against the spread. Still, it's hard to ignore a Commanders team that will likely never be this big of a favorite again all season. At the current 1% selection on ESPN, they are a good pick, though I expect them to be significantly higher picked in high-stakes pools.

 
 Chance to win: 64% (ESPN Analytics), 79% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Commanders -5.5 (-218 moneyline) 
 Future value: 24th 
 Availability: 100% 
 ESPN Selection: 1%

title: What has gone wrong for 2025 running backs? Ashton Jeanty, Omarion Hampton, more
summary: We thought last year's running back class was going to be great. But Ashton Jeanty, Omarion Hampton, TreVeyon Henderson and others haven't lived up to the hype.
full_text:
About a year ago, I wrote about the then-rookie class of NFL running backs and how excited I was to see them thriving. During Week 4 of the 2025 season , first-year rookie backs combined to run for 737 yards, the most by any set of rookie rushers during a week of September football since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger. It looked like a class that was regarded by prospect mavens as one of the deepest and most compelling groups in recent memory was quickly taking over.

 One year later, things aren't looking quite as rosy. In Week 6 of the 2026 season , the class of 2025 combined for just 246 yards on the ground, its collective worst total in any given week so far. With benchings and injuries plaguing so many standouts, the leading rusher from the 2025 class that week was Corey Kiner , an undrafted free agent who was the third-string option on the Patriots. Things were better in Week 7 , but the class has collectively topped 600 yards in a single week just once since that big breakout in Week 4 one year ago.

 What has gone wrong? Injuries have plagued many of the class' most promising backs. Ashton Jeanty ,  Ollie Gordon II  and  LeQuint Allen Jr . are the only three 2025 draft picks at running back to be active in every one of their team's games since entering the league, and Gordon and Allen have been backups for most (or all) of that time. Jeanty has played through several ailments, including an ankle issue that he dealt with this preseason.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Jeanty himself might be a microcosm of the class' struggles as a whole. He entered the league as a highly touted running back out of Boise State, drafted by the Raiders ahead of other offensive options such as tackles  Armand Membou , receiver  Tetairoa McMillan , tackle  Kelvin Banks Jr . and tight end  Colston Loveland , who were the next four picks off the board. Jeanty has certainly flashed at times over his first year-plus in the league, and there are excuses that can help justify his lack of consistency, but he wouldn't be taken ahead of any of those players if the league took a second shot at the 2025 draft.

 I will run through many of the most notable contributors from the 2025 rookie running back class -- Jeanty, Omarion Hampton , Quinshon Judkins , TreVeyon Henderson , Bhayshul Tuten , Cam Skattebo and others -- and deliver a sort of progress update on where they stand. There are certainly success stories, but they're coming from surprising places. And while their final NFL story is far from written, it's fair to start wondering whether we'll see some of the most promising and highly touted backs from 2025 live up to what we saw from them as rookies, let alone as prospects.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Jeanty | Hampton | Judkins 
 Henderson | Tuten | Skattebo 
 Best of the rest | Disappointments 
 Will this class be all-time great? 

 
 

 

 Ashton Jeanty , Las Vegas Raiders 
 Let's start with the first running back selected (No. 6) in the class. Jeanty has been available every week for a Raiders team that hasn't had great playmakers beyond tight end  Brock Bowers , which is valuable in its own right. But it would be difficult to argue that the production has been what the Raiders hoped to get. Since entering the league, Jeanty has turned 372 carries into just 1,303 yards, an average of 3.5 yards per attempt. He has averaged minus-0.27 EPA per rush attempt over that timeframe, the worst mark among backs with 150 carries or more since the start of 2025. And Jeanty is second to last in success rate (32.8%) and last in first downs over expectation, per NFL Next Gen Stats (minus-16).

 There has understandably been an effort to contextualize Jeanty's struggles within the broader Raiders offense, which was particularly awful in 2025. Jeanty averaged just 1.3 yards before contact during his rookie season, the worst mark in the NFL by a considerable margin. He was hit at or behind the line of scrimmage nearly 52% of the time, per Next Gen Stats, a figure topped by only fellow 2025 draftee Quinshon Judkins . A league-high 93% of Jeanty's rushing yardage came after he was initially contacted.

 

 It was certainly reasonable to see what Jeanty could do with an improved line and a much better coaching staff in 2026. The Shanahan zone scheme that Klint Kubiak was going to install as his primary mode of attack on the ground has made stars out of dozens of backs over the years. It promised to make life easier for Jeanty, too.

 Instead, Jeanty has been worse this season. He is still getting hit behind the line more often than league average (47.2%) and still gaining a significant portion of his rushing yardage after first contact (91.3%), but the offense is functioning far more effectively around him than it did a year ago. Sure, there are still too many plays in which Jeanty ends up in a hopeless situation because a lineman busts, and he has run for no gain or a loss on a league-high 26.4% of his carries. But he isn't doing enough in the situations in which he does have an opportunity to break something big. Jeanty doesn't have a single run of more than 20 yards and has just five runs of 10 yards or more on 105 attempts. That 4.8% clip is less than half the league average (10.3%) for backs with at least 60 carries. Plus, he's forcing missed tackles on just under 18% of attempts, below the league average of 25%.

 We've also seen another back look more explosive as a runner in this same offense. Rookie  Mike Washington Jr ., a fourth-round pick, has averaged 4.9 yards per carry playing behind the same offensive line. And while he also doesn't have a great success rate, Washington has been able to create explosive plays on the ground. He has picked up 10 or more yards on 15% of his carries and already has 21- and 35-yard rushes this season.

 Explosive plays can be subject to significant amounts of variance, so I wouldn't go as far as suggesting that what we've seen from him in 2026 means Jeanty can't create big plays. He does have five catches of 20 or more yards. But the fact that Jeanty has struggled to create those big plays on his own undercuts the idea that he was the sort of transcendent back that justified a top-10 pick, especially in a draft with so many other exciting prospects lurking in later rounds.

 One way to generate value while those explosive plays come and go is to succeed in short-yardage situations. However, Jeanty has been frustrating there throughout his career. Running backs have converted about 66% of their rush attempts over the past two years on plays with 1 or 2 yards to go for a first down or a touchdown. Jeanty has converted 45% of the time. That's the worst mark among backs with at least 20 attempts in short yardage since the start of 2025, and it weighs heavily in Jeanty's league-worst first down over expectation of minus-16.

 Are there plays in which Jeanty has no chance of succeeding because someone shoots a gap past a befuddled lineman? Yes. There are also plenty of snaps in which Jeanty simply doesn't exhibit the combination of decisiveness and power needed to pick up first downs. Those short-yardage plays don't need to turn into explosives, but Jeanty needs to be able to make a defender miss, follow his blocks or run through contact to pick up the 1 or 2 yards he needs. Trucking a defender is great if you can do it, and it's always nice to have huge holes, but good short-yardage backs either find narrow windows or run through contact and fall forward on the way down to move the chains. Jeanty does not do that on a consistent basis, an issue that popped up in 2025 before continuing to afflict the young back in 2026.

 

 The bright spot in Jeanty's game has been his work as a receiver, where he has 34 catches for 312 yards and three touchdowns this season. Jeanty is averaging just over 2 yards per route run, which is excellent for a running back. And while most of those catches are checkdowns and screens, we're seeing Kubiak expand Jeanty's route…

title: Fantasy football buzz: Vikings defensive dilemma? Check in on the Jaguars
summary: As the Vikings head to their toughest matchup of the season, pick up an under-the-radar defense.
full_text:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values.

 Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

 
 Oct. 28: Need a defense as the Vikings head to Detroit? Get the Jags 
 By Tristan H. Cockcroft 

 We're officially entering the week where the No. 1 D/ST, the Minnesota Vikings (12.3 fantasy points per game, plus-2.8 over the next-closest team and plus-6.9 versus the league's average) face the toughest schedule-adjusted matchup in the Detroit Lions . And it's a road game, no less. Anyone care to guess the last time a visiting D/ST scored in double digits at Ford Field? It was the Green Bay Packers (10 fantasy points), back in Week 12 of 2023. Since then, only these same Vikings (9, Week 9 of 2025) and Tampa Bay Buccaneers (7, Week 7 of 2025) have scored as many as five points there.

 It's remarkable that in this topsy-turvy NFL season -- the Cleveland Browns are division leaders and the Los Angeles Chargers and RB Omarion Hampton are off to a disastrous start , for two obvious examples -- that Week 8 presented perhaps my fewest Vampire league lineup dilemmas thus far.

 Humble brag: Perhaps that's the result of my four-game winning streak, bolstering the roster with claims of Bhayshul Tuten , Bijan Robinson , Nico Collins and Jameson Williams . (On that note, sarcastic "thanks" to the manager who sat all his stars to protect any being claimed last week -- except Williams. You know who you are!)

 But even putting those aside, only one lineup spot stood out and perhaps it's one that has been a frustrating spot to manage for many of you: Team defense/special teams.

 

 Managers of the Vikings D/ST face a pair of decisions: Keep them around, or which unit to pick up as a substitution?

 As far as the former, it doesn't get much easier for the Vikings over the coming weeks, much as they're a supremely talented defense. After the Lions game, the Vikings' remainder of November goes like this: BUF (on Monday Night Football), @GB, @SF (on Sunday Night Football), ATL. Using past-five-weeks, schedule-adjusted data, those are the Nos. 16, 18, 24 and 31 offenses for D/STs in terms of matchups. (The Buffalo Bills , by the way, are 27th if using full-season data, and the Green Bay Packers are 24th.)

 I have no qualms about releasing a D/ST with a bad matchup, and that's any defense, though it'd be understandable if the only ones you're avoiding as a Vikings manager are the two Lions games (Week 15 at home is the other) and Bills. If you've got the bench space -- not an easy thing in these four-team bye weeks -- by all means keep them around. But you've got my permission slip to cut them otherwise.

 Among pickups, there's one team that stands way, way out: The Jacksonville Jaguars , fresh off their bye week following a pair of games overseas. They play one of their six scheduled games all season at EverBank Stadium and they face the Indianapolis Colts , the No. 6 schedule adjusted matchup for D/STs and and that's before they traded an offensive lineman (G Quenton Nelson ) and a defender (DT DeForest Buckner ) on Tuesday, with Jonathan Taylor also rumored on the block .

 While the Vikings are at a low point in their D/ST schedule, the Jaguars are at a high point. Their rest-of-November schedule looks great: @BAL (on Thursday Night Football), @TEN, @NYG, TEN. Those are the Nos. 14, 2, 10 and 2 matchups over the past five weeks, and in the case of the Baltimore Ravens , consider that quarterback  Lamar Jackson 's iffy status for Week 8 raises the question how healthy he might be with the quick turnaround next week, too.

 From a rest-of-season perspective -- it's possible that managers with tighter rules on in-season pickups need more of a locked-in D/ST -- the Jaguars have few truly scary remaining matchups: In Weeks 13 (@CHI), 16 (@DAL) and possibly 14 (PIT).

 Among other encouraging defenses to consider for Week 8: The Cincinnati Bengals , who have scored seven-plus fantasy points four times and get the Tennessee Titans at home; and the Washington Commanders , who have averaged six points in home games and face the Philadelphia Eagles , the No. 7 D/ST matchup over the past five weeks and No. 6 if using full-season data.

 I'll have more full-November options for you in next week's updated D/ST Road Map, but for now, go get the Jaguars, still available in roughly 45% of ESPN leagues.

 

 Oct. 27: Cowboys go off, Saquon scores but hurt again 
 

 By Michael F. Florio 
 The big story of "Monday Night Football" was Jay-Z being announced as the Super Bowl halftime performer. However, outside of that, the  Dallas Cowboys  stole the show by getting their offense back on track.

 
 Dak Prescott  bounced back in a big way, throwing for 212 yards and three touchdowns, He finished with 23.28 fantasy points. It was his second-best fantasy game of the season. Prescott has a great chance to stay hot against the  Arizona Cardinals , who have allowed the most passing TDs in the NFL. 
 Prescott's success translated to his top receivers having big days as well. CeeDee Lamb saw 12 targets, catching five of them for 74 yards and two scores. He finished with 24.4 fantasy points. He's surpassed 20 fantasy points three times and has just one game with less than 15. That's elite, high-end WR1 production. George Pickens caught four out of six targets for 57 yards and a touchdown, good for 15.7 fantasy points. He brings an extremely safe floor, but we have not seen as many big performances like last year. Still, you should start him weekly. 
 Javonte Williams was the other star for the Cowboys in this one. He rushed for a career-high 155 yards and a touchdown on 25 carries. That was good for 21.5 fantasy points. Williams brings an extremely safe floor and sees so much volume that he is also a weekly must-start. 
 Saquon Barkley returned from a hamstring injury -- before exiting last night's action due to a back injury. Before he left, he ran seven times for 62 yards and a touchdown, adding two catches for nine yards. If he's able to suit up next week against the  Washington Commanders , you start him. Dameon Pierce , who turned 15 opportunities into 48 yards and a touchdown, also exited late.  Elijah Mitchell finished the game for Philly. The health of both injured backs needs to be monitored. Pierce, or perhaps Mitchell, would be a streaming option if Barkley misses time. 
 Tanner McKee threw for 211 yards, one touchdown and one interception. He finished with 10.54 fantasy points. McKee played well given the circumstances, but still has not had a big fantasy showing. He remains a streaming option for those diving deep (or in superflex leagues) against the Commanders next week. Washington has allowed the fourth-most passing TDs and the second-most QB fantasy PPG. 
 Makai Lemon   and Dallas Goedert were the top targets for the  Philadelphia Eagles . Lemon saw a team-high eight targets, catching seven for 67 yards and a touchdown. All were career highs, as were his 19.7 fantasy points. Lemon should be added off the waiver wire this week. He'd be in play once again if DeVonta Smith sits again next week. Goedert saw seven targets, catching five of them for 48 yards and scoring 9.8 fantasy points. The volume he sees, paired with his safe floor, keep him as a low-end TE1 -- especially next week against Washington.

title: Why Micah Parsons' ACL recovery is taking longer than Patrick Mahomes'
summary: They were injured the same day, but while Mahomes was ready for Week 1, Parsons has yet to practice.
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- A few hours apart on Dec. 14, 2025, Patrick Mahomes and Micah Parsons went down in a heap. First, in Kansas City, the  Chiefs  quarterback's season was over after his left knee hyperextended on a scramble. Less than two and a half hours later in Denver, the Green Bay Packers ' pass rusher stumbled without contact and immediately grabbed his left knee.

 Two star players. Two ACLs ripped apart. Two vastly different recoveries.

 When Chiefs rookies and quarterbacks reported for training camp on July 24, Mahomes was fully cleared. From that day on, he has had no reported issues.

 For Parsons and the Packers, the process has taken much longer. More than three months after Mahomes was cleared, Parsons remains on the physically unable to perform list with no set date for a return to play. However, coach Matt LaFleur this week offered the first hint at when Parsons might return when he said there's a chance he could start practicing next week . 

 "The fans always want to know, 'Why is it taking so long?'" said Dr. Michael J. Alaia, a sports orthopedic surgeon at NYU Langone Health. "When you do enough ACLs, you just know the variability of the recovery can be so vast, and every patient brings their own set of physical and psychological needs."

 Parsons was never going to be ready for Week 1, even if he had undergone surgery the day after his injury like Mahomes did. Not only did Parsons wait two weeks for his surgery, but the Packers almost never put a player recovering from a torn ACL on the practice field until nine months after the date of surgery.

 

 Tight end Tucker Kraft , who tore his right ACL on Nov. 2, had one of the fastest returns to practice by a Packers player in recent years: 8½ months from the date of his surgery (271 days after the injury). He was cleared for full team drills 2½ weeks later and made his season debut in Week 1. Last year, receiver Christian Watson practiced 274 days after tearing his right ACL and played in his first game 20 days later.

 Based on those timelines, Parsons should have been back by now, as it's been 319 days since his injury and 304 days since the surgery.

 In fact on Sept. 1, general manager Brian Gutekunst said that once Parsons became eligible to come off the PUP list after Week 4, "We're going to be pretty close." Gutekunst went as far as to suggest that the new rule this season that allows players to return to practice after Week 2 if they began the season on the PUP list could be in play for Parsons.

 Those who know Parsons say he always believes he can do things other players can't. It's why in January, less than a month after his surgery, he said he believed he could return within the first four weeks of the season. Early in training camp, Parsons adjusted that timeline but still said it was "very realistic" to return for the Week 6 game against his former team, the Dallas Cowboys .

 None of that happened, and, according to a source familiar with Parsons' recovery, it was never in the cards. A November return was always the most likely, even without any setbacks.

 "It was the only thing that made sense knowing he wanted to be 100%," the source said. "Micah has to play a different game than most guys and relies on his speed and athleticism -- on top of the fact that he had the meniscus [tear, which] made it a longer recovery period. 

 "When he wasn't going to practice at all in training camp, it solidified where he was at in his recovery process."

 

 No two knee injuries are the same, even if it's a torn ACL. Parsons' injury was not simple. Neither was Mahomes'. Parsons revealed in the spring that he also tore the meniscus in his knee. At the time, it was unclear whether his surgeon, Dr. Neal ElAttrache, did a simple trim or a full meniscus repair, but Parsons told ESPN this week that it was the latter.

 "That makes a huge difference," Dr. Sharif Tabbah, who runs Alkemē Sports Rx in South Florida and has worked on rehab with several NFL players coming off ACL injuries. "When it's a repair, you're not allowed to bend your knee past 90 degrees for between four to eight weeks, depending on the surgeon's protocol. 

 "So that obviously leads to a lot of stiffness and gives guys a hard time getting back into that deep knee bend, which even positionally could make a big difference."

 

 Because of that, Parsons told ESPN this week that he did not walk without assistance for eight weeks. Most ACL patients are walking without crutches within two weeks.

 "That leads to a much slower recovery process because you have to protect it," Tabbah said.

 Mahomes didn't have any meniscus issues, but he did have a torn lateral collateral ligament (LCL), which is why his surgeon, Dr. Dan Cooper of Dallas, operated immediately . According to LaFleur at the time, Parsons' surgery was delayed in part because he was awaiting the birth of his child. Also, some surgeons believe it's best to wait for initial swelling to go down before operating.

 "That's usually right," Alaia said. "The reason Mahomes had his done early was because he had a tear in his LCL. So they wanted to go in early and fix the LCL because sometimes, if the ligaments are ruptured in a certain way, the earlier you fix it, the easier it is to fix it and perhaps the better they do. 

 "So there's a reason why he went in early, at least from the reports that you read. I have no personal connections to the actual surgical procedure, but that's usually why."

 

 The surgery is merely one part of the process because the recovery and rehabilitation can create unpredictable turns.

 Watson worked with Tabbah, a doctor of physical therapy, during his recovery. According to Tabbah, Parsons reached out to him immediately after his injury and expressed an interest in working together during his recovery, but it never happened.

 "We stayed in touch throughout the process," Tabbah said. "He sent me some videos and updates and I kind of gave him some guidance along the way from afar, but he never actually ended up coming."

 Because of that, Tabbah couldn't speak specifically to why Parsons still hasn't practiced.

 

 Two weeks ago, before the Packers were getting ready to play the Cowboys,  he said on his podcast , "The Edge with Micah Parsons," that if the Super Bowl were that week, he would have played. 

 Kraft and Watson have tried to help Parsons through the process -- Watson more as a sounding board because he knows what it takes to come through better on the other side and Kraft because he was often rehabbing side by side with Parsons when both were at the facility.

 "Every ACL recovery's different," Kraft said. "[Parsons] had a little bit more work done, so his surgeon held him back from full weight bearing and running a little while longer. It's just different. And that's something he'll overcome very soon."

 Said Watson: "Anytime I've got a chance to check in on him and he's doing stuff, I'm telling him, 'Oh, he's not doing enough,' to kind of just push him because when I was going through it, there was always people there to kind of push me along through it. And honestly if there wasn't, I feel like there needed to be."

 Watson wasn't implying that Parsons wasn't doing enough; it was merely his way of pushing him. But the reality is that every player attacks their rehab differently.

 "I've had guys commit really heavy where they're doing three, four hours a day, and we're hitting this thing from every angle," Tabbah said. "We're finding ways to do the most without crossing that line of doing too much. 

 "Versus just doing what's expected or just doing the minimum where you can come in and do an hour of rehab instead and be like, 'Yeah, I did my rehab every day or I did it three days a week and I traveled and I kind of messed around.' So I've seen all ends of the spectrum with that process."

 

 Earlier this month, LaFleur offered perhaps a hint at what might be the holdup for Parsons.

title: CC Sabathia, J.J. Watt top social media reaction to Brewers' World Series win
summary: Wisconsin's teams also chimed in to shout out the Brewers after Milwaukee wins its first World Series.
full_text:
For the first time in franchise history, the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions.

 

 The Brewers' title came in dominant fashion, as Milwaukee completed a 4-1 series win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night following a 4-1  victory. Milwaukee spread its production across the first six innings with one run each in the second and fifth before two in the sixth. Brewers ace  Jacob Misiorowski  exited after 5⅔ innings, giving up two hits and no runs. Their bullpen handled the rest, giving up one run and closing out the Rays at Tropicana Field in front of a heavy contingent of Brewers fans.

 Milwaukee won a franchise-record 103 regular-season games. The Brewers are now the third team in MLB history with their first 100-win season and their first World Series title in the same year, joining the 1910 Athletics  and 1969 New York Mets , according to ESPN Research.

 The state of Wisconsin was fired up about the hometown ballclub finally getting over the hump and bringing home a title. Other local teams in the Badger State shouted out the Brew Crew. Former Brewer CC Sabathia and Wisconsin native J.J. Watt chimed in, too, leading reaction to Milwaukee's championship.

title: With Davante Adams out, Rams leaning on the run game
summary: In Sunday's victory over the Raiders, the Rams looked to be leaning on the running game, something Los Angeles has struggled to find consistently in this season.
full_text:
LOS ANGELES -- After the Los Angeles Rams lost Davante Adams for six to 10 weeks with a hamstring injury, quarterback Matthew Stafford was clear it would take a team effort to replace the wide receiver.

  "You're not going to one-for-one sub a guy that's going to be wearing a gold jacket one day," Stafford said. 

 In Sunday's 35-21 victory over the Las Vegas Raiders , that looked like leaning on the running game, something the Rams have struggled to find consistently in this season. 

 In the game, the Rams -- led by running backs Kyren Williams and Blake Corum -- rushed for a season-high 201 rushing yards and two touchdowns. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, the Rams' 60.0% rushing success rate was a season high and the fourth highest by a team in a game this season.

 "It was beautiful," Corum said of the success the Rams were able to have on the ground in Week 7. "I feel like when you're able to run, that's how you break their will."

 The Rams will attempt to continue that success on Sunday against the Los Angeles Chargers (4:05 p.m, Fox). The Chargers had a Week 7 bye, but in their Week 6 loss to Kansas City, Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III ran for 128 yards and two touchdowns on 19 carries, forcing seven missed tackles for 60 yards and both scores.

 While Rams head coach Sean McVay entered the season knowing he wanted to share the load at the position between Williams and Corum, this was the closest the Rams have come. Part of that earlier in the season had to do with the game script. After the Rams' Week 6 loss to the Arizona Cardinals , a game in which quarterback Matthew Stafford attempted 33 passes and Los Angeles ran the ball 20 times, McVay said, "I would like to be more balanced, no question about it."

 

 "Any good offense that we've had here that I've been a part of, you have to be able to do both," McVay said on Sunday. "You have to be able to have balance, or you at least have to have the threat of if they overcommit to something, then you have to be able to make them pay."

 Williams played 36 (52.9%) of the Rams' offensive snaps on Sunday and ran for 99 yards and a touchdown on 16 carries. Corum played 29 (42.6%) offensive snaps, running for 93 yards and a touchdown on 17 carries. He also had a 43-yard run erased by a phantom face mask penalty.

 "When you're able to [run the ball well], you're not in a bunch of bad spots on second down and on third down and a lot of things can come off of that," McVay said. "I thought that was the first game that was reflected. We were able to really do some of the things that I've been in alignment with when we've been able to operate at a pretty decent clip offensively.

 "Both Blake and Kyren did a great job. I think to be able to get them both involved and both allow them to get the amount of touches that they did and really for us to get the amount of rushes off while still being able to be efficient."

 In an interview on "The Pat McAfee Show"  on Monday, Stafford joked that sometimes when he gets into the huddle, "I don't know which one of them is in the damn game."

 "I haven't had a tandem like this where they both can do everything," Stafford said. "You usually have one big guy, one small guy, a big slow guy that can run over people and a small fast guy that can run around people.

 "And this is a really unique instance in which we can call our entire offense with both those guys in the game and not bat an eye."

 McVay said Monday that while he thinks Williams and Corum are "similar in stature," there is a difference in their run style that makes opponents have to defend different things.

 "I think they both have the ability to run all the types of runs that we're activating and be factors in the pass game," McVay said. 

 The head coach called the pair "nice compliments off of one another" and said, "I think as you start to see each of them get opportunities in the game, I think they really play off of one another."

 "The benefit is not necessarily feeling like you can't call certain things," McVay said. "I think as a playcaller, the best thing is you just call the plays. It's not like I have a specific menu of plays for Blake or for Kyren or vice versa. That's where we're able to rotate those guys accordingly.

 "I think they both do some things really well. They're both really good, productive, all-purpose types of backs. I think there is a play style that's a little bit different that makes it more challenging on a defense without hindering our ability to run everything we want to run with either one of them in the game."

 And while the running backs remain competitive with each other, Corum said he and Wiliams feed off of the success each other has on the field.

 "Being able to have a partner back there like Kyren just makes you want to go harder," Corum said. "Seeing him do some things that he does on the field, it's just like, 'All right, let me go do it.' And so I feel like we just make each other proud, and we feed off each other's energy, and it's really good."

title: Why Vikings' astronomical 70% blitz rate isn't a gimmick
summary: Minnesota blitzed Indianapolis 85% of the time Sunday, as they redefine what a 'normal' pass rush can be in the NFL.
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- If you do the same unusual thing every week, is it still unusual? 

 That's the question hovering over the Minnesota Vikings ' defense, which is now in its fourth season of blitzing more than any other NFL team. It has gotten to the point where safety Harrison Smith , speaking last week on the "The Richard Sherman Podcast," wondered why a standard rush is classified as four pass rushers -- and that anything beyond it should be considered an exception.

 "Was that decided when Walter Camp came up with football?" Smith said with a laugh. 

 The Vikings' ascension to one of the league's top defenses this season has coincided with a nearly unprecedented surge in their blitz rate. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores sent five or more pass rushers on 85.3% of the Indianapolis Colts ' dropbacks in Sunday's 16-10 win at U.S. Bank Stadium, the second-highest blitz rate in the past 20 years of NFL games. And after posting a combined blitz rate of 44.9% during his first three seasons in Minnesota, Flores has pushed that rate to 69.9% this season. 

 

 To put those numbers in perspective, consider that no team has blitzed more than 59.9% of the time through Week 7 of a season, or 52.4% of the time over a full season, since ESPN Research began tracking pass rushes in 2006. The NFL average during that time period has been 28.9%. Speaking this week to reporters in Minnesota, Flores grinned widely when asked about it. 

 "I don't want to say we've normalized it," Flores said, "but we've run it enough that guys understand where the issues may be and what we need to do so that those spaces on the field in the pass game are covered up enough that hopefully the pressure can get there. And so there have certainly been some hard times with that. We've given up plays as well, but I think our guys, they feel comfortable playing an aggressive style."

 

 In theory, the Vikings are vulnerable to explosive downfield plays if their opponents can get the ball over or through their suffocating presence on the line of scrimmage. The Vikings have allowed 10 gains of more than 30 yards, either via long passes or runs that broke through the line, tied for eighth most in the NFL. But those instances have seemed a fair tradeoff for the Vikings' work on the 330 other plays they have defended this season.

 Entering Week 8, the Vikings continue to lead the NFL in nearly every defensive metric, from fewest points allowed (12.3) to opponent's QBR (49.7) to expected points allowed (50.8). They are tied for the lead in sacks (21), despite having already had their bye, and rank No. 2 in yards allowed per game (252.8). And because they surprise teams not by blitzing, but when they don't blitz, their defensive EPA is actually substantially better (40.6) when they send four or fewer rushers than when they send five or more (10.2).

 That performance has come against what ESPN's Football Power Index (FPI) considers the ninth-easiest schedule in the NFL, however, and the Vikings will face FPI's sixth-most difficult schedule the rest of the way. That begins Sunday at Ford Field, where the Vikings (6-0) will face the NFL's third-best offense by EPA in the 4-2  Detroit Lions  ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ). Might it be time for Flores to mix up the playcalls?

 "Anybody who's doing the same thing over and over again," Flores said, "inevitably somebody's going to catch it. There's a lot of really good coordinators in this league and really good teams. We're going to face one coming up."

 

 To be fair, the Vikings have been playing themselves into circumstances that are conducive to successful blitzes. This week, coach Kevin O'Connell noted that Flores' work has triggered the kind of long down and distances that can shrink an offense's play selection. 

 The Vikings lead the NFL with eight sacks and a 53.6% completion percentage on first down, and their defensive rush success on first down (72%) ranks No. 2. As a result, their opponents are averaging 9.3 yards to go on second downs and 8.4 yards to go on third down. 

 Flores laughed and said "we'd still pressure if it was second-and-5 or second-and-3," but acknowledged that the long distance from the first down sticks has "put pressure on the offense to call a play or get into a set that they feel comfortable with assuming that they're probably going to get some pressure."

 Another factor in setting up friendly blitz circumstances has been an NFL-high 2.83 offensive holding penalties per game against their opponents, who are forced to grab blitzers as they get close to the quarterback. That also speaks to the Vikings' comfort level in Flores' scheme. 

 Of the 11 Vikings who have started most of the games this season, all of them are in at least their second year in the defense and nine are in their third or fourth. There isn't much hesitation visible on the video of their games. 

 "We see those conversations about the blitz rates," Smith told Sherman, "and everybody thinks it's wild. And rightfully so. It is wild. ... [But] I was there kind of from the start and almost part of the experiment in a way. It doesn't feel crazy. It looks [like that] when you look at the numbers of pressuring with more than four essentially. 

 "There's value in doing it so many times because you build comfort in it and it just allows you to see the game a little bit different."

title: After bringing back DeForest Buckner, will the 49ers make more trades?
summary: The 49ers addressed their defensive line by adding Buckner, but will they make more big moves to help the WR room before the Nov. 10 deadline?
full_text:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- Occasionally around this time of year, tight end George Kittle , fullback Kyle Juszczyk and offensive tackle Trent Williams will see  San Francisco 49ers  general manager John Lynch on his office patio overlooking the practice fields and begin chirping in his direction.

 A few weeks ago, Kittle asked Lynch if he was trying to trade for Chargers pass rusher Khalil Mack . More recently, Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner also came up both privately and publicly. Juszczyk commented "Come home" on an Instagram post from Oct. 18 that showed Buckner speaking about his frustrations in Indianapolis.

 "I just like to chirp him and ask what he's interested in, see if he'll give me anything," Kittle said. "We all chirp him just to see if he'll actually tell us anything."

 

 Lynch and his staff answered in the affirmative Tuesday, striking a deal to send a 2027 fourth-round pick to the Colts to bring Buckner back to San Francisco. It was the first, but perhaps not the last, meaningful addition the 6-1 Niners made before the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

 It was no secret that the 49ers have long wanted a reunion with Buckner, who was drafted by the team with the seventh overall pick in 2016. Upon trading him to Indianapolis in March 2020 , Lynch said it was the "toughest thing" he'd done on the job. That held true in the ensuing years, as the 49ers failed to replace Buckner with significant draft capital ( Javon Kinlaw ), big free agent money ( Javon Hargrave ) and a smaller combination of the two ( Maliek Collins ).

 In recent years, as the Colts struggled, bringing Buckner back has always been at least a passing thought. In 2026, with the Niners unable to consistently rush the passer, multiple injuries on the defensive line , and Buckner unhappy in Indianapolis, the conditions were right for it to become a reality.

 The move elicited joy in San Francisco's locker room. Kittle, Juszczyk and wideout Deebo Samuel Sr . celebrated on social media. And now, with the rest of the bye week to evaluate the roster, one big question remains: Will the 49ers make even more big moves before the trade deadline?

 

 In San Francisco, nobody is denying that now is the time for urgency. Kittle, Juszczyk and Williams might be joking when they push Lynch and coach Kyle Shanahan for trade information, but there's at least a kernel of truth in it. Sometimes, that means Shanahan and Lynch seeking their input on potential acquisitions they have played with or against.

 For Williams, 38, retirement isn't far off, and the only thing left for him to accomplish is to win the Super Bowl. It's why he acknowledges that he and the other veterans wouldn't mind seeing the Niners swing for the fences, even if it means trading top picks if the right opportunity arises.

 "As a player, you don't know how they value draft picks, but nobody in here ever values draft picks because we look at them as being a gamble," Williams said. "You don't know what anybody can turn out to be. You had people come in and they swear they're the best they've ever seen, and you got people that can go to the last pick in the draft and turn out to be All-Pros.

 "For us [players], you always want the proven product. But it's a happy medium ... I don't look at it the same way they look at it. They look at it in a whole picture view."

 

 The Niners' first loss of the season in Atlanta made that picture less blurry, laying bare San Francisco's two biggest needs. The defensive line struggled to generate pressure with zero sacks, and a depleted receiver corps didn't offer much pop aside from second-year wideout Jordan Watkins .

 When asked about using the bye week to get a jump on the trade deadline, Shanahan said Lynch and his staff have already been working on it with those two positions front of mind.

 "We still have the week when we get back [before the deadline], but if there's stuff that makes sense that can improve our team in any spot, we'd love for that to happen," Shanahan said. "The obvious injury spots to us have been receiver and D-Line. We are getting a number of those guys back at both positions, but that also doesn't exclude us from looking to something that would make sense to help us."

 Shanahan said the Niners "have a chance" but aren't guaranteed to get Samuel ( hamstring ), DE Nick Bosa  ( calf ), DT C.J. West  ( knee surgery ), WR Mike Evans ( Achilles tendinitis ) and WR Demarcus Robinson  ( ankle ) back as soon as Week 9 against the Raiders . Rookie wideout  De'Zhaun Stribling  is more likely to return in December from ankle surgery .

 The danger in counting on players returning from injury is that the Niners, of all teams, can't presume they will stay healthy once they return or that others will remain available. And even if they do bring someone in, Shanahan said it might make sense for one or two weeks until players return from injury and they have to start making cuts.

 "We would love to just stockpile some players in case some people get hurt going forward because the odds are people do ... You've got to kind of see where you're at and try to guess the future," Shanahan said.

 

 Adding Buckner, who has missed just 14 games in 10 seasons, should lessen the need on the defensive line and bolster a pass rush that is 31st in the NFL in pressure rate (23%) when rushing four players. However, they would be wise to operate as though Bosa might not be available for every game the rest of the way after his return from a calf injury.

 An addition such as Mack -- or other potentially available edge rushers like the Jets' Will McDonald IV , Cardinals' Josh Sweat or Bucs' Yaya Diaby -- would make sense to round out San Francisco's rotation for a reasonable cost in terms of what they need to give up.

 As with Bosa, the team has to be cautious with Evans to ensure he's ready for the playoff push. Jacksonville's Brian Thomas Jr ., Cleveland's Jerry Jeudy and the Colts' Josh Downs  ( who requested a trade Wednesday ) are among the wideouts who could be available for something less than a premium draft pick.

 If the Niners truly want to swing for the fences, they could try to pry loose a superstar. Raiders end Maxx Crosby and Jets wideout Garrett Wilson are names that move the needle, but they're unlikely trade candidates barring a significant offer -- one with multiple top picks, probably including multiple first-rounders.

 As always, San Francisco would only do a deal like that for a player they believe could be a part of the long-term foundation. Lynch has pulled off such trades for Williams in 2020 and running back Christian McCaffrey in 2022 .

 Whether another big move is a pipe dream or realistic depends on a lot of factors out of their control. But the Niners know what's possible with this team, and the chance to finally break through is one they don't want to take for granted.

 "To be in this position earlier in the year, I think you do get that sense of excitement or confidence knowing that, OK, we're not just talking," Williams said. "We really could do the things that we set out to do. And with that being the case, obviously we all want to go for broke."

title: Jayden Daniels focusing on faster operation at the line of scrimmage
summary: John Keim breaks down Jayden Daniels' emphasis on improving the Commanders' tempo.

title: Why Commanders believe they aren't done yet in the NFC East
summary: Washington returns from its bye with renewed belief despite a 1-4-1 start. And its QB is a big reason why.
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- The Washington Commanders ' hopes of climbing into the NFC East race focuses on a variety of factors: The NFC East isn't good; the schedule eases up; Jayden Daniels is healthy and playing well.

 What they need to provide legitimate hope, though, is something that hasn't occurred nearly enough: wins.

 As Washington returns from its bye week, it does have renewed belief despite a 1-4-1 record heading into Sunday's game against the Eagles (2-5).

 

 "Belief is really powerful," Washington coach Dan Quinn said, "knowing that you're capable of doing these things. And so, my belief in them as a group is really strong."

 But that belief does need to turn into wins soon in order for Washington to have any realistic shot at being a factor in the division the rest of the season.

 It also can impact Quinn's job security. While multiple team sources say there's no immediate jeopardy, a second losing season in a row -- they were 5-12 last season -- would lead to much speculation about a fourth season for Quinn.

 Players say they're not focused on that aspect. With 11 games remaining they still believe they have a chance -- and the next three games will be pivotal as divisional games between Philadelphia and New York are sandwiched around a conference one vs. the Rams.

 "We certainly know what's ahead over the next three games," Quinn said.

 They also haven't lost faith in who they have.

 "We've got everything we need in this locker room to compete with anyone in the NFL," nose tackle Tim Settle said. "Execution has been the hard [part] or lack of being able to execute and stop shooting ourselves in the foot will be critical to our season from here on out."

 It does help that they play in the NFC East, in which the Giants are in first place at 4-2-1 and coming off an impressive road win at Houston in quarterback J.J. McCarthy 's first start.

 Otherwise, the division has been a mess. The Eagles have lost five in a row; Dallas is only 3-4, and Washington is just 2.5 games out of first and plays everyone in the division once more. The Commanders are 0-2-1 in the division after blowing a 14-point fourth-quarter lead in a 27-27 tie vs. New York earlier this month.

 Blowing a chance to win in overtime vs. New York because of a botched sequence on the final play and then having a rally fall short at San Francisco a week later would test any team.

 

 "This team is probably the most mentally tough team I've been on," running back Austin Ekeler  said. "There's not one moment where when we've been down that there's a disbelief in anybody. The energy, the mental discipline to stay locked in is still there. The mental fortitude is extremely strong. That's reassuring ... but that doesn't guarantee you wins."

 Still, because only one team has a winning record -- and is on its third quarterback -- it provides at least the illusion of hope for others. But the Commanders also know that's not enough.

 "We have to take care of our business," Ekeler said. "As much as we can look at the division, it all comes back to us. We've got to win our games. It's great for us [that no one is pulling away], but we've got to win now. I guess that's a positive, but it won't matter until we take care of business."

 Washington's schedule also eases up, at least on paper. The Commanders opened the season with road games at Philadelphia and Dallas before hosting Seattle. They capped the first six games with a Monday night road game at San Francisco. Washington finished 1-3 in those games. They also lost to the Colts in London, in part because backup quarterback Marcus Mariota injured his knee in the first quarter and rookie seventh-round pick Athan Kaliakmanis made his NFL debut.

 But in the next seven weeks Washington plays only two teams that currently have a winning record -- the Giants and Cincinnati. Also, Washington has first-year coordinators on both sides of the ball; if they hired the right people -- and have the right players -- they should improve as the season progresses. To this point, however, there has been uneven play.

 "This is a very capable team," Ekeler said, "but we are like a bucket of water poking holes in ourselves. We're carrying it, we're going and now it's starting to drain. That's the most frustrating part about it, but also one of the nice parts because we can fix that."

 Perhaps the biggest reason for optimism remains Daniels. He's played two consecutive games wearing a brace on his left elbow that he dislocated in Week 2. In those games, Daniels has thrown for a combined 499 yards and two touchdowns while rushing for another 113 and two scores. As one player said before the Week 6 meeting in San Francisco, "when he plays like that, we always have a chance."

 Even with receiver Terry McLaurin done for the season with a torn patellar tendon, there's confidence in the offense because of Daniels. But there is one caveat: They need to protect him better. He has been hit on 27.3% of his dropbacks -- third highest in the NFL. But he also has a 90.5 quarterback rating out of 100 in the second half of the past two games.

 "We have to keep him off the ground," Ekeler said. "Jayden has taken a lot of hits. When we keep him up, we can go. That's what it will come down to and there's no sugarcoating it."

 Quinn said they want Daniels to stick with some routes a little longer, pointing to missed opportunities vs. San Francisco. They also would like to see him throw more when he scrambles -- then again, he scored on touchdown runs of 38 and 26 yards vs. the Giants in Week 5.

 "That's kind of the blessing and the curse of when do I scramble? When do I move out? When do I go?" Quinn said. "Those are fair comparisons when you see a window like, 'Hey, man, this is the time to go let it rip.' One of the things I appreciate from Jay is he puts the ball in the right location when it's contested or when it's not."

 Washington wanted to improve in the turnover differential this season and it has. so far, the Commanders are plus-six for the season, having turned the ball over only twice in the first six games. Of the top eight teams in this category, six have winning records.

 But of the 10 teams that have played only six games, Washington has committed more penalties than all but two. Here's why that matters: 25 of their 69 drives this season have featured at least one penalty; the Commanders have scored a touchdown on two of those series.

 "It throws us off rhythm," guard Sam Cosmi said.

 And they need to run the ball better. Washington ranks ninth in rushing yards per game and 10th in yards per carry. But, when it comes to just running backs, the Commanders are 24th and 25th, respectively. Some of that comes down to better play fakes; better blocking by tight ends and receivers and backs finishing EEruns. In other words: Everything that makes up the run game has to improve.

 "I want to make sure that the finishing of run plays, that's noticeable to you in the weeks ahead," Quinn said Monday.

 Washington's last two quarters were among its best as it rallied from a 23-3 deficit and had the ball in the final minute with a chance to upset the 49ers on the road, only to lose 23-17. The defense played well in the second half -- after allowing 85 points after halftime the previous four weeks combined, they allowed just three.

 Not everyone was celebrating.

 "We lost," safety Jeremy Reaves said. "We measure progress in wins and losses."

 But, perhaps, there was a mentality they can -- and need to -- carry forward. Not just as a defense but as a team.

 As Settle said, "We got tired of getting hit in the mouth."
